en: The Compendium on Daily Duties and Other Rites.
Śrī Brahmā said:
What should be performed here by those who have been initiated, both upon waking from sleep and after eating?
"O Maheśvara, tell me where those devoted to you should remain.
The Supreme Lord said:
Those who desire to study must possess the capacity for the study of Śiva."
The true meaning of the mantra should be heard by those who desire to hear it. Whether walking, standing, sleeping, or sitting, one should meditate upon the supreme reality, Śiva;
and by restraining Vāgīśvarī, one shall never be empty [of that realization] in any way.

But this is not the practice for an aspirant; it is the practice for those bound by the observance of the sons [of the teacher]. For the mantra-practitioner is constantly intent upon the ritual procedure and indeed upon recitation.
The preceptor, however, is declared to be independent in the world of Śiva.
Whether he has eaten or not, he remains as he pleases. Householders, established in their own duty, intent on protection within their independence,
devoted to the common scriptures, and always delighting in the Śiva scriptures.
The Śiva-siddhānta was indeed entrusted to Vāgīśvarī by Śiva.
Having performed the sacrifice of Vāgīśvarī, one should undertake the study of the Śiva[-tantra] as instructed by the Guru in the chapter concerning study.
And one who desires to hear should listen with a single-pointed and concentrated mind,
just as it was shown by the Guru in the chapter on exposition. This study is said to be established in two ways.
The self which has been correctly described as consisting of mantra and tantra—
the teacher and the practitioner alike— should both possess equal study and auspiciousness;
once their learning is complete, they should be made into a guru and a practitioner respectively.
Neither the initiated one nor the holder of the pledges would reach the further shore of knowledge;
therefore, those who know the worship, the fire-ritual, and the mantras should be made holders of the pledges and initiated.
Furthermore, one who has been initiated and desires to know the complete Saṃhitā for the sake of his own thorough awakening should study it here;
and he should listen to it with diligence, based on the authority of the scripture.
From conviction in the scripture, his own conviction will clearly arise;
otherwise, the teacher would not cause the disciple to study,
and the one who does not study would go to a state of disappearance.
[He is] the proclaimer of the arising of knowledge and likewise the one who causes [others] to enter into knowledge.
... In knowledge, there is the grasping of the word "reality" (*tattva*). Having stated the connection with the scripture as well as the purpose of the scripture...
The application of the sūtra to the reality [of the meaning],
the application of the sūtra within the sūtra itself, and indeed the analysis of the words (*padaccheda*) along with the formation of compounds (*samāsa*)— all these belong to the sūtra.
Having diligently proclaimed the intermediate insertion regarding the reality,
[he established] there the eightfold site and the thread...
[he was] indeed free from doubt and undisturbed.
One should practice the tantra by explaining it through the very methods of the tantras (tantrayukti).
The authoritative tradition (āptāgama) is the means of valid cognition for the attainment of the object of knowledge. The accomplishment of a word is said to arise from its definition.
The establishment of the sentence is firmly grounded in the definition of the sentence;
the accomplishment [of meaning] through words is proclaimed to be uniform everywhere.
Furthermore, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) established by the treatises on epistemology are recognized as such in all respects.
(2a) One should not examine the knowledge of the Lord based on the capacity of animal-like cognition.
That [knowledge] should be examined according to one's own tradition, and it must be heard by those who have been initiated.
Through the investigation of the knowledge of the Paśu, one should investigate the knowledge of the Pati.
Whether it be the teacher or the disciple, they may proceed toward the state of concealment (tirobhāva).
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the *prakriyā* with the *bindus*, and likewise having performed the placement of the *sūtra* with the *padas*.
The lord of teachers should deliver the exposition after having placed Śiva in his mind;
the disciple, too, with a focused intellect, should gaze upon the mouth of the teacher and listen with diligent effort,
asking again and again whenever there is doubt.
The Guru should undoubtedly lead [the disciple] through the Sūtra according to the tradition,
so that there may be no contradiction between the preceding and subsequent statements.
At the conclusion of the exposition, he should worship the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Having bowed at the feet of the Guru, one who is steadfast should then desist.
Thus has the exposition been stated; now the tantric methodology (tantrayukti) is demonstrated.
This eighteenfold methodology is established as pervading all tantras.
The very arising of worship from the body of Śiva is knowledge itself;
it becomes eighteenfold as it rests upon the [eighteen] Vidyās,
and again eighteenfold by virtue of resting upon the [eighteen] incarnations.
Furthermore, there are eighteen types [of reasoning] from the comprehensive grasp of the principles (*tattva*),
and again eighteen types from the grasping of that which pervades space (*vyomavyāpin*).
These ninety principles of reasoning (*tantrayukti*) are to be known within this scripture of knowledge.

Those [teachings] previously spoken by Śiva establish the true meaning of reality. One who provides an exposition there without knowing them would be a speaker of incoherent nonsense, devoid of the logic of the Tantra and the traditional scriptures.
(2b) The teacher who provides the explanation of a tantra for his disciple should show that disciple the origin of that tantra.

"This such-and-such knowledge has arisen from the body of Śiva; one should communicate it through that specific part [of the body] with the corresponding intention. The proclaimer of this such-and-such knowledge is named so-and-so."
The one named so-and-so is the introducer of this knowledge.
This knowledge, having been thus introduced, remains with those like us;
it has come down through the succession of lineage and rests upon the tradition of the gurus.
"This [teaching], having come from such-and-such a guru, has reached this guru;
until the end, O Guru, you are the expounder upon this earth.
The first is the principle of origin (utpattiyukti), the second is designated as 'Cloth' (vastra)."
The third is called *avasāna* (conclusion), and the fourth is *gurusantati* (the lineage of the teacher).
Relying upon the two types of liberation, the instructor should provide an exposition for the disciple of great intelligence who has been awakened by the fourfold reasoning.
Indeed, these two methods should rely upon the nature of exposition for the sake of grasping the reality of the state whose essence is Śiva:
"This is such-and-such a reality; this, however, is that."
Knowledge has proceeded forth, for the knower indeed [attains] this state which is of the nature of Śiva.
That reality unfolds at the time of exposition through the succession of principles (*tattva-santati*);
and the state [of the word] unfolds through the succession of words (*pada-santati*), as indicated by the limits of the Tantras.
When another reality-level arises during the course of explanation,
that which is connected to the connection therein is the manifestation of that particular reality-level.
Furthermore, the occurrence of another word in the course of an explanation arises as an indicator;
the connection with the sentences of the *tantra* is the manifestation of that word.
That which is the occurrence of another aphorism within one aphorism after another is [the same].
The commentary is connected to the sūtra; it is the unfolding (*vijṛmbhita*) of that sūtra.
Unfolding means the expression of expansion, which is expansion itself, a thorough investigation.
There can be no meaning whatsoever that is not based on the reality (*tattva*) [of the sūtra], nor is there anything that is not a sūtra, nor likewise anything that is not a word (*pada*).
The reality, the word, and the aphorism proceed in an interwoven manner;
yet in some places they are not interwoven, and in some cases they are neither beginningless nor endless.
In some instances they remain exactly as they are, while in others they are bound together like a chain.
In some places, there may be a succession of steps that must be explained by means of the *tantrayukti*s (methodological principles).
Not even a single word can be understood in this great ocean of Śiva-knowledge without the application of the *tantrayukti*s.
The first three methods of reasoning rely upon three principles:
Śiva, Sadāśiva, and Īśvara as a principle.
Śiva, however, is declared to be the supreme principle, which is partless (niṣkala).

Sadāśiva is proclaimed as the state called Ātman (the Self), while Īśvara is that called Vidyā (Knowledge); these are seen as three distinct states. These correspond respectively to authority (adhikāra), experience (bhoga), and dissolution (laya).
For these three states are proclaimed as the knowledge (vidyā) of reality;
this third one is celebrated as established in the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva).
The tantra is the principle whose essence is knowledge, and its speaker is Sadāśiva.
Established in the pure reality of the self, he is both the impure one and the one who leads others [to purity].
That which is known as Śiva is the supreme reality, remembered as that which brings about the attainment of it.
Through the union with knowledge, when the supreme, auspicious reality is attained,
those who abide in the state of the principles (*tattva*), established in conjunction with the principles,
are considered to have correctly understood the designation of the principles and to have realized their sublation.
That which is called *tantra-śakti* (the power of the system) is dependent upon the lineage of gurus.
Among all the methods of the tantras, whose nature is established through a sequence of prior and subsequent [elements],
that is declared to be the "method of lineage" (*santāna-yukti*), wherein there exists only the lineage itself.
No characteristic of exegesis (*vyākhyāna*) is found in her expansion (*jṛmbhita*) within the *tantra*.
Thus ends the *Tantrayukti*.
From the head [emerges] the *vijaya* knowledge, and from the forehead, the *parameśvara* *tantra*.
From his eyes he emitted the unsurpassed King of Knowledge;
from his ears, the Udgītha; from his mouth, the Mukhavimvaka;
likewise, from his neck and shoulders, the Siddha; and from the region of his armpits, the Kartṛ.
From the chest [he manifested] Nārasiṃha, from the two breasts the one named Candra,
from the heart the one called Vīrabhadra, and likewise from the belly Sāyaṇa;
from the region of the navel Svāyambhuva, and from the two sides Visara.
From the region of the back, Raurava [emerged]; from the region of the hips, Tantraja;
from the linga, that known as Kiraṇa; and from the pair of thighs, Lalita.
From the two knees, Saurabheya emerged here in the presence of Śiva.

The methods for the arising of knowledge should be known as being of eighteen kinds. At the time of exposition, the Guru should demonstrate this arising of knowledge [by showing] the deities who illuminate knowledge from his heart and the heart-mantra from his Śiva-body.
Arising simultaneously with the gnoses, the impurities [arise] in succession;
the Blessed One is revealed as being without beginning for Vijaya.
The ten-syllable [mantra] of the Supreme Lord’s breath is Śrīrūpa;
that of the Prodgīta is named Bhadra; that of Praśāntamukha is known as Saṃjñita; the Binduvyāpin belongs to the Siddha lineage and is the means for accomplishing Śiva.
The Saumya [mantra] belongs to Nārasiṃha; that named Ananta belongs to Candra.
Sarvātman belongs to Vīrabhadra, and Vyoman, known as Āgneya, belongs to him.
Nidhana belongs to Svayambhuva, and Tejas belongs to Visara.
Brahmaṇeśa is the lord of Raurava, while the one named Śiva is that of Umākuṭa. Kiraṇākhya is the deity of Lalitālaya; likewise, Devapati is proclaimed as the lord of Prakāśa and Saurabha.
Thus, these eighteen methods for the illumination of knowledge are to be understood.
The wise teacher should explain to the intelligent disciple both the meanings of the Tantra and likewise the deities who are the manifestors of the knowledges.
From the primordial form, the Blessed Lord Parameśvara attained victory;
from the form of Śrī, the sage Uśanas attained the supreme mastery;
and from the ten-syllabled breath, he reached the state of liberation.
The sage Kaca obtained the *prodgīta* from the one named Bhadra;
the muni Dadhīca obtained the facial orb (*mukhabimba*) through tranquility (*praśama*);
and from the one called Binduvyāpin, he attained the perfected *caṇḍeśa* who had arrived among the gods.
The sage Vaiśampāyana obtained the lineage from the one named Śiva;
likewise, Nṛsiṃha again received it from the gentle one in the Nārasiṃha [Tantra];
and Vīrabhadra, however, obtained the Bhadra [Tantra] from Sarvātmadeva.
(4b) Bṛhaspati obtained from Ananta the [mantra] known as Candra;
likewise, the god Skanda and Anala obtained the Āgneya from Vyoman.
Brahmā indeed obtained the Svāyambhuva [Tantra] from Nidhana;
the divine Prajāpati received the Visara from Tejaspate;
and the sage [Durvāsas] obtained the Raurava from Īśāna and the Prāndīśa from Brahmā.
Bhairava obtained the Tantraja from Mahākāla, who is known as Śiva; he attained the Vidyālaya from Vilaya;
and the sage Saṃvartaka received the Kiraṇa from Devapitṛ.
The divine Dharma completed the discourse on the bovine [sacrifice] for the Lord of the Gods.
Thus, eighteen applications of the Tantras have been declared by Jñānāvatāra.
In this way, fifty-four applications of the Tantra were taught by the Guru.
But at the time of exposition, for disciples who are of keen intellect, the subjects to be explained [should be presented].
Thus concludes the instruction on the principles of methodology (tantrayukti).
All the methodological principles have been explained; now the non-study period (anadhyāya) is being defined.
One should never study during the periods of twilight, nor during an ominous portent;
nor indeed during an eclipse of the moon or sun, nor at the transition of the zodiacal signs;
nor on the eighth, the fourteenth, or the fifteenth day of either fortnight.
On the fourth lunar day, however, with great effort during the fortnights, months, solstices, and so forth,

as well as during the supreme study of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*), and for the sake of the king— especially in the event of the loss of his kingdom, or when misfortune has befallen him, or particularly when misfortune has befallen himself.
But when there is an excessive wind, during all festivals,
during those times which are among the interdictions for study,
and when occupied with the words of the teacher, one should never recite.
(5a) One should never engage in recitation in the presence of animals;
one should keep yawning, belching, coughing, and the like far away from the presence of the Guru.
If one performs it otherwise due to negligence, one should recite the Vāmadeva hymn a hundred times. If a student recites it incorrectly, or if a teacher teaches it incorrectly,
or if it is forgotten through negligence, it shall lead to the state of concealment (tirobhāva).
Brahmā said:

O Lord, having diligently studied the entire collection of the sacred fires (agnis) along with their ritual manuals, what further duty remains here for those who have been initiated by preceptors and others?
The Supreme Lord said: The initiate (*samayin*) and the spiritual son (*putraka*) should perform the worship of Śiva;
the practitioner (*sādhaka*) should constantly perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) and the practice of mantras (*mantrasādhana*).
The teacher, having understood that teaching, exposition, and the favoring of others—
whether resulting in material gain or spiritual liberation— are truly Śiva himself, should contemplate that Lord of Gods and perform all his duties with wisdom.
Otherwise, the entire fruit of the scripture is lost.
Thus concludes the rule for study.
The rule pertaining to study has been declared, preceded by the principles of tantric methodology and the like.
Endowed with the [teachings on] non-study days and so forth from the venerable Pauṣkara-śāstra,
it is taught specifically according to the Śrīkaṇṭhī,
as follows: from the supreme cause, Śiva, who is beyond the end of the unmanifest form (adṛṣṭavigraha).
The great form of knowledge emerged from the mind, possessing a face;
when it attained the state of being the cause, it was called the Unstruck (Anāhata).
Because it flows forth as that which is supreme, it is celebrated as the Imperishable (Akṣara).
(5b) That which they call inconceivable is the sustainer of the life-force of living beings;
it is the conscious self, all-pervading, established in itself, self-cognizable, and without support.
Residing within the lotus-heart of all living beings, [the Lord] speaks in the form of sound (nāda).
From cowherds, women, and children, down to barbarians who speak vernacular tongues,
and even those creatures that move in the water— having realized this— they too constantly utter it.
O lady of excellent vows, the letter *ha* is of the nature of sound (*nāda*), [expressed as] "haṃsa, haṃsa.
From this, all this has arisen, bestowing the fruits of the four aims of life.

Now, therefore, [I shall explain] the Vedas, grammar, logic, history, the Purāṇas, and the tenets of the Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Saura, Bauddha, Ārhata, Sāṅkhya, and Yoga systems, as well as the Kula, Kaula, and Akula traditions.
Through such primary divisions as these, it is established as Śabdabrahman;
likewise, it is divided manifoldly by many other pure distinctions of names.
These seventeen divisions have been proclaimed by me according to their principal categories.

I shall explain their differentiation as it arises from the scripture of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā). That which first perceives [the object] by means of the path proclaimed in the scriptures, emerging from the infinite mouths [of Śiva], is declared to be fourfold.
The *Ṛgveda* is the earth, Brahmā, and water; the *Yajurveda* is remembered as Viṣṇu. Rudra is the splendor (*tejas*), while the *Sāmaveda* is Bhava; the *Atharvaveda* is said to be Vāyu and Īśa.
It consists of a thousand chapters and many hundreds of thousands of *ṛks*.

Through my grace, the Ṛgveda was brought down by means of a mouth born from my favor, together with innumerable common scriptures filled with many mantras and the like, and joined with thousands of sacrificial sciences along with their primary and secondary limbs (aṅga-upāṅga).
And from that, the scripture was prophesied according to the conditions of different times:
the Atharva is the auspicious southern face, the abode of secret mantras.
The Ṛgveda is the eastern face, which sets forth the Brahman of Sound;
the Smārta [Yajurveda] is complete in all its limbs and is filled with various ritual actions.
The Sāmaveda is said to be the western [face], adorned by the study of meters.
The letter *ha* is in the form of a swan; it is called *hau*, it moves, and it is sung.
Residing within the mouths of the Yajur, Ṛg, and Sāma Vedas, it is recited in four ways:
the letter *a*, the letter *u*, the letter *m*, and the half-mora (*ardhamātraka*).
When one analyzes all [words]— such as Śaiva and Vaidika terms— for the sake of understanding words and their meanings,
and for the purpose of [grammatical] application,
that is traditionally known as *vyākaraṇa* (grammar).
And that [grammar] should be known as ninefold, according to its different times and causes:
those composed by Indra, Gālava, Śākalya, Gārgya, and Vātsya,
as well as those composed by Kātyāyana, Bharadvāja, Guha, and Ātreya.
Thus, the nine grammatical treatises (navavyākaraṇa) are the cause of all words and their meanings;

they are the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the objects of perception and other means of knowledge, and they are eightfold according to the relationship between the signified and the signifier, characterized by the inferable and so forth.
From the mark (liṅga) comes the bearer of the mark (liṅgin); this is the general rule, as fire is inferred from smoke.
The seen is the seer, the form of darkness is the progenitor, just as the one who is born is the progenitor.
[This inference] is caused by the existence of dry wood and so forth, yet it is without a [substantial] cause.
Error is the universal that is beyond perception; the perceptible is imperishable.
The relation cognized through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) is without cause.
Reasoning (tarka) is an instrumental cause; it is momentary and beyond perception.
The connection with mere cognition and so forth is characterized by the notion of existence and the like.
All this is mere cognition, caused by the state of things as they truly are.
Forms are without objective causes; the cause itself is without a further cause.
(6b) The reason is common to direct perception, and the object of cognition serves for the establishment of the goal.
There is rebirth, characterized by selflessness, the absence of intrinsic nature, and so forth.

The Buddhists consider this eightfold direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) to be common [to all]. History and so forth concerning Viṣṇu are both with cause and without cause. Beyond that, everything characterized by persistence and so on is internal (*ādhyātmika*).
All that is characterized by ritual action and so forth, consisting of the duality of the object of worship and the worshiper;
the natural order of pervasion and its constraints, characterized by the yoga of action and the like—
all this is established everywhere with reference solely to the Self, and is thus characterized by self-awareness.
That which proceeds with signs ceases when it is signless;
all this is indeed Vedic, and this is sung as Brahman.
Ritual acts such as sacrifice, which arise from the flow of the qualities (*guṇas*), [are likewise included].
The definition of the Pāñcarātrika is connected with the renunciation of ritual action (*karmasaṃnyāsa*).
With reference to that, ritual actions both exist and do not exist.
Ritual action, which has sacrifice as its basis, is considered to be fivefold yoga.
Having attained co-residence (sālokyatā), the manifestation of the Supreme Self and other principles occurs;
just as a mass of life-force described as its own radiance, when struck with great speed,
emits sparks, so too does the manifestation of the elements and other principles arise.

For some, there remains only a mere possession [of the truth], like powdered frog-meat. "This is to be done, this is not; having done this, one shall attain that"—such is the gravity of the reality established through the instruction of a reliable authority.
That which was composed by Brahmā and others is celebrated as "Smārta" (based on tradition);
it was performed in ancient times by the ancestors, having been established by those who came before.
Primary creation, secondary creation, genealogies, the duration of the Manvantaras,
and the history of the dynasties and their successors— this is proclaimed as the Purāṇa.
I shall describe it in its eighteenfold divisions according to the different incarnations.
The first is called the Cosmic Egg (Brahmāṇḍa); the second is said to be Vāyu;
the third is Maṇa; the fourth originates from Sūrya;
the fifth is named Viṣṇu; and the sixth arises from Vidyā.
The [scripture] known as Soma, that which is born from Sāmba, Bhairava, and likewise Vijaya—
thus the Purāṇa is proclaimed to have eighteen divisions.
The activity of the mind and its abandonment, characterized by direct realization and so forth, [are its subject].
Union with the Self is considered to be of six kinds:
breath control (prāṇāyāma), meditation (dhyāna), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), reasoning (tarka), and absorption (samādhi); this is called the six-limbed yoga.
The syllable *oṃ* is its designator, as is the term "the person who is the reflection of the heart.
Īśvara is untouched by afflictions, karma, their maturation, and so forth;
he is the cause of the knowledge that sustains the objects of perception through the means of valid cognition.
"The object of worship is of the nature of light, and its minute particle is the transformer"—
this and other such views constitute the Pātañjala determination of the Self.
"The smeller, the toucher, the speaker, and the self of light"— this is the view of the Yogins.
The knowledge of the objects to be established (sādhya) by way of enumeration is indeed twenty-five-fold in nature:
the elements beginning with earth; sound and the other [qualities] which are the sources of the elements;
the internal organ as threefold; and the ten organs of action and cognition.
O Goddess, Prakṛti consists of the three guṇas, while Puruṣa is the twenty-fifth principle.
He is both the agent and the enjoyer; through their conjunction, he experiences the fruit [of action].
The accomplishment [of this] is like a lame man and a blind man, or as a magnet is to iron;
likewise, the determination of the elements is like a crystal by the power of the sun.
However, due to the reversal of the qualities and because of the distinctness of the enjoyer's activity, [the self is established].
Having understood many established principles through the means of valid cognition and the cognizer,
one who remains constantly in the state of *prakṛti* does not attain liberation.
Only after perceiving the distinction between *pradhāna* and *puruṣa* does one become isolated (*kevala*).

The wise of the Sāṃkhya declare that the unmanifest (prakṛti) is non-agential in the production of objects of experience, being as insentient as a clod of earth; yet it is not entirely isolated [from the Puruṣa]. Beyond the Puruṣas there is something further—that is the ultimate limit, that is the supreme goal.
This knowledge, which has been declared by way of enumeration to consist of three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
is the *Pañcarātra* that extends over a hundred crores in its extent.
Within it, there are a full hundred divisions, plus sixteen more.
O Goddess, Viṣṇu has declared the exposition of the five times (pañcakāla).
I shall briefly describe them according to the different names of the Saṃhitās:
Nārāyaṇī, Saṅkarṣaṇī, Pradyumnī, and Aniruddhikā.
Vaihāyasī, Kapilā, Ātreyī, Kālapauṣkarī, Bhāradvājī, Kālākhyā, Aindrī,
Baudhāyanī, Svarbhānavī, Jayakṣenā, Kūrmākhyā, and Śāṅkupāyinī.
Nāradī, Kautukī, Tathyā, Prahlādī, and Pauṣkarī;
Jayā, Hayaśirā, and likewise Kālavapīyakā; Padmodbhavā, Pañcakālī, Māyā, and Vaibhavikā.
The Vāsiṣṭhā is the supreme enumeration, as are the Aurvā and the Sārasvatī;
likewise the Sāndarśanā, the Lakṣmī, and the Naranārāyaṇī. (8a)
The Hiraṇyagarbha, Paulastya, Asuravadā, and Nāradī;
then the Jājvali, Śāṇḍilya, and the Saṃhitā called Kaustubha;
the Śeṣa, Ananta, Sātvata, Bārhaspatya, and Gālava.
O Goddess, there is the Saṃhitā called Sadya, as well as the Kāśyapi; also the Saumantā, the Viśvā, and likewise the Trailokyamohinī;
the Catuścayāvatārā, the Nārasiṃhī, and the Trivikramā.
Dattātreyī, Sanatkaumārikā,
likewise Lauhamarṣiṇikā, as well as Vihagendramata;
Pārāśaryā, Kāpitthī, and Sauparṇaketukā.
The Cāturātrī, the Vāyavyā, the Jaigīṣavyā, the Māṇḍavī, the Mālvā, the Kālaparā, the Vaikuṇṭhī, the Adbhutagautamā,
the Lāciketā, the Jāmadagnī, and likewise the Vaiśampāyanikā.
Śrīpatnī, Śākalyā, Aiśvarī, Pārthivī, Hautāśanī, Dhruvāntā, Mahāmāndārimānavī,
Navātmikā, Āṅgirasī, Āruṇā, and Śākaṭāyanī.
Avyaktā, Ādivārāhī, and likewise Pradyumnakāmikā;
Brahmodbhavā, Kiñjalkā, and likewise Tejosravaṇikā; Kaṇvakrūrā, Satyabhāmā, Mārkāṇḍeyā, and Bhavodbhavā.
The ocean of secrets, the lion of the *sphoṭa*, and likewise the Pātāla-lion—
she who possesses these forms is declared to be the fivefold form, the source of the universe.
Śatadhārā, Viśvamukhī, Viśvaksenā, Anuṣṭubhā,
Deśāvatārā, Praṇavā, Padmagarbhā, Lomaśā, Suparṇā,
and likewise Deveśī— these indeed number one hundred and sixteen.
O lady of excellent limbs, among those who are united [in practice], this is proclaimed as the Vaiṣṇava path.
It is characterized by the commonality of both direct perception and indirect inference;
it is the transformation resulting from that yoga, and not characterized by rebirth.

This world is devoid of intrinsic being, empty of the notion of karma, and like a bubble upon the water—what has passed away has simply passed away. For those whose minds are destroyed by pride, what agent is there here, and what is it that is acted upon? Such is their view.
That which resides in the heart as the "living sun" (jīvāditya), which dispels the darkness of the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa)—
that is the supreme doctrine of the Sauras, characterized by the attainment of that light.
This entire world, both stationary and moving, is of the nature of light.
That [tradition] is sung in many ways, arising from the divisions of Saura and others;
I shall now explain its accomplishment according to the meaning of the *Saṃhitā*.
First was the *Mārtāṇḍī Saṃhitā*, and likewise the *Mahāmārtāṇḍikī*.
The third is Bhargaśikhā, and likewise Bhairavaśekharī;
the fourth is Jaiminīyā, celebrated with Vedic mantras and the like; the fifth is Saṃhārā;
the sixth is likewise [called] Saṃhārā; and the seventh is Bhāskarī.
The eighth is declared to be Parākhyā, and the ninth is Saṃyamā; the tenth is called Guhyacakrā, and Mahālakṣmī is likewise the eleventh;
Sahasrā is declared the twelfth, and Karaṇā is the thirteenth.
(9a) Caṇḍā, Vyomagarbhā, Khaśolkā, [and] Nakṣatriṇī;
Vāḍavī, Kāruṇyā, and likewise Yamunā were conquered.
Likewise, there is the mistress of birds (Khageśvarī) named Sūryaśikhā and Raśmicakrā;
Maholkā and she called Maholkā; Nabholkā and Vyomamālinī;
Kalmāṣā and Puṣkarāvartā; and likewise the one known as Sāmbhāsaṃhitā.
Vaiśvānarī, Prakāśā, the one named Saṃvartā, Piṅgalā, the one named Hanumā, Yājñavalkī, Jānakī, Yajñamekhalā,
the one named Uccaiḥśravas, Aruṇā, and Kālavaiśvānarīprabhā.
Caṇḍacetā, Mahādevā, as well as Vyājīvatārikā;
Tārikā, Tejati, Yakṣikā, Mokṣatārakā;
Jīvārkā, Paramārkā, Praśāntārkā, and Vaidyutā.
Dharmadhvajā, Jñānagarbhā, Tattvagarbhā, Hairaṇyagarbhā— who is foremost among them— and likewise Harimardinī;
Bhacakrā, Ātmacetā, and Piṅgalacetakā.
*Svasā*, *Ātreyī*, *Āruṣī*, *Vyomā*, and *Sāraṇā*; *Revatī* (known as *Revandā*), *Hetirājñī*, *Sahirā*, and likewise *Draviḍā*; *Aurvā*, *Sāratipatā*, *Bheruṣpandā*, and likewise *Antrikī*.
Maheśvetā, Tejagarbhā, and likewise Mahākairātikā;
Sūryadharma, Trayodaśātmā, and likewise Sūryadharmottarā;
Vyomāṅgarā, and Vyomagarbhā—these are the eighty-five Saṃhitās.
O Goddess, these Saṃhitās are declared in the Pārameśvara [Tantra] according to their primary divisions based on the Sun (Saura),
by the distinction between those consisting of a hundred thousand verses and those that are not, and by the distinctions of being in quarters (pādaka) or in half-verses (āvaka),
as well as by the extent of their textual bulk.
(9b) This work,
titled *Pratyakṣalakṣaṇa*, is by the Sauras; it has been correctly expounded there according to that authority, wherein the subject matter is not cluttered by excessive scriptural citations.
They know that [work] to be concise in text yet great in meaning, possessing the sense of a compendium;
it is proclaimed as the Tantra that has arisen,
and by it the chapter on the method of subtle discourse is distinguished.
O Goddess, the expansion of its meaning from beginning to end, along with the sequential determination of its doctrines and its account of creation, is set forth here from various texts;
it is a collection of distinct subjects, crowded with the meanings of many books.
That discourse which proceeds in due order and is preceded by systematic analysis [declares]:
the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed established as distinct, characterized by what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted;
its bondage arises from *māyā*, the atoms (*aṇu*), and *karma*, preceded by the cognition of the conscious and the unconscious.
Because it exists in a state directed toward objects of enjoyment, for the sake of attaining dispassion,
one who desires to know the supreme reality [should understand] the characteristics of the descent of power (śaktipāta),
the causes of its bestowal and destruction, and so forth, as well as the dissolution of the subtle body.
One certainly attains that supreme, peaceful state which possesses a Lord;
indeed, that mantra known as *prasāda* is proclaimed as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
From the perspective of ultimate reality, all entities are of the nature of the eternally manifest.
The conjunction consisting of that [power] is called the "conjunction of attainment" (*prāpti-saṃyoga*), which is proclaimed as being "of power" (*śākta*).
They say that "kula" is the body; nothing exists anywhere that is not *Śiva*.
The accomplishment of the fruit is one's own nature (*svabhāva*); there is nothing higher than that.
That which consists of the fourfold [categories] beginning with the *piṇḍa* is known as the *kula*;
however, that [kula], beginning with the non-duality of substance (*dravya-advaita*), is established in four ways. (10a)

The revelation of secret mantras and so forth, characterized by the withdrawal of all things— O Goddess, that is the Kaula meaning, which produces immediate conviction. Now, the Śaiva meaning is proclaimed in ten ways.
The characteristics of the divisions of Rudra and so forth consist of ten and eighteen varieties.
This seventeenfold division arises from sound and the other [sensory objects].
O Goddess, when the primary nature has been declared, there is a slight internal distinction within the various sounds.
Īśāna is remembered as having sound for his body and being the essence of all sciences;
whatever worldly knowledge exists, all that has issued from Brahmā. But Vedic knowledge, on the other hand, arose from the splendor of Viṣṇu, which is certain within the self.
And Īśvara [received] the path called Mantra from Sadāśiva.
These four categories are established within the state of pervasion.
Now, [this concerns] the God beyond gods, who consists of the five mantras.
Five streams have arisen from the cause of the origin of the scriptures,
in sequence from above, from the east, from the front, from the south, and from the north.
Within these streams, there shall be divisions of knowledge born of those known as Śiva and Rudra in ancient times.
Kāmika, Yojaka, Citrya, Nākuṭa, and again Aṃśumān;
Dīpta, Sūkṣma, Sāhasra, Ajita, and likewise Anantaka—these are declared to be the divisions of Śiva. Now hear, O beloved, the divisions of Rudra.
The Vijaya, the Pārameśa, and the Niśśvāsodgati;
the Mukhabimba, the Siddha, the Santāna, and the Nārasimhika;
the one called Candra, the Vīrabhadra, the Āgneya, and the Svayambhuva.
(10b) O Maheśvarī, they declare that the Tantras are Viśara, the one called Raurava, Vimala, Kiraṇa, Lalita, and Saurabheya.

The upward stream (ūrdhvasrotas) has emerged in twenty-eight divisions. Those twenty-eight tantras which were revealed by Tūrṇoka are produced from the likeness of Śiva and others, bestowing the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.

I shall now declare those twenty-eight divisions according to the various meanings of many scriptures. These twenty-eight divisions constitute the embodied form of the Supreme Goddess; the body of the God of gods is established in the Śabdabrahman (the Absolute as Sound).
The manifestation of the body is for the sake of favoring living beings, and not otherwise. The Blessed Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, who is the embodiment of mantra and is designated as Sādākhya,
possesses a body composed of the various divisions of Rudras and the various divisions of Śivas, O Pārvatī.
He who knows [this] even in the state of all mantras is a knower of the Veda.
I shall now explain that [mantra], beginning from the head and ending with the feet:
from the head, the self of victory (vijayātman), and from the forehead, the supreme lord (pārameśvara).
From the eyes, he [emanated] the breath, the supreme King of Knowledge;
from the two ears, the *prodgīta*; and from the mouth, the *mukhabimbaka*. From the shoulders came that which is known as the *siddha*, and from the region of the armpits, the *santāna*.
From the chest [emanates] Nārasiṃha, from the two breasts Candrasaṃjñaka;
from the heart the one named Vīrabhadra, and from the belly Āgneya;
from the region of the navel Svāyambhuva, and likewise from the two sides Visara.
From the region of the back comes Raurava; from the region of the hips, Vimala;
from the genitals, that which is named Kiraṇa; and from the pair of thighs, Lalita.
From his two knees [arose] Saurabheya; likewise, from the tip of his crest-lock, Kāmika.
From his crest-lock [arose] Yogaja, and from his tongue, the one known as Cintya.
From his crown was born Makuṭa, and from his two arms, Aṃśumān.
Blazing from the three eyes, subtle, and having emerged from the throat; likewise, the thousandfold [teaching] by means of the teeth, as well as the *Ajita* in the two hands,
and the *Tantra* known as *Antarnāma* in the feet, which arises from the host of stars.
Another division of the Śiva-mantra is recited as being further [than the previous].
Its summary (saṅgraha) should be understood through the words of the Ṛṣis and the hosts of gods.

Likewise, we shall explain the eight divisions of the Left (Vāma) and Right (Dakṣiṇa), characterized by the head (mūrdhan). Furthermore, that [division] should be described as having eleven distinct parts, distinguished by the causes of their connection, their designations, their measures, their faces, the listener, and the nature of the scripture and its meaning as seen by the speaker.

The relationship between the signified and the signifier is characterized by all [categories] such as difference and so forth. The signified is the object, and the signifier is the word; and that object may be manifold: it may have a cause, it may be an undertaking, it may be preceded by a substance, or it may be without cause.
The commonality of practice and so forth, together with reasoning, is to be inferred;
but the verbal [cognitions], O Goddess, are as before, and likewise manifold in their divisions. The cognition of the external Naiyāyikas is the delusion of silver in mother-of-pearl.
For he who would perceive the past and the future through similarity [of form] proceeds without expectation;
his cognition and other faculties cease to function.
Moreover, because it has entered into another state of being, it is manifested only by that which is to be cognized.
O Goddess, the definition of *ūha* and the other [subsidiary sciences], along with the word (*śabda*), which has many divisions,
is proclaimed as the instrumental cause for the sake of favoring living beings.
Because he is independent, that Supreme Lord exists for the sake of turning back the cycle of transmigration;
by his very nature, he is the supreme benefactor of living beings.
For the purpose of [severing] the bond of *māyā*, he liberates the bound souls (*paśu*) from that bondage.

O Goddess, the various divisions of the scripture concerning omniscience and other attributes have been proclaimed; these many divisions arise from the multiplicity of the texts and their extensive details.
Thus, there is a difference of opinion among the Buddhists regarding the Buddha, and likewise among the Śaivas regarding the Lord (Īśvara).
The diversity of opinions regarding the meanings of the doctrines, the origin of knowledge among the Sauras,

the various divisions of Rudra among the Tantrikas, and the manifold distinctions of the faces [of Śiva] are recited; likewise, the divisions of Śakti, the divisions of ritual action, and the divisions of mantra are taught.
Because it is the source of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman), and due to the distinctions such as celibacy (brahmacarya) and so forth,
the various manifestations of the descent [of the Lord] are cited under different names.
Furthermore, the six means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) previously mentioned— namely those established as perception (pratyakṣa) and the rest— are also included.
Self-awareness and likewise other experience are recorded as such;
O Goddess, in this Śaiva system, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is proclaimed to be eightfold.
Following the stream [of the teaching], one should ascertain the meaning of the words in order to eliminate doubt.
The deity, through many divisions according to the distinctions of incarnations and so forth,
is the speaker with whom [this work] is connected; he is the initiator of all scriptures,
who, having arisen from doubt, exists for the sake of turning back from cyclic existence.
What is this, by whom, and for what reason is it characterized by a connection with the current (*srotas*),

having arisen from [the transmission] beginning with Āyāta and so forth, yet not brought down according to one's own will? Indeed, it has come from Śiva through Anantanātha to myself, who am infinite.
"From his mouth fell upon the earth that which is called the *Aṣṭāvatāra*.
(12a) Such is the connection of the scriptures; thus proceeds their traditional transmission in due order.
The definitive conclusion of the true scripture is that the essential nature [of the Self] is the cause.
For what purpose, then, has it descended? It has done so for that very purpose through many divisions:
for the sake of instruction, ethics, and other matters, as well as for the sake of yoga, characterized by the realization of the Self.
The attainment of the Lord is for the sake of Śiva; the object of knowledge is said to be for the sake of knowledge;
the realization of the meaning of the sentence is for the sake of the sentence; and liberation is said to be for the sake of initiation.
Thus, the purpose—which is of many forms—is discerned through its various aspects.
This meaning is this treatise; thus, the meaning [of the term] is manifold.
That which was designated as "the seer" (*darśaka*) is inferred through the perspective of the treatise (*śāstradṛṣṭyā*).
Whatever action is not seen in the treatise, such as that characterized by chewing and so forth, [is also included].
And that which is performed from the perspective of the Śāstra is considered the "Visionary" (darśaka);
thus we shall describe these eleven subjects according to their respective modes,
whether by way of the Śambhu-pakṣa or again by way of the Śakti-pakṣa.
That side by which [liberation] is attained is called the Śakti-pakṣa;
that by which the supreme, eternal [state] is attained becomes the Śambhu-pakṣa.
Due to the presence of a cause, there is a dull manifestation of the individual souls (aṇu) in their state of limitation.
Having descended, they bestow grace; the meaning of the mantra belongs to the faction of Śambhu.
Formerly, the Gāruḍa-hṛdaya consisted of twenty-eight divisions.
That which is known as Sāvitra-uttara is the measure of a digit (kalā), the nectar of the digit.
The *Harahuṅkāra*, the *Bindu*, the *Bindusāra*, the *Kalottara*;
the *Pakṣirāja*, the *Śikhāyoga*, the *Śikhāsāra*, and the *Śikhottara*; the *Pañcabhūta* known as the *Bheda*, the *Śivabheda*, and the *Mānasa*.
(12b) Nīlakaṇṭha, Kālākhya, Kālakūṭa, Śatadrūka, Vākoja, Kambala, Kāka, Kākatuṇḍa, and Kahakamī.
Suvarṇalekha, Sugrīva, Trotula, and Trotulottara—
thus have twenty-eight varieties been briefly declared by me,
out of compassion for living beings and for the purpose of destroying the six [internal enemies].
For the protection of noble lineages and others, it is crowded with the meanings of many mantras.
It is known as the *Harahuṅkāra* through twenty-four divisions;
first, that called the *Pakṣirāja* consists of five divisions.
Hayagrīva, Kumāra, Gormāda,
Vajratuṇḍa, and Śubhāṇḍa are proclaimed as the five divisions.
The application of their crests (śikhā) is described in seven ways in successive order.
Śikhāśaiva, Śikhā itself, Sāra, Mahābhaṭa,
Karṇarāja, Saurabheda, and the seventh is indeed Amālina.
O Goddess, Śikhāsāra is threefold, characterized by Caṇḍasāra and the others.
Tuṇḍigrīva, Mahākāla, and then Vajraśikhottara; Pātāla, Tālacaṇḍa, and Aṭṭahāsaviṣolbaṇa;
Agādha, Ghoratuṇḍa, and likewise Viṣadharamata.
Holākhya, Vegaṣaṇḍa, Vivartaka, Gonāsa, Bhiṇḍicaṇḍa, Śākala, Jīvarakṣaṇa,
Daśapañca, and Bheda— these fifteen have been declared to you as the Śikhottara.
Nīladaṇḍa, Śiva, Tālaghuṣṭa, Vilambika,
Bhairava, Śivāṇḍa, Rājamūla, and Mahābala. (13a)
Karṇāmoṭa, Paradaṃśa, Indravajra, and Mahāgada—
these twelve varieties are said to arise from the fifty [letters].
They are all known by the name Sāvitrī and are considered to be of one mind.
Indeed, these divisions have been declared by me according to the nature of my disciples.
In the Western [tradition], there is that which is called Bhūtatantra, belonging to the division of Śiva.
Therein are Holā, Hayagrīva, Karaṅka, and Kaṭakāmaya.
Karoṭī, the one called Muṇḍamālā, Kārkoṭa, Khaḍgarāvaṇa, Caṇḍa, the one called Daṇḍāsidhāra, Vikaṭa, Kaṭimaṇḍala,
Bhūtrāsa, Śikhārāva, Gharghara, and Siṃhakoṭara.
Ghoraṭṭahāsa, Yamaghaṇṭa, and Ghaṭotkaca—
these were designated for the purpose of turning back the wicked and out of compassion for living beings,
as well as for the destruction of all diseases; indeed, here the division [of mantras] is based on the human [source].
It contains the meaning of fierce mantras, is crowded with garland-mantras (mālāmantras),

and is endowed with medicinal prescriptions for healing and the like; it shatters evil planetary influences and is filled with hundreds of [remedies for] untimely deaths, by the knowledge of which they are destroyed.
The first, known as Helā, is characterized by Āyurveda and other such sciences;
the second, renowned as Hayagrīva, is proclaimed for the purpose of protecting children and for the destruction of Kaṭaṅkaṭa and Rūpikā [demons].
The fourth, called Kaṭaka, is for the purpose of fulfilling desires for pleasure;
it brings about the destruction of eye diseases and initiates the treatment of extraneous objects lodged in the body.
The fifth is remembered as the *Karoṭī*, which is joined with the treatises on ethics (*nītiśāstra*) and so forth;
it is characterized by alchemy (*dhātuvāda*) and the like for the sake of achieving success in the extraction of essences (*rasavāda*).
For that purpose, the sixth tantra called the *Muṇḍamālā* has been revealed.
All [the rites] beginning with the discourse on mining (khanyavāda) are characterized by the extraction of treasures;
the seventh is remembered as Karkoṭaka, which involves the summoning of serpents.
It is fully equipped with garland-mantras for [overcoming] planetary afflictions, fevers, poisons, and the like.
The eighth is Khaḍgarāvaṇa, which pacifies all diseases;
the ninth is known as Caṇḍa, for the destruction of Rākṣasas and Piśācas;
and the tenth is considered to be Caṇḍasidhāra, consisting of three hundred and fifty thousand [verses].
The ten names were established for the purpose of obtaining all medicinal herbs.
As for the characteristics of the herbs, they are distinguished according to their individual ritual procedures (*kalpa*) and so forth.
By means of the collection of king-mantras, the eleventh is known as *Vikaṭa*.
The propitiation of sparrows and other birds for the purpose of destroying enemy armies;
the various types of offerings for the spirits (*bhūta*); and the *Amaraṇṭhaka-maṇḍala*.
This is the twelfth [chapter], O Great Goddess, by knowing which one becomes a possessor of mantras.
All beings perish, as do the Yoginīs and Śākinīs.
Thus has been declared the thirteenth [chapter], the "Terror of Beings," which is designated according to its true meaning.
Therein, the cry uttered by the beings eightfold increases their fear.
All the varieties of mudrās and the characteristics of the yoginīs have been taught;
likewise, the distinction of the crest-lock has not been omitted.
O Goddess, this fourteenth tantra is filled with the meaning of secret mantras;
it possesses a single division for all beings and is characterized by pervasiveness and other such qualities.
It contains both the descent of fever and its very cessation.
That tantra by which the portions of that [Principle] are known without distinction within all the wombs of beings— that *Gharghara*, the fifth string—
extends over nine hundred thousand verses and is crowded with many divisions.

O Goddess of the gods, that which is the primary mantra-discourse has been taught in the Siṃhakoṭara [Tantra]; it contains the terrible loud laughter and is the destroyer of spider-bites. It is conjoined with the knowledge of the stages (bhūmikās) and endowed with the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhi).

In this [sixteenth chapter], the sixteenth [type of magic] is proclaimed as that which consists of common applications characterized by the "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) and the "vanished" (*naṣṭa*), intermingled with sorcery (*indrajāla*) and the like;
it concerns the proportions of deities and their worship for the purpose of rites for prosperity.
The *Naktayāga*, the *Guhyasūtra*, the characteristics of subduing and attracting women,
and whatever minor rites (*kṣudrakarma*) and so forth that are encompassed by fierce mantras—
this is to be known as the seventeenth tantra, named *Ucchiṣṭa*.
From retention (*dhāraṇā*), however, there arises the differentiation of knowledge, adorned with the power of leaping and other such feats;
stability of the physical body and its constituents, the destruction of old age and disease,
the ability to desire the actions of others, and the entry into the light of another.

O lady of beautiful hips, that which describes the combination of medicinal herbs and the persistence of Rudra’s seed as taught by the Lord who desires the welfare of all beings— that remaining work is known as the eighteenth tantra.
The playful activities of beings, characterized by their natural disposition, dress, and so forth—
wherein all these elements of beings have been described in their entirety, that is the authoritative source. (14b)

In every case, it is determined by the distinction of the texts and the distinction of the ritual actions. Furthermore, the arising and the withdrawal of mantras have been described here. Now, the complete measure [of the mandala] and the characteristics of the world-protectors and so forth [are explained].
Where the entire earth, along with its oceans and forests, is described as being within the Supreme Lord;
where that which was asked by Vainateya and that which was asked by the son of Bhṛgu is all set forth— that they know as Yamaghaṇṭa.
The nineteenth [chapter], with an extent of one and a half crores.
Furthermore, O Goddess, there is another auspicious [chapter] which is the abode of all mantras,
uneven [in its power], descended from Rāvaṇa, and [known as] Ghaṭotkaca.
The first section is the Pātālakhaṇḍa, known as Hāṭakeśvara;
it is declared to consist of ten parts, which I shall describe according to their essence:
Hāṭakeśa, the one called Ghaṭa, and likewise Viṣamasambhava.
And another is the Sarvasaṃhāraka, and beyond that is the Pātālaśikha; the Kusumāli-mata and the seventh is the Kāmapañjara;
the Guhyārṇava and the Picu-mata are known as the ten Sāmanikas.
I shall now describe, according to their true meaning, the section on the two-fold entry:
first the Kulārṇava and likewise the fourfold Krama.
I shall relate the Kulārṇava in its tenfold form exactly as it is.
The Kula, the Mahākula, and likewise the Mahākālikula;
the Viśvākula, the Kāmikula, and likewise the Śubhāmaṇikula;
the Bhairavasāmānyakula, and likewise the auspicious Mātṛkula.
(15a) The Viśvākula, Śaktikula, and Kula have been proclaimed;
O Goddess, hear from me in brief how their sequence is divided.
The sequence of emanation, the sequence of time, that which is joined with the sequence of withdrawal,
and another, the sequence of descent— thus is the fourfold sequence. O Pārvatī, the sequence of emanation becomes fourfold through its divisions.
The first, the *Rāgāvatāra*, consisting of fifty thousand [verses], was spoken by me;
the second is the *Kulāvatāra*, and likewise the *Mantrāvatāra*. That which is called the *Varṇāvatāra*—thus the emanation is said to be fourfold.
The Kālakrama is indeed declared to be fourfold according to its divisions:
first the Kālakrama, then the Mahākālīkrama,
the Kālasaṅkarṣaṇīkrama, and the Pīṭhakrama is remembered as the fourth.
O Supreme Goddess, I shall likewise describe the withdrawal (saṃhāra) exactly as it is:
preceded by the sequence of withdrawal, joined with the power Bhairavī,
the second name is Kālākhya, which effects the withdrawal of all states of being.
The fourth is proclaimed as having the name "Universal Withdrawal" (sarvasaṃhāra).
Sequential emanation (kramasṛṣṭi), clan-emanation (kulasṛṣṭi), and the third, state-emanation (bhāvasṛṣṭi),
along with teacher-emanation (gurusṛṣṭi)— these they know as the sequence of emanation (sṛṣṭikrama).
That which is called the third section is known as the Ayodhyākhaṇḍa;
it is declared to be eightfold—listen to that, O lady of great asceticism! [They are:
the Bhalla-vijñāna-dṛṣṭi and the third is the Vindhyakhaṇḍa.
There was one resembling a fragment of moonlight, another arising from a cluster of stars;
one named Jayadratha, and yet another consisting of scattered stars.

Indeed, they know these three sections by the name *Sarvavīra*; this *Ghaṭotkaca-tantra* exists in many millions of divisions. It is the most secret of secrets, and it is the supreme [teaching] concealed by mantras.
This western face has been described by me in brief.
In the south lies the southern path with its twenty-four divisions;
among them is the most terrible, the most fearsome face of the directions.
Also [the one] known as Bhīmakhaṇḍa, the one named Mahāvetāla,
Asitāṅga, Mahocchuṣma, Krodha, Unmattabhairava, the one called Caṇḍa,
the one called Kamala, and Mahābhairavaśekhara.

The *Siddhayogīśvarītantra*, the *Yoginījālasaṃbhava*, the *Pañcāmṛta*, the one called *Prapañca*, the *Viśvabhairavakaṇṭha*, the *Bhairavāmṛta*, the *Utkoca*, the *Tilaka*, and likewise the *Yāmala*.
O Great Goddess, I shall describe these divisions to you exactly as they are.
First is Ghoraghoṇa, which is proclaimed to be fourfold:
Vidyudghoṇa, Vetāla, and Malicaṇḍa as the third.
O you of great asceticism, the fourth is the secret *surāsava*;
that which is the *mahāvetālaka* is proclaimed to be of two kinds:
first, *aṣkāloḥ*, and second, *ruṣṭasarvasva*.
In the Mahāghora [Tantra], I shall proclaim that which arises from the Rightward Current (dakṣiṇasrotas),
which is extensively spread over many millions and divided into twenty-four sections.
First is the Mahāghora, and likewise the Ānandabhairava.
The Lākula [tantra] preceded by the illustrious [Aghora], as well as the Vijñānabhairava;
the Aghorīśvarī-svacchanda and the Vidyā-svacchanda. (16a)
The *Sāra*, the one known as *Svacchanda*, likewise the *Rasasvacchandaka*;
the *Rājaputrīyaka*, and he who is *Svacchanda* and *Svatantraka*; the *Ceṭikā* named *Tāluka*, and the auspicious *Guhyasāra*.
Bindusvacchandaka by name, and likewise Nādasvacchanda;
Raurava and Kāladaṇḍa, as well as Ulūkādi;
Kramojjhita, Sāṭopa, Candragarbha, and Surārcita.
The twenty-fourth [chapter] concerning Death is declared to be most terrible.
I shall now proclaim the eighth, which is celebrated as Ghoraghoṇa;
this first Ghoraghoṇa extends over ninety million verses.
O Pārvatī, the eighty-eight thousand [verses] concerning Bhairava and his supreme consort—
the Goddess known as Candrikā— have been sung in various divisions.
She is Lambodarī, eternally satisfied, and indeed free from rising and setting.
It has been taught through the differentiation of mantras out of a desire for the welfare of devotees.
Beyond this is Mṛtyujihva, then Śuṣkākula,
followed by Vahnipāda, Bhīmaśiva, and likewise Heḍanormikula.
I have proclaimed these eight as Cittuvāda and Kāmadaṇḍa;
now, according to the differences of opinion, there are eight types of Diśāmukha,
and the ninth is indeed Kaula, known as Mahāvetāla.
Now, O Goddess, at this present time, Asitāṅga is being proclaimed;
it is renowned as being fourfold, known as Kālapakṣa. (16b)
Brahmavādya and Durākhya are sung of as Kalmaṣaṇḍa;
thereafter, O Goddess, Mahocchuṣma is recited in ten ways,
followed by Śikhocchuṣma, Kaulī, and then Vīrabheda.
And another is Aṣṭavīreśvara, which is most wonderful for those desiring supernatural power (ṛddhi);
also the Śuddhaśikṣāmata, as well as the Sārasvatamata;
likewise the Kālajihva, the one called Kuvīra, and the Siddhasantānaka.
Henceforth, O Pārvatī, I shall proclaim the Krodha-Unmattabhairava,
which is declared in two divisions along with its secret [teachings].
The first is the Nameless (Anāmaka), and likewise the Moon-Crested Jewel (Candracūḍāmaṇi).
O auspicious lady, the Jayākhyasaṃhitā is sevenfold: first the Vaijaya, then the Vāruṇa, the Bhadracūḍa, the Sārāmṛta, the Mahotkaṭa, the Parāvarta, and the Kākaśi... [and so forth].
(17a) Furthermore, what else? The Vidyātilaka and the Tilaka known as Bhairava, which is the stainless Dayāmala, are recited.
O Goddess, I shall describe to you the eightfold Yāmala within the Sūtrānta:
the Rudrabheda, the Brahmabheda, and likewise the Viṣṇubheda;
O Goddess, these contained within the Yāmala constitute the southern face.
In the Udaksrotas [tradition], there is that which is called Vāma, consisting of twenty-four divisions.
Among them are the Mahātantra, the Nayasūtra, and the Nayottara;
as well as the Mahāsaṃmohana, the Vīṇātantra, and the Śikhottara.
Furthermore, there is Ajita, Vijaya, another called Cintāmaṇimahodaya, and Vidyābhyudayānta; these four are the wonderful nectars of the quarters.

The sixth is known as the marvel of time, while the marvel of the secret is likewise remembered;
these six kinds of marvels are thus honored by all.
The supreme essence known as Lakṣārdha has been described,
wherein the five-faced sisters are remembered together with their brothers.
O Goddess, this is a great secret, named after the [sisters] themselves.
Hereafter, the Kāmadhenu is recited in four parts:
first, Vāmaguhya; likewise, Śāntika and Mānasa; and Ajatuṇḍa as the fourth. After that, I shall describe Karambaka.
That first [type] is divided into seven varieties:
Karambaka, Samudrormi, Stambhādya,
Mohana, Siṃharāja, Vājimukha, and Naurbandha is recorded as the seventh.
I shall now describe to you, O Gaṇava, the Ananta [Tantra] in its fivefold form:
the Anāmaka, the Bhinnaśīrṣa, the Ekavīra, the Balotkaṭa, and the Apsarāja; likewise, O Goddess, there is the Śaukra, which issued forth from Śukra.
Vāmadeva, desiring the welfare of Bhārgava,
composed the auspicious Saṃhitā known as Śaukra, consisting of twelve thousand verses;
it is filled with a multitude of great mantras and contains secret doctrines, O Pārvatī.
O Goddess, that which is surrounded by eight auspicious beings equal to herself in nature—
namely Brahmā and the others, numbering ten million, who delight in the left-hand path (vāmācāra)—
I shall now describe its fourfold division, which is proclaimed as being of four kinds.
The first is the group of four called Jaya, and likewise the one named Vijaya;
the third is called Jayantī, and similarly Aparājitā. (18a)

Wherein the fourfold set and the ninefold division are proclaimed—that secret abode of the Great Mantra is indeed the Bījapañjara (the Cage of Seeds). That is declared to be fourfold: the Pañjara and the Śaktipañjara.
O Goddess, it is considered the Bījapañjaraka as well as the Sārasvata;
it is called Ānanda, containing the meaning of the Saṃhitā, with an extensive scope of a hundred thousand verses,
joined with all mantras and the like, and arising from Bhava and Rudra.
The one called Sarva, Candraśakala, Somarāja, Kalāmukha,
and likewise Siddhamata— O Goddess, this is recited as fivefold.
Next, I shall describe Kiṅkareśa, by the knowledge of whom one attains success.
O Goddess, I shall likewise describe these sevenfold [teachings]: Kṣīrodakamata, Nitya, Hāṭakeśa, Virājita, Dūtīmukha, Tattvabheda, and Mūlavākya Manonmana; as well as Parāṅmukha.
Siddhakaula, known as Nāga, and likewise the auspicious Vidyāṣṭaka,
Kāmeśvara, and Siddharāja— these are proclaimed as the fivefold [traditions].
Through twenty-four principal divisions, they have emerged from the mouth of Vāma.
The Vāmavaktra [Tantra] is proclaimed as being expanded across ten million verses, containing secrets and hidden mantras that accomplish all desires and goals.
I shall now speak briefly of another [tantra], the Gīta, which was sung by the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin).
I shall explain their divisions according to the sixty-fourfold classification:
Bhairava, Yāmala, O Goddess, that called Matā, and likewise Piṅgala;
Cakrāṣṭaka, Śikhāṣṭa, and Bahurūpa as the seventh.
The eighth is proclaimed as belonging to Vāgīśī, O Goddess worshipped by heroes;
this Sādāśiva Tantra I shall now relate in brief. (18b)
Svacchandabhairava, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmattabhairava,
Asitāṅga, Mahocchuṣma, and Kāpālīśa is considered the eighth;
this is declared to be the Brahmayāmala, and Vetāla is remembered as the eighth.
Likewise, the Viṣṇuyāmala;
the Skanda, the Umārudra, and the Atharvaṇa is remembered as the sixth;
the seventh is called the Rudra, and the Vetāla is remembered as the eighth.
These are indeed known as the fierce divisions within the Bhairava [tantra], which is devoted to heroes.
Bhairavī is declared to be the first, originating from the Piśutantra.
She is renowned as being twofold by division, and the third is likewise mentioned.
The fourth is Brāhmī, while the fifth is called Vijayā;
the sixth shall be Candrā, then Maṅgalā and Sarvamaṅgalā.
These are the divisions of Maṅgalā as proclaimed by Krodheśa.
The first is the wheel of mantras, the second is the wheel of phonemes;
the third is the wheel of powers, and the fourth is the wheel of digits.
The fifth is the wheel of the point (bindu), and the sixth is indeed known as the wheel of sound (nāda).
The seventh is the Guhyacakra, and the eighth is considered the Khacakra.
These indeed are the various divisions of the Cakras taught by Asitāṅga:
Andhaka, the division of Ruru, that called Aja, and the one known as Mūla.
Karṇāmoṭa, Viḍaṅga, Jvālinī, and Mātṛrodana—
these are the varieties of Svacchanda, spoken of in many forms.
Bhairavī is declared to be the Śikhā, and Vīṇā is the second.
The third is Vīṇāmaṇi, while the fourth is Saṃmoha;
the fifth is named Ḍāmara, and the sixth is Atharvaka. (19a)
The seventh is known as Kabandha, and the eighth is Śiraccheda.
O Goddess, these varieties of the *śikhā* were spoken by Unmatta;
this is the wheel of Sādāśiva, divided into sixty-four parts.
This infinite merit arises from the stream [of the lineage] and is adorned by that;
it was spoken by Ananteśa, who is like an infinite sun. It is permeated by the three powers and spread forth by the jewel of the mudrās.
The Great Maṇḍala Leader, distinguished by manifold aspects,
is intermingled with thousands of Vidyās and originates from the divine lotus-face. Those Tantras residing in the Heart are proclaimed to be twenty million in number.
O Bhairavī, the *Siddhayogeśvarīmata* extends over ninety million [verses]. O fair-faced one, other tantras numbering three and a half crores have subsequently appeared,
divided into fifty thousand and twenty-five thousand sections.
O beautiful lady, there are three thousand and fifty-five hundred [deities] in the Kṣatra [tattva];
then, some are in the Sādāśiva principle, and others in that which is named Ananta.
Others are hidden within Rudra, and likewise others in that which is called Vidyā;
[others] in the Great Principle (mahātattva) of Prakṛti, and likewise in the three lineages of gurus.
[Others are hidden] in the intellect (buddhi), and likewise in the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) by the Guru, the Higher Guru, and the Great-Guru.
Then, in the ocean of creation, it was forgotten by the Lord Śrīkaṇṭha.
Śiva, Śikhā, Jyotis, and Vimala as the fourth—
from these [sources] it was declared, and from there it reached the mortal world.
The Mudrā-maṇḍala-pīṭha, as well as the Pañca-pīṭha; likewise,
the Vidyā-pīṭha is proclaimed— thus the Saṃhitā consists of four pīṭhas.
Śrīkaṇṭha, Saumakaumāra, Mausalija, Jājali, as well as Vimala, Aṣṭahāsa, Ghorasvacchanda as the eighth,
Dūrvāsāmechaka, and likewise the supreme Sārasvata.
Jayadratha and Phetkāra are proclaimed as the fifth;
Raktākhya and Lampaṭākhya—thus the Brahmayāmala is sevenfold. [The others are] Haṃsa, Yakṣiṇī, Mātaṅga, Ekavīra, Ambu, and Pauṣkara.
The Pārameśvara [Tantra] is sevenfold, including the Vāmadeva;
that which is the Haṃsapārameśvara is recited in two parts. The one called Haṃsa, in the southern recension, extends to ninety lakhs [of verses].
The *Yakṣiṇī* and the *Parameśa* are recited as the ninefold [scriptures]:
the *Kiraṇa*, the *Nandimata*, the *Haṃsinī*, the *Brahmamaṇḍala*,
the *Svāyambhuva*, the *Skandamata*, the *Pratiṣṭhā*, and the *Pārameśvara*.
The *Liṅgakalpa* together with the *Gārgīya*, which extends to ninety million verses, and that tantra known as the *Mātaṅga*— that is recited in three ways:
the *Kalpaśākhā*, the *Mātaṅga*, and the *Mṛgendra-saṃhitā*.
O auspicious lady, they know the *Ekavīra* to be twofold, consisting of three hundred thousand [verses].
Then there is the *Paitāmaha-ekavīra*, which is called the *Ambā*;
that is known as the *Ambā-sajña*. Likewise, the *Guhyasūtra* and another, the *Piṅgalā*, are considered [to be parts of it].
The *Pratiṣṭhā*, the *Ṣaṭkadīkṣā*, and the *Arṇa*—these exist in five ways;
O Goddess, that *Tantra* which is the *Pauṣkara* is recited as being sevenfold.
Puṣkara, Brahmavallī, and likewise Nārāyaṇīyaka;
Kuberaṣaṭka, Kāliñja, and Hālāhala are considered [tantras];
Yoginīmata and another, Vāmadeva, are now mentioned.
O Mother of the Gaṇas, [I have taught] Vāmadeva, the one called Catuṣka, as well as Tumburupañjara; this Sarvajña and another, the Guhyaṣaṭka—
the supreme ocean of all mantras, which is the branch of reality and the divine creeper.
O Goddess, it is said to be eightfold, with an extent of seventy million verses:
Nīlāmbara, Sutāra, Sandhyā, Yoginī, Ḍāmara, Svāyambhuva, Siddhamata, and that called Gaṇa, as well as Khecarīmata.
These eight are known as the Kaulas, which produce immediate conviction.
But the ninth is the Mahākaula, which is difficult even for the gods to attain.
It consists of the Mūla, the Samudbhava, the Pīṭha, and the Tantra called Kaula.
The Pūrṇapīṭha is recited by the yogis as being fourfold:
Yogapīṭha, Upapīṭha, Guhyapīṭha, and Samāttikapīṭha.
Furthermore, the Mattapīṭha is tenfold; I shall describe them to you exactly as they are.
The seat of Matta is called Siddha, and the seat of Jālandhara is the highest;
the seat of Śrī is the desired Ardhakūṭa, along with the seat of Satti and Śambhu.
O Maheśvarī, there is also the seat of Nāda, the seat of Bindu, and the seat of Cakra.
The *Samyagvāma* is proclaimed as fivefold on the left and right;
this Śaiva [system] of the six currents (*ṣaṭsrotas*) is superior to that which arises from the five currents (*pañcasrotas*).
First is the *Śikhākameśvara*, and the supreme *Kiraṇa* is called *Mīna*.
The *dhātrī* doctrine consists of *haṃ*, *kṛ*, and *lōri*; Vāsuki is remembered as the fifth.
These varieties, originating from the downward flow (*adhassrotas*), are designated as the netherworlds (*pātāla*).
They know the scripture to be sevenfold: Tantra, Saṃhitā-sūtra, Saṅgraha, Śāstra, Kalpa-śabda, as well as Kalpa, and Āgama.
Furthermore, [the divisions are] that which resides in the Cakra, that which is spoken by the retinue, the fourth, and the Pañcaka.

Furthermore, for the sake of those belonging to the six classes of birth, that which abounds in deities—well-composed by both the sacrificer and the officiating priest—is here proclaimed as the *Tānti*. As for the meaning of the *Saṃhitā*, it has been previously stated; [now] the number is given for the sake of determining the purpose.
That which is the essence of essences is said to be the meaning of the *saṃhitā*.
That which has a hidden meaning, consists of few words, will be explained in various ways,
and is determined by its beginning, middle, and end— that is designated as the meaning of the *sūtra*.
A summary is proclaimed for the sake of brevity, due to the cause of a different time,
being of little meaning and few words; whereas that in which there is an instructor and the characteristics of those to be instructed and so forth is the detailed [treatise].
That which is indicated by the authority of the scripture is called the "teaching" (śāstra) because it instructs.
Śiva is one and possesses a single power, yet he is designated by many distinctions.
However, such distinction is merely a mental construction characterized by [the attribution of] specific parts and so forth.
Because those of very limited wisdom are blinded by the objects of cognition, a "kalpa" is here conceptualized by them.
That which is a collection of such kalpas is the "avatāraka" (the means of descent). This definitive [teaching] is its own kalpa; that is called a "skandha."

Thus, the connection of the Āgamas has been proclaimed in seven ways. Those divisions which have been described along with their secret doctrines are the divisions of Śiva; indeed, they are said to consist of the six currents (ṣaṭsrotas).
Whatever mantra-tantras there are, which are the authorities for the ocean of sound,
they have been drawn forth from the ocean of knowledge and bestow the fruit of the goal of liberation.
Thus has Śiva demonstrated the distinction of the Śrīkaṇṭha stream. [This concludes] the investigation of the streams.
Having studied the entire chapter and having heard it with great effort, [one attains realization].
O Lord, what task should one who is initiated perform here, headed by the preceptor? A *samayin* and a *putraka* should perform that single act of worshiping Śiva;
a *sādhaka*, however, should constantly perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) and the practice of mantras (*mantrasādhana*).
The teacher’s duties are teaching, exposition, and the favoring of others;
having correctly understood the *āsana* (posture) as both worldly enjoyment (*bhauktika*) and liberation (*mauktika*),
all ritual actions should be performed by the wise while meditating upon that Lord of Gods.
Otherwise, the entire treatise becomes fruitless.
Having understood this ritual as proclaimed in the Pauṣkara, one should perform the bath.
Those who have received initiation according to the tradition should perform the worship of Śiva with devotion.
"Because they are unworthy, the fruit of initiation for them is undoubtedly in vain"—
thus [it is stated] in the *Svacchandadalā*.
This concludes the rule for study (*adhyayanavidhi*) in the *Nityasaṅgraha* extracted from the Āgamas, composed by the venerable Rājānaka Takṣaka.
Now, for one who is fit for the virtuous rites beginning with worship,
bathing— which generates such fitness— is described in seven forms by means of the words proclaimed by the Lord:
the Vāruṇa, the Taijasa, the Bhauma, the Ānila, the Divya, and the Gaurava.

And "mental" (mānasa)— this is stated as their definition in brief. The Varuṇa bath consists of water, preceded by the general procedure, performed with obstacles removed, purified by the Lord, and accompanied by consecration and self-restraint.
The shaking off of ashes from one purified by that [rite] is performed according to the prescribed method;
it involves the use of wind and the service of air joined with the pure dust of cows and other such substances. (21b)

The terrestrial bath (*pārthiva-snāna*) is performed according to the prescribed rite with water from the Gaṅgā and other holy rivers that has been purified by mantras; the celestial bath (*nābhasa*) is performed with rainwater;
and that which is obtained from the lotus-feet of the Guru is called the upward-moving (*ūrdhvaga*) bath.
The mental and the Śākta methods for these are now described. This sevenfold procedure for bathing is proclaimed in the *Mṛgendra* Tantra:
either with water containing mantras according to the tradition, or with divine wind.

In that regard, first there is the water bath (*jala-snāna*), which is for all castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*). After that come the fire-bath (*āgneya*), the wind-bath (*māruta*), the divine bath (*divya*), and the one called the mantra-bath (*mantra-ākhyam*).
For those established in celibacy (*brahmacarya*), however, the water bath is prohibited.

Those who are free from the defects of passion, established in austerity, and devoid of attachment—[for them] all religious duties are preceded by bathing; bathing removes the impurity of sin. Whether it be a great lake, a river, a pond, or even a sacred ford (tīrtha).
In the absence of these [wells], one should resort to water drawn by human effort;
having drawn seventeen lumps of earth, one should perform the bath.
This applies to reservoirs belonging to others; otherwise, it is never sanctioned.
Since the god Vāmadeva is omnipresent and consists of the essence of water,
nevertheless, the rule is prescribed regarding gods, brahmins, and fires;
one should never transgress that which is ordained by the gods and proclaimed by the sages.
Having taken earth, *kuśa* grass, and sesame seeds, one should perform the ritual bath.
Regarding the purpose of the *śikhā-kāmeśvara* [bath], an ordinance was established by the Lord.
Now, for the sake of accomplishing eligibility (*adhikāra*), I shall describe the bath according to the ancient tradition.
(22a) By means of which one becomes fit for eating, consecration, sacrifice, and burnt offerings—
one should perform a twofold bath for the purification of defilements and impurities.
Having bathed according to the general rule, one should then perform the specific rite.
The general bath is the worldly one, while the specific is remembered as that performed with mantras.
[This applies] in rivers, in places renowned for deities, and in ponds and pools.
For one who has been initiated, bathing in a lotus pond is the best; in a well, it is said to be middling;
and bathing at home is proclaimed as the lowest.
However, for the four [classes of officiants], beginning with the preceptor, that [bathing at home] is equal to the others.
Regarding the procedure for bathing in water, this has been declared by you in the Śrī-Pauṣkara:
"Having taken earth with the Astra-mantra, one should place it on a pure spot near the water;
having sprinkled it with the Sadyojāta and Vāmadeva mantras, one should consecrate it with the Aghora mantra."

Having touched it with the mantra and enveloped it with the armor-mantra (varman), one should divide it into three parts for the purpose of bathing away impurities, cleansing the hands, and ritual bathing. Then,
having extracted one part with the supreme [mantra] and recited the weapon-mantra (astra) which removes impurity, [one should proceed].
This rule for the acceptance of clay has been demonstrated by the Lord of Beasts (Śiva).
The feet, the shanks, and the hips are purified respectively by three applications of clay;
furthermore, they are purified again by seven applications with intervals between them.
Having consecrated the earth seven times with the Astra-mantra,
the knower of mantras should heat it before the face of the sun and subsequently smear his body with it.
For the purpose of pacifying the multitude of obstacles, he should wash his body and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
When this *dalasnāna* (leaf-bath) taught by the illustrious Mṛtyuñjaya has been performed,
the constant washing of the hair with *āmalaka* and other such substances is auspicious;
it is beneficial for the eyes, removes impurities, and destroys diseases of the head.
Flour of barley, wheat, or even rice, along with grains and water,
should be mixed with sesame paste.
Anointing with sesame oil cleanses the head, promotes the flow of vital fluids, and destroys obstacles; therefore, the application of sesame is highly praised.
Anointing with sesame, bathing, libations, and the consumption of sesame are likewise recommended.
"The gift of sesame seeds is remembered as removing sin from the mouths of men.
Thus ends the procedure for bathing according to the *Vidyāpurāṇa*. Now, the ritual bath (*vidhisnāna*) is described: having prepared that remainder, one should take another third portion of clay.

Having divided the water held in his hand into three portions situated in the east, south, and north, he should touch [the disciple] with the *astra*, *brahma*, and *śiva* mantras. With the first mantra, he should drive away obstacles from the water;
with the second, he should consecrate it as nectar (*amṛtī-kuryāt*); and with the third, he should touch the body.
Then one should bathe with a third part [of the water], performing purification of the hands again and again.
This is declared to be the ritual bath (*vidhisnāna*) in the *Mṛgendrottara-śāsana*:
first with the left hand, then in sequence on the right and the left.
Then, one should consecrate the eastern part seven times with the Astra-mantra;
likewise, O fair-faced one, having consecrated the southern part with the [five] faces,
and having similarly consecrated the northern part with the root mantra accompanied by its limbs.
Having taken the eastern portion, one should cast it in the ten directions;
with the northern portion,
however, one should consecrate the water while recollecting Bhairava at a distance of one cubit.
Having covered oneself with a cloth, O lady of excellent vows, one should bathe according to the royal custom using fragrant *āmalaka* and other such substances with the right hand.
And in the illustrious Svacchanda Śāstra, the consecration of the clay is taught:
one should first cast it in all directions, beginning from the east.
By the mere utterance of the *nārā* weapon-mantra, the flood of obstacles is certainly destroyed.
By that [water] thrown into the water, those things situated in the water quickly go to destruction.
Having made the sacred ford (tīrtha) auspicious by circling it with one's arms while standing in the water,
one should touch one's own body, beginning with the head, while standing on the right side.

One should perform a bath in the auspicious waters (Śivāmbhas), which destroys sin and follows the feet [of the Lord]. As for the sacrifice called Chākrītu that has been proclaimed, there is no sacrifice superior to it. He was appointed by the Creator as the leader of all the gods.
By one situated in that direction, there shall be the eradication of obstacles in this world.
As for the northern quarter, Īśāna is born from the nectar;
the Moon, stirred by Śiva, preserves the nectar alone.
Since that sacred ford (tīrtha) is nectar (amṛta), one who bathes therein becomes immortal.
Dharma is the lord of the southern quarter; he is the remover of sin.
Therefore, by touching the deceased situated in that direction, one [is purified] by him.
The distinction among the earths for the destruction [of obstacles] according to the different directions has been explained in the *Śrīparāgama*:
