"One should fashion a circular sacred site (*tīrtha*) measuring one cubit or five cubits;
there, one should scatter earth by means of the application of the *nārāca* weapon."
Indeed, the obstacles within the water— headed by sea-monsters and crocodiles—
flee in terror, swiftly tormented by his weapons.
Furthermore, the supreme consecration of the sacred site (tīrtha-saṃskāra) is here further described.
The practitioner of mantra should perform the retention that dries up the sacred ford, joined with fire,
as far as the seventh netherworld, up to the cosmic egg of Prajāpati. (23b)
The practitioner of mantra should mentally fill [the vessel] with fire, [visualizing it] as being filled with garlands of flames.
For thus occurs the drying up and likewise the burning of the sacred site (tīrtha).
The practitioner of mantra should recite the Saṃhitā and wipe that [site] with his hand.
By means of the tip of the key, through the application of the hook-like form, Śiva previously taught the forceful extraction of that [power].
The sacred site (tīrtha) is said to be threefold: divine, atmospheric, and terrestrial.
Having visualized [it], one should cause it to descend into that place according to this procedure.
By this very application, the wise one [should know]:
the sixth [vowel] joined with the end of the Sādhya, accompanied by the nasal bindu.
The disciple, joined with the end of the reality of emptiness (*śūnyatattva*), is directly of the nature of water.
This shall be the seed-syllable of the sacred ford (*tīrtha*), which destroys all sins.
The practitioner of mantra should repeatedly recollect the heart-mantra as being all the sacred fords.
A downpour of nectar fell, flooding everything on all sides,
by means of those [rays] that had reached the fourth station, entered the sun, fallen within the sphere of the sacred fords,
resembling the moon, and comparable to a mass of streams of milk.
One should contemplate the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) as being inundated by showers arising from nectar;
for this is indeed remembered as the nourishment of the *tīrtha*, without a doubt.
Furthermore, one who knows the mantras should perform the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) within that sacred bathing place.

Facing north, one should contemplate the Śivatīrtha. There, one should install Ananta, endowed with dharma, jñāna, and the other [guṇas], as well as the lotus, the group of powers (śaktigaṇa), and then the three mandalas.
(24a) One should place Śiva upon that, endowed with the body of Brahmā—
white, resembling ten thousand moons, and filled with the essence of nectar.
The *netra* mantra, accompanied by the *anusvāra* and consisting of the essence of *svadhā*, should be joined to the eyes.
This is declared by Lord Śambhu to be the "Śiva-tīrtha" (the sacred water of Śiva).
Otherwise, water filled [with other mantras] is inert and devoid of sanctifying power.
It is not the cause of either spiritual perfection or liberation, nor does it remove sin.
Therefore, one should diligently perform the rite of *śivīkaraṇa* (consecration as Śiva) there.
Once that sacred site has been made into Śiva, one should bathe with full concentration.
Having recollected the seed-syllable of Śiva, the wise practitioner should perform immersion and emergence in the midst of the Śiva-tīrtha while reciting the Vāmadeva mantra.
Then, having leaped up, the mantrin should behold the Sun as Śiva, whose very nature is the sacred ford.

Having thus meditated upon the sacred ford (tīrtha) consisting of Śiva as declared by the venerable Vāmadeva, one should fix the mind within the midst of the restrained vital breaths (prāṇa) and, with the heart,
recite the Tāraka mantra— which delivers one from suffering— in order to destroy the flood of sins.
This procedure for the internal water [ritual] has been fully prescribed by Mṛgendra.
Thereafter, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) and restrain the activity of the mind.
By restraining the activity of the mind, one removes whatever mental sin exists.
By reciting the *praṇava*, which destroys sin, one is liberated from verbal sins.

Thus, while there is a general destruction of ordinary sins, there is another specific [destruction] pertaining to particular [sins]. This specific [destruction] occurs when one is within water; this has been declared in the *Śrīparāgama*.

Having leaped up and turned around, having washed his hands and the lower garment, he should then perform the consecration with mantras using the *kalaśa-mudrā*. The two hands are joined in the *saṃhitā* [mudrā], with the thumbs and little fingers extended and the palms facing outward.
Having joined the thumbs and the joints of the fingers firmly together,
this is declared to be the Ghaṭa-mudrā, which fulfills the rites of bathing and other such procedures.
This procedure for the *ghaṭamudrā* has been declared by you in the *Śrīmṛgendra*.
Having performed the ritual bath according to the rules,
one should put on a loincloth (*kaupīna*) twelve finger-breadths in width and twice that in length.
The ascetic should make a cord of eight threads and a loincloth hanging from three parts; he should wear white cloth as prescribed, or a firm saffron-colored garment.
The definition of the loincloth has been declared in the *Vāmadevīyasaṅgraha*.
If a man, out of delusion, should offer water with a loincloth that has been sprinkled with water,
his ancestors—
along with the hosts of gods who depend on the water of that waterfall— will be satisfied when he proceeds to bathe.
The winds follow after him, afflicted by thirst and seeking water;
they depart from him in despair once the wringing out of the garment has been performed.
Therefore, one should not wring out the garment without having first offered libations to the ancestors.
A prohibition against [receiving gifts] from one wearing wet clothes was declared by Devātitarpaṇa;
it is also indicated in the *Smṛti* by the Lord in the *Analasiddhānta*:
"Whatever one wearing wet clothes might perform—be it recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), or the acceptance of gifts (*pratigraha*)..."
One should know that all [the water] for the Rākṣasas is that which is poured outside the knees;
however, when there is an intervening garment, as in the libations to the gods and ancestors,
one should perform it with water reaching the navel— such is the rule declared by the Smṛtis.
Having sipped water according to the rule, the practitioner of mantra should consecrate the Śiva-tīrtha with the five mantras in sequence by means of the five Brahmans.
One should place Īśāna, who has the luster of crystal, before oneself at a distance of one cubit in each of the four directions;
one should meditate on Tatpuruṣa in the east, reddish like yellow pigment (rocanā) and saffron (kuṅkuma).
In the south is Bahurūpa, resembling a mass of crushed collyrium;
Sadyojāta is in the west, with the luster of pure silver;
and Vāmadeva is in the intermediate direction, similar in color to the pomegranate flower.
One should install these with their respective mudrās, having meditated upon the desired sacred site (tīrtha).
Indeed, the sacred site is of two kinds: celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial.
Having properly drawn it forth by means of the Aghora deity and the goad-mudrā (aṅkuśamudrā), [one should perform the installation].

Or, by means of the *saṃhāramudrā*, the mantra-knower may deposit it before himself; by means of the *samantapuṣpā* [mudrā], that becomes the *śivatīrtha*. Having thus meditated upon the *śivatīrtha* as taught in the *Pauṣkara-śāstra*:
Having washed his hands and feet, he should purify his own body.
Then, purified by the Astra-mantra, he should take his place upon the seat of the Praṇava in a spot that is stainless,
very beautiful, pure, or covered with green grass.
One should purify the water with water using the *śuddhi* [mantra] held in the hand;
then, having assigned the mantras according to the ritual procedure for fire (*agnikarma*), one should offer libations (*tarpaṇa*) to the gods,
the Brahmins, and the ancestors, respectively, by means of the front, the left, and the right [hands].
"svāhā," "namas," and "svadhā"— with these, they are to be gratified in due order. When gratified with water, the deities, ancestors, siddhas, and sages, who bestow boons, always grant peace to men.
(25b) Having performed this act of satiation at the water's edge or on dry land,
if one then withdraws the foot, one goes to the sacred ford while protecting oneself.
This has been declared by way of summary in the *Vāmadevīyasaṅgraha*.

Having sprinkled the feet first, the water from the throat is gathered as the "Śiva-tīrtha. That [water] should then be used for the consecration of the head with the *saṃhitā* [mantra] and the *kumbha-mudrā*.
For the sake of self-protection and for the destruction [of obstacles],
one should scatter water consecrated with mantras toward the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Once the placement of the mantras (*mantranyāsa*) has been performed, one should then pay homage to the Vaiṣṇava twilight devotion (*sandhyā*).
Having performed the *mārjana* and the *Māghamarṣaṇa*, one should perform *ācamana* again.
With the *Śiva-mantra* ending in *svāhā*, accompanied by *kuśa* grass, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*),
one should offer a handful of water as an *argha* to Śiva and recite the *Gāyatrī* mantra according to one's ability.
With the sacred thread worn in its natural position, one should satisfy the mantras and the gods;
the seven ṛṣis with a salutation (namaskāra), human beings with the vaṣaṭ-call,
the spirits and others through the application of the vaṣaṭ-call, and the ancestors with the svadhā-calls.
With the sacred thread (upavīta) resting on the neck, one should offer these three [libations] in sequence;
with the sacred thread resting on the right shoulder, one should satisfy the ancestors accompanied by the utterance of *svadhā*,
using the middle of the thumb and forefinger of the right hand.
In all these cases, the heart-mantra preceded by the *praṇava* (OM) is common.
They declare the root-mantra, joined with the faces, limbs, and enclosures, to be the mantra.
The deities are known as the Vidyās, the Vidyēśvaras, and the Tattvas and Tattvēśvaras.
The Vasus, Viśvedevas, Rudras, Sādhyas, Maruts, Bhṛgus, along with the Aṅgirases, and those headed by the Ādityas— these are proclaimed as the eight classes of gods. (26a)

They know the seven sages to be Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, Kratu, Bharadvāja together with Viśvāmitra, and Marīci. They remember Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanātana along with Sanatkumāra, and Kapila with Pañcaśikha as the seventh of the Ṛtus. All beings—beasts, birds, wild animals, reptiles, oceans, rivers, mountains, seasons, and so forth—are declared to be devoid of numerical reckoning. The ancestors (Pitṛs) are considered to be of two kinds: the Devas (gods), the Pitṛs (manes), and the Pretas (spirits). Among them, Kavyavāhana, Anala, Soma, and Aryaman are [the chief].

The Agniṣvāttas, Barhiṣads, and others, as well as the Somapānas and others, are the Pitṛs; among them are the Pitāmahas and Prapitāmahas, and likewise the Mothers. The Mātāmahas are those preceded by the honorific prefix *pra* (i.e., Pramātāmahas, etc.). Similarly included here are brothers, maternal uncles, kinsmen, friends, teachers (*upādhyāya*), preceptors (*guru*), and others, as well as other relatives and so forth. These mantras are for the deities, sages, humans, spirits, and Pitṛs who are to be satiated.
Having sipped water (*ācamya*) and offered a handful of water with the appropriate mantra to the Sun, [one should proceed].
Having recited the root mantra, one should offer it to the deity.
Having placed the sacred water (tīrtha) within one's own heart and wrung out the bathing garment, one should wash the hands three times with earth; such is the procedure for the external rite.
The libation to the gods and others is prescribed in the *Śrīviśveśvarapaddhati*.
Thereafter, one should bathe at home with cool, pure water.
However, this specific rule regarding ritual bathing (*vidhisnāna*) is proclaimed therein.
Having washed the clay, it should be consecrated in a jar as if it were the Śiva-tīrtha. It is said by me in the *Kiraṇa* that the mantra residing in the tantra must be withdrawn. (26b)
The bath with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā" is declared to be the Prājāpatya bath.
The Mantra-bath is performed with the Brahma-mantras or according to the Śivasaṃhitā,
using nine, eight, or five jars prepared as the Śiva-tīrtha.
Even at home, the bath may be performed by those who have received initiation on ground that has been smeared;
the procedure for bathing at home is described in the *Pārameśvara-pauṣkara*:
"Water is pure by its very nature, even more so when it is in motion or combined with fire."
Therefore, the wise have declared that bathing with water consisting of praise, [the water of] ablution, and flowers— even with warm water—
is the thirty-sixfold bath enjoined by the *Mata*. Thus,
this is described as the "Vāruṇa" (watery) bath for practitioners.
When this is performed, there is purification from existence through the great fear of all sins;
it is a bath that purifies the mind, destroys the evil dreams of the Kali age,
and eradicates the effects of magical spells, scorpions, Vetālas, impurities, and indigestion.
It removes mental distress and dejection from the mind and intellect;
it nourishes the limbs, is beautiful, and bestows the pleasure of sensual enjoyment.
In this world, those who are not deprived of bathing are honored for their merit, religious rites, and wealth.
"And the foremost of practitioners become [successful]"; thus spoke Maheśvara.
"The physical sin of one who has bathed perishes instantly.
The ṛṣis, gods, and gandharvas are constantly devoted to bathing."
For one who has bathed, there is an increase in prosperity, and the gods stand face-to-face with him. The planets always rejoice in a man as soon as he has bathed;
his mind attains steadiness, and forgiveness arises immediately.
(27a) By giving to the gods, one’s glory becomes inexhaustible;
bathing is said by Rudra to be the bliss of all sacrifices within the sacrifice.
The merit arising from daily bathing is equal to that of all sacrifices.
Even for a man who is excluded from bathing day after day,
the fruit of bathing for an entire fortnight is obtained by bathing on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days.
Furthermore, for one who is devoted to bathing with devotion upon seeing the full moon,
it is no wonder that the rivers yield infinite fruit;
bathing in warm water is meritorious, but bathing in cold water shall be twice as meritorious.
Just as the fire from a flint-stone strikes a heap of cotton, so does [this practice], performed continuously for seven days, burn away a mass of demerit accumulated through hundreds of ritual baths.
Whatever fruit is obtained from bathing in water according to the illustrious *Abhayasiddhānta*, [that too is attained here].
And it is stated in the Parāgama how that is taught:
"Varuṇa [bestows] pure water, which is the form of death yet joined with immortality.
Having bathed in that, one becomes like death and stands upon the path of immortality."

During bathing, the offering to the deities, the fire sacrifice, eating, ritual worship, yoga, essential duties, and recitation of mantras, the wise man should always remain silent. Thus ends the procedure for bathing with water.
Alternatively, one should bathe with ashes and avoid bathing in water.
All the deities, beginning with Śiva, perform their ablutions with ashes.
The bath with ashes possesses countless qualities superior to the bath in water.

Whatever merit is found in all sacrifices and whatever fruit is found in all sacred fords, one obtains that fruit constantly through the ash-bath; of this there is no doubt. Even one joined with great sins, or even one joined with all sins.

One who constantly practices the bath of ashes is liberated from all sins. The fruit that belongs even to a single day for one whose firm foundation is established in the ash cannot be attained by a householder even through hundreds of sacrifices.
Therefore, having abandoned the Varuṇa bath, one should perform the Ātreya bath;
for it is there that the renowned Śiva-bhasma remains, held in worship.
Therein there shall be neither thieves nor fire, neither diseases nor predatory beasts;
there shall be no approaching obstacles, nor piśācas, nor rākṣasas;
there shall be no suffering from fear of kings, nor shall any other inauspicious thing occur.
Struck with this ash, the seizing spirit perishes instantly;
one is likewise immediately liberated from fevers such as the quartan and others.
The practitioner of mantra should bathe with ash at the proper time and at other intervals as well.
In the morning, at midday, and likewise at the third libation (the afternoon),
as well as midnight as the fourth—
these times are prescribed for one to perform a bath after voiding wind, urine, or feces.
That interval between times was ordained by the wielder of the trident (*Śūlapāṇi*).
From bathing with water at the three periods [of the day], diseases of phlegm arise;
there is headache and the breaking of limbs. Therefore, one should avoid that.
Having bathed once with water, one should therefore perform that ritual ablution;
when practiced daily, it destroys all diseases,
as well as the afflictions of dreams, evil associations, and harmful winds.
Having bathed with water according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the fire-bath (āgneyasnāna).
This bath is always dear to the Rudras and the Gaṇas;
it is favored by the Vidyeśvaras, and Śiva always holds it most dear.
That [mantra], which possesses great power, should be constantly practiced by teachers and practitioners;
it should be served by Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are established in their vows.
Since fire has ash as its substrate, it dissolves into that very [ash];
by means of the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna), the sage is seen to possess brilliance like fire.
In the Parāgama and the Pauṣkara, praises have been composed for the ash.
Wherever one sees [the deity] consumed by the fiery splendor of the mantra and Śivā,
or wherever the Lord of Gods, Sadāśiva, appears as a mass of radiance—
there, if he has not been dismissed, one should offer [the oblation] according to the rite of ashes.

Alternatively, one should previously cast a brand from the fire of Śiva into the midst of the ashes by means of a multiformed [mantra], using either the *Saṃhitā*, the *Vartitu* [method], or the *Turuva* [method].
In this way, it becomes the ash of Śiva; one should employ it for the purpose of bathing.
Having obtained [the materials] according to the rule, the mantra-practitioner should accomplish supreme prosperity.
With that, one should perform a bath by means of the rite prescribed by the rules.
Taking dried, pure cow-dung, free from defects.
Or else, excellent fuel originating from milk-trees and the like [should be used].
Thus is the procedure for the ash proclaimed in the *Vāmadevīyasaṅgraha*:
"Then the ascetic should bathe with ash, or with cow-dung and stones found in the forest."
Or [one may perform it] with wood such as *palāśa* or *candana*,
brought by a *pracchambara* [spy], fanned with flowers, kindled by the *ghora* fire-altar of Vāmadeva,
encircled by the *varman* [armor-mantra], gazed upon by the *astra* [weapon-mantra], and situated on a pure ground.

Having taken the ash produced by Śaṅkara, the Lord should consecrate it with mantras. O best of the twice-born, having brought forth the fire while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra and the Aṅgavata-āgama, he should cause it to blaze, having performed protection and always reciting the immortal hymn of praise.
Then, the wise one should dust that [powder] over the entire body, following the sequence of the head, face, torso, shanks, and so forth, excluding the hands and feet. (28b)
The purification of the hands for the subsidiary rites is performed as before with the Astra-mantra.
Ritual ablution with mantras, the twilight devotions (sandhyā), and so forth are excluded, as is the worship of the Sun;
this is declared in the *Mṛgendra* to be the "ash-bath" (*bhasmasnāna*).
Having taken ash consecrated with mantras according to the prescribed rule,
one should perform a bath to remove impurities with a mind focused on the visualization.
Then, having turned around, he should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyā) as previously described.
One should perform the ritual bath while recollecting Bhairavī;
O fair-faced one, the twilight salutation should be performed as before.
This is declared to be the ritual bath in the Svacchanda-śāsana.
Having meditated upon the supreme, fierce splendor as ashes, one should bathe in this sequence from the beginning.
Others— Kṣatriyas and the rest, or even women— should apply the Tripuṇḍra on the chest,
the neck, both arms, the thighs, the heart, and the sides.
One should dust the back, the waist, the thighs, the shanks, and the private parts in succession.
Then, the wise practitioner should bathe in order, starting from the northeast (Īśa), according to the [sixteen] digits (kalās).
Thus it was declared in the Purāṇa by the one whose crest is the crescent moon.
The practitioner should sprinkle the ashes five times on the head with the *Īśāna* mantra;
the wise one should dust the face four times on the face with the *Vaktra* mantra;
and likewise, having dusted the heart eight times with the *Bahurūpa* mantra.
The secret [mantra] should indeed be applied by Vāmadeva in thirteen divisions;
one should dust the body and the two feet with Sadyojāta in eight ways.
Each individual location has been indicated by me in brief.
And indeed, smearing all the limbs with ashes is prescribed in the teaching of Śiva for those of all four castes who are lifelong celibates and free from passion. (29a)
The smearing with ashes is recommended for those who possess learning, virtuous conduct,
and ritual action; or else, a steadfast knower of mantras, being skilled in mantra, should diligently apply the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) with Śiva-ashes according to the rite prescribed by rule.
The wise practitioner, using the index, middle, and ring fingers of both hands,
should rotate that [ash] which has been mixed with water;
thereafter, he should apply the *tripuṇḍra* on the forehead according to the prescribed rite.
One should perform [the placement] on the throat, the heart, the crest-lock, the head and neck, the two ears,
the two shoulders, the navel, the hips,
the buttocks, the pair of thighs, and likewise on both the left and right shanks.

By this method, the knower of mantras should always apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ashes for the constant increase of prosperity; thus it is declared in the Vāmadevīyasaṅgraha. That which is inaccessible to the right hand is to be done with the left hand.
One should properly dust the limbs by touching both hands to one another.
Having put on a clean inner garment and covered the hands, one should wash them with earth and pure water;
likewise, one should wash the feet with earth seven times.
In the venerable *Mataṅgaśāstra* as well, this has been declared with its underlying rationale.
Thus ends the procedure for the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*).
As for the earthen bath, it is a bath with clay; the water-bath is as previously described.
The fire-related bath with ashes is now declared; its procedure is as follows:
having obtained the dung of a tawny cow, the wise man should burn it while reciting the *Śivahṛdaya* mantra.
Having consecrated it according to rule by repeating the *Saṃhitā* once, [he should apply it].
It should be applied to the mouth, the head, the heart, and the navel in sequence;
then to the secret place, the knees, and the feet, according to the order of the Gāyatrī mantra. (29b)
Then, one should scatter ashes in all directions with the Pāśupata weapon;
by that, the obstacles flee in the ten directions, afflicted by fear.
One should perform another ablution, the Āgneya, and meditate upon the body as blazing intensely.
The Vāyavya bath has been described as being performed with the prescribed breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
The fifth is the Nābhasa bath, which destroys all sins;
one should meditate upon the world as blissful and resembling pure crystal.

Thus, the threefold bath has been proclaimed in the Hāṭakeśvara-śāsana. By means of the *saṃhitā*, one obtains earth from the confluences of the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sindhu, Sarasvatī, and so forth, or even earth born within my own sacred field.
With that [earth], one should likewise apply the *tripuṇḍra* marks on the head and other limbs.
This is declared as the *pārthiva* [rite] in the *Mṛgendrottara-śāsana*.
Thus ends the procedure for the *pārthiva* bath.
That which has become [the wind] when mixed with the mother-spirit (mātariśvan) from the dust of the *rajas* [element],
by bathing with that one becomes pure-limbed and purified like the wind.
Thus is the "wind-bath" (*māruta-snāna*) described in the venerable *Parāgama*.
Thus ends the Vāyavya bath.
Reciting the auspicious [mantra] "Śiva," one should sustain the meritorious rain accompanied by the sun's heat.
One should proceed toward the seven divine primordial sounds with that water of Śiva.
In the venerable *Mṛgendra*, that which was taught by Vāmadeva is now stated:
from the descent of rain from a cloudless sky, [the rite] of Indra-mījana occurs.
With arms raised, eyes restrained, facing the east, and intent upon bathing;
It is said that one should repeat the seven lines; that is the *viśeṣaka*.
Thus ends the divine bath (*divyasnāna*).

With a pure head, one should offer salutations to the Guru while uttering "Śiva"; one should contemplate that Guru with a mental disposition of reverence until the mantra becomes purified. Then, by bathing in the Śākta water touched by him, one attains equality with his vehicle.
Thus, these two types of bathing have been fully elucidated by Mṛgendra.
This concludes the mental bathing characterized by reverence. As for the mantra-bathing, it should be performed by sprinkling the head with mantras using the *ghaṭamudrā*.
Thus has the mantra-bath been declared by Maheśa in the Parāgama.
This concludes the mantra-bath.
The mental bath (mānasa) is to be performed with the mind, and it is considered to be accompanied by the *āvarta* [mantra].
"By means of the *sarvamantra* and other mantras, together with breath control (*prāṇāyāma*)—
thus is the mental bath (*mānasasnāna*) described in the *Svāyambhuva-śāstra*.
Thus ends the section on the mental bath.
Thus has been described the water-bath; now learn the mantra-bath.

That which one should perform in the absence of water—during a time of distress, in a difficult place, during cold weather, when traveling, for the sake of swift success, or in a matter of great importance—is the most independent [form].
O great lord of sages, when this portion of the day’s night has arrived,

one should wash one’s feet and perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with water drawn up [from a vessel]. Then, having performed the purificatory rite for the place and the ten directions as before, one should sit down.
Having applied the Astra-mantra to the palms of the hands, one should then perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the body in due order,
beginning with the root mantra and employing the entire collection of mantras.
[One should know that] from mere bathing with water alone, devoid of the purificatory rites (saṃskāra)...
O Nārada, the fruit that belongs to one who has performed the ritual bath at sacred fords such as Prabhāsa should be known to be a hundredfold greater than that of the mantra-bath. After this,
I shall describe the bath of meditation, which is superior to both of these.
One should meditate upon the omnipresent Lord, the lotus-eyed one, whose form is the mantra, abiding in the heart;
[and one should meditate upon] the stream born from the water of his feet falling upon one's own head.
One should visualize [the stream] entering one’s own body through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
With that, one should wash away all impurity located within the body.
At that very moment, the practitioner becomes free from passion (viraja) and becomes like a crystal.
This best of bathing mantras is remembered as being a hundred times more effective than ordinary bathing.
Therefore, one should perform at least one of these baths accompanied by purification,
because all ritual acts preceded by bathing yield their full fruit.
Therefore, one who desires to attain perfection should first perform the ritual bath;

by its mere performance, a living being becomes stainless. O best of the twice-born, what need is there to mention that [bath] which is accompanied by ritual action, since even this [simple bath] produces such purity through lack of discernment?
This bath has been proclaimed in many ways for Śrī Jayā in the Vaiṣṇava tradition:
one should meditate upon her as being in the center of the heart-lotus, having the form of a *kadamba* flower,
situated in the middle of the night, and flowing into the lake of the moon of Śiva.
Having restrained the collection of the senses and established oneself in the abode of consciousness,
one should meditate upon that river for the sake of purification;
with the brilliance of the fire of time, one should thoroughly burn away the net of bonds.
Thus, internal bathing has been briefly described as being of two kinds.
Having performed either one of these and having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, the practitioner should perform the worship of Śiva; never, however, while remaining unbathed.
This spiritual bath (*ādhyātmika-snāna*) has also been declared in the *Vidyāpuraṇa*. Thus ends the section on the mantra-bath within the daily rites extracted from the *Āgama*.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme procedure for the worship of the Liṅga—
Śambhu, who assumes the form of the Liṅga and possesses both manifest and unmanifest aspects.

In a *liṅga* established by nature (*svarapratiṣṭhita*) or one fashioned by men, one should worship the Lord situated within it—the embodiment of the mantra, who is both supreme and non-supreme. By whatever [deity] one desires, that desired goal is attained; this entire path culminates in Śiva.
Therefore, one should worship that very Lord of Gods, who has assumed the form of the *liṅga*.
The glorification of the *liṅga* is meritorious, and its sight destroys sin.
Those who touch it go to Śiva, and those who worship it are freed from rebirth.

Those men would be of great merit and would not fall under the sway of Time. Since the Great Gods themselves are eternally established in manifest form within the *liṅga*, and because it bestows grace upon the worlds, one should therefore worship the *liṅga*.
He who, out of delusion, does not worship the Liṅga adored by the hosts of gods,
is not a recipient of heaven, nor of liberation, nor of sovereignty.
But he who worships with devotion the Liṅga, the Lord of the three worlds—
The cultivation [of devotion] toward heaven, liberation, and sovereignty occurs swiftly.
All sacred sites (*liṅga-tīrthas*) are present; everything is established within the *liṅga*.
Through the *liṅga*, supreme liberation is attained as a perfected state (*siddha*), and through its worship, worldly happiness is gained.

Those devoid of the *liṅga* do not attain perfection, nor do they reach the supreme state. Therefore, Śiva, who resides within the *liṅga*, should be worshipped according to the prescribed rite with flowers, fruits, and water consecrated by mantras, to the best of one's ability and with devotion.
The supreme majesty of the Liṅga has been declared by the venerable Vāmadeva:
"Those who are perfected ones (siddhas) in the world according to the Āgamas, who are self-manifested Maheśvaras—
they are Rudras, the supports of the worlds, the lords of the vowels within each principle (tattva), O Dear One."
Those who are designated as "Earthen" and so forth exist as embodied forms within the causal state;
for the sake of favoring living beings, they have entered into the state of immobility.
Likewise, there are arrows that are self-manifested and perfected according to the Purāṇas.
Those established by Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, Munis, Devas, Asuras, and Uragas are equal to them; they do not abandon their fixed positions.
The descent of the Liṅga is seen in the *Aghorīpañcaśataka*.
Thus ends the majesty of the Liṅga.
O you whose form is the Liṅga, likewise in the lotus, in fire, and in the orb of the sun.

One should worship the Supreme Lord either within one's own body or in the intermediate space (antarikṣa). Thus, there is the purification of the self, the purification of the place, and likewise the purification of the ritual materials;
fourth is the purification of the *liṅga*, and fifth is the purification of the mantra.
He who knows the fivefold purification is worthy to perform the worship.
Bathing is declared to be fivefold, and that is remembered as the purification of the self (ātma-śuddhi).
By the binding of the directions with the Great Weapon [mantra], the purification of the place (sthāna-śuddhi) is proclaimed.
One should always perform the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of substances with water containing *apāmārga*.
This is declared to be the purification of substances, which bestows success in sacrifices, fire-offerings (*homa*), and other rites.
As for those very powerful obstacles that reside in temples, pedestals, and *liṅgas*—
The warding off [of obstacles] with the most terrible weapons preceded by the *tāla* gesture is declared to be this purification of the *liṅga*, which brings great benefit to practitioners.
The purification of the mantra is proclaimed to consist of beginning with the *praṇava* (OM) and ending with *namaḥ*.
Purification is declared to be fivefold in the Hāṭakeśvara scripture.
Having understood this, the practitioner shall swiftly attain perfection even in this world.
Thus ends the fivefold purification.
Taking a very beautiful vessel made of gold, silver, or the like,
or one made of clay, or even a vessel of lotus leaves;
Having obtained any one of these according to availability, the instructor should wash [the site] with water consecrated by the *astra-mantra* and smear it with sandalwood paste and other substances.
Therein, he should prepare the *argha* offering as prescribed in the scriptures, purified by the *astra-mantra*.
Water, milk, tips of kuśa grass, unbroken rice, jasmine flowers,
sesame seeds, barley, and mustard seeds— this is proclaimed as the eightfold arghya.
One should illuminate the arghya with the Astra mantra and purify it with the Kavaca mantra.
Then the knower of mantras should perform the nourishment (āpyāyana) with the root mantra;
he should constantly unite the Power (Śakti) there, conjoined with Dharma,
along with knowledge (jñāna), dispassion (vairāgya), sovereignty (aiśvarya), and endowed with Māyā and Vidyā.
One should place Īśāna above that, Puruṣa in the eastern mantra-position, Aghora in the southern mantra, Vāmadeva likewise in the north,
and one should assign Sadyojāta to the western petal-section.
One should contemplate the heart in the southeast corner and likewise the head in the northeast;

one should apply the crest-lock (śikhā) in the southwest and contemplate the armor (kavaca) in the northwest. One should contemplate the face in the front region, and the wise know that the crown (masta) is all around.

Then, having formed the *dhenumudrā*, one should recite the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). This [mantra] is the pervader of all mantras; one should conceive it as nectar, white like the moon and surging with streams of ambrosia.
Then, one should sprinkle the substances with the mantras residing in the *argha* vessels;
one should strike them with the *astra* mantra and purify them with the *varma* mantra.
One should drench them with the root mantra and sprinkle them with the auspicious water (*śivāmbhas*).
Then, during worship, those [limbs] shall become stainless and of the nature of Śiva;
joined with the splendor of Śiva, they shall bestow both supernatural powers and liberation.
For they shall go to liberation, which is beyond illusion and stainless. Thus ends the procedure for the arghya vessel.
As long as the mantra-soul remains in the linga, or on the fixed or mobile sacrificial ground, [so long does the presence endure].
Until then, all those substances are indeed not considered *nirmālya* (remnants).
For this is known as the property of the deity; it must not be given to anyone whatsoever.
One must certainly not neglect it, nor should one use it for one's own personal purposes.
Having taken up the *argha* vessel and paid homage to Maheśvara,
as well as to the God, the Goddess, the lords of the Gaṇas, and likewise the three Gurus,
one should thereafter worship Śiva, who bears the form of the self, with flowers.
Then, having worshipped the Sun, as well as the trident and the bull,

one should worship them within the circle of light with extensive offerings such as water for the guest (arghya) and flowers; thereafter, O Brahmin, one should cast into the temple waters consecrated by the recitation of the weapon-mantra.
The great hosts of spirits with physical bodies who were stationed there on the ground were quickly driven away by them;
struck by them, those fierce ones who caused obstacles to the sacrifice fled.
Having performed this Vāmadevīya rite, one should worship the guardians of the doors;
one should then worship the group of Āśās and Mātṛs, Lakṣmī, Nandin, and Gaṅgā,
as well as Mahākāla and Yamunā, and thereafter worship the threshold (dehalī).
Having performed the expulsion of obstacles (*vighnaproccāṭana*), the binding of the directions (*digbandha*), and the armor-rite (*kavaca*) thereafter,
one should arrange a beautiful foundational power (*ādhārikā-śakti*) for the sake of one's own seat.
Then, having sat down, one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) in due order.
There, one should begin the concentration (*dhāraṇā*) simultaneously through the processes of drying and so forth;
one should meditate upon that [body], which consists of the six sheaths and is impure, as being utterly consumed by fire.
One should contemplate consciousness alone there as empty and all-pervading:
"I do not exist, nor does another exist; and here no object of meditation is found.
The mind, dissolved into the state of bliss, has attained a state of uniform flavor.
Thereafter, one should contemplate one's own seat situated upon the Support-Power (ādhāraśakti).
One should remember pure consciousness alone there— void and all-pervading—
as a lotus as vast as the ocean of the earth, illuminated by the crescent of the lunar orb.
One should sprinkle with water scented by the powder of the sixty-four arts from the hem of one's garment.
One should then manifest the three principles (tritattva) as the embodied form using the root mantra alone.
Thereafter, one should again project the limbs upon the body using both hands.
One should contemplate the mantra and indeed the self-conception through the yoga of meditation;
having formed the Amṛta-mudrā or the Padma-mudrā,
one should meditate upon the Lord of Gods within oneself, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons.
One should recollect him as worshipped with entirely white offerings.
Then, according to the distinction of one's disposition, one should recollect him as resembling a wish-fulfilling gem—
gentle, fierce, terrifying, or deformed, through the various distinctions of mental state.

Having thus meditated upon Sadāśiva, Bhairava, Tumburu, and Vīranāyaka, one should worship the God with auspicious mental flowers. For the sake of attaining all perfections, one should subsequently perform worship externally within the heart-lotus.

Worship performed with mental flowers is considered sattvic, stable, unwithered, supremely pure, auspicious, bestowing liberation, and granting spiritual perfections. This should be performed first; afterwards, one may proceed with elaborate material offerings.
In one's own home, in a temple, at a confluence, on a mountain peak,
or on a highly praised stretch of ground, or in a beautiful cluster of lotuses—
this is declared to be the "Mṛtyuñjaya" [rite], consisting of the worship of the door and the purification of the body.

The seat ending with the [deity’s] form and the meditation [performed] in the sequence beginning with pacification (śānti) and so forth— having first reflected upon that which lies within those [stages], it is now being described. Then, outside the door, are the supreme guardians of the sacrifice.
(33b) The Mothers, who reside in the ten directions, bestowing auspiciousness, are to be worshipped:
Umā, Durgā, Bhadrakālī, Svasti, Svāhā, and Śubhaṅkarī.
"Śrī, Gaurī, Lokadhātrī, and Vāgīśī is remembered as the tenth.
Thus, these [deities] were indeed described by Śiva to Śrīkaṇṭhī in a manner sweet to the quarters;
they should be worshipped either simultaneously or separately, in brief or in detail.
Having paid homage to the Mothers of the Directions and having diligently sprinkled the door with auspicious water while reciting the mantra, the expulsion of obstacles shall occur.
One should likewise [worship] the Lord Gaṇeśa and Śrī above the two door-panels.
Having worshipped [the deities] in sequence with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as incense and other offerings,
and then with water for the guest-offering (*argha*) and water for the feet (*pādya*),
one should worship Nandin and Gaṅgā at the northern door, and Mahākāla at the southern [door].
Having worshipped Kālinda, one should worship Dehalī below.
Having recited the Bhairava-weapon mantra, the practitioner, being meditative, should take up a flower and empower it seven times with mantras, so that it becomes filled with blazing crests of fire.
One should cast [the weapon] from the middle of the house by employing the nārāca-weapon.
Having placed the hand palm-upward, one should extend the three fingers;
through the joining of the index finger and the thumb, one should move them repeatedly.
Thus ends [the section on] Anantavijaya.
Then, for the sake of protection, one should discharge the weapon-mantra in the ten directions,
having produced the sound of clapping (*tāla*) by employing the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ*.
By joining the heel with the lower hand, one effects the expulsion of obstacles;
one should strike those on the ground with the heel and those in the air with the palm-clap.
Having purified the divine [deities] with missiles, one should then enter the sacrificial hall.
Thus ends the worship of the door.
Having worshipped Brahmā in the center with perfumes and flowers in due order—
Then, seated upon the seat previously practiced and established upon the *praṇava* throne in the southern image,
one should smear the hands with fragrant substances and purify them with the *astra-mantra*.
Having enveloped those two with the Kavaca mantra, one should drench them with nectar.
Having thoroughly agitated the Supreme Śakti, one should then manifest Ananta.
Having assigned the Mūrti, one should subsequently assign the faces and fashion Svacchanda.
One should assign the five limbs from the thumb to the little finger;
having likewise conceived the Bhairavas while recollecting the supreme reality,
one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) as the cause for the purification of the body.
One who is impure should fill the body with the pure [air] by means of the *svama* and *rudra* [breaths].
Having performed *kumbhaka* and *recaka*, one should cause the self to rest within the void—
subtle, resembling a firefly, and devoid of the sense organs.

Listen now to how one who is devoid of all activity, whose sphere of experience has been destroyed by Māyā, becomes truly identical with Śiva through that very nature; O Dear One, having grasped the supreme state, the body must then be consumed.
By means of that very [mantra], conjoined with the *saṃhāra* (withdrawal) seed-syllable, differentiated and joined with the seed-syllable of Rudra,
the burning should be performed; however, with the head [of the mantra] joined with fire (*ra*),
and the letter of Vāyu (*ya*) with its bindu (*m*) joined below, conjoined with Viṣṇu (*ha*).
For this indeed causes the flow of that [nectar]; it is remembered as the Vāruṇa [mantra] for the flooding.
"The drop [of nectar] breaking forth from the crown"—thus are the mantras of concentration (dhāraṇā). Thereafter, there should be the placement of power (śaktinyāsa).
One should bring that [consciousness] back as it was brought, and then flood it with nectar;
for its consciousness has been obscured by impurity and it remains dependent upon *kalā* and *vidyā*.
There, the self is colored by passion (rāga), measured by time (kāla),
further limited by necessity (niyati), and increased by merit and demerit; it has entered the state of primordial matter (pradhāna) and is endowed with the three qualities (guṇas).
The principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva), seated together with the ego (ahaṅkāra),
along with the mind, the organs of cognition and action, the subtle elements (tanmātras),
and the gross elements— all that which causes the production of the body is [awakened] by the syllable Om (praṇava).
O Goddess of gods, one should place them in sequence, numbering thirty-one.
O lady of beautiful countenance, the six principles (ṣaṭtattva) are to be known here;
the body is constructed from Pradhāna down to the earth.
O lady of excellent hips, the twenty-four principles should be seen as devoid of consciousness, yet they are presided over by the Puruṣa;
indeed, all of them should always be understood as being endowed with consciousness.
This indeed is declared to be the primordial twenty-five-fold [system].
Thereafter, O Goddess, one should install the form as previously indicated.
Thus has it been briefly proclaimed by Bhairava in the Svacchanda.

Having assumed a posture as desired— whether the Svastika, the Padma, the Ardhacandra, the one called Vīra, the Yogapaṭṭa stretched out, or the Paryaṅka— these are declared to be the eight postures according to their arrangement.
Having led the right foot behind the left by a double measure,
and having made it crosswise by a double measure so that it touches the shank,
one should place the two feet doubled over each other, one upon the other.
(35a) Thus the lotus has been fully described; now hear about the half-moon.
Having positioned both feet in that same manner, with the soles resting against each other, [one should perform the half-moon mudrā].
Listen now to that which is called the Vīra posture, which is like a half-moon.
Having placed the left foot doubled and dropped down above the right [foot],
with the soles of the two feet resting against each other, it is then called Vīrapaṭṭa.
Having first doubled the two [hands], slightly [extended] across and upwards,
one should place the hands like a bandage with the white [palms] joined and the fingers touching.
Then, having stretched out both feet, the face is likewise stretched forward.
Having extended both feet behind while standing on the buttocks,
according to their natural position and stability—
having bound this [posture] by stretching the chest evenly across the abdomen.
Placing the palm of the right hand upon the left hand, one should hold that water situated on one's own lap; then,
extending the left arm,
one should place the right hand upon the left knee while remaining seated in the lap-posture.
Or, with palms joined in reverence and a vision of complete satisfaction,
one should offer this "Eightfold Seat," which is indeed proclaimed in the *Kiraṇa*.
[The Eightfold Seat]
Having assumed a posture, one should gradually perform the purification of the hands, body, and so forth.
Seated firmly in the lotus posture (padmāsana), one should carry out the purification of that [channel],
for it is joined with innate impurities and actions that have not been purified.
Having burned away all that [impurity], one should recover the wealth situated within;
for that life-force (jīva), which is the wealth, resides supported by the wind.
One should grasp it with the inhalation (pūraka) and stabilize it through the retention (kumbhaka).
(35b) Raised up by the exhaling breath, one should establish it in the abode of the power (*śakti*).
This ritual action was conceived by him through the application of the purified body.
Through that [purification], he should purify the impure so that he may obtain the fruit of the pure mantra.
With that, he should establish the individual soul (jīva) in the locus of power (śaktisthāna), which consists of impurity.
He should make that body void and burn it away with that [power] like a piece of wood.
This [body] has been burnt away by a weapon resembling fire and reduced to ashes;
those ashes, consisting of darkness and devoid of support, have been washed away with water.
Having made the individual soul (jīva) pure like a grain of stone, one establishes it as the refuge of power (śakti).

In the venerable Parāgama, the method of attainment is described as follows: first, having burned the body from the tip of the big toe with the Astra-mantra, which possesses a brilliance equal to the fire of cosmic destruction,
one should contemplate [the self] both externally and internally.
Having meditated on that ash being scattered by the wind of the armor-mantra (kavaca),
one should contemplate oneself as having the form of a drop (bindu) within Śiva.
The characteristics of the burning of the body and so forth are declared in the Śrīpūrvaśāsana.
Impurity (*aśuddhi*) takes the form of a dwarf (*vāmana*); it moves along the path of the breath (*prāṇa*).
By means of that [impurity], the mountain of all powers of vision and action is obstructed.
Indeed, the cause of its fragmentation is proclaimed to be the burning of the body.
Ignorance, latent impressions, and aversion do not abandon one who is like a beast;
therefore, the means for the purification of the internal organ is proclaimed.
Just as a process is prescribed for gold in order to achieve its state of purity.
For the penetration of the essence of beating, cutting, burning, and so forth is performed by someone [through initiation];
likewise, through the sight of the mantra-path, sacrifice, mudrās, and maṇḍalas.
Through the practice of the retention of the vital breath (*āyāma-dhāraṇā-yoga*), the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are perceived.
All this is eternally pure, just as the practitioner should contemplate it. Then, all his actions [are purified] by virtue of his having attained the state of a disciple from the teacher.
It is stated in the Śrīmaṅgalāśāstra regarding the cremation of the body:
"The Weapon [mantra], raised from the tip of the big toe, blazing with the fire of Time,
should burn the body both externally and internally with its flames."
Burning and destruction are said to be identical; that which destroys is known as the fire.
This fire, called "desire," is permeated by the sap of its own mental constructs.
By means of that internal fire, there is burning in the body and likewise in the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*).
The destroyer of the body and the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) arises precisely from [the realization of] annihilation;
for it is not by mere existence that one becomes bound to a body, as is the case with ordinary embodied beings.
Indeed, this "I-ness" constitutes embodiment; therefore, once it is thoroughly destroyed, it certainly burns away that [embodiment].
Then, having become ashes, he remains as the residual impression (*saṃskāra*) of that body;
shaken by the wind of its attributes, he abides in the pure conscious self (*śuddhacidātman*). Having attained absorption (*samāpatti*) in that waveless ocean, he remains there.
Because consciousness possesses the nature of creation, it assumes that initial state of movement;
that very state is known as the "Form" (mūrti), which is the great self of the expansion of the Tāra.
This has also been stated in the Tantrāloka; now, the Form is further investigated.
Thus ends the justification for the burning of the body and so forth.
Having uttered [the mantra] while immersed and having offered it aloft into the abode of the Śiva-tattva,
[the soul] is drawn by its limbs— the radiance of that [tattva]— through the attraction of its fragrance, namely omniscience and the other [perfections].
Once it has been performed, one should place that supreme form upon the pair of bodies;
or else, by a single utterance, there is the purification of that which consists of thirty-two syllables.
Therefore, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) should be performed once upon the hand and likewise once upon the body.
Thus, the form is described as being both partless (*niṣkalā*) and with parts (*sakalā*), as well as supreme (*parā*).
I shall now explain the material cause (*upādāna*) of the form, together with its various divisions.
And Sumanā is in the lower region, along with Śuddhavidyā and the group of Kalās.

She is to be abandoned during the withdrawal of the Vidyeśvaras for the sake of the devotee, the disciple, and the Self; she resides within the belly of Sumanā for one who enjoys worldly experience at the break of day.
The Pralayākalas are pure, to be known as abiding beyond the state of *heṣā*;
they are always to be abandoned [by the seeker], being stainless through pure consciousness. Above them is the power Unmanā, and below that, no [such beings] are situated.

The pure principle of the Self (śuddhātmatattva) is to be known by them; from its agitation arises that which is designated as the "Self" (ātman). That is his formless (niṣkalā) form; above that is the one called the "Self" (ātman).
From its agitation arises the embodied (sakalā) form, and from the agitation of Śiva arises the supreme body.

When she, being partless (*niṣkalā*) and herself beyond mind (*unmanā*), is pervaded by the Self through the Self, she becomes the manifest (*sakalā*); she is the unfolding of Śiva (*śivonmeṣā*), known as Parā, who is higher than the highest Śiva. Her material cause (*upādāna*) is threefold; such is the lineage of the Guru.
That supreme power which is beyond mind (unmanā) is proclaimed to be the [ultimate] form (mūrti).
Śiva is not its material cause, nor are the individual soul (ātman) and the presiding deity (adhikārin) its causes.
And she, established upon the six causal agents, remains pervading the entire universe.
She is worshipped as a single form, as fourfold, sevenfold, manifold, and eightfold; she is the noble, auspicious, and virtuous one who is treated as a physical manifestation.
That which was sung by the illustrious Mataṅga is now being proclaimed here in its verses.
Then, in that heaven, the abode of the Lord— which consists of the rays of his own power—
he, whose nature is brilliantly luminous, remains unmoving yet possesses a mobile form. (37a)
She is the ultimate limit, exceedingly subtle, whose nature is to face all directions;
she has destroyed all veils, is peaceful, intensely devoted to pure reality alone,
free from beginning and end, virtuous, and is figuratively designated as having a form.
She is to be known as *liṅginī* when she is undifferentiated (*niṣkalā*), and as *nirliṅgā* during the purification of the body (*piṇḍaśodhana*).
She is fourfold—known as *vidyā* and *śivā*—and sevenfold thereafter.
Here, she is to be expressed as that which illumines the expansion, the beginning, the pervasion, and the awakening.

The states beginning with *sthiti* and ending with the nature of consciousness (*saṃvit-svabhāva*) consist of vowels, consonants, and the *sabindu*; they end with the half-moon (*ardhendu*), the resonance (*nāda*), and the power (*śakti*). The state of *unmanā* pertains to the form and the phonemes.
This expansion is said to be in the heart, while its pervasion (*vyāpti*) is proclaimed to be in the throat.
That which is called *bodha* (awakening) is said to be in the palate; *prakāśa* (illumination) is within the space between the two eyebrows;

its *sthiti* (abiding) is at the crown of the head; and *saṃvitti* (consciousness) is thus described as being in the state of Śiva, which is its own name—so it has been stated by the masters of the Mūrti school.
Through the various distinctions of forms, doubts, and bodies, she is the possessor of marks;
she is presided over by that [power] through the eightfold modes known as Vidyā, Earth, Fire, the Flame of Fire, Sun, Water, Wind, Moon, and Sky.
And because she is the supreme essence of the reality of the Self whose form is distinguished by consciousness,

she is known as the Supreme Śiva who bestows grace upon all; and due to the unfolding of that Supreme Śiva, she is the solitary heroine (ekavīrā) for yogins regarding the forms and mantras not explicitly mentioned.
Based on the threefold pervasion, one should conceive of the three [aspects] within the one;
having meditated upon the heart of reality with a form described according to one's own ritual action,
and having performed the commencement of recitation as previously stated, one effects the differentiation of the rites and so forth.
(37b) At the conclusion of the cessation of the fuel and so forth, one should conceive of the sixfold group of actions.
The fuel is the awakening of the power of gnosis within the space of the heart.
From the heart up to the palate, there is an ancient [channel] shaped like a bow.
By meditating upon it in its center, there is the kindling of one's own radiance;
by striking it through the path of the Śakti, [this occurs] between the fire and the wind.
One should purify the mantra defiled by the practitioner according to that path.
One should awaken [the mantra] situated within the heart in the confluence of the Bindu and the end of the Nāda.
Afterwards, one should effect its cessation in the immovable, eternal state.
Having performed yoga together with the qualities of Śiva, which transcends the state of ultimate reality,
and having understood the Form as proclaimed by the illustrious Dharmaśiva, the practitioner [attains success].
Thus ends the description of the nature of the Form.
Then, O Goddess, one should install the form, well-characterized by the preceding mantra;
having installed the complete Bhairava, O fair-eyed one, for thirty-two days,
one should subsequently assign the faces from the head down to the feet.
Thereafter, one should fashion the faces— the upper, the eastern,
the southern, the northern, and the western— according to their proper divisions.
One should then arrange the path to be purified according to its previous division into *kalās*.
The nine principles and the three principles are the limbs of knowledge, the three eyes;
the knife (kṣurikā) is beyond the classes of phonemes, the lamp of fire above and below.
That [state] at the end of the sixteen through forceful effort (haṭha) is the protector and the destroyer of obstacles.

One should first arrange the nine [syllables] on the head, the face, and the throat; then on the heart, the region of the navel, the secret place, and from the thighs down to the knees, and finally to the ends of the feet, while remaining endowed with the qualities of excellent meditation.
Action, knowledge, and likewise will reside in the right, the left, and the center;
for thus is Bhairava, the leader of mantras, remembered as the King of Vidyās. (38a)
The deity is described according to one's own preference, yet it is stated again regarding the rites of pacification and so forth:
for the purpose of pacification, one should contemplate the mantra as resembling pure crystal or like snow and the jasmine flower; for the rite of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), it has the luster of gold.
In rites for subjugation (*vaśyākarma*), one should visualize [the deity] as red in color;
in all rites of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), meditation on the black form is prescribed.
Thus it is at Hāṭakeśvara, and now the Niśvāsa is being told.

One should meditate upon Śaṅkara, the Lord of all beings, who is the form of light. [He is] seen by the gods, sages, siddhas, yakṣas, vidyādharas, and uragas. (*The reading is "darśate vibhoḥ". (*The reading is "taṃ devādayo...")
Those of firm vows constantly meditate upon Rudra, the Mother-goddesses, and the Lords (Īśānas).
His forms are indeed manifold— blue, yellow, and ruddy—
and are worshipped by wise men endowed with austerity according to their various fruits.
In that regard, whatever red form there is, eternally possessing the luster of lac-dye,
should be meditated upon by one desiring sovereignty through yoga in its proper sequence.
Therein, it is endowed with yellow radiance, gentle, lovely, and possessed of splendor.

The practitioner of mantra, in whatever stage of life he may be engaged, should constantly meditate upon that [disc] which eternally attracts the women of the gods and asuras, and which is as pure as clear crystal for the sake of purifying sins.
One should contemplate for the sake of Dharma that which resembles the rising sun.
Thus, the terrible diseases that destroy the body always perish,
even without the destruction of the planet Kavi (Saturn), for the sake of one's own victory.
And when the sun has set,
one should visualize that form as having the luster of golden light, intensely radiant, and facing in all directions. (38b)
One should meditate for the sake of the prosperity of the Dharma, or for one's own nourishment;

or, for the destruction of obstacles, one should contemplate [the deity] as dark-complexioned and flickering with sparks. Through the ritual application of a fierce mantra, he is wrathful, with eyes bloodshot with rage.

One should meditate upon the light as eight finger-breadths in size for success in all undertakings. This was indeed proclaimed by Nandin during the descent [of the Lord] at Nandīśvara, according to the sequence of the phonemes, exactly as they follow one another in order.

Having placed Īśāna on the head with the Bhadrā and the Liṅga-mudrā, one should place the face upon the mouth with the Vaktra[-mudrā], and Bahurūpa in the heart with the Hṛdaya[-mudrā]. One should then install Vāmadeva in the secret region with the Guhya[-mudrā].
Beginning from the two feet,
one should apply the Sadyojāta [mantra] up to the head across all limbs with the *bhadra* or *sūkti* mudrā;
this is done by joining the thumb with the index finger and so forth in successive order.
The Bhadrā mudrās begin with the face [mudrā], while the Liṅga mudrā is formed with the fist.
This is the definition of the mudrās for the faces as proclaimed by Puṣkara;
or else, the syllables are joined with the Saṃhāra [mantra].
The faces of Bhairava, pierced at their crowns by the *bindu*,
should be joined according to the sequence of Brahmā, starting from the head and ending with the feet. Furthermore,
the principal face should be conceived as facing upward, followed by the southern and then the northern faces.
Having further conceptualized [the directions], one should perform the placement according to the division of parts:
the east, the south, the north, and likewise the west;
and above, joined with the head and so forth, the letter *kṣa*, which has the form of Īśvara.
In this way, one should apply the four faces to the [four] faces themselves;
as for the fifth face that may exist, one should indicate it by the syllable *kṣa*.

One should place [the mantras] upon the heart, the neck, the back, the navel, and the abdomen; likewise on the back and the chest, in due order with the *aghora* mantra. Similarly, one should place them on the private parts, the anus, and likewise on the thighs and the knees.
One should place them on the two calves, the two thighs, the waist, and both sides;
and indeed, on the left side of the body in due order.
I shall now declare their names correctly and in sequence.
Tārā, Sutārā, Taṇī, Tārayantī, and Sutāriṇī—
these are the five digits (kalās) of Īśāna, which follow the state of Nirañjana.
They are Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti.
These four are proclaimed as the kalās of Puṣa:
Tamas, Moha, Kṣudhā, and Nidrā; and by Māyā, [comes] Mṛtyu and Jarā.
Thus, O woman of excellent complexion, there are eight kalās of Aghora.
Rajā, Rakṣā, Rati, Palyā, Kāsyā, Tṛṣṇā, Mati, Kriyā, Ṛddhikāyā, Rātrī, Bhrāmaṇī, Mohanī,
and the one renowned as Manonmanī— these are the thirteen [powers] in Vāmadeva.
Siddhi, Ṛddhi, Dyuti, Lakṣmī, Medhā, Kānti, Sudhā, and Sthiti—
these are proclaimed as the eight kalās of Sadyojāta.
This is the arrangement of the faces and kalās according to the Svacchanda Śāstra.

The placement [of the mantra] should also be performed with both hands; therefore, it should be done for both hands. Since all ritual action preceded by the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) and so forth must be performed with those two hands, one who performs the rite becomes the embodiment of all mantras.
(39b) A twice-born man should place the [mantras] beginning with *kanyasā* on the fingers beginning with the little finger in sequence;
thereafter, he should place them on all the limbs and the individual limbs by means of those two [hands].
One should project the form like a *piṇḍa* with the *udgītha*, which possesses stainless luster.
That manifestation is the construction of the body by means of the five [syllables] beginning with *aja*:
*sadyojāta* is earth, *vāmadeva* is water, *aghora* is fire, *tatpuruṣa* is air, and *īśāna* is ether.
Īśa is the withdrawal into space; Nyāsa is that which extends from the feet to the top of the head.
Liberation results from the total withdrawal of all things; such is the nature of Nyāsa among them.
Beginning with Īśa and ending with Sadhya, Nyāsa is intended for the purpose of enjoyment.
Since emanation (sṛṣṭi) consists of eight [units] from which enjoyment arises, and maintenance (sthiti) is that from which [the world] remains,
the placement (nyāsa) begins from the top and ends with the feet. Therefore,
the arrangement of the body of the Lord was first fashioned by the Lord for His own form.
These five, by their very nature, are like the individual limbs of the Lord.
First, from the east, south, north, west, and the center—these are indeed the faces;
through these, one should contemplate the form of Nara.
Then, with the fierce [weapon], he struck the heart, throat, shoulders, chest, back, navel, and abdomen;
with the goat on the left, he struck the anus, genitals, thighs, buttocks, shanks, hips, and the sides;
and with the goat on the right, he struck both feet, the hands, the nose, the head, and the arms.
One should conceive of one's own body with these five mantras as they abide therein:
the earthly element of flesh is present, pervading all limbs;
and in that limb resides the deity who dwells within all beings like the self.
The placement (nyāsa) declared according to the authoritative tradition bestows both enjoyment and liberation.
Furthermore, O Goddess, the practitioner [should perform it] on all the limbs in due order:
the nine principles, the three principles, and the group of nine known as Bhairava.
(40a) One should first arrange nine [syllables] on the head, the face, and the throat;
then on the heart, the region of the navel, the secret place, and from the thighs down to the knees.
One should likewise install the eight [deities] at the end, conjoined with the qualities of one's own meditation.
According to the teachings of the *Svacchanda*, there is an installation (*nyāsa*) of the Bhairavas and their essential principles (*tattvas*);
therein, there is a group of nine for Śiva and Suśiva.
The spheres of the Lord, of knowledge, and of the two who govern illusion and time, as well as the stations of the individual soul and primordial nature—
these are to be contemplated by the Bhairavas in the threefold reality at the throat and the heart.
This arrangement with substances has been proclaimed as it is taught in the Śrīpauṣkara.
This installation (nyāsa) is indeed performed upon Śiva, the fire, the fetters, and the self,
using purified perfumes, leaves, flowers, and incense.
The heart and other centers are dissolved into their respective locations by means of the *svastika-bandha* on both sides.
This is the all-pervading Śiva, situated above the big toes of the feet.
Just as in the state of Nandīśvara’s descent, this is the placement of the limbs and the root [mantra].
Praśasanī, Śivā, Jvalinī, Stambhinī, Ghātinī,
and Jñānanetrā are proclaimed as belonging to the heart and the other [limbs].
Having raised the thumb and formed a fist, it is called the heart [mudrā].
Having placed the thumb in the *puṣṭi* [mudrā], the *śikhā* is raised toward the head;
that same [gesture] turned sideways is the *kavaca*, and here it is raised three times for the *astra*.
Having placed the index finger on the forehead and formed a downward-facing fist, [this is the *netra*].
In the great Āgama known as the Purāṇa, this is appropriately called the Netra.
Thus spoke the venerable Vasiṣṭha, the goad.
Previously, that *brahmapañcaka* was fashioned as belonging to the major and minor limbs.
What is the use of these imagined limbs, which merely designate the heart and so forth?
Thus spoke the Lord Sun, the Light.

The status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) that belongs to the *udaṅgas* is established by the rules of metaphorical application (*upacāra-vidhi*), because even they have attained the state of being auxiliaries here in what is called the "Sword of Dharma" (*dharmakṛpāṇa*).
Since [the primary] does not lose its nature as an auxiliary when it has become an auxiliary, it is therefore caused by the auxiliary.
The *hṛdaya* is for the protection of the heart, fastened with the band of Dharma; the *śiras* is for the protection of the head, serving as a turban for the head;
the *śūlikā* is for the protection of the skull, and the *kaṅkaṇa* is for the protection of the limbs.
Once he has taken up arms, the minister stands like a terrifying warrior;
he becomes a source of affliction for the base, just as the sight of Tārkṣya is to serpents.
Just as there is a physical arrangement of the body, so too is the arrangement of his limbs.
At that time, the practitioner should cultivate a firm conviction rooted in self-confidence.
Having become Śiva both internally and externally, and having thus become Śiva himself, he should worship Śiva.
Pratoda said:
Since the relationship of the worshiped and the worshiper is seen as if between two unequal parties,
how could Śiva— who has become Śiva himself— be a worshiper?
Prakāśa said:
The husband, residing in the palace of the pure path, is identical to that attainment;
as long as he remains equal to it, he is capable of worshiping it.
For friendship between those of similar character is seen to lead to the ultimate fruit.
Thus has been spoken regarding those who desire to ascend the Parā [path].
Now I shall speak concerning those who have already ascended, with respect to the six limbs (*aṅga*) pertaining to the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
They know that omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is the heart and perfect satisfaction (*paritṛpti*) is the head.
Primordial awakening is the crest-lock; sovereignty is the armor of the All-pervasive Lord;
the unimpaired power is the eye; and that which possesses infinite power is the weapon.
This sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya) is indeed remembered as the six limbs of this [king];
this is the general pervasion residing in the six limbs of the science of kingship.
Just as fire [shines] with its own flames, and just as the sun [shines] with its rays.
Śiva is likewise capable and invincible by means of his own limbs;
because he pervades both the states of sorrow and bliss, he is the knower.
By this reason, the omniscience of Maheśa is demonstrated.
That is declared to be his heart; it is called the first limb.
Complete satisfaction is the second renowned quality of Maheśa. Maheśvara remains indifferent amidst both enjoyments and non-enjoyments due to his equanimity.
Then, being declared fully satisfied, he is called "the Steadfast" (Tasthira) of the Lord.
By virtue of his primary nature, he becomes the primordial warrior of the Lord;
through the state of possessing all characteristics, he is the seer of all and the knower of all.
Not seeing [the object] yet perceiving it through the awakening of even that which is already awakened, the third quality is spoken of; she is declared to be the Crest (Śikhā).
The sovereignty of Śambhu is always present, distinguished by its gross and subtle aspects.
Because he bestows grace upon all and because he is indivisible,
that sovereignty of the God of *varman* is called the fourth quality;
O Maheśvarī, the Blessed Lord is eternally possessed of unimpaired power.
The power of the Supreme Lord is never impaired;
therefore, it is designated as "light" within the Great Lord.
The Blessed One possesses infinite power, and its end is not perceived.
O Maheśānī, because it causes the fallen [soul] to burst asunder the bonds (pāśas),
it brings about the loosening of the bonds through its inherent power and leads him to a state of equality.
Because it possesses infinite power, it is therefore called an *astra* (weapon).
(41b) This object of knowledge has been explained as pertaining to the six limbs of the deposition upon the body.
Now I shall speak of the Śikhātantra according to the venerable Mṛtyuñjaya mantra.

While the worship is being performed, this concise sequence for the worshipper has been declared, based on the principles of the established doctrine of the ritual of *nyāsa*. It is also briefly stated here as the essential core extracted from the compendium of all the currents (*srotas*). Having performed the *mūrti-mantra* in a pervasive manner throughout the entire body, one should place the three mantras known as Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman at the locations of the crest, the heart, and the throat.

One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the principles (*tattva*) with the two thumbs, and of *prakṛti*, the heart, and the other [limbs] starting from the heart. One should also place the *astra* (weapon-mantra) in the middle of the hands; these same [mantras] are to be placed upon the body according to their respective locations. Having performed the placement of the *astra* as before on the two hands and on the body in an all-pervasive manner, one should meditate upon the Lord as the Embodiment (*mūrti*). Having performed the placement of hand-gestures (*karāmudrā*) as prescribed in the Siddhāntadarśana, one should worship Mṛtyujit. Alternatively, having performed the placement as taught in the Mṛtyuñjaya, one becomes Sadāśiva. For it was thus declared by Maheśa in the scripture named Mṛtyusañjaya:
"In the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), in worship, and likewise in the case of the Vidyā and the argha-vessel."
In the consecration by fire (agnisaṃskaraṇa), as well as in the placement of mantras (nyāsa) and meditation (dhyāna) and so forth,
no hesitation should be made regarding that which is common to all;
since no confusion arises therein, one should therefore abandon doubt.
Thus indeed did Śrī Viśvānta declare in his own manual:
"Having invoked the Niṣkala [form], one should arrange the limbs (aṅgas) in their proper order—
the heart, the head, the crest-lock, the armor, the eyes, and the weapon."
This host of Bhairavas accomplishes all desires and goals;
[they are to be honored] with perfumes, flowers, incenses, and various kinds of food and edibles.

One should worship the Lord of the gods of gods with offerings mentally conceived. Then, one should meditate upon oneself as Bhairava according to the heart-āgama. Having established the bulb (kanda) at the navel, its stalk extends for twelve finger-breadths.
One should conceive of the heart; there, one should visualize a lotus—eight-petaled, greatly radiant, with filaments and a pericarp.
The bulb at its base consists of power (*śakti*), and those which are the thorns are indeed in the stalk.
O lady of excellent complexion, those very worlds belong to the Rudras;
[therein are] Ananta, the support of Śakti, the feet beginning with Dharma,
the limbs such as Nityadharma, and likewise the pins for the joints.
One should provide the lower and upper coverings, the filaments and pericarp of the lotus,
the lotuses, the power (*śakti*), and the mandalas and their presiding deities;
one should then offer the seat ending with the corpse by means of the *dhruva* mantra, which is the primordial form.
The form is the array of the portions of Brahman, consisting of nine principles or three principles;
it is the thirty-two-syllable deity, as well as the eight Bhairavas,
the Vidyā-aṅga-kṣurikā, and likewise the three eyes.
One should assign the three powers to the supreme deity together with the collection of limbs;

one should likewise apply the mudrās, mantras, and ritual substances to their respective places. Having performed the visualization according to the rule, one should arrange everything as is appropriate and fitting.

One should assign Sadyojāta, Vāma, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna—the [five faces] of the God—as they have been described; one should likewise arrange the petals situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions. Then, one should place the five [mantras], beginning with Hṛdaya, in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Outside, from the east up to the northeast, is the enclosure of the Bhairavas;
then, from the east to the northeast, are the world-protectors and their weapons.
One should recite the mantras in sequence for the weapons, the world-protectors, the eight Bhairavas,
the five Brahmās, and the limbs; these are the enclosures (āvaraṇas),
continuing until the Lord who is the embryo [of the mantra].
Listen now to this union of mantras, which indeed effects the supreme state.
Then one should utter the deity, endowed with short, long, and protracted vowels;
one should recite the mantra for as long as it remains within the sphere of Nirvāṇa.
From below the *cakras* up to above, within the path of the Moon and the Sun,
by means of the central channel (*madhyamārga*) of Piṅgalā and through the sequence of the utterance of the phonemes (*varṇoccāra*),
one [perceives] the five deities, Śakti, Vyāpinī, Samanā, and Unmanā.
Having sequentially differentiated everything up to the very end of dissolution—
that which is waveless, pathless, all-pervading, and beyond the mind— one should,
by means of superimposition in the direct order, establish it within the heart-lotus.
O Goddess, one should thus install that pervasive [mantra] upon all the coverings (*āvaraṇas*).
By being presided over by it, all [the deities] bestow the fruit of the abode of Śiva.
And those mantras which have been described by me according to their respective forms—
In that manner, O Bhairavī, they should be employed in the mind by means of the mind alone. Having established Śiva upon the pericarp, existing in two states,
resembling pure crystal and adorned with all mantras.
There too, it should be known from another source as being inexpressible and free from disease;
where there is no duality and no conceptualization of phonemes or mantras,
you should point out the dissolution of the syllable *oṃ*, the bindu, and the nāda.
That state is difficult to attain; a meditator may perhaps reach it at some time.
It has neither top nor bottom, nor cardinal directions nor intermediate directions;
it possesses no sound, touch, taste, or form, nor is there space, nor is there smell.
O Goddess, having known that, the yogi is liberated, O Mistress of the Gods of Gods.
And thus is the union of mantra and the union of the channels.
