One should perform the act of supreme transformation by means of the supreme Pervasive One.
Having offered various kinds of food offerings, one should display the mudrās.
The preceptor, intent on the sacrifice, should perform prostrations and the recitation of mantras.
Whether on one's own body, on a sacrificial mound, on a *liṅga*, on a mandala, or likewise in the sacrificial oblation (*caruka*),
as well as in water or fire— one obtains the supreme fruit of initiation (*dīkṣā*).
Without performing the mental sacrifice, one should not undertake any other sacrifice.
But that which is inauspicious should be known as not being prescribed for liberation.
O Goddess, when the sacrifice of the self (ātmayāga) is performed, purification of the body arises.
One should designate that teacher alone as being presided over by Śiva.
This mental [sacrifice] is proclaimed solely for the purpose of self-purification.
Having understood it correctly, the teacher becomes a god who severs the bonds.
In whatever place he may reside, he who thus abandons the mental [sacrifice] [is liberated].

Even a slayer of a Brahmin would be liberated, how much more so one who [practices] day after day! Having obtained the desired fruit even in other tantras through the performance of sacrifice and other rites according to the rules as prescribed in this system, [one attains liberation here].
Endowed with various supernatural powers (*siddhi*) and qualities, it bestows the fruit of manifold enjoyments.
One attains the perfection of yoga (*yogasiddhi*) and certainly achieves liberation (*mukti*). All the gods know it, and the imperishable Śiva understands it.
The placement [of the deity] in the region of the heart, mental worship, and the praise of that [deity]—
this which has been proclaimed in the venerable *Svacchanda* and other [texts] is called a limb of worship.
Listen, O Goddess Ambikā, I shall declare how the hosts of true devotees come to my presence, which is difficult to attain, without effort;
O Goddess worshipped by the Lord of Devas, I act through various dispositions.
For the sake of their own worship within themselves, O You of equal splendor,
that steadfastness which arises through the collection of materials for their adoration is known as Earth (Sādhara).
Water, by its nature of fluidity and joy, is eternally established within itself.
Then, for the sake of honoring him, joy arises;
that which is there in the form of radiance is proclaimed by me as Fire (Tejas). That which has the nature of touch and mobility is indeed established as Wind (Vāyu).
Among those, O slender-waisted one, because they are devoid of the fortune of possessing excellent channels,
my own quality of space manifests there;
and because of its pervasive nature, they appear as they do once again.
O Goddess, those two, the Moon and the Sun, who abide therein, are nourished and grow.
O Great Goddess, these seven [rays] constantly nourish the essence.
And that eighth form, O Goddess, exists as the sacrificer (yajamāna).
Thus, O Mistress of the Vowels, O Queen of the Gods, the potency of my own self is seen within all living beings among the objects of worship, such as the water for the feet and other offerings;
for they are born from my potency, equal to me, and possess my own prowess.
"O you who enjoy my worship, all beings are the implements of my worship;
relying upon them, my devotees are intent upon my worship.
O Goddess of the Suras, those who worship [thus] attain the supreme goal.
Worship is remembered as being performed according to the sequence of the eight *pūrṇās*, following the *Niśvāsa*.
Having performed the previously mentioned *vyāsa*, one should offer the eightfold nourishment (*aṣṭapuṣṭika*).
Listen to those eight flowers mentioned by name:
the aquatic, the lunar, the auspicious, the aerial, the earthly,
then the sixth is the arboreal, and the seventh is the progenitor-born (prājāpatya).
Now hear from me the eighth, the Śiva-flower, which is the quintessence of those [offerings]:
water is to be known as the lotus-born (vārija), milk as that with ghee (sapuṣṭata), incense, lamps,
and so forth as the airy (vāyavya), and sandalwood paste and the like as the lunar (candana).
The terrestrial flower consists of bulbs, roots, and so forth; the arboreal, of flowers, fruits, and the like;
the prājāpatya, of footprints and such; while the śivapuṣpa is the latent impression (vāsanā).
Thus, the Lord Sadāśiva is always to be worshipped with these eight flowers.
In both cases, this "Eight-Flower" [rite] was spoken by Śiva in the *Kiraṇāgama*:
"Offering the body of the mantra with a mind free of conceptual construction,
one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantra for the sake of attaining the state of being identical with that [mantra]."

For mental activities, which take the form of volition, are indeed very firm and bring about auspicious results. O Goddess, within the mind all this is situated; both bondage and liberation, as well as merit and demerit, are eternally bound to the mind.
Name-and-form, conceptual proliferation, as well as birth and death—
the mind, defiled by beginningless ignorance, is called saṃsāra.

That very [state], when it has become absolute, conduces to Nirvāṇa. Therefore, having accomplished renunciation (nyāsa), one should perform the sacrifice of yoga (yogayāga) with [mantras] that are not exhausted,
untainted, free from deceit, and imperishable.
One should worship the deity who assumes a physical form with mental enjoyments.
Thus, according to the system of Cakreśvara, the heart-visualization (hṛdyāga) bestows all perfections (siddhis).
— Nārada.
Since the heart-sacrifice (*hṛdyāga*), accompanied by both primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) and discerning consciousness (*vijñāna*), bestows all accomplishments,
for what purpose should external worship be performed within the mandala? The Blessed One said:
This firm latent impression (*vāsanā*) regarding external objects, acquired over many lifetimes,
has indeed caused the pure Self to become agitated by that which is of an impure nature.
That mantra-related practice, however, is pure and bestows the tranquil state of one's true nature.
That [practice] is proclaimed for the purpose of destroying its origination;
one should become absorbed in that through both external and internal actions.
However, for those whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) regarding objects are firm, their attenuation occurs only very gradually.
O Brahmin, whatever one is absorbed in while currently abiding in the body,
that in which one becomes absorbed upon the fall of the body— this is what has been declared by me.
The justification for two modes of worship has been declared in the *Śrījayā*:
"In the absence of an abundance of material offerings, one should resort to mental proximity [to the deity].
But those who, out of greed, favor the mental ritual while possessing wealth..."
For those whose souls are thus impaired, initiation is in vain and sacrifice is in vain.
Therefore, [this] has been proclaimed as the method for worshipping Cakreśvara.
Thus ends the section on the mental sacrifice (*manoyāga*) in the *Nityādisaṅgraha*, extracted from the Āgamas.
(45b) Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, by whom and in what manner should that sacrifice be performed?
At what time, in what place, with which substances, and for what purpose, O Maheśvara?
Thus urged by the Goddess, the Supreme Lord spoke:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the unsurpassed Śiva-sacrifice,
knowing which embodied beings are swiftly liberated from the bondage of worldly existence."
Whether he be a teacher, a practitioner, one bound by the observances, or even a spiritual son,
the knower of mantras, having procured the sacrificial materials suitable for the rite, should worship the auspicious seat of yoga (yogapīṭha) as Śiva.
Having performed the protection rite, with a serene mind and having purified the ritual substances and so forth,
one should perform the purification of the site by touching it with water consecrated by the recitation of the *astra* mantra, or even with ashes,
or by clapping the hands or using a mudrā.

One should perform the *argha* offering and so forth for the purification of substances and for their sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) by means of the *śivodaka*, the *pavitra*, the limbs (*aṅga*), the *śaktis*, or by Śiva himself. One should establish the earth-mantra below and the weapon-mantra (*astra*) in the directions as a rampart with the staff-gesture (*daṇḍamudrā*).
One should perform the binding of the circle of elements and the net of rays with the *samudrī* [mudrā].
Above and below are Fire and Sun; in the middle is the mandala of the Moon.
Seated there, one should worship the God with action, mind, and speech.

Having purified the sacrificial materials, one should mentally recollect the Śivāstra-mantra. Then, with the Gāyatrī, one should satiate them while causing nectar to flow. According to the ritual and according to the time, one should join the materials with the materials.
One should employ flowers in these eight [rites]: the invocation, the offering of arghya, worship, bathing, incense, unguent, the food offering, and the dismissal. (46a)
One should employ fragrant paste (*gandha*) in three instances: for the *arghya*, for anointing (*vilepana*), and for bathing (*snāna*).

Likewise, one should employ water in seven instances: for the offering of flowers, the *arghya*, the foot-water (*pādya*), as well as for bathing, sipping water (*ācamana*), washing, and sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).
Incense should be offered everywhere; having understood what remains, one should employ it accordingly. Just like incense, the divine mudrās are prescribed for all ritual actions.
[One should offer] that which is enriched with eight [qualities], beginning with the three fragrances, and saturated seven times with water.
Having understood the ritual action pervaded by the procedure for mantras and incense, one should worship Śiva.
Due to the maintenance of the established tradition of the Āgamas, there is the presence [of the deity], as well as water for the feet,
the offering of honor (*argha*), and food to be tasted, following the sequence beginning with the worship.
Bathing, the gift of garments and so forth, and again the offering of worship and the *argha*;
the recitation (*japa*) of the mantra and other rites, the renunciation of action (*karma-saṃnyāsa*), and then the dedication of the recitation;
again the offering of worship and the giving of the *argha*, and likewise, O Goddess, the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*).

Wherever all these— the eight flowers and so forth, as well as the rites beginning with the invocation— are remembered, that is proclaimed to be a sacrifice (yāga). This procedure for sacrifice has been recorded in brief in the Vidyā-purāṇa.
The characteristics of flowers and other such items by which one should worship Śiva have been declared.
Thus, when that most excellent of teachers has attained the state of Śiva, [he is fit for initiation]. (46b)

At that time, all the flowers and other offerings are lifeless, yet they become endowed with life when they are consecrated by Śiva and established in Him. Otherwise, like a flower offered to a dead body, the offering remains [lifeless].
The deity would not have been worshipped even for a hundred past kalpas had he not been thus duly honored with an abundance of various flowers,
along with fragrant incenses mixed with ghee, honey, and guggulu.
With beautiful lamps filled with ghee, abundant and resembling stars;
with various delightful perfumes, auspicious offerings joined with sweet flavors;
and with various drinks, O Goddess, that are most delicious and fragrant.
O Pārvatī, having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with pearls, sapphires, all kinds of gems, various eyes, and garments,
one should thus [worship] the one whose nature is immeasurable everywhere, as taught in the Śrīkaṇṭha-śāstra.
Reflecting upon the ritual procedure, one should first examine the materials.
Among them, the vessel for the *arghya* offering should initially be made of gold, silver, or likewise of conch, mother-of-pearl,
pearl-oyster, copper, or even clay.
Having taken lotus petals for the purpose [of the ritual], washed them with water,
O Goddess of the Lords of Gods, and smeared them with *gurucandana* over which the *astra-mantra* has been recited,
one should then fumigate them with refined incense and fill them with *kariṇa*.

It is proclaimed that [the water] should be filtered with a cloth and made pure; this is known as *svacchanda*. From among these, one should offer the eightfold *argha* into whichever vessel is appropriate, according to the procedure for the *puryaṣṭaka*: namely, water, milk, *kuśa* grass, and curd.
Rice, unbroken grains, white mustard seeds, and sesame seeds are to be used respectively;
water has Soma as its presiding deity, and milk is remembered as having Sarasvatī as its deity.
Sāvitrī resides on the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass, and Viṣṇu resides in curd.
Rice grains have the Earth as their deity, while sesame seeds have the ancestors (*pitṛ*) as their deity.
Barley has Brahmā as its deity, and white mustard seeds have Rudra as their deity.
Thus, the eight-limbed arghya-vessel should be understood by the most excellent of teachers.
The belly is the cosmic egg, the lotus is said to be the earthly principle (pārthiva-tattva);
it is endowed with sixteen petals and adorned with the eight directions.
Taking that vessel of oblation (arghapātra), which contains the eight-fold flowers of the Vidyās,
the determination of the eight-limbed oblation (aṣṭāṅgārgha) is declared in the *Vāthula* [Tantra] regarding the worship of Bhāva.
With that, one should sprinkle everything that has been presented, such as the flowers and other offerings.
Having recited the eight-limbed *arghamantra*, one should discharge [the water] by means of the *dhenumudrā*.
Then, one should sprinkle oneself on the head with drops of that water.
One should then consecrate the sacrificial materials situated there with the water of the *astra-mantra*.
Having consecrated it with the heart-mantra, one should envelop it with the *piṇḍas* and the *tantra*.
Having displayed the *amṛta-mudrā* and offered a flower upon one's own seat,
and having applied a *tilaka* on the head, one should join the flower with the root-mantra (*mūla*).
Thus has the procedure for the *tilaka* been shown by Somaśambhu:
one should make a *tilaka* that is circular, crescent-shaped, square, or in the form of a vulva (*bhaga*),
and the fifth [type] should be a vertical line.
A circular [shape] is said to bestow wealth; a square bestows dharma;
a half-moon bestows liberation; and the shape of a vulva bestows all desires. One should likewise cause an upward line to be drawn, for it brings about all prosperity.
In Kāmākhyā, it is circular upon the net-throne;
in Pūrṇagiri, it is square; in Oḍyāna, however, it has the form of a vulva.
In the case of the *vyantara* seats, one should indeed draw half a line.
The index finger is for victory over enemies; the middle finger is for rites of pacification (*śāntika*);
the ring finger is said to be for withering (*śoṣaṇa*); and the little finger is for the activities of a Buddha (*buddhakarma*).

The thumb should be used for the śrāddha rite, and the application [of unguents] is on the fingers. They say that sandalwood has the Moon as its deity, while saffron is said to belong to the Sun. Vermilion has Agni as its deity; thus, the tilaka mark consists of these three divine sources.
Having performed this, the practitioner will quickly become the very body of his desired deity.
In some places, the characteristics, the object, and the substance for the *tilaka* have been described.
Then, one should worship the gurus to the east of the Brahma-sthāna.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa in the direction of the wind (the northwest) with perfumes, incense, and so forth in due order,
one should pay homage for the sake of removing obstacles and contemplate that he has granted permission.
In the Svacchandabhairava Tantra, the worship of the Guru and other rites are prescribed [to begin] from this point.
Assuming the form of the preceptor, Śiva bestows knowledge.
Therefore, Śiva should always be worshipped with every effort;
for the spiritual accomplishment of all practitioners is established therein.
Without worship of the Guru, even for the Siddhas, success is difficult to attain.
Therefore, one should first worship the Guru with a mind endowed with devotion;
for Maheśvara himself, having assumed a human form, [bestows it].
Out of compassion, in the form of a guru, [the sages] extracted the mantras for the sake of living beings.
In the Vājasaneyī [Saṃhitā], the primary worship of the guru has been proclaimed;
having thus worshipped the gurus in a single spot upon a stone surface.
Then, having informed them, the minister should commence the fierce sacrifice (caṇḍayāga).
The great hosts of mantra-bodies are subtle and have entered within the physicians.
The fierce ones who create obstacles to the sacrifice, even if they have risen up forcefully,
are struck by the wise with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra; having been thus struck,
they abandon the sacrificial seat (*pīṭha*) from their bodies, after which one should perform the worship.

Then, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon two pure vessels, the practitioner of mantra should worship Caṇḍarudra with five Brahma-mantras, as well as with parched grains, flowers such as lotuses, and other substances.
With those two [hands], the wise one should touch the body from the head down to the feet;
furthermore, he should always meditate upon Netracaṇḍa in the place of the eyes.
One does not become defiled by the remains of the offering (nirmālya) or by drops of sweat adhering to the limbs.
At the time of sacrifice, the practitioner must always remain pure.
One should not invoke Caṇḍarudra in a *liṅga* made of stone and other such materials;
nor [should one do so] in a *liṅga* fashioned by humans, even when using mantras belonging to the Siddhānta.

When those [deities] have been worshipped, the wise one should perform the placement (*vinyāsa*) and the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) at the feet; and during that very procedure of worship, he should offer the worship of Caṇḍa. For this purpose, he should carry out the ritual injunctions beginning with "Ibha" according to the prescribed method.

Oṃ śuddhendudhautāya svāhā. Oṃ dhunicaṇḍa huṃ phaṭ. Homage to Netracaṇḍa. Then, the second vessel for the offering (arghapātra) should be prepared with the Caṇḍa mantras. Thereupon, one should arrange the seat (āsana), namely Ananta, beginning with the syllable Om (praṇava).
Having recited the heart-mantra ending in *namaḥ* just once,
one should visualize Caṇḍa in its center, endowed with the six limbs.
Having worshipped him, one should then perform the excellent seat for Caṇḍa.
The wise one should meditate on the city of Ardhacandra situated in the northeastern direction;
within its center, he should visualize Ananta with the heart-mantra ending in "namaḥ.
One should meditate upon the fourfold attributes— dharma, jñāna, vairāgya, and aiśvarya—
in the corners beginning with the southeast (āgneya). Above that, upon a white lotus, one should contemplate the Form (mūrti) within the pericarp (karṇikā), its essence marked by the syllable *caṃ*.
Joined with the root mantra and ending with a salutation,
one should contemplate his heart in one's own heart and his head upon one's own head.
Afterwards, one should worship the five-faced white Lord with water for the feet and other offerings.

One should meditate upon the god Caṇḍeśvara, who has ten arms, large eyes, and is adorned with divine ornaments; thereafter, one should offer worship. The name "Caṇḍa," joined with the syllables *ca* and *ka*, followed by *namaḥ*, [constitutes the mantra].
This shall be the root mantra, expressing Caṇḍarudra.
The letter *ca* joined with a dot (*dīpa*) expresses the heart and the other limbs.
Therein, the weapon-mantra (*astra*) should be with the *anusvāra*, while [the head-mantra] is with the *visarga*.
Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the collection of mantras, one should display the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*).
Thereafter, one should offer worship to him, consisting of the form established as the Linga.
Placing a flower in the left hand, one performs the worship with the right hand.
Having grasped [the flower] from the top of the *liṅga*, one should place it upon the pedestal.
Swiftly taking the flower from the left hand with the right hand,
the wise one should offer it by tossing it onto the top of the *liṅga* without touching it.
Having made the head of the *liṅga* empty, the practitioner should never remain there;
for when the head becomes empty, a terrible obstacle arises.
Therefore, the wise one should perform that worship upon the back of the pedestal (*pīṭha*), accompanied by the *Caṇḍa-mantra*.
Having taken it, one should offer it to Caṇḍarudra with the head restrained;
for that which has issued from the pedestal of the Liṅga and been offered to Caṇḍarudra is called "nirmālya" (remains of the offering) consecrated by mantra, as stated in the Tantra.

Having offered the *argha*, the mantra-practitioner should dismiss [the deity] with the words "Forgive me," and by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā* and inhalation (*pūraka*), lead [the deity] back to the heart.
The ritual service, however, should be performed with the heart-mantra beginning with the *praṇava*.
One should prepare a seat for him and worship it with this very mantra.
Then, having worshipped the pedestal (*pīṭha*) with the five mudrās, the practitioner of mantras should worship [the deity] upon it.
One should send all the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) into the hand of a disciple to be discarded;
the wise one [should never] neglect it by casting it into a river or into fire.

One should quickly purify that place with three balls of cow dung. Having thoroughly washed both hands and feet, one should perform the bathing of the *liṅga* using fragrant water consecrated by reciting the Astra-mantra seven times.
Thereafter, one should wash the pedestal, and immediately after that, the temple;
furthermore, one should smear it with cow dung if it is made of clay or stone.
Then, one should wash one's hands, feet, and especially the shanks.
When the head [of the deity] has been sprinkled, one should then perform the ritual bath.
One must not step over the *liṅga* with the arm, nor should one wash one's hands there.
One should not perform the hand-washing in front of Caṇḍeśa by using the back of the pedestal.
One should cleanse the ground with proper method and never cause any impurity there.
One must never let drops [of liquid] fall upon the seat when rising. The Lord never accepts a worship that is defiled by intoxicants.
This is taught in the Caṇḍayāga within the Vāmadevīya-saṅgraha.
Then, with flowers in hand, the mantra-practitioner should enter the temple of Śiva;
with the syllable *phaṭ*, he should cast the garland before the face of the deity.
Those Vināyakas who assume the form of liṅgas and engage in fierce deeds flee in terror when [the yogin] repels them, being devoid of desire for the body.
Having offered the *argha* oblation to Mahādeva together with the remains of the previous offerings (*nirmālya*), the practitioner,
having properly clothed the most excellent of gods along with his mandala,
should first place him in the northeast during the sacrifice to Caṇḍīśvara.
One should meditate upon the exceedingly fierce Caṇḍarudra, mounted upon the emblem of Agni,
with quivering bimba-like lips and chin, possessing six arms and holding an axe,
bearing a sword and a shield, terrible in appearance, and adorned with a mass of matted locks.

One should offer [the oblation] with this mantra: "Salutations to Caṇḍarudra, the divine one who wears a rosary, who is clothed in a tiger-skin garment, whose head is bound by a crown, and who is stationed in the northeast direction."
One should offer that Śaiva garland and food offering to him.
Indeed, in former times, he was chosen by the God of gods, who was gratified by his ascetic penance,
through the granting of a boon concerning the remains of the offerings (*nirmālya*).
Whatever garland is given to him is supremely and most pure;
that same [garland], when given to others, is impure like excrement.
By its very nature, the *nirmālya* is not impure; it is the destroyer of sin.
Otherwise, by [offering] from an impure source, one would insult the god Caṇḍīśa;
he would undoubtedly be burdened with a great weight of sin.
Therefore, one should offer whatever food has been brought down as an oblation.
Having taken what is to be given, one should offer it to Īśāna and to Caṇḍeśvara.
The sacred sanctuary thus meditated upon brings about the destruction of all obstacles.
Having offered that to the deity there, one should dismiss him immediately.

The Lord, the God, being pleased and unwearied, bestows the fourfold aims of life for the sake of the next world; therefore, one should take refuge in the God. Having performed this, one should bathe Śiva with water consecrated by the recitation of the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra).
Together with its pedestal, its floral remains, and including the prostrations within;
if, in this manner, the floral remains remain in any one of these locations.
By the power of Caṇḍīśvara, no fault whatsoever shall arise from that.
In the Siddhānta known as Nila, it is stated that the sacred *nirmālya* is pure;
one should wear the *nirmālya* of Śiva with devotion, but one must not consume it out of greed.

By eating [the offerings], one goes to hell; by transgressing [this rule], one goes to a lower state. Śaṅkara does not accept his bathing water, worship, and so forth—[the merit of] him who worships Śiva while consuming the food offerings and the remains of the garlands.
Just as no one would resort to a patch of ground covered with leftover food,
so Rudra does not accept a man defiled by the remains of offerings (nirmālya).
He who drinks the bodily impurity of another becomes untouchable to him.

Therefore, a person should not touch ashes defiled by *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings). If one performs bathing and other rites with water from jars or similar vessels mixed with *naivedya-nirmālya*, Śaṅkara does not accept those [offerings].
Thus has this defect regarding *nirmālya* (remnants of worship) been declared in the Śivadharmas.
O sinless one, listen attentively as the knower of mantras explains the purification of *nirmālya*:
having first worshipped those mantras beginning with Sadāśiva.
Thereafter, one should worship the Lord who is the leader of the Mothers together with his retinue.
(Arudra:
"O Lord, what kind of *nirmālya* causes obstacles for the practitioner?"
"Tell me, O Lord of the World, [what is the rule] before the God of gods.
The Blessed One said:
"There would be no fault regarding the *kaivalya* [state], yet one should avoid the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings)."
As long as the essence of the mantra remains present in the liṅga, the fire, the sacrificial ground, or the water,
so long all those substances are certainly not considered *nirmālya* (remnants).
Whether in the liṅga, on the sacrificial ground, in the image, or upon a lotus in the water—

O son of Kaśyapa, through the worship of the Guru’s feet alone, everything attains the state of being *nirmālya* (offering remains), even without the attainment of *kaivalya* (absolute liberation). One should meditate thus.
And the continuous path of consciousness, born of the mind, intellect, senses, and self— abiding in its own nature and self-realized— this is Kaivalya in the Imperishable.
When established in the state of Kaivalya, the discarded offering (nirmālya) never returns.

Otherwise, O Nārada, the deity may be seized by fierce defects; likewise, there is no *nirmālya* (remnant offering) in the case of mobile liṅgas, those made of clay, those made of wood, those made of stone, those made of crystal, those consisting of mantras, or those [installed] within the body.
Having understood that the sequence is without support, those [offerings] are indeed not to be discarded as remains.
Then, having performed the cremation rite, one should place the mantra in the sky.
Thereafter, one should extract the original mantra in the form of the Manu.
Their forms are like the dust of stars, established within the wheel of Brahmā. Having relied upon meditation in the lotus of the earth and then in that which belongs to the sky,
otherwise they do not accept even the mere offerings of a consecrated guest.
There is no purification from the state of the Supreme Brahman;
nor [is there] that which has become stale, even if it stands before the deities.
When the Lord of Mantras has been dismissed, the oblation remains as the refuge of the deities.
All [lingas] devoid of mantras and the absence [of such] would become discarded offerings (nirmālya).
A linga made of earth, stone, gold, silver, or copper,
if marked with lines for the eyes, all becomes a discarded offering.
Having extracted the portion, those who know the mantras should place it under the protection of the mantra.
Having cast it into unfathomable waters by means of the piercing of the exhalation of the wind,
everything that has come down through the sequence of the eastern stream shall attain the state of being discarded as floral remains (nirmālya).
For thus it was said by Maheśa in the *Pārameśvara* known as the *Haṃsa*:
"He who is proclaimed as Caṇḍīśa is indeed [the lord] of the unmanifest *liṅga*.
O Pārvatī, whatever has been seen by him, as soon as it is offered—
even if it merely touches the liṅga, such as an infinite offering of flowers and the like—
whether it has been formally given or not, that is called *nirmālya* here.
That which has not been offered should not be taken, especially in the case of a manifest *liṅga* made of metal that stands upon a separate pedestal;
indeed, for those made of metal, there is no such thing as *nirmālya* (remnants of an offering).
O Pārvatī, that which is given to Caṇḍarudra and smeared with ashes is to be known as *nirmālya*;
it does not exist otherwise.
Even one who is initiated, having known [this] again and again, should not step over the *nirmālya*.
For him, the initiation, the observance of the vow, and likewise the ritual of ascending the sacred thread (*pavitrārohaṇa*) must be properly performed by the Guru; otherwise, one would go to hell.
If an initiated person, struck by delusion, should consume the remains of an offering (*nirmālya*), [he falls].
Even one who performs a hundred million recitations may fall into the Raurava hell;
I do not see any auspicious accomplishment for him by any means whatsoever.
For if one who holds *darbha* grass should consume [the substance] even once without knowing [the rules], [he will suffer].
Having performed three *candrāyaṇa* fasts, he attains purification of his body.
Thus, O Pārvatī, by eating the sacrificial offering (*bali*) of Lord Caṇḍeśa,
one incurs great sin through leaping over [the food], touching it, or giving it away.
If a fool, for the sake of the *liṅga*, even takes so much as a mere *likā* (a small measure) stuck on the tip of his nail,
he causes his lineage to fall— ten ancestors and ten descendants.
That [food] which neither the gods nor guests or Brahmins accept [is likewise lost].
Upon seeing one who lives off the emblems [of the deity], one should recite the Aghora mantra ten thousand times;
if seen through negligence, one is purified by a hundred thousand recitations.

Upon seeing one who sells *kaṭha* incense, one who engages in sexual intercourse with women of a different caste, or one who subsists on his own genitals, immediate bathing is prescribed. A killer of a Brahmin is purified in a *kalpa*, as is a killer of an embryo and a killer of a father.

And one who steals the property of Śiva shall not be purified even in hundreds of millions of kalpas while remaining in the Raurava hell; this is the truth, and not otherwise. Thus, in the *Śrīkaṇṭhī*, Śrīkaṇṭha has prescribed the rule regarding the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*).

The property of the deity (*devasva*), the substance belonging to the deity (*devatādravya*), the offering (*naivedya*), the one who presents the offering (*nivedaka*), the substance for Caṇḍa (*caṇḍadravya*), and the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*)— these six types of *nirmālya* are traditionally taught.
The property of the deity belonging to the Lord of the village and so forth is *devasva*, while cloth and other such items belong to the deity (*devadravya*).
The food offering prepared for him is the *ucchiṣṭa* (remnant) of the God, which is presented to the *nivedaka*.
That which is given to Caṇḍa is the *caṇḍadravya*; the *nirmālya* is cast outside.
Furthermore, even the *nirmālya* remaining on the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) [is discarded] once the God has been dismissed.
From the gift of meat one is born as a flesh-eater; from eating it, one becomes an elephant.
From leaping over [the offerings], there is a loss of spiritual power (*siddhi*); by going and taking them, one becomes a wolf.
Just as by giving to a *caṇḍāla* one becomes a dog, so too by selling them one becomes a corpse-eater.
From touching [the *nirmālya*], womanhood arises; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever has been touched by the *nirmālya*, whether by a human being or a beast, [the merit] therein is reduced by one-quarter due to touching, stepping over, and consuming it, as previously stated.
But that which enters as a secondary consequence through the grace of sandalwood and the like—
[it is found] in the fourth part of the remains of offerings (nirmālya) at the abodes of perfected liṅgas and so forth,
and in those of the Guru, the sacred books, the Nāgas, the Fire, and the host of yogins.

Just as there is no *nirmālya* for the mountain-dwelling Yakṣas and Mothers in the case of Śiva, so it is not [forbidden] regarding lingas made of jewels, gold, and the like, nor in the case of mobile images, paintings, or circumambulation. (52a)

One should not offer remains of offerings (*nirmālya*) even to gurus or to divine images. However, in the case of a river current, the offering of scents, lamps, and so forth— including mantra-worship during worship— is never considered defiled by such remains.
When a *liṅga* has been consecrated— whether it be mobile or immobile—
no impurity arises from the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*) until the completion of the fourth-day rite (*caturthī-karma*).
This applies to *bāṇaliṅgas*, mobile *roha-liṅgas*, *siddha-liṅgas*, and self-manifested (*svayambhū*) *liṅgas*.
And in all images, one should not appoint Caṇḍa;
likewise even in the ritual procedure for the Lord on the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) when it is joined with the meditation on non-duality (advaitabhāvanā).
Having thus consecrated the Caṇḍas, one should remove the defect of Caṇḍa.
The characteristics of *nirmālya* (remnants of worship) have been declared in six ways by the venerable Somaśambhu:
that which is known as the property of the deity (*daivadravya*) must not be given away to anyone;
it must not be neglected, nor should divine property such as ornaments and the like be taken by oneself.
The impure [substance] given by Caṇḍīśa is purified when established in the *liṅga*.
Indeed, the substance that has undergone transformation and modification falls away from the *liṅga* to the outside.
[I offer this] to the one washed by the pure moon, O River; *oṃ svāhā*, to the one with the sound of Caṇḍa, *huṃ phaṭ svāhā namaḥ*.
One should meditate on Krodha and likewise the Netra-caṇḍa mantra in the location of the eyes.
That which is constantly touched by the remains of offerings (nirmālya), such as the mouth and other parts, does not become defiled.
Daṇḍa, together with his limbs, should be worshipped with his own āsana-mantra.
One should worship the bull, the trident, and the two door-keepers with the *argha* water consecrated by their respective mantras.
As before, there is the expulsion of the three obstacles (*vighna*), the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), and the worship of the heart.
Then, as previously, one prepares the *argha* vessel, performs the worship, and subsequently the invocation (*praveśana*).
A slight distinction regarding those who have been initiated is here briefly stated:
when one dismisses the mantra, the liṅga should go to the state of Caṇḍa.
Whoever removes the worship from Śambhu when he is present in the *liṅga* incurs a fault equal to the breaking of the *liṅga*.
Therefore, one should perform worship here through the method of Brahman, beginning with the Unborn (*Ajāta*) and ending with the Lord (*Īśa*).
Having cast [the flower] into the middle of the *liṅga*, one should meditate on the Lord whose body is the *bindu*.
One should place the offering from the *liṅga* upon the back of the pedestal in the direction of the Lord (the northeast).
Taking a flower with the left hand, one should perform the worship with the right hand.
Quickly, with the left hand one should offer a flower,
and with the right hand the wise one should offer it upon the head of the liṅga.
A liṅga whose top is empty is obstructed by terrible obstacles.
One should then withdraw that worship dedicated to the mantra of Caṇḍīśa from the back of the pedestal.
Having offered a flower with a highly valuable oblation, one should dismiss [the deity] saying, "Forgive me.
Then, [one should perform this] at a Liṅga consecrated by the aforementioned mantras, or at a Bāṇaliṅga, or even at a mobile Liṅga.

One should not perform the visualization of Caṇḍīśa when throwing [the offering] into fire or into deep water; rather, one should purify the dwelling with the water of the weapon-mantra and the ground with cow-dung. When [the ritual] is performed threefold upon the body, it is done without touching the *bindu* or the head.
One should wash [the deity] up to the teeth; however, if the head is touched, one must perform a ritual immersion (*majjana*).

Afterwards, the wise practitioner should offer [the water] once upon the *liṅga* with the *saṃhitā* mantra. With the water from the *argha* vessel, one should likewise make the *tāla* gestures and the scattering of drops (*vipruṣ*).
One should deposit [the seed-syllable] at the top of the *liṅga*; this is declared to be the "purification by evacuation" (*recana*).
Whatever substance may be present there—whether gross, subtle, or supreme—the obstacles residing in the pedestal and the chamber of the *liṅga* exist in the form of those very substances.
The practitioner of mantra should destroy [impurities] with his mind and perform the ritual bath with weapons;
this is the procedure prescribed for the offering remains (*nirmālya*) by those engaged in ritual action.
The Gaṇas are said to be of two kinds, existing in reliance upon the *liṅga*.
One should effect their expulsion so that purity may be attained.
Some have bodies born of the elements (*bhūta*), while others have bodies consisting of mantra and are bestowers of liberation.
The powerful obstructors of the *liṅga* reside in three places:
those born of spirits (*bhūtajāḥ*) are to be known as residing in the temple, while those whose bodies are composed of mantra reside in the sacred seats (*pīṭha*).
Those whose bodies grant liberation indeed subsist upon Śaṅkara within the *liṅga*.
Thus it was taught by Śambhu in the *Bṛhatkālottara* scripture:
"The Gaṇas are said to be of two kinds, just as they are described in the *Bṛhadvāthula*:
the first consists of those dominated by *rajas*, and the second is Caṇḍarudra."
The third is Raudrarūpa, while the fourth is Caṇḍāgra;
the fifth is Mahācaṇḍa, and the sixth is Sitavaktra.
They know the seventh to be Sitanāda and the eighth to be Grasana.
Assuming the forms of Umā, they are free from obstacles and established on the path of the seats (pīṭha):
Piṅgala, Harahuṅkāra, the radiant Kṛṣṇapiṅgala,
Kālāntaga, Kapālīśa, and likewise Saṃhārakāraka.
These obstacles, assuming the form of lingas, are situated upon the linga. These obstacles are all extremely fierce and are stealers of the sacrifice;
they must be worshipped with effort by means of the Śiva-weapon (śivāstra) in its foremost form.
The wise one should wash the *liṅga* with the *Śivāstra* mantra; of this there is no doubt.
One should wash the pedestal (*pīṭha*) with the *Mahāpāśupatāstra*.
For all mantras, the *Netra* mantra is traditionally held to be common to them all.
In the same way, for those whose *liṅga* is unmanifest (*avyaktaliṅga*), the *bāla-liṅga* is praised;
this applies to both the support and the supported, as well as to the *bāṇaliṅga* and the *mṛtyujit*.
Indeed, the state of being common to all is established in the Mahālakṣmīmata: "Wherever the Śrīmṛtyujit mantra— whether it be one for a specific purpose or common— is practiced,
there exists neither *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) nor any impurity."
And so it is seen in this *Pañcāśikāgama*:
"I do not know how that remains of the offering (*nirmālya*) arises through this mantra;
[it is used] during consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), worship (*pūjana*), and for the two vessels of the *argha* offering."

In the consecration by fire (*agnisaṃskaraṇa*), as well as in the placement of mantras (*nyāsa*) and meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth, no conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*) should be made, because [the practice] is common to all. No confusion (*saṅkara*) shall arise; therefore, one should abandon [such differentiation].
This was indeed taught by Śiva even in the *Mṛtyuñjayavidhāna*.
Thus ends the ritual of ablution with the Weapon-mantra (*astrasnāpana*) for the pacification of the threefold obstacles.

There, upon that which has been washed with the Weapon-mantra, one should perform the preparation of the seat (*āsana-kalpana*) as before. Having offered the *argha* water together with flowers, one should contemplate the dissolution [of the universe] starting from Kālāgni. First, one should contemplate the Support-Power (*ādhāra-śakti*), and above that, the Root-nave (*kanda*), the Spine (*ṛṣṭhī*), and so forth.

Having fashioned the lotus of Vidyā, which has the stream of Māyā as its interior and the fifty phonemes as its stalk; which stands upon that [Māyā] as its foundation and possesses the eight petals of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvara), who are exceedingly white and radiant; which has a mass of filaments consisting of the multitude of Niyata-mantras; whose interior is beautified by being encompassed by the pericarp itself through Śakti; and which possesses the nine seeds of the nine powers, beginning with Vāmā—[one should contemplate it].

Having meditated upon the triad of measures (mātrās) that constitute the *praṇava*—an incomparable radiance like the orbs of the sun, moon, and fire—as the source of bliss and illumination within the filaments and the pericarp [of the lotus], one should install the supreme blue form. This is indeed the "contracted seat" (*saṃkṣiptāsana*); it is then described as expanded in sequence: having invoked Kālāgni-Śiva, who reaches down to the seven netherworlds, there arises the earth, then the ocean of milk, and above that, the thousand-petaled lotus.

One should place Dharma and the other [qualities] upon those petals starting from the southeast (Āgneyī). On the northern, southern, western, and eastern lotuses are Dharma and the rest. This group beginning with Dharma is placed for the sake of increase and to prevent obstruction.

White, red, yellow, and black are their colors in sequence; here, the fourfold group beginning with Dharma resides. That which is in the middle of these two is variegated (*śabala*), due to the application of their respective colors. Dharma and the others are: Dharma, Knowledge, Dispassion accompanied by [the power of] Sovereignty.

Furthermore, the subsequent [elements], beginning with Dharma, are those same four. The eightfold group beginning with Dharma has been declared to be the foundation (*pādabhūta*). For that which has four, its ages—Kṛta and so forth—are to be meditated upon like staffs (*daṇḍavat*).

To the east of that, below it, are those very [staffs], white-smeared and black-hued, holding staffs in both hands. Above that are the Vedas, possessing four faces, endowed with two colors, facing toward Śiva, and with their hands joined in *añjali*.
Moreover, the ages here are Kṛta, Tretā, and so on, as well as Dvāpara and Kali; the Vedas are also the Ṛgveda and Yajurveda, sung under the names Sāma and Atharva.

(54b) Having fashioned the illusory animal (*māyātiryak*) upon the pedestal (*pīṭha*), one should place [the syllables] starting from the southeast in the form of the sun and resembling the moon, and likewise beginning from the northeast with the *vidyā*. This pedestal, becoming extensive, possesses a pericarp and a hundred-petaled lotus. Its filaments are fashioned by the groups of letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ha*, along with the *ya-śa* group. With petals and filaments... [the goddess] whose cheeks possess a reddish luster like the shadow of a broken earring at the waist, and whose face has surpassed the bimba fruit in beauty, rests upon her beautiful hips.

Regarding the designations of the vowels: starting from the petal in the southeast (Āgneyī), there are the eight Śaktis, beginning with Vāmā; namely, Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Śakti, Kālī, Kalavikaraṇī, Balavikaraṇī, Balapramathanī, and Sarvabhūtadamanī. Behind these, situated like a girdle, is to be known the supreme goddess named Manonmanī, the ninth and most excellent Śakti. Thus was the excellent [teaching] spoken by the Lord in the *Rurusūtras* according to the method of the descent of Nandīśvara.

The practitioner of mantra should gradually distinguish the forms of the seats as they were spoken [by the Lord]: the Mukulyā and the Āsanākṛti. Thus there are two mudrās of the seat. One should bind them in sequence upon the teeth.
Their characteristics were stated by the All-pervading Lord in that very same place:
"Having fixed the *añjali* [gesture] and being composed, one should [place it] on the various parts."
One should recognize the *mukulī* [mudrā] as having the fingers slightly contracted;
one should extend both hands, restrained at the region of the heart.
The fingers should be spread out, and thus one should display the *padma* (lotus) mudrā.
"The ritual placement (*nyāsa*), however, should be performed with sprinkled flowers and balls of fragrant paste.
Thus, in the *Pauṣkara*, there is a distinction of materials regarding the procedure for the placement upon the seat.
The immeasurable supreme deposition is shown for the practitioner and others.
First there should be the deposition of power (*śaktinyāsa*), and immediately after that, the ritual action;
one should then perform the [deposition] beginning with the sprout (*aṅkura*).
Consisting of light, greatly radiant, and blazing with shimmering rays—
thus one should sequentially place knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty.
White, red, yellow, and black are situated in the southeast and the northeast directions.
Those feet, which have the form of lions, possess three eyes and are renowned for their ferocity;

they consist of Śiva and Śakti and should be installed by the mantra-practitioner, O Goddess worshipped by heroes. Adharma, lack of knowledge, lack of dispassion, and lack of sovereignty [are to be placed] in the eastern direction.
The northern limit should be established; the limbs, the smiles, and the colors,
as well as the connecting pins which resemble the flax flower—
these, O beloved, are to be known in sequence as the Vedas and the Yugas.

One should visualize the lower covering as red and the upper as white; one should know that to be *tamas*. One should visualize the filaments as white, red, and yellow, according to their positions at the base, the middle, and the tip.
The pericarp is like gold and the seeds are green.
One should place Vāsā on the eastern petal, Jyeṣṭhā residing on the southeastern petal,
Raudrī on the southern petal, and Kālī on the one that is beyond the range of sight.
One should place the goddess Kalavikaraṇī on the western petal;
one should place Balavikariṇī resting upon the northwestern petal;
and one should seat the goddess Balapramathinī in the northern direction.
One should place the Sarvabhūtadamanī-śakti in the northeast,
the goddess Manonmanī in the center, and the Śakti-maṇḍala in the northwest.
In the center, one should contemplate Manonmanī, possessing the splendor of a thousand suns.
Having placed the Sun upon the petal and the Moon upon the filament,
O Goddess, one should not place the Vaṃ-maṇḍala upon the pericarp.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara are recorded as the names for the mandalas.
One should subsequently place the great preta (mahāpreta), laughing and conscious.
One should place the entire seat of Bhairava with the syllable Om (praṇava).

Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, one should then effect liberation. When [the time comes] for the form of the flower, one should visualize the complete Lord Bhairava above the head, who is the enemy of the mass of frost.
O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, one should fashion the faces with the thirty-two syllables, blazing like a flickering lightning flash, through profound meditation;
from the head down to the feet, beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.

One should perform the visualization for purification according to the division of the thirty-eight *kalās*. One should also visualize the nine principles (*navatattva*), the three principles (*tritattva*), the group of nine called Bhairava, the limbs of the Vidyā, the immovability, and the Razor (*kṣurikā*).

Then one should project the three powers (*śaktitraya*) in the right, the left, and the middle region, O Mistress of the Gods; thereafter, one should contemplate the form of the Lord Svacchandabhairava, who bestows the fruits of all desires.
The man who, with a disciplined mind, meditates upon her, quickly attains perfection.
That supreme power Aghorī, who was previously described,
should be placed upon the lap of Bhairava after he has been worshipped.
Indeed, just as the form of Bhairava is, so too is that of Bhairavī. Then, by means of the supreme seed-syllable, [one contemplates] the Supreme, the ultimate cause,
which is self-quiescent, partless, pure, all-pervading, and stainless.
Having invoked the Supreme Lord, who is unwavering and beyond all instruments,
and having established the God according to the prescribed rite, one should then perform the placement of the six limbs.

O Goddess of gods, one should offer water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), the respectful offering (arghya), and thereafter a welcome (svāgata); then, one should effect the presence (sannidhāna) [of the deity] and restrain it within Niṣṭhurā.
Having fumigated with perfumes, flowers, and incense, one should worship her.
The ritual of placement (*nyāsa*) and the procedure for invocation (*āvāhana*) are clearly elucidated in the *Svacchanda*.
Consciousness, the imperishable light, resides in the center of the heart-lotus;
it has the form of a *kadamba* flower, is the universal form, and possesses the luster of a gem.
O twice-born one, like a great jewel-lamp whose form is clearly manifesting its vast radiance,
[the light] issued forth from the apertures of the ears and the nostrils,
filling the cavities of the hollow gourd-like vessel that was joined with the great lamp.
Just as light departs from the body when it is obstructed by a mass [of darkness], so indeed does [the deity depart].
Having thus previously understood the power of the mantra according to its true nature,
one should act so that its presence may be established when the time for worship has arrived.
One should contemplate one's own awakening, the great bliss, within all things;
O Goddess, it surges outward like a reflection in a mirror.
Just as the wind, though omnipresent, is perceived by means of a fan.
In the same way, the omnipresent God is invoked in sacrifices and other rites;
for the Great Self, who is independent and whose purpose is manifold,
there is no need for the village of physical movement arising from summoning or dismissal.
Just as a lamp is lit from another lamp, so too does one's own consciousness manifest externally;
one should contemplate it as both distinct and non-distinct, as a libation and a reflection.
This is the correct invocation, as described by Śrī Jayā.
This very [purpose] has been revealed by the Goddess according to the opinion of Cakreśvara.
(56b) Thus ends the purpose of the invocation.

Afterwards, they call Śiva that which pervades all principles without exception within the form [of the body]. Having ascended from the levels frequented by the lords of the causes, beginning with Brahmā, by relying on the state of the Emitter (Udyantṛ) and uttering the root mantra ending in a prolation (*pluta*), one should dissolve slightly into the abode that is the terminus of sound (*dhvaninidhanadhāman*).

Then, having returned by the process of emanation and experienced the state of essential identity (*sāmarasya*) among consciousness, mind, breath, the designator, and the designated, one should contemplate [the deity] in the center of the heart-lotus, whose form is like a shimmering, incomparable light-star, and lead it up through the path of the Suṣumṇā.

Having grasped [the hand] with the *śāntamudrā*, one should place it on the neck of the venerable Nārāyaṇa. This is not desired in one’s own ritual manual (*paddhati*). This *śāntā* is proclaimed as having the thumb well-extended toward the right;
it should be employed by the wise in the installation of all mantras.
Thus, in the Svāyambhuva Śāstra, Śiva taught the Śāntamudrā:
having placed the two hands face upwards with the thumbs positioned in the middle of the palms,
this is declared to be the Āvāhanī mudrā for the rite of invoking the mantra.
With the fists clenched and the thumbs pointing upward— this is the supreme mudrā for installation.
Having again formed the fists and placed the two thumbs in the middle of the hands— this is declared as the *niṣṭhurā* mudrā for the confinement of the God of gods.
The wise one, having bent the little finger, should press it with the thumb;
this is renowned as the Śakti-mudrā, considered to be that which brings about the presence [of the deity].
Thus, having bound the four mudrās in sequence as declared in the Kiraṇāgama.
(57a) One should perform [the ritual] joined with summoning, causing to remain, arresting, and bringing into proximity. Here is the application:
Oṃ, Blessed One, come! Come! Oṃ, Blessed One, remain! Remain! Oṃ, Blessed One, become arrested! Oṃ, Blessed One, be present!
Having raised the thumb and formed a fist with the right hand,
the knower of mantras should place the hand of the left [into it];
likewise, he should place the remaining fingers over the right hand.
Having stated in the *Rauravaśāsana* that "the *liṅgamudrā* is of great power," one should,
having bound the mudrā called *āliṅga*, perform the veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*),
because it is seen in the world as the abode of bliss and is most secret.
"Therefore, because its nature is bliss, there shall be the veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*) of Śiva.
Thus indeed did the venerable Brahmaśambhu declare in his own *Paddhati*.

Having first pervaded [the deity] with the Brahma-kalas, one should effect the ritual of integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) according to the procedure for the placement upon the body (*tanunyāsa*). Then, by continuously bringing about oneness with the companion who is present, this rite of nectarization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) should be performed with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).

The arrangement of the seat, the preliminary sakalīkaraṇa, and likewise the invocation—this triad of rites which has been taught for the worship of Śambhu, one should know that it is called the *vidyā* [tattva], and this is what is termed the *tattvanyāsa*. And so the Lord spoke in the venerable *Pauṣkara-pārameśvara-śāstra*: "This entry into the *vidyā-tattva* of Śiva is indeed called *āsana*."
Then, having performed the placement (*vinyāsa*) of the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*), one should next perform the ritual of complete manifestation (*sakalīkaraṇa*).
Thereafter, one should invoke the supreme deity, both with form (*sakala*) and without form (*niṣkala*),
who is known as the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*), resembling pure crystal.
Having understood these three principles of Śiva, Ātman, and Vidyā in their proper sequence, the practitioner will swiftly attain the accomplishment of mantra.
Thus, in the *Rurusiddhānta*, the Blessed One proclaimed the fruit arising from the realization of the three principles (*tritatva*):
"One should touch with both hands [the body] from the feet upwards as far as the head;
this is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), which accomplishes all desires and aims."
Thus was it previously declared by Śambhu in the *Kālottara-śāstra*:
"Thereafter, one should perform the binding of Mahāmudrā with the hands in a pleasing manner. The union of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga* occurs through the pressing of the index finger and the thumb."
Oṃ, you are Gaurī, the goddess, and the liṅga is indeed [united] with the bhaga and so forth.
Oṃ, O Gaurī, holder of the lotus!
Oṃ, the heart of the bhaga is the liṅga; the heart of the liṅga is the bhaga.
"Salutation indeed to that Bhagaliṅga, to Rumārudra.
When the procedure as declared in the Pauṣkara Śāstra has been thus performed,
the rule for the offering of water for the feet and other items is now set forth.

One should perform the rites beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and ending with the incense (*dhūpa*), including the water for the feet (*argha-pādya*) and so forth. Since this was taught by the Lord in the *Raurava-tantra* regarding the *astra-mantra*, therefore: the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), and the offering (*argha*) should be given to his feet, mouth, and head respectively. Likewise, the flower should be offered above the head with the right hand facing forward. Herein is the ritual application: *Oṃ bhagavan pādyaṃ gṛhāṇa namaḥ*.
Oṃ, O Blessed One, accept the water for rinsing the mouth; svadhā! Oṃ, O Blessed One, accept the arghya offering; svāhā! Oṃ, O Blessed One, accept the flower; vauṣaṭ!
Thus, the invocation and other rites are performed, as conceived by Śrī Viśvāvarta.
Having invoked Śaṅkara with the Āvāhanī [mudrā] and the heart-mantra, having established him with the Sthāpanī [mudrā],
and having brought him into close proximity with the Sannidhānī [mudrā], one should inform him with the Niṣṭhurā [mudrā].
Then, with the Kālakarṇī [mudrā] ending in "phaṭ," one should [ward off] obstacles and those who cause misfortune.

Having formed the *liṅgamudrā* and paid homage with the heart-mantra, one should perform the veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*). Facing [the deity] with devotion is here called "invocation" (*āvāhana*). The wise have stated that "establishment" (*sthāpana*) is the act of seating [the deity] there with devotion.
O Jagannātha, that acceptance [of you] expressed as "I am yours" is the very vision [of you];
even though you are omnipresent, your presence [is felt here] and not otherwise.
Your proximity must be understood as extending throughout the entire ritual section (karmakāṇḍa).
The concealment of Śambhu is proclaimed as being due to his all-pervasiveness;
for Śiva, who is the seed of bliss and consists of the bliss of consciousness,
that which is his non-manifestation toward those who are not devotees constitutes his veiling.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa with the six mantras, one should then effect the unification and the immortalization of the self together with the possessor of the limbs (the deity),
so that one becomes invincible and empowered, like the sun with its fierce rays.
In that same way, the Supreme Lord, the God, should be meditated upon with His own limbs:
consciousness is His heart, sovereignty is His head, and the eight [siddhis] are His [eight] faces.
That which is not dependent on another and is mastery itself is celebrated as His crest-lock (śikhā).
The armor of the Supreme Lord is said to be impenetrable.
That light which serves for the purposes of burning, nourishing, and illuminating resides in the eye;
it is his irresistible majesty, the scripture that removes all obstacles.
Having uttered "namaḥ svāhā," likewise "vauṣaṭ," "huṃ," "vaṣaṭ," and "phaṭ" in their proper sequence,
one should present the water for the feet and other offerings while first reciting [the mantra] from the heart.
He offers water for the feet at the pair of the Lord’s lotus-feet, water for sipping in His mouths,

and the respectful offering (arghya) consisting of flowers, dūrvā grass, and unbroken rice grains upon the head of the Supreme Lord. Having thus purified the Supreme Lord with these consecrations performed by the Ṛṣis, [he continues].
One should worship according to the ritual procedure with the fivefold offerings, beginning with flowers and so forth,
as instructed by the venerable Somaśambhu in his *Paddhati* starting from the invocation.
Those [mantras] which liberate individual souls (*aṇu*) who are seized by sins and the impurities of their bonds.
They release various fruits from the tree of mantras;
they nourish the sufferings of worldly existence and awaken the deluded.
They [subdue] rākṣasas, yakṣas, serpents, and the like, as well as cruel grahas and vināyakas.
They cause thousands of other wicked beings to flee;
they, in turn, flow toward the excellent practitioner with sprays of the nectar of bliss.
For the sake of accomplishing the dual purpose, they have been declared by Śiva to be liberated.

Mudrās are called "seals" because they seal away the flood of obstacles; they are the powers of Hara, for such an effect is not seen to be produced by anything else when [the mantra] has been deposited. A mudrā should be known as threefold, arising from mind, speech, and body.

The delightful [mudrā] residing in the mouth of the Guru is the Vāgbhavā, whose form is the mantra; that which arises from the body through the movements of the limbs is known as the Kāyikī. This mudrā is remembered as being threefold: the Kāyikī by means of the binding of the hands, and the Vācikī preceded by the mantra.
"From the utterance of the blazing power (śakti), the mental mudrā is to be known. Thus, the definition of mudrā has been shown in three ways in the Umāyāmala, the Mṛgendra, and the Vāsiṣṭha.
(59a) The salutation, the banner, likewise the moon-petal, the pearl-string, the lotus mudrā, and the summoning [mudrā] should be formed.
Niṣṭhurā, Kālakarṇī, and likewise Liṅgamudrā—
these nine great mudrās should always be employed in ritual practice. O Brahmin, understand now as they are being proclaimed their defining characteristics.
Having understood the characteristics of the four kinds of mantras as they exist within their retinues,
and likewise the nine mudrās exactly as they are,
such a wise person attains completeness in all respects.
Having formed a hollowed cavity with both hands, with the fingers joined and extended,
it becomes the *namacchara* mudrā, with the left thumb serving as the sacred thread (*upavīta*).
Then, having grasped the left index finger with the right fist—
Having raised the thumb and joined it with the fingers of the left hand as a banner;
then, having joined the tips of the index finger and thumb of both hands, with the wrists turned upward—
this is the *śaśikarṇikā* mudrā.
When the two hands are in the shape of buds in the space [before one], that is known as the *mukulī* [mudrā].
That same [mudrā], with the fingers extended everywhere, becomes the *padma* (lotus) mudrā.
Having placed the two hands palm-upward and joined with the fingers extended, [it is the *saṃhata* mudrā].
By bringing the two thumbs across [the palms], this is the *āvahanī* mudrā.
When the two fists have the thumbs tucked inside and are joined together, it is known as *niṣṭhurā*.
That same mudrā, with the thumbs facing upward, is proclaimed as *kālakarṇī*.
With the fingers of the left hand forming a parasol and the right thumb raised upward,
this shall be the Liṅga-mudrā, the foremost leader among all mudrās.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the powers upon the two hands as prescribed, [one should proceed].
(59b) The practitioner must perform the binding of the mudrās within his own heart; indeed,
the binding of all mantras is intended to be performed in the region of the heart.
Others, however, should be performed by the wise exactly as instructed.
The practitioner of mantra should not reveal the binding of the mudrās;
he should practice the binding of the mudrās in this manner while residing with his guru.
The manifestation of the binding of mudrās is directly perceptible to those who know the conventions;
one should never perform it elsewhere without instruction.
Having placed both hands in the six-fold concealment (*ṣaḍgupti*), the mantra-practitioner, skilled in mudrās, [should proceed].
Otherwise, obstacles will arise during the rite to cause agitation.
On the seat, the practitioner should join the *mukulī* and the *padma* mudrās. There should be three prostrations at the feet, ending with the invocation.
The knower of mantras should apply the *mukulinī* mudrā to the pericarp, the *padma* mudrā to the lotus petals,
and likewise to the filaments and the seed-syllables.
By means of the power of the Lord, he should also employ the *dvija* mudrā upon the Lord of Knowledge.
And on the seats and on the four limbs, the knower of the ritual procedure [should place] Āvāhanī on the unborn (the head), Śaśikarṇikā on the left (the left leg),
Niṣṭhurā on the non-ghora (the right leg), and Kālakarṇī on the face (the right arm).
One should apply the *liṅgamudrā* of Īśa and Śiva;
the *namaskāra* for the head, the *dhvaja* for the heart,
the *śaśikarṇī* for the crest-lock (*śikhā*), and the *niṣṭhurā* for the armor (*kavaca*).
Then, one should employ the *kālakarṇī* [mudrā] on both of his arms.
For the *śaktis*, there should be the *padmamudrā*; one should apply those ending with the *mukulī*.
For the *hṛdaya* and other [limbs], there are the *dhvaja* and others, concluding with the *namaskāra*.
(60a) For the embodied [deities], one should sequentially perform eight [mudrās] preceded by salutation;
for all forms, whether upright or inverted, one should employ the liṅga-mudrā.

One should employ the invocation and so forth for the lords of the wheels, beginning with Ādyā and ending with Padmā. For Nandin, one should use the banner mudrā; for Mukula and Ṣaṇmukha, [the appropriate gestures];
and for Kāla, one should apply the harsh [mudrā], as well as the invocation with the limbs.
One should offer salutation to Gaṇendra with the lotus mudrā;
to Īśāna with the liṅga mudrā; to Kubera with the karṇikā mudrā; to Samīra (Vāyu) with the banner mudrā; and to Varuṇa with the bud mudrā.
One should employ Kālakarṇī for Nivṛtti and for Yama;
one should employ Āvāhanī for Agni and the banner for Brahmā.
The best of those who know mantras should employ the lotus mudrā for Ananta.
The knower of mantras should employ *kāśakarṇī* for every kind of weapon; likewise, for the hosts of Mothers and Bhūtas that have not been mentioned,
he should employ the fierce *uttiṣṭhadhvaja-mudrā* for the purpose of invisibility.
For summoning, one should use the Kālakarṇikā mudrā; for walking on foot, the Pātāla mudrā; for good fortune, the Padma mudrā; and likewise for attraction, the Vāhanī mudrā.
In all the aforementioned [rites], one should employ the Liṅga mudrā.
One should pay homage with a prostration and practice meditation with the banner-gesture.
Restraining the ears like those of a rabbit, one assumes the form of the seat;
the practitioner of mantras should gradually arrange the seat using the lotus-mudrā.
One should employ the *āvāhanī* [mantra] for the *argha* and *pādya* offerings, as well as for the incense (*dhūpa*).
One should ward off misfortune with the *niṣṭhurā*; likewise, one should obtain good fortune from the *aniruddhā*. One should drive away ill fortune (*kālakarṇī*) when it is applied to all locations.
One should employ the lotus mudrā upon the leaves and the flowers;
one should employ the *namaskāra* [mudrā] upon the food, the drink, and the various kinds of edibles.
Indeed, the *yojanā*, the *liṅga*, and the *mudrā* are proclaimed as the very form of Śiva.
The binding (*bandha*), the application of mantras (*mantraprayoga*), and likewise the ritual procedure of action (*karmayogavidhi*)—
these nine *mudrās* were taught at Puṣkara in the *Pārameśvara*.

Having thus worshipped Śiva with water for the feet and water for sipping, one should massage and rub [the image] and then bathe it according to the prescribed rule. Having rubbed it with lukewarm scented milk and washed it, one should sprinkle it with powders.
One should apply *bandhūka*, *karkaṭa*, and *toda*, along with *haridrā* and *priyaṅgu*, combined with *uśīra* and *candana*, at all times.

Thus, the bath prescribed for Gaurī in the *Amala-śāstra* regarding fragrant substances has been explained; one should therefore bathe [the deity] with that water using the Heart-mantra, and then offer incense with the Armour-mantra and the water-offering (*argha*) from the vessel.

In a secluded and auspicious location, one should perform a bath for the Liṅga— measured according to its size— with a thousand, a hundred, half of that, half of that again, or with ten or eight [pounds] of gold and other such materials.
"Or else, in the absence [of others], with earthen jars that have roots [or] are without [roots],
according to the number prescribed in the rule in the *Śrīgaurīyāmala-tantra*:
'O Goddess, those who perform the worship with earthen jars...'"
O Goddess, they dwell in the world of Rudra for a hundred brahman-years;
in copper it is a hundredfold more, and in silver it is increased by a lac. With those made of gold, the great happiness in the world of Rudra is multiplied ten millionfold.
O Goddess, as the fruit of merit has been proclaimed in the Śivadharmas:

a golden or similar vessel filled with four *pala*s of water is beneficial for the ritual bathing (*snapana*) of even a small, moving image measuring only one finger-breadth, such as one made of mung beans.
(61a) For the remaining [liṅgas], the increase is calculated by finger-breadths according to the intellect, starting from three palas and so forth;
when the stationary liṅga is one cubit in measure, the mobile [liṅga] should be one prastha and a half.
The increase for others should be by increments of eight *palas* according to the sequence;
thus the teacher Vairocana has declared this procedure for the *gaḍukas*.
The procedure for the offering of *kaḍukas* was taught by Śrī Somaśambhu.
That which was stated in my own manual (*svapaddhati*) is now being examined through its verses.
Immediately thereafter, one should bathe [the deity] at will with water that has been consecrated by the recitation of mantras, provided it is not warm; the procedure for this is now described.
Having placed the water-pot on the palm of his left hand, he removes the flower previously placed upon the top of the *liṅga* with that arghya-water; then,
having washed his hands with his own mantra, he is immersed in the *śaṅkha-mudrā*.
One should bathe [the deity] with waters that do not splash upward and which are not incomplete;
one may use milk, curd, ghee, honey, or even sugar.
Having performed the bath by means of these five nectars (amṛtas), one should then offer [the remaining substances] separated by water.
In this manner, the knower of mantras should sequentially visualize the Ocean of Milk and the others to provide pervasion; for the bath with ghee, he should imagine the Ocean of Ghee,
and for the bath with milk, the knower of mantras should imagine the Ocean of Milk.

In the *Pauṣkara-śāsana*, this fruit is proclaimed for the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*): [the fruit of] sprinkling with curd is like that of the ocean of milk; [the fruit of] honey is in the honey-bath; and [the fruit of] sweet water is in the sprinkling with the waters of the sweet ocean.
As many as there are [atoms] on the earth, the fruit of bathing at that [ordinary] linga becomes equal to that number through the act of giving;
from that, bathing with water at a [sacred] linga yields a hundredfold more.
Bathing with scented water yields a hundredfold more than that, and likewise, bathing with milk yields a hundredfold more than that.
A bath with curd yields a hundredfold merit, and one with clarified butter yields even more than that;
yet the fruit of this is equal to [the merit of] immediately drinking a draught of mṛdvīkā juice.
This has been prescribed for the practitioner by the illustrious Dharmaśiva:
namely, the self-arisen arrows (bāṇas) joined with non-dual mantras;
their propitiation (tarpaṇa), moreover, is said to be performed with substances such as the nectar of the left (vāmāmṛta) and others.

For indeed, when the ritual mark (liṅga) has been established according to the established doctrine (siddhānta) as conceived by the mantra, the fragrance [of the water] is a hundred times superior to water; the liquid (payas) is a hundred times superior to fragrance;
curdled milk (dadhi) is a hundred times superior to milk; and it is traditionally taught that [the clarified butter] is a hundred times superior to curdled milk.
In the teaching of the Right [Dakṣiṇa], a bath with wine is a hundred times superior to ghee;
a bath with honey is equal to ghee, as is a bath with grape juice or sugarcane juice.
A bath with liquor or with a corpse is even more excellent than that.
Even by performing the bathing of the *liṅga* and the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with only a drop as large as the tip of a blade of grass,
it becomes equal to [the merit of] a hundred horse-sacrifices.
One should always perform that which is prescribed in the Vāma, Trika, Siddhānta, and Bhairava traditions.
For those who have taken refuge in Bhairava, bathing with water yields fruit even greater than ordinary bathing;
this was indeed proclaimed by Śambhu in the Aghorīpañcaśataka:
"With water, milk, curd, ghee, and likewise with honey..."
With rice, herbs, fruits, and flowers in brief;
likewise with white mustard seeds, parched grain, and fragrant waters—for the one of great intellect.
Thus, O Maheśvarī, the great ablution (mahāsnāna) is said to be twelvefold.
This procedure for the great bath (mahāsnāna) is prescribed in the Svāyambhuva-kalpa.
It should be known that one hundred palas constitute the [ordinary] bath, while twenty-five palas constitute the anointing (abhyaṅga).
However, two thousand palas are prescribed for the great bath.
(62a) Thus has been declared the measure of bathing substances for the auspicious dharmas. Bathing is said to be of three kinds: inferior, superior, and middling.
O lady of beautiful hips, for each of these—curd, ghee, milk, and honey—the bath with one hundred and eight [palas] is middling; with one thousand and eight, it is excellent;
and with eight palas, it is the lowest.
Thus has the Yamala scripture been taught by Maheśa to the Goddess:
one should perform the daily *āhuti* with mantra, or even with water alone.
Thus satisfied, his ancestors shall emerge from the ocean of hell and attain heaven.

Having bathed Śiva with the *Śruti* [mantras] using *gaḍuka* measures of *pittṛdela* [water], and having worshipped the full vessel with fragrant water, fruits, and flowers while reciting the *saṃhitā* mantras; having consecrated the auspicious jar held in the hollow of both hands, one should contemplate that [nectar] as merged in one's own *dvādaśānta*, like the full moon, and as a continuous stream of nectar falling within it. One should bathe the Deity with that [stream], raised up until it reaches the station of the *bindu*.

Having thus consecrated this white, soft, and fragrant cloth along with the pedestal, having wiped it with sandalwood paste and other substances, and having offered loose flowers, one should then sprinkle water from the *śāntika* pitcher all around while reciting the *astra-mantra*. Then, the knower of mantras should perform the ritual of dismissal (*nirbhartsana*) with this mantra:
"O spirits dwelling in the temple, accept this offering intended for Śiva."
The five mantras, the spirits, and those who are their followers—
[these] are the two self-imagined mantras consisting of threats.
The form of the offering should be made in the shape of a parasol with white and yellow pigments,
or it may consist of a half-moon made with red and black colors; or else,
O Dear One, it may be a pure svastika or a śṛṅgāṭaka.

"It must indeed be made variegated with paints of diverse colors; [one should create] specific arrangements of flowers," so Śiva declared to the Goddess in the *Devīyāmala*. Having worshipped the God of gods with garlands, ornaments, fine silken garments, the sound of bells, fragrant incense for lovemaking, and the performance of the *ārātrika* rite with lamps kindled by worthy vessels, and having prostrated and requested permission for the external worship, one who has received that leave should worship the enclosures (*āvāraṇas*) in their proper order.
"One who is not veiled is not worthy of splendor, for by him the Lord is veiled.
Those who are to be surrounded by the Lord must first be surrounded by mantras characterized by power.
Thus it was stated by Maheśa in the Parākhya, within the *Sahitā*.
The worship of the outer enclosure is the duty of the Supreme Lord.

Then, in the places of enjoyment (bhogasthāna), [one should worship] Īśa in the east, Dakṣiṇa in the south, and Uttara in the north; likewise Brahmā, the five Hṛdayas, and those situated at the tips of Īśāna, Niśācara, and Anila.

Outside, in the eight directions, one should worship the Weapon (astra), as well as Viśva, Gaṇeśa, the Guardians of the Quarters (dikpālas), the Mothers, the Planets (grahas), and the Nāgas, within the lotus and the moving [elements].

The weapons beginning with the Vajra are worshipped in sequence; that is the external worship. This is the inner enclosure (*garbhāvaraṇa*), and that which follows consists of seven enclosures. Beginning from the east, there are eight [deities] joined with the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*) and the Blissful Ones (*sukha*). Among them, Ananteśa is in the east, followed by Sūkṣma, and then Śivottama and Ekanetra.

The first goddess follows Śrīkaṇṭha and Śikhaṇḍin, who are the forms of one and three Rudras respectively. Her attendants are Bhairava, Parameṣṭhin, Viṣṇu, Vighnakṛt, Bhṛṅgin, Skanda, and Aitī; likewise, there are eight lords of the Gaṇas. The practitioner of mantra (mantrī) should meditate upon Caṇḍeśvara and Vṛṣarudra according to their respective positions. From them [proceed] Indra, Anala, Yama, Kṣiti, Jala, Pavana, Dhana, Īśvara, Jayā, and Subhagā.

The Vijayā goddesses go forth from the unfortunate ones together with Aparājitā and Karālī; such is the group of Mothers (*mātṛgaṇa*). From them [arise] the planets: Ravi (Sun), Śaśin (Moon), Kuja (Mars), Budha (Mercury), Śukra (Venus), Śani (Saturn), and Rāhu.

After them come Ananta and Kulika, Vāsuki and Śaṅkha, then Mahāpadma, Takṣaka and Kārkoṭa—these are the seven—and likewise the eighth is Padma. Now, the weapons: the thunderbolt (*vajra*), spear (*śakti*), staff (*daṇḍa*), sword (*kṛpāṇa*), noose (*pāśa*), goad (*aṅkuśa*), mace (*gadā*), and trident (*śūla*).
