These are the weapons of the enclosure (*āstrāvaraṇa*) which, having been invoked, should be joined starting from there. In the *Niśvāsa*, consisting of nine thousand verses, within the *Nandīśvarāvatāra*.

Thus has been explained the sequence and the division for the worship of the seven enclosures (*saptāvaraṇa*). This is the sequence found in the *Gaurīśvarāgama*, which has emerged from the *Siddhayogīśvarītantra*. When [the ritual] is performed in brief, it should be done with the weapons (*āyudha*) and the world-protectors (*lokeśa*). Thus was it spoken by Maheśa at Śrī Hāṭakeśvara.
First, one should worship the lineage of gurus (gurukrama), then Gaṇeśa and the Mothers (mātṛkā);
finally, the world-protectors (lokeśas) together with their weapons should be worshipped with diligence.
Thus is described the single enclosure (ekāvaraṇa), which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

The procedure for the worship of the retinue of Nandīśvara’s incarnation is well known. Let the temple of the Lord face any desired direction, such as the east; however, the faces beginning with Tatpuruṣa do not abandon their positions in the directions starting from the east. Even in those cases where the faces beginning with Tatpuruṣa are indeed not situated in their own respective directions during the rite of worship, they must nevertheless be mentally conceived as being located in the east and so forth. [Objection: "This retinue, consisting of Dharma and the others, is fixed in specific directions while bathing; how can there be a rule for them based on a rotation according to the direction facing the Lord's face? [Response: Thus it is said.
"All these groups of mantras are directed toward Maheśa for her," so it was declared by Maheśa in the *Pārameśvara* [Tantra] of the *Pauṣkara*.
However, in the *Maheśa*, it is heard as: "directed toward Maheśa for him."

Having worshipped those [liṅgas] according to one's capacity with all the prescribed methods of ritual service and with various kinds of food offerings, one should worship the Supreme Lord. Thus it has been stated by Maheśa in the Indrāśāstra regarding the aforementioned touch.

"One should offer all ornaments, a fly-whisk, lamps, libations, divine weapons, garlands, betel, food and drink, a canopy, and a brilliant banner here, either with the *hṛdayodgītha* or with the mantra that is a limb of the sacrifice. Thus, having performed the invocation and so forth, [this was] spoken by Śrī Viśvāvarta.
(64a) Now, from the perspective of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), I speak within the teaching of Bhairava;
having performed the ritual action situated therein, according to the teaching of Bhairava.
Having clothed [the image] in beautiful garments made of silk scarves,
one should anoint it with agallochum, camphor, pearls, and other substances, and then adorn it.
One should worship it with various kinds of white flowers and further offer incense.
Having offered the *argha*, O Great Goddess, one should again display the mudrās;
having prostrated before the god Bhairava, the independent Lord of the Universe,
one should then, O fair-faced one, arrange the external enclosure.
One should install the five faces, each endowed with five mouths, starting from the northeast, proceeding to the east, south, and ending in the north.
One should worship those situated in the four directions: southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest.
One should contemplate the heart, head, crest-lock, armor, eyes, and weapon according to their respective divisions:
the heart has the luster of red, the head has the brilliance of yellow orpiment,
and one should meditate, O Goddess, on the crest-lock as resembling a flash of lightning.
One should know the armor (*kavaca*) to be smoky-grey and the weapon (*astra*) to be tawny-brown.
The eye (*netra*), resembling the form of light, is situated in the center.
Bhairava and the others are remembered as the mantras; they are the lords of the seats (*pīṭheśāḥ*) and the protectors of the seats (*pīṭhamandakāḥ*).
And on the second enclosure, one should likewise place the eight Bhairavas:
Kapālīśa in the east, Śikhivāhana in the southeast,
Krodharāja in the south, and Vikarāla in the southwest.
One should likewise place Manmatha in the western quarter, Meghanādeśvara as well,
and one should install Somarāja in the northwest and in the north.
One who is well-concentrated should place the Vidyārāja in the northeast;
and in the third [position], one should likewise arrange him from the Weapon of Lokeśvara. I shall state their names correctly and in proper sequence.
O fair-faced one, Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Samīraṇa (Vāyu),
Soma-rāja (Candra), Kubera, and Īśāna, the Supreme Lord—
these should be meditated upon in the form of the eight Bhairavas.
The vajra, the śakti, as well as the daṇḍa, the khaḍga, and likewise the pāśa;
the dhvaja, the gadā, and the triśūla—these indeed are the weapons of the world-protectors (lokapālas).
The vajra is enriched with many colors, and the śakti has a luster like gold.
One should visualize the staff as having the luster of split collyrium, the sword as having the brilliance of a blue lotus,

the noose as resembling the *kiṃśuka* flower, and the banner as white. One should likewise visualize the mace as having the appearance of coral and the trident as possessing a radiance equal to lightning.

Having worshipped the entire retinue, the connection with the Lord of Mantras should be performed by means of the root mantra; likewise, the connection of the channels (nāḍī-sandhāna) should be made. [One should worship] the weapons, the world-protectors (lokapālas), and the eight Bhairavas.
The five Brahmans, as well as the ancillaries and these enclosures,
one should pronounce in sequence until that which is the Lord within the womb [of the mantra].
Listen now to this union of mantras, which is indeed the process of supreme unification.
One should utter the deity endowed with short, long, and protracted vowels;
one should recite the mantra as long as it remains within the sphere of *nirvāṇa*,
from the lower wheel up to the upper, within the interval between the paths of the Moon and the Sun.
(65a) By means of the central path of Piṅgalā, through the sequence of vocalizing the phonemes,
[arise] the pentad of deities: Śakti, Vyāpinī, Samanā, and Unmanā.
Having sequentially divided everything down to the very end of the destruction,
and having visualized it as far as the ultimate limit, one should present the food offerings:
*ghārikā*, *vaṭaka*, *śaṣkulī*, and *modaka*.
One should display a sword, as well as shallow bowls containing various kinds of food— rice cooked with *śāli* grain, lentil soup, and clarified butter—
and many types of appetizers that are both pungent and sweet.

Free from stinginess regarding wealth, one should fill the foremost vessel of Śambhu with curd, milk, various types of fermented liquors, many kinds of human flesh, and whatever else is fit to be licked or drunk.
Afterwards, the *argha* offering should be presented with well-scented liquor.
Having declared the worship consisting of the enclosure (*vṛti*), the food offering (*naivedya*) is revealed.
Here, the worship within the enclosure is taught according to the *Svacchanda-śāstra*.

In this [tradition], because the eastern direction is conceived as being face-to-face with Bhairava, the worship should be performed by the devotees starting from the east, and not from the northeast (prājāpatya). This dialogue,
according to the Śrī Lakṣmī Kaula scripture, is for the purpose of providing consolation.
It is said there that, in connection with the performance of sacrifice and worship,
the three doors should be closed, but one should not close the western door. She, however, should first know [the way] facing the Goddess and the God.
The east is to be known as the west, and the west indeed as the east;
the south is to be known as the north, and likewise the north as the south.
This is the sequence common to all mantras, as spoken by Śiva.
(65b) This must be guarded with great effort from disciples of wicked intent.

Thus, I shall now describe the food offering (*naivedya*) according to the Siddhānta scriptures. In the east, one should arrange curds, milk, rice-pudding (*pāyasa*), ghee, meat, and wine; in the south, various edibles; and in the north, the food offering consisting of *pāṇisat*, which is pleasing to the heart of the physician.

One should offer an oblation (*bali*) here to Śiva with the placement of all the *mukuṭas* (crown-mantras) facing upwards, while performing the play of splitting and breaking pieces of the Guru’s body with the left limb.
Whatever food offerings (*naivedya*), including edibles and drinks, are presented to Śiva,
all that becomes equally pure according to the Vāma and Dakṣiṇa traditions.
In eating, wearing, giving, or even stepping over [it], one incurs no fault;
except for Caṇḍeśvara, O Vināyakas, it brings auspiciousness even according to the Siddhānta.
Thus it is stated in the Gaurīyāmala regarding the food offering (naivedya) in the five faces.
That which is offered at the tip of the door and other such places from the enclosure of the non-favorable [deities] is designated as *nirmālya*;
one should cause it to be given to Caṇḍarudra.
This specific distinction is proclaimed in the *Anala-siddhānta*.

Now I shall explain the mudrā, which consists of the substances mentioned by Śiva. That which is remembered as the form and substance of a substance in the rule for its division is indeed the mudrā of the substance; it is proclaimed to be both single and manifold.
Having joined the fingers together and placed them with the palms facing upward,
this is the mudrā of the right hand to be employed in the ritual.
Having placed the thumb upon the palm, this is the mudrā known as Gandharūpiṇī.
The ring finger and thumb of both hands joined at their tips, while the remaining fingers are extended;
this is the *rūpiṇī* mudrā of the garland (*sraj*).
With the wrists of both hands well-knit together,
the fingers slightly separated— this is the mudrā in the form of a flower.
Having brought the fingers together and turned them upward...
This mudrā, representing the form of incense substances, is to be employed in the ritual procedure.
With both hands, the index fingers and thumbs are joined together;
the remaining fingers are extended, and the mudrā is worn like a sacred thread (yajñopavīta).
With the palms facing upward, the two hands are joined at the tips with the thumbs bent;
this mudrā, which represents cloth and wealth, should be displayed.
In both hands, the index finger and thumb are joined at their tips.

This is indeed the *mudrā* of armlets; it assumes its form in the ritual procedure. Having extended the little finger of the right hand, the remaining fingers, beginning with the thumb, take the form of a ring.
With the tips of the two thumbs joined together and the two little fingers likewise joined in both hands,
while the remaining fingers are extended, this is the form of the *mukuṭa* (crown) mudrā. Having bound the *aṅgada* (armlet) mudrā, one should enter into union with the other.
With both hands, one forms the mudrā representing Kuṇḍala;
likewise, forming the mudrā representing the Kaṭisūtra,
one should join the two ring fingers (anāmikā) to form the mudrā representing the Graiveya necklace.

The mudrā of the crest-jewel (cūḍāmaṇi) consists of the index finger of the right hand placed upon the joint at the base of the thumb; the mudrā of the necklace (hāra) is that which wears a sacred thread. The mudrā of the cow (dhenu), however, is the personification of all food and drink.
These mudrās have been fully described as signifying the forms of the ritual substances.
Furthermore, regarding the mudrā of Sadyojāta, it has two names.
The wise practitioner should then cover the tip [of the finger] with the joint of the thumb.
For she indeed bears the form of all substances; thus,
in the ritual procedure, the single mudrā should be known as the embodiment of substance.
Having bound this mudrā in the form of a substance while remaining established in the ritual procedure,
the mantra-practitioner should contemplate all substances as being of the nature of mind.
Accompanied by the dhenu-mudrā, this [mudrā] brings about abundance.
The substance of the officiants is established by rule, as is the human substance itself.

*Oṃ, to Śiva, the sovereign lord of the form of substance.* This mantra, accompanied by the appropriate mudrā, is prescribed for the fulfillment and completion of the category of substances—both fixed and unfixed—as taught in the Pauṣkara-śāstra. One should offer water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) and water for the feet (*pādya*), and remain standing with the gesture of salutation (*praṇatimudrā*).
Thus ends the procedure for the ritual of the food offering (naivedya) mudrā.
Then, having performed prostration, one should subsequently begin the recitation (japa),
having taken up that rosary which is appropriate for the accomplishment of the mantra.
One who has renounced worldly undertakings should perform *japa* with the palms of the hands or a rosary of shells;
a householder, however, should perform it with a rosary of seeds.
That [rosary] is of three kinds, according to its sequence: *tāmasī*, *rājasī*, and *sāttvikī*.

Having offered it one hundred and eight times, or half that number, the Guru should cause [the disciple] to grasp the beads— though naturally devoid of qualities— as now endowed with qualities. This is done by means of ashes consecrated with the Astra-mantra and water interspersed between them.
One should worship with the five products of the cow, with fragrant scents, and with the auspicious water;

having performed the sacrifice, one should smear [the image] while reciting the mantra, and then offer prayers. This should be done by one who has fasted, who is pure, and whose mind is overflowing with devotion.
With rudrākṣas, conch shells, and crystal; with lotus seeds, leaves, and jīvika beads;
with gems, pearls, and corals of various colors; and sometimes with iṣṭaka stones—there stood men holding ten-bead rosaries for householders and those observing vows.
That cord is made of three types of material: wool, iron, or hemp; it may also be made of kuśa grass, triple-stranded, and joined together with cotton or some other strong fiber.
One should contemplate the Śiva-sūtra, the Self, and the senses as being mutually composed of networks of moonlight, or rather as a single unity; these,
clearly joined with the power of resonance (nāda-śakti), are the hands.
One should contemplate all [the mantras] as being illuminated by flickering lamps;
one should contemplate them for the disciple as having the form of supremely radiant splendor.
Having placed the right hand upon his back, one should mutter [the mantra] there for a long time.

One should consecrate one hundred and eight [offerings] for the heart-mantra and the others by means of a tenth part [of the total recitation]. One should sprinkle them with water fragrant with camphor and sandalwood.
The practitioner of mantra should display the mudrā prescribed in the sequence of his own ritual manual (kalpa).
"O Blessed One, Supreme Lord, grant me your own rosary.
Having received permission, one who is humble with devotion should take it and then illuminate the mantra.
While reciting the mantra daily, the summit of Meru must not be transgressed.
One should go, keeping Meru to one's right, making a circumambulation of it with the head turned toward the peak.
If, through negligence, one oversteps Meru or fails to maintain the threefold vision,
or if [the ritual] becomes worn, torn, or one becomes terrified, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred times with hands and feet joined.
Upon touching [the rosary] by one who has not been initiated, one should perform a thousand recitations (japa).
When the rosary is lost or frightened, then the japa should be ten thousand (ayuta).
One should dismiss it, worship it, and install the mantra day after day.

One should behold the god Śiva directly, five-faced and three-eyed. By drawing in the index, middle, and ring fingers from the thumb onwards, success shall arise; one should place [the thumb] between the two little fingers.

While the sun has not yet risen, he remains in Siddhārtha, which is delightful with incense and protected by garments, parasols, and weapons, engaged in the practice of giving, fire-offerings, and recitation. (67b)

Then one should perform ablution with water purified by the sun. Whether standing, waking, sleeping, walking, eating, or engaged in sexual intercourse, one should mentally recite the mantra; thus, even when afflicted by various diseases, one is not oppressed.
Then one should perform the bath with water purified by the sun.
This procedure for the rosary has been described to you for the sake of performing ritual acts.
Now I shall fully explain the characteristics of the rosary.
One should fashion [the rosary] from conch shells, or made of conch, or from *pautrajīvaka* seeds;
or it may be made of *raudrākṣa*, or of gold or silver, or from the hair of a cow's tail;
or it may be made of lotus seeds, or of crystal, or of *rājavartaka*.
One should make this rosary from auspicious gems endowed with stainless luster; it should be free from [excessive] knots,
with round beads that are well-proportioned, flawless, uniform, and beautiful.
The best of practitioners should not have the mouth [of the beads] made with a gap.
He should have a beautiful rosary made from beads that are neither too thick nor too thin, which are uniform, smooth, well-rounded, and as perfect as possible.
That which is made of great conch-shell, with an upward perforation that is even,
smooth, free from blemishes, bright, and reddish-brown in color—
that is declared to be "equal" (sama), and it is employed for the accomplishment of spiritual powers.

O Padmākṣa, the rosary made of putrajīva beads serves the purpose of all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*). Furthermore, another rosary string used here for the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) may be made of coral;
such a coral rosary is to be employed for rites of subjugation (*vaśya*) and the like.
For rites of inciting enmity and eradication, [the mantra] inscribed on gold is praised;
for procedures such as killing, it is traditionally held that [the mantra] should be made of rājavarta stone.
For burning and heating, it is traditionally held that [the mantra] should be made of ruby (padmarāga).
One should employ gold for worldly enjoyments and in rites such as subjugation;
silver is to be known by the wise for use in pacifying rites and for the sake of prosperity.

In rites for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), one should use [beads] arising from conch; likewise, in the ritual of Mṛtyuñjaya, one should use crystal. O fair-faced one, a rosary made of pearls is said to accomplish all things and indeed destroys all diseases.
Thus, all these sūtras, established and upright, O illustrious lady, must be applied according to the distinction between gain and loss— in rites that are obligatory,
occasional, or optional, and in every action as prescribed by the ritual manuals.
O beautiful one, I shall now describe the arrangement of the rosary:
it may be shaped like a cow’s tail, or have a middle like a barley grain, or likewise have a middle like an ant; it should also be uniform.
And thus this characteristic of the arrangement has been declared as uneven:
when it is coarse at the beginning and gradually becomes subtle at the end,
this rosary is known as "cow-tail-shaped" (*gopuccha*), O beautiful one.
That which is fine at both ends and thick in the middle is the beautiful *akṣasūtra* known as "barley-middled" (*yavamadhya*). It should be thick,
then fine, then thick again, then fine, and then even finer.
This is declared to be the "poison" (viṣa) [breathing], occurring when the movement of the breath is coarse at the beginning;
likewise, it is "subtle" (sūkṣma) in the middle and "increased" (vṛddhi) at the end, as long as one practices it.
This is the "ant-middle" (pipīlikā-madhya), which remains equal when observed with equal eyes.

One should perform the rite with Rudrākṣa beads according to the sequence of the face and back, like the method of the cow-path (gopatti), using lotus-seed beads for the livelihood of the grandson. One should place a knot on both sides and arrange the beads facing each other.
(68b) Even when it is half-equal, that [posture] is praised as virtuous action.
For this [posture] is situated in pairs; indeed, one is facing forward while the other is turned away.
One should employ the sūtra from the *Granthisūtrāntika* for the purpose of immobilization (*stambhana*).
For [the rite of] death and so forth, one should apply it in the opposite manner to the sūtra that is half as long as the knot. Furthermore, one should apply it on the side facing the knot.
Indeed, the *tarjanī* [mudrā] is praised for causing enmity and eradication, as well as for intoxication and delusion;
likewise, for quarreling and provocation, for casting down and destruction,
and for crushing enemy armies.
The *nāmikā* (name-finger) is said to be for liberation; such is the characteristic of the rosary (*akṣasūtra*).
O Goddess, one should cause it to be made, or else one should not bypass what has already been made.
For one desiring the highest accomplishment, O fair-faced one, the middle [finger] is used.
For subjugation, attraction, and good fortune; for the breaking of fetters;
likewise for rites of pacification and enrichment, as well as for the ritual of Mṛtyuñjaya;
for assemblies, the attainment of supernatural powers, and the protection of one's own army.
On a day when anger has subsided or on another auspicious day,
O fair-faced one, one should pull the rosary with the middle finger;
this is remembered as the rule for the rosary regarding the extraction of the beads and so forth.
In the daily rites, the occasional rites, the rites for desired ends, and in the procedures for attaining supernatural powers as taught in the Kalpas;
likewise in the previously unestablished rites, in those for pacification and nourishment,
and in the procedure for Mṛtyuñjaya, there is the method for quelling malevolent influences.

One should employ the *yavamadhyam* (middle-heavy) formation for the purpose of destruction, intimidation, causing [the enemy] to fall, and the act of paralyzing (*stobha*), as well as for the protection of one's own army.
However, for the increase of fortune and sovereignty, or during times of creation and the like, one should employ the *sṛṣṭā* (expanded) formation.
And during the *melaka*, O highly fortunate one, one should turn the cow's tail;
likewise for inciting enmity, eradication, provocation, and oppression.
In cases of insanity, causing terror, casting down, and the rite of paralyzing (stobha),
the mantra-practitioner should visualize that rosary as having its beads reversed.
Likewise, in killing, deluding, causing insanity, and crushing an enemy army.

In a quarrel, when the eye fails, or when the eyes have become distorted, one should employ [the mantra] for the paralysis of all goddesses, as well as of wind, water, and the mindless. Likewise, it is used against an enemy army, or for the piercing of a jar, or for causing miscarriage and the like.
O fair-faced one, a rosary in the shape of an ant is recommended for one engaged in all ritual actions who desires all accomplishments. However,
a rosary with an equal number of beads is supreme for accomplishing the meaning of all the scriptures.
The rules for the rosary (akṣasūtra) appropriate for all rites have been stated;
by performing them in their proper sequence, one shall attain the desired success.
The ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa), established according to its various applications, should be performed in accordance with the prescribed rule.
Having first performed the cleansing, one should place [the image] upon a cloth.
There, the ritual placement (nyāsa) should be performed according to one's own worship-rite. Having applied all the conjunctions and having worshipped in due order, [one should proceed].
The rule for the rosary is prescribed for daily rites, occasional rites, and rites performed for specific desires.
Understand the virtues and faults according to the method of attraction (ākarṣaṇa).
O Dear One, if the rosary swings while reciting, confusion arises.
One should likewise prescribe salt for the rite of eradication (uccāṭana), and also the Kali age. If the sugarcane thread is excessively long, the loss of wealth occurs.
For the sake of purification through expiation, one should perform daily recitation (japa).
(69b) And when there is a bursting, as well as when the channels are slack or drooping, O lady of good vows,
one should cause the penance to be performed through the increase of the piercing of the cakras.
When one who knows the mantra performs the *āsphoṭa* [ritual] day by day,
twenty-five thousand recitations are proclaimed as the expiation,
accompanied by the procedure for the personal sacrifice to the Lord Mṛtyuñjaya.
O Dear One, when a practitioner does not perform the rite of atonement,
his spiritual accomplishment (siddhi) will perish, or he will suffer from a very great disease;
or else death will come to him before long— of this there is no doubt.
When one is indeed weak in knowledge, one should perform the daily *sphoṭa* rite established by the ritual procedure of the self-sacrifice (*svayāga*) of the god Mṛtyuñjaya.
If performed with a rosary (*akṣasūtra*) ending in an odd number, a loss of merit arises.
If [the rosary] has been made without being recognized [as such], one should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
One should not make it with large beads, nor with very small ones, O fair-faced one;
rather, one should have the rosary-string fashioned from beads that are uniform, smooth, and round.
"One should have a rosary made of fifty-four or twenty-seven [beads]; thus Bhairava has spoken.
Regarding the ritual for the rosary: it should be ancient, intact, uncracked, unshattered, not mounted by oneself, and not prepared by another."
One should avoid using [the rosary] for activities such as the *argha* vessel or the *akṣasūtra*. If it becomes old, it destroys human power; if it cracks, there is the destruction of one's lineage.
If it is worn out, illness should always be known to follow, and if it breaks, death occurs even for one who has conquered death (*mṛtyuñjaya*).
One who performs ten thousand recitations after hearing [the teaching] once,
and likewise having made a "burst" (*sphoṭa*) while reciting the sūtra with his hand, and having performed his daily duties (*āhnika*), shall become one of the ten [who are freed from] poverty.
For that which is occupied by another practitioner will indeed cause the destruction of success.
However, in the case of attaining liberation through the mental [practice], or in the accomplishment of the powers such as *aṇimā*,
or in the *melaka* and other rites with sky-farers (*khecara*), the *pāśu* [should be] *karṣara*.
One should accomplish rites such as killing and expulsion through the power of speech.
A rosary made of gems, crystal, rudrākṣas, gold, pearls, rubies,
or great conch shells indeed bestows the highest siddhis.
With beads made of trapu, puruṣya, īri, sīsa, copper,
lotus seeds, coral, rājāśma, putrajīva seeds, and likewise with arishta, kī, kācī, clay, conch, and pīluka, one who desires middling success [should use them].
The *darbha* [mudrā] is produced from the fruit [of the hand], while that produced from the fingers is the youngest (*kanīyasī*).
Indeed, the drawing together of the index finger and the thumb is proclaimed as the best;
the drawing together of the middle finger is middling, and among men, [the drawing of] the little finger is the youngest.
One hundred and eight *mātrās*, half of that, or even a quarter;
one should not exceed this if one desires supreme accomplishment.
This is the classification of rosaries for optional rites according to the auspicious scriptures.
In the Vaiṣṇava tradition, however, it is specifically seen that this [method] is prescribed:
a beautiful rosary should be made, unseen by other people,
with beads (akṣas) the size of bones, made of large, well-rounded gems.
The size of an *dhātrī* fruit is considered the medium measure;
that which is the size of a *badarī* stone is declared the smallest.
[This may be] a full one hundred and eight, half of that, or even a quarter.
And one should perform that in all rites according to the procedure prescribed by the rules.
For the sake of attaining wealth, one should have an excellent golden [image] made therein;
for the sake of nourishment and the attainment of beauty, a silver one; and in rites for the ancestors, [one should use] [silver].
O tiger among sages, one who desires wisdom, vigor, and likewise splendor should indeed make the rosary out of copper of medium quality.
For the accomplishment of yakṣas and yakṣiṇīs, the three-colored [thread] is prescribed;
likewise, for the subjugation of rākṣasas and piśācas, it is made of hemp (sīma).
For the purpose of accomplishing the netherworld (pātāla), however, it is said to be made of yellow silk (harīta).
For the propitiation of the pannagas and nāgas, it should be made of bell-metal (kāṃsya).
Likewise, for the younger [spirits] and in rites of minor power (kṣudrakarman), one should make it of iron. Thus is recorded the application of threads made of various metals.
O best of those who dwell on the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), at the end [of the ritual], there is a division among those made of gems:
all those made of jewels increase longevity and health;
however, crystal specifically bestows liberation and is used for rites of pacification (śāntikarma).
I shall now describe, according to tradition, the supreme procedure for seeds originating from roots.
For the sake of good fortune, the first three should always be made of coral;
for the sake of liberation and the pacification of the eight defects, they should indeed be made of gold.
I shall now describe the objects found in water, which grant all accomplishments:
one desiring prosperity should perform recitation with lotus seeds and conch shells;
one desiring long life, progeny, and fame should do so with pearls, which bestow all accomplishments.
By means of the threefold classification beginning with "excellent," this triad bestows all accomplishments.
One of these should be selected from among them on an auspicious day.
Thus it is taught that the fruit [of practice] differs according to the distinction of form, specifically regarding the "victory" (jayā).
One should hold the rosary with the right hand;
one should place it only on the right side, never on the left.
One should fashion an upward knot for the *sadāmāla* [garland] of the highest [initiates],
a horizontal knot for those of middling capacity, and a downward knot for those who are not of the highest.
Having brought it around clockwise, the mantra-possessor [should place] the right hand [upon it].
One should receive this garland, fixed with knots,

from the presence [of the teacher] while meditating on the Lord of all Vidyās; it is said that by means of the exhalations moving forward along the line situated at the base of the little finger, it becomes "dark" (tāmasa).

Having performed the recitation (*japa*), the wise practitioner, by moving the middle finger and the thumb, and through the movement of the ring finger, the ring finger grants all desires. The middle finger is praised for attracting and nourishing, as well as for the recitation (*japa*).
In all rites such as killing and the like, one should perform the ritual action with the index finger.
A circumambulation should also be performed, like the circumambulation of the Lord of Nagas.
This is auspicious and brings about all accomplishments for all mantras whatsoever.

Thus has the rule for the rosary been shown in the Pauṣkara-Pārameśvara: the procedure and the characteristics of the rosary according to one's specific desires. Having understood this, the practitioner, possessing all accomplishments, should perform the recitation.
The Chapter on the Rosary:
Having taken up the rosary, which has been worshipped with perfumes and flowers, he—
his speech restrained and his self purified— should remain seated upon a lotus throne.
Having uttered the root mantra, one should contemplate it as dissolved into the *nāda*. Then, opening one's eyes and reflecting [on this], one should begin the recitation (*japa*).
The succession of syllables should be neither too fast nor sluggish.
Those desiring liberation should perform recitation throughout the day, making it equal to their very life-breath;
that should be understood as the process of withdrawal, which bestows the fruit of the abode of Śiva.
When the sound, having reached the ether, returns once again,
that should be known as the night; it is declared to be the very creation (sṛṣṭi) which brings about the fruit of all accomplishments, as long as it has returned to the heart-lotus.
O fair-faced one, the form of Bhairava within oneself should always be contemplated.
By means of the practice of inhalation (*pūraka*), it is joined with the three [syllables] ending in *ṣṭha*.
O Goddess, this is declared to be the secret that bestows the attainment of the triple perfection.
In rites for pacification (*śāntika*), recitation is performed mentally; in rites for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), it is said to be whispered (*upāṃśu*);
and in rites of sorcery (*abhicāra*), it is with audible sound. Facing north, east, or south, that which one hears oneself is proclaimed as mental recitation (*mānasa*).

Know that which one hears by oneself to be *upāṃśu* (whispered); that which others hear, O Goddess, is declared to be *saśabda* (audible). Thus has the procedure for recitation (*japa*) been proclaimed in the venerable *Svacchanda-śāsana*.
Even those devoid of bodies are slain, yet first those perfumed by virtues are liberated;
even embodied beings are released once they have reached the ground of mantra.
Because it protects through the act of contemplating (*manana*), it is therefore proclaimed as "mantra."
The wish-fulfilling gem has been realized through sacrifice as being like wood or a clod of earth;
it possesses neither measure nor accent, nor is it characterized by the difficulty of phonemes. It contains no deceptive letters, no [fixed] words, and no dependence upon the sequence of words.
There is neither blindness, nor consciousness, nor the object, nor the arising of intuition;
nor is there the manifest sound, the mantra, or the worldly [utterance] based on the organs of speech—
wherein the state of Agni and Soma exists through mutual conformity.
Therein, the speech that proclaims Brahman finds its firm foundation;
it is the source of mantras, the supreme reality, whose body is the universal nature of consciousness.
The first unfolding therein, which is filled with the perception of its own light,
eternal bliss, of a radiant nature, and devoid of the divisions of space and time—
standing at the very limit of volition, that is called the *nāda* mantra.

That very [consciousness] gradually attains grossness within worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*). Whatever is a mundane action is called a transaction; the engagement in transaction is established as being based upon objects.
O Beloved, that object is twofold in the form of the grasped and the grasper;
its life depends upon the conceptualization of mental constructs by infinite powers.
That object is the abode of conceptual thought, and its life is rooted in volition.
Volition rests upon the sentence; the sentence rests upon the word.
Words consist of phonemes, and those phonemes consist of the *tattvas*.
By means of the union of seed-syllables (*bīja*) and matrices (*yoni*), they attain the sovereignty of mantra.
Thus, those who worship the mantra whose essence is established consciousness enter the pure, supreme abode that is free from conventional signs.
When the mantra takes the form of the Person (Puruṣa), it then becomes inactive.
One attains freedom from delusion through that form; therefore, one should employ it within the power (śakti).
All this network of mantras has been declared as brought forth by power.
Situated in the center of the bulb (kanda) of the triangle, she flows through all the pores of the skin.
Slender like the awn of wild rice, flickering like a streak of lightning,
spreading with a curved form like a fine vibrating string,
the supreme *Kulakuṇḍalinī* is permeated by the essence of bliss.
(72b) That creative power, Sañjīvanī, gives birth to the sixty-four phonemes.
From that, the mantras awaken; from that, the powers of the senses [arise].
Then the mind, then the ego, then the intellect, and then consciousness.
One who has grasped the meaning of the Tantra should perform the recitation; otherwise, it is as described in the *Araṇya*:
"Those mantras that are devoid of their constituent parts are like clouds passing away."
Those who are burnt, those who are shattered, those whose lineage of teachers has been severed;
those who are pinned down, those who are bound, those who are deficient, those who are strung together, and those who are interlaced;
those who are asleep, those who are fainted, those who have grown rigid, those who are mangled, those who are shorn, and those who are slain.
Through the infusion of this power, they become bestowers of fruit.
Mantras existing in the state of the bound soul (paśu), consisting merely of the form of phonemes,
are fit for liberation only when their forms are nourished by Śakti.
The first three divisions—Paśyantī and the others—are indeed those primary qualities under discussion;
however, the fourth, or even the third, is merely its own innate form.
Its definition is established through its locus, its instrument, and its effort.
The three-word sequence of the mantra in its manifest form has been declared.
Having ascertained the meaning through the intellect, the embodied being joins the mind with the desire to speak;
he then stirs the fire of the body and attains the state of vital breath (*prāṇatā*).
From the region of the navel, the vital air known as *prāṇa*, impelled by strength, constantly moves upward; reaching eight locations, it is then divided.
Thereafter, through the impact upon the internal cavities, it attains its various objects.
The single form of the mantra becomes manifold in appearance by relying on states such as waking and so forth,
just like the manifestation of a wish-fulfilling gem.

The waking state consists of the senses, while the dreaming state is that which occurs without them; both are characterized by memory. From these, there arises a fourfold distinction for each of the others through mutual combination: the object of knowledge (*meyam*), the means of knowledge (*mānam*), the act of knowing (*pramāṇam*), and the knower (*pramātā*), respectively.
The conscious self (cidātman) is proclaimed as being with body, without body, and bodiless;
it is also celebrated as the transcender of the states such as waking and the rest.
It is without appearance, free from phenomenal proliferation, and overflowing with the bliss of the mass of consciousness.
The state beyond the fourth (turyātīta) is fully described as being devoid of both manifestation and emergence.
Consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, and action— these five powers, in their respective order,
have issued forth in the form of the states beginning with the one beyond the fourth.
By these very [verses] the Lord is described as having a great body consisting of five powers;
and this sequence of principles (tattvapaddhati) exists in the form of five pentads. Furthermore, through immersion in the essence of worshipping Him, that [sequence] is also said to be "I" (aham).

Of that very All-pervasive One, whose nature is not dependent on anything else for subsistence, there exists a prior power called Akula, which is distinct from Him and possesses His attributes as its own. Through its union with bliss, will, and sovereignty, it undergoes a state of diminution due to its unfolding (unmeṣa).
Due to the application of the fire of desire, [the power] becomes blunted;
yet, through the union of the emergence of desire with the mutual bliss of Nāda and Kula,
the Bindu flows forth in four ways as the withdrawal of the Light.
O Goddess, Kula-mālinī is sealed in three ways by the Visarga.
From Akula, the second group has emerged, consisting of five powers;
and beyond that is the Will, whose form is uncolored [by external objects].
Then, from the two banks of that [vowel] which partakes in the activity of fire, the pair beginning with *pa* arises through unfolding; thus, these are proclaimed as the consonants (*sparśas*). (73b)
Through the conjunction of powers, the differentiated will (icchā) attains the state of *ya-ra-la-ta*.
O fair-faced one, the power of unfolding (*unmeṣa-śakti*) indeed becomes the letter *va*.
By entering into the beginning and end of the will and so forth, they are proclaimed as being situated therein.
Desire itself, when overcome by the *uṣman* and resting upon the three times,
reaches the state of the *visarga* and dissolves into its own self.
These six short vowels are the root cause of all things.
And those rays of the sun are to be known as being of the nature of light.
Within the web of the solar digit (sūryakalā), the six digits born of the moon reside.
This is the supreme, true knowledge; this is the eternal yoga.
This is that state of the Lord of the Wheel within the wheel of the Śakticakra.
Here, O Goddess of the Gods, just as the Mantras approach the Mantreśvara,
so too do we, impelled by the Lord of the Wheel, constantly come forth as the Cillās.
O fair-faced one, whoever— even if uninitiated— knows this in such a way, he is liberated and rejoices, while others remain bound as sacrificial victims.
For this is indeed the supreme pervasion of mantra, just like that of the Lord of the Wheel.
Knowing thus the true nature of mantras, one always employs them;
all [mantras] abide in Śakti, bestow power, and grant the fruits of both enjoyment and liberation.
When the practitioner of mantra does not perceive [the distinction between] the paths of creation and dissolution, [he attains the supreme state].
Mantras that possess the nature of rising and setting yield little fruit;
even when impelled by the command of Śiva, they do not bestow enjoyment or liberation.
However, when the practitioner of mantra truly knows creation, maintenance, and dissolution, [he attains these goals].
(74a) By means of the form of their rising and setting, the mantras of immeasurable power then enter into the state of being servants; then they become the bestowers of knowledge.
And these [deities] appear before the practitioner, O fair-faced one.
In the *Śrīmad-mṛtyuñjaya* as well, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) resulting from recitation (*japa*) is revealed in this way;
how one should perform the recitation and the corresponding pervasion are here explained.
Having restrained the senses with the mind and being seated upon a lotus throne,
one should recite the root mantra and meditate within the heart upon the form of one’s own mantra as prescribed for one’s specific ritual action, dissolved into the *nāda* within its own cause.

The subtle body should enter Śiva within the lotus of the heart, which is the body of Śiva. From that state of being the *bindu* (the point), it attains the form of the *nāda* (the sound) and reaches the state of *śakti*. Having ascended there, one should press and gradually pierce the *kanda* at the root of the penis.

Moving counter-clockwise, one should pierce in sequence the supreme [state] located within the six causes of the navel; thus, for the sake of the goal, the mantra should not become absorbed in the *nāda*. One should contemplate the mantra neither in the *puṃs* [the individual soul], nor in the *para* [the supreme state], nor in the *pattra* [the petals], nor in the *śakti*.
One should contemplate those syllables as being strung upon a power (śakti) like jewels on a thread.
That power is to be known as fivefold: the gross, the subtle, the supreme (parā), the ethereal (vyomātmikā), and the auspicious (śivā), which arises there from the space of the heart.
And she abides as the support within the channels of the moon, sun, and fire.
Having equalized her while seated in the equinox (*viṣuvat*),
and having rendered the two instruments both artificial and natural, one should lead the power of Kuṇḍalinī.
The mantra, made manifest in the heart by means of the *pūraṇayantra*,
[is joined] with the two big toes resting on the earth and the two thumbs within them.
One should make the body erect, relying on divine means;
or likewise, by pressing the sides, one should fix the gaze in the form of Bhairava,
or, with the gaze fixed on the tip of the nose, remaining steady therein, one should fill [the breath] from the outside.
In that very place, one should fill [the breath] according to one's capacity; in an instant, the equinox (viṣuva) arises.
Having meditated upon the Lord of Mantras, whose form is the Bindu, situated in the center of the heart-lotus, shaped like a Kadamba bud, and located within the path of the Brahma-nāḍī.
Pervading the interior of the cavity of the palate by means of obstructing the force of the upward flow,
when a hundred tālas have been completed, the equinox (viṣuvat) arises in an instant;
at that time, there is no movement even by means of the breath, and this is known as the "artificial" [equinox].
In the Bhairava scripture, it is said that the hundred stages (*bhūmikā*) along with the twelve,
when focused upon as one, become an equinox (*viṣuvat*) by its own will.
Or, if one desires the pressure on the sides, there is the flow through a single channel (*nāḍī*).
As long as that thief remains within the body,
he may carry away its wealth from the left to the right, or from the entrance to the neck by force; yet, due to the absence of any further purpose, he turns back after having moved the limbs upward.
The vital breath (prāṇa) should be made to fill [the body] and carry [it] within the cavity of the heart;
thus is the gross Khecarī. The subtle Khecarī has the nature of the *bindu*. She flows like the fluid within a peacock's egg, consisting of the nature of internal discourse (*sañjalpa*).
Emerging from the two knots and following the path of the cavity of the palate,
the Vaikharī [speech] is like glowing embers, reflected in the orb of the fire-god's mouth.
That Madhyamā, joined with mantra, is its cause and its mistress.
The supreme [power] should be known as consisting of sound (*nādātmikā*), which is always undifferentiated;
it has the form of a flame of fire, and the unstruck (*anāhatā*) [sound] is within the lotus of the mouth.
Perceiving as pure consciousness alone, she is the Vidyā-Śuddhā who moves through the void.
She is the ground of all mantras; from her arise the rites of subjugation and so forth.
Having reached the Suṣumṇā, she is the Vyāpinī who reaches the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) due to the attainment of the supreme state.
The state called Śivā is indeed samanā, whose nature is the arising of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā).
It follows the path of Śiva through the six levels of sound beginning with "Bhu.
When the mantra becomes the Supreme Self (parātman), it then becomes inactive (niṣkriya).
Through association with a man, she falls into a state of delusion; therefore, one should establish her in the Śakti.
One should cause her to perform the sixfold ritual beginning with Indhikā, as will be described hereafter.
By means of these four [powers], she is constantly presided over by gross speech.

One should perform the recitation (*japa*) with that power (*śakti*), in accordance with the vital breath (*prāṇavāta*). Śītalā, whose navel is like a lotus, is the one who effects the arrival [of the breath]; the recitation performed while established in her attains perfection, even if it is devoid of [external] characteristics.

The supreme characteristic is always declared to be that which follows the crest of the vital breath (prāṇa-śikhā). The mantras, endowed with qualities such as omniscience and the rest, are ever-present.
[This applies] to the accomplishment of fierce rites and the like, as well as to the supreme entry into another's body.
The supreme [power] is said to be that of the Bindu, which impels all sentient beings;
the other is to be known as born of Nāda, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
It destroys suffering, generates peace, and accomplishes auspicious deeds.
The constant recitation of the Nāda is said to bestow health and nourishment, increase happiness and good fortune, and grant all perfections;
it should be performed upon arriving at the forenoon, the midday, and the end of the day.
The rites of recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth, [should be performed] with the flesh of gods and yakṣas;
with bulbs, vegetables, fruits, and leaves that have not been received as gifts.

One who desires accomplishment for oneself should subsist on alms and perform oblations; he should accept worship and the fire-sacrifice (*homa*) with substances acquired through righteous means. Regarding the purity of substances, such as those used in recitation (*japa*) and other rites, it is not required when one subsists on alms.
A yogi should never perform his recitation (*japa*) too hurriedly,

because that recitation which is undertaken for the sake of attaining dharma and liberation depends upon the cessation of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Therefore, he should perform it constantly and with focused alertness.

The self alone performs one [type of recitation], while the self does not perceive the other. That which is heard by others and that which is muttered (japya) are remembered as being threefold: the whispered (upāṃśu), the mental (mānasa), and the audible; these respectively grant tranquility, fulfillment of desires, and the subjugation of enemies.
One should daily offer water mixed with [milk] to Bhānu, clarified butter (*ghṛta*) to Vahni, and flowers along with the breath-retention of *sthūla-sthāyāsara-cakra* to Śambhu;
one should employ these with heart-pleasing mental flowers through the practice of *pūraka*.
Having performed the recitation (japa) with a tenth part of the limbs of Brahmā, one should offer it.
This knowledge is taught for the sake of duality; therefore, one should then apply it for the sake of non-duality.
In the Śaiva tradition of the five currents (pañcasrotas), the recitation is taught differently than in the Kula system.
And as long as one contemplates that, the arising of the mantra occurs in due order;
once you have attained stability, there shall be the cessation of mantras.
When the mind is exhausted and devoid of both existence and non-existence, [the goal is reached].
Having thus understood the nature of the mantras, one should then recite them:
three hundred times for the sake of expiation, likewise for daily rites, and for the sake of propitiation;
this is the prescribed rule for recitation regarding the Śiva-mantra as well.
One should recite with a one-pointed mind; if exhausted, one may cease the recitation.
On whatever day the wise person remains single-minded, on that day he should perform the recitation.
After yawning, sneezing, spitting, or coughing, one should sip water and recite [the mantra] again.
After voiding wind, urine, or feces, one should bathe and then begin the recitation.
One should avoid bathing, worship, recitation, and fire-offerings while suffering from indigestion.
Having performed the recitation, one should offer it to Śiva, the remover of misfortune.
With three drops of scented water purified by the syllable Oṃ,
the practitioner of mantra should observe the rules for recitation as declared in the Pauṣkara.
Oṃ! You are the protector of the most secret of secrets; accept this recitation performed by us. May it lead to my accomplishment through your grace, for it is established within you.
O Lord, whatever we do, whether good or evil deeds, [may it be for our success].
"O Śaṅkara, for me who am stationed at the feet of Śiva, destroy [my sins] with *hūṃ kṣaḥ*!
These two mantras have been proclaimed by the venerable Svayambhū and others for the rite of offering recitation (*japa-arpaṇa*) to Śambhu, leading respectively to worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having thus offered the recitation,
the wise one should have the rosary placed in a beautiful casket made of *śrīparṇī* wood,
provided with a silk cloth, fine cotton, or silken fabric, and equipped with a pillow.
When protection has been performed with the Gāyatrī, or when one is absorbed in it,
the rosary must never be shown to an uninitiated person, nor to one who recites a different mantra;
otherwise, there is an expiation of a hundred [recitations] of the Śrīsūkta.
Purification from the recitation of another mantra occurs again through the rite of re-consecration (*saṃskārakarman*).
The procedure for installation and so forth has been declared in the *Pauṣkara-śāsana*.
[The Chapter on Recitation]
At the gate of the circle of light, during the rite of invocation to the Guru,
and finally with incense and the food offering, one should worship the messenger and cause her to enter.
O Supreme Goddess, the power called Kriyā is designated as the messenger (dūtī);
she who is superior to that through the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) is the Great Mistress, the Mother of Mantras.
Since mantras are unmanifest and supreme when established in resonance (dhvani), [she is their source].
Sound (*dhvani*) is of the nature of action (*kriyā*), and that resonance (*nāda*) is indeed the power of sound (*nāda-śakti*).
Because it exists for the manifestation of speech-sounds (*śabda-vyaktyai*), this power of action is eternal.
Therefore, it attains identity with the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).
O Goddess, divide that which is desired into sixteen parts:
let there be three divisions for the first pitcher, numbering five, four, and three;
or alternatively, it is said that those [remaining] ten should consist of groups of four, three, and three.
Now listen to [the description] of the weapons that are unmanifest as well as those that possess form.
First, having divided the egg-born [mandala] into three sections, one should determine the measurement of the parts:
the portion from the tip of the hand is declared to be for the goddesses; one should fashion them with that portion.
Or indeed, O Maheśvarī, one may worship the King of Weapons (Astrarāja) directly as Ekapāda with three heads,
established through the sacrifice of the axe and other implements, or alone, seated upon a lotus;
or in the form of the Goddess, as previously described, as the King of Weapons.
The circumference is three times [the width], auspiciously marked with lotus petals;
the hand-hold is fashioned as emerging from the pericarp (karṇikā),
and it is constructed as a "house of sound" (śabdaveśma) adorned with lattices and other ornaments.
Emerging from the finger-joint of the field (*kṣetra*), fashioned from sharp iron,
it is called the "manifestor of sound" (*śabdavyañjaka*) and is designated as the "middle breath" (*madhyamaprāṇa*).

Thus fashioned, this auspicious bell, which bestows all accomplishments, remains in whatever house it is located; there Śiva himself is truly present. Having been cleansed and consecrated, it produces a beautiful sound during the performance of worship.

The bell that bestows both goals is known as the source of the *dūtī* mantras. She is called the *Dūtīḍāmara*; her specific nature will be shown hereafter. She is the power (*śakti*) of the all-pervasive Lord of Power, known as the Point (*bindu*) and Sound (*nāda*).
O Goddess, this very Ghaṇṭā is known as that which follows the path of the way of Śiva.
Its resonance (nāda) resides in sound, and its drop (bindu) resides in form.
Now, that [Ghaṇṭā] will be described according to its various distinct forms.
Its pervasion is established as extending from Kālāgni up to Śakti.
That power, known as Mahāvidyā, exists in the form of a bell.
Emission (sṛṣṭi) is declared to be the sounding [of the bell], and withdrawal (saṃhāra) is its turning over.
And its object of knowledge is declared to consist of the five principles (*pañcatattva*):
the principles beginning with the earth and those belonging to the three divisions, ending with space;
likewise, they know them to extend up to the principle of the Person (*puruṣa*).
Or rather, by means of five groups of five, there are exactly seven pentads;
thus it is said that its object of cognition is endowed with five instruments.
There is a bell made of the five metals, devoid of harsh sound.
One should not make [the sound] too sharp, nor likewise too short. By a sharp sound, death is indicated; by a subtle sound, loss of wealth.
By an excessively long sound, one is hated among all living beings.
One should have a bell made with effort, marked with five lotuses,
or bearing the signs of a wheel or a footprint, and producing an auspicious sound.
The spear, the trident, and likewise the thunderbolt; Vāgīśī, the bull, and the bird;
the water-pot, and Gaṇeśa—whatever one’s chosen deity may be, for all those who have been initiated, their body consists of the thunderbolt weapon and the rest.
One should diligently produce the previously mentioned auspicious sounds, which bestow perfect accomplishment.
Having worshipped, fumigated, and anointed [the image], with its form infused by the mantra,
one should unify it with one's own voice through the inner self situated in the heart.
The bell that liquefies the three worlds is the destroyer of all the wicked;
she is indeed the messenger of mantras, the awakener of those who are asleep,
emitting a flood of mantras and endowed with the blazing radiance of mantra.
And even when being praised by Brahmā and the other exponents of Brahman,
by ṛṣis, munis, and siddhas who act for the benefit of the worlds,
she is never at all remembered as "Nāsā" during the time of worship.
Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā! Hūṃ phaṭ! To the Mother who has arisen from Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā), [I offer] this mantra.
Since mantras are grounded in sound, they originate from the resonance of mantra (mantrānāda).
O Supreme Goddess, that resonance, flowing through the ears, is heard eternally.

O Śivā, what is this [practice] called "alms" (*abhikṣā*) consisting of the seven mantras? O Goddess, it is to be employed in every way for invocation, installation, and likewise for dismissal; it is the awakener of the vow of the seven mantras.
One should play [the instrument] with the left hand; one should not move it without incense.
Thus, having explained the messenger (dūta) as an incidental topic, the subject at hand is now stated.
Here ends the section on the female messenger (dūtī).
(78a) One should perform special worship and fire-offerings according to one's ability;
one should worship Śiva with instrumental music, song, dance, and other such offerings, as well as with hymns of praise.
Having prostrated with eight limbs and addressed the Supreme Lord:
"O Blessed One, the Lord has been distressed by the practice of dharma for the sake of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Therefore, O God, O Lord, you should always forgive me, who abide in the prescribed order."

The worship described by me in the scriptures was performed even when deficient in its prescribed rules; it was not made complete through further elaborations or heaps of prayers. Indeed, I have performed whatever ritual procedure was possible by relying solely upon devotion.
"May all that bear fruit for me while you, the All-pervading Lord, are well-pleased.
One should contemplate the gracious-faced, joyful Lord as having granted the boon.
Then, O Dear One, having presented the sacrifice, one should withdraw it gradually."
Having requested the best portion, one should take it and place it protected by the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
Having offered special worship and the *argha* water, one should perform prostration.
Then, having offered the *devinirodha-argha* to the left and right, [one should proceed].
Then, while recollecting the mantra of the abode (*dhāman*), one should dismiss the deity;
having performed the exhalation (*recaka*) for oneself, one should cast a flower toward the deity.
Then, by means of the *saṃhāriṇī* [mudrā], one should withdraw those [deities] who were stationed at the sides and in front from the mantra.
One should meditate on the playful movements of lightning within the left body;
then, one should cause the body of knowledge of Maheśa to dissolve into the form of the *bindu*,
and cause the *bindu*— situated within the power of *nāda*— to flow as the form of *śakti*.
The Praṇava, with its pervasive essential nature, is enclosed by the two syllables [of the mantra].
Having withdrawn it by means of the Saṃhāriṇī [power], one should join it at the dvādaśānta.
Then, having deposited it in the heart by means of inhalation (pūraka), one should contemplate it as established in its own place.

O Dear One, one should meditate upon the Lord who resides in the heart— the Master of His own Mantras— existing in the states of being with parts (*sakala*), without parts (*niṣkala*), and likewise both with and without parts (*sakalaniṣkala*). These are distinct states of His own nature.
The procedure for dismissal is as follows, according to the *Svacchanda-śāstra*:

"In this manner, regarding the manifest lingas and others, one should withdraw those [souls] who are atomic; however, for those who remain in the body while still engaged in experience, one should perform the rite but not effect their withdrawal."
For the sake of measuring those [deities] who are beyond [the senses], for worship, and not for dismissal;
invocation is not for the sake of bringing them near, but for the permission to perform worship— I,
having reflected thus even regarding the Seat of Knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), should worship with a single utterance.
One who possesses faith and is skilled in the ritual procedures should worship the Lord with garlands, perfumes, incense, and food offerings—
whether He is in the solar or lunar mandalas, in the sky, in the preceptor, or in His footprints; likewise, in water, in fire, on the head, or in one's own self, until the end of the kalpa.
This specific procedure for dismissal has been revealed by the Lord of Beasts (Mṛgendra).
[End of the Section on the Ritual of Dismissal.
Indeed, there is no dismissal of the mantras residing in the bones, nor is there any dismissal of the bones themselves.
For this practitioner is indeed independent and eternally identical with that [deity];
thus, when he says "Come," it is an invocation directed toward his own self:
"O Blessed One, may I truly become one with you for the sake of officiating at the sacrifice."
This is the invocation: whatever sound emerges from the heart outward, at the conclusion of the worship, one should say "Go" and place it back within the heart. One should say:
"O Blessed One, I am departing; forgive me for my mental actions."
This [procedure] for the invocation and dismissal of the pervasive powers is taught for all-pervading mantras, but certainly not for others. (79a)
One should not approach them with the request "forgive me" as if they were ordinary beings;
rather, having recognized their true nature, one should subsequently perform worship within the bodily cakras located on the earth.
This [practice] has been established by the Siddhas and the wise from the manifest [state].
When these [images] have been installed by Brahmins and others as the form of the divine Brahmin,
whatever mantra was placed therein becomes its limb-mantra (aṅgamantra) along with the marks;
it then departs to its own abode, leaving the image behind once the ritual action is completed.
One should [worship] the preceptor Śambhu and the artisan for whose sake [the deity] was installed.
Piśācas, bhūtas, vetālas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas take refuge in the site,
the pedestal, the image, and everything up to the flagpole.
Having understood this, O Greatly Intelligent One, one who desires auspiciousness should act accordingly so that the consecrated image attains auspiciousness through worship,
fire-offerings, and gifts, along with musical instruments and yellow-colored items.
In one's own home, the placement of flowers, incense,
and so forth before a mobile image should be performed at all times according to one's capacity and with devotion for the sake of attaining auspiciousness.
This should continue for as long as life lasts, established by means of the true mantras.
The practitioner of mantra should worship his own mantra of the moving image three times a day;
thus, by means of this uninterrupted rite, the procedures for worship, invocation, and so forth,
have been taught in the *Pauṣkara-śāstra* by Viṣṇu, who was born from the lotus.

Having first prepared the *arghapātra* (offering vessel) according to his own chosen mantra, the wise practitioner should sprinkle everything— the mandala, the sacrifice, and so forth— with its water. Then, right there, he should mentally resolve upon the sequence of the doors, the seats, and the lineage of gurus.
(79b) One who is fully permeated by Śiva should worship, beginning with his own body;
thereafter, that entire sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) is as pure as the crystal of the sky.
Having beheld one's own host of deities as identical with awakening,
one should likewise perceive them as reflections through the power of realization;
this is the primary invocation, like the wind arising from a fan.
Just as the wind, though all-pervading, is brought to life by a fan,
so too the mantra-wheel, though all-pervading and effective in its purpose, becomes manifest through such practice.
And this very reality is declared in the *Catuṣpañcāśikā*:

In the illustrious *Svacchanda-śāstra* as well, that very point was declared by the All-pervasive Lord: "O Goddess, how can the omnipresent Lord Śiva be without limits? O Queen of the Gods, he is invoked and yet he is beheld. Being thus questioned, the All-pervasive Lord spoke.
O Goddess, latent impressions (vāsanā) are carried away, and latent impressions are firmly established.

Having thus worshipped and praised [the deity], one should dismiss the God from within the heart. Furthermore, he who does not perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for the mantra that has arrived [should be known as such].
"He takes [the impurity] from the body; may Śiva grant that to him"—thus one should instruct.
In the *Tantrāloka* as well, the invocation and other rites were taught by the Guru.
Hereafter, I shall explain how the world-protectors (lokapālas) are situated.
Heruka is in the eastern seat, while Tripurāntaka is in the southeast. Agnivetāla is in the south, and Agnijihva is in the southwest.
Kālākhya is in the western seat, and Rājarājeśvara is traditionally taught [to be there].
And as their limbs are the sixty-four [sites] of great power;
likewise, others are situated everywhere in the secondary seats (*upapīṭha*), the junctions (*sandeha*), and so forth.
They dwell in every field (*kṣetra*), in every city, and in every village.
(80a) Even those guardians, commanded by Śiva and others, carry out their duties;
they take the form of obstacles for the gods and for heroes who desire spiritual accomplishment.
When worshipped, they create vulnerabilities and cause destruction.
[The deities are] Ajara, Āpabhūti, Iḍādhāra,
as well as Īśamūrti, Ulkāli, Raśmādi, and Nṛpumardana.
Ṛrdhamūrti and Ktyaṣtakāya; Lṝphapāda and Ekadaṃṣṭrin; Airāvata and Ojoghna; likewise another, Auṣadhaghna;
Añjana, Aḥhavāpa, Kambala, and Kharānana.
Gomukha, Ghaṇṭākhya, the one named Oṭa, Caṇḍarāvaṇa, Phaṭāṭopa, the one named Jaṭāla, Jhāṅkāra, Ñabhaṭeśvara,
Ṭaṅkapāṇi, and another, Dhānubandha, and Ḍāmara.
Phaḍphakarṇa, Uṇarīkānta, Tapanas, Sthavira, Dantura, Dhanada, Nāgakarṇa, Parātmavān,
the letter Ḍha, Bībhatso, Bhaṅgurākṣa, and Mahāsura.
Yugānta, Raurava, Lamboṣṭha, Vasana, Śaṅkukarṇa, the one named Ṣaḍāla, Surādha, Hūhuka,
and Kṣayānta— these are declared to be the fifty Kṣetrapālas.
They are situated embracing [the deity] at the beginning, end, or middle of the field (*kṣetra*), village (*grāma*), syllable (*akṣara*), and so forth.
Just as it is in the field, so it is in the village; such is the characteristic of the beginning, middle, and end.
One should worship that deity by whose name the field is designated.
Now hear from me the names of those who have fallen from their respective fields:
in the Ekaliṅgas, Huṅkāra; in the cremation ground, Bhayāvaha;
and in the terrible Mahālakṣmī forest, Jvālāmukha shall always abide.
Likewise, on a single tree he is Jvāla; he is Biḍālavadana;
he dwells in a cave as Ghaṇṭākarṇa; and he is Pralambana in a lotus thicket.
In battle he is Bhūridhāraugha, and likewise Māruta on the mountain;
in the ocean he is Pravaha, and in the treasure-house Maṇibhadraka;
he is Parādhyakṣa in the field of nectar, and Kroṣṭaka in the sacrificial enclosure.
One should know the Śavara in the forest, and the Madhupa stationed in the garden.
These sixty-four of great prowess are established throughout the world.
There, in whichever sacred field (kṣetra) the Ācārya resides, he should present the offering of oblations (balipūjā).
Therein, four types of beings—beginning with the twice-born and ending with the kings—are the recipients of the offering (*bali*).
The earth-dweller, the sky-goer, the tree-dweller, the bird, and the dog are those who desire the offering.
These are the permanent claimants (*nityādhikārin*), including all people from the eaters of raw flesh (*kravyāda*) down to others.
The barbarians have tawny hair, and their eyebrows, beards, and eyes are tawny;
they are terrifying with their fangs, extremely fierce, and radiant with ornaments of skull-bowls.
These are the offering mantras for all of them.
There are eight other great heroes born of the maternal lineage who dwell everywhere— in the city, at the crossroads, in the home,
and in the house of a woman of noble birth. They are the divine mothers of knowledge.
From instruction, they are born fully manifest with supreme knowledge.
They dwell there eternally, in their own abode, wherever they may have come from.
[There are] Daṇḍādhāra, Pracaṇḍa, Jaṭa, and Śaktipāṇika.
Śaktituṇḍa has a mace in his hand; Daṃṣṭrāla has the face of a boar;
Vajratuṇḍa is a Kāpālin; and the eighth is remembered as Triraśmi.
Thus, the deities beginning with Brāhmī are established in the temple according to their respective portions;
having recognized the house of the deity by its characteristics, marks, and inherent natures,
one should then establish the Kṣetrapāla within that field.
Where there is a self-manifested linga (svayambhū), or any other [linga] of Śiva;
or at a solitary linga or a single tree, on a mountain, in a mountain cave,
at a waterfall, a stream, or a world-renowned confluence of rivers.
In a lotus grove, by a pond, or indeed in a lake or at a crossroads; at a four-way junction, on a solitary peak, or even in a cremation ground or a forest;
Mahālakṣmī [is worshipped] in formidable places, as well as in excellent fields and lands of the Siddhas.
Where there are methods for elixirs (*rasāyana*), perfected substances,
gardens, fires, broken forms, and lakes;
where there is the abode of the Mothers (*mātṛs*), and the sacrificial arena in the great battle.
In Gokula, at the city gate, or likewise in the capital of a great king;
wherever there is the splendor of Yakṣas or Nāgas, or even in the temple of Caṇḍikā;
in a shrine of Mahādeva, Viṣṇu, or Ambikā.
Indeed, in the city of the asuras, there is a path leading to Pātāla;
there stands the Kalpavṛkṣa, a great tree such as the Nyagrodha,
where there are fragrant gardens and a delightful place.

Wherever Svayambhū or other deities such as Śiva reside, they constantly protect that place; yet there, the obstructing spirits (vighnas) are exceedingly powerful. O Great Goddess, these [spirits] have been appointed as guardians in these very locations.
Indeed, during the time of austerity, these [deities] never initiate obstacles for men;
nor do the gods, though they may be provoked by the guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas), achieve success.
For these very ones create disturbances and obstacles here for the practitioner.
(81b) O Goddess, when they are neither known nor worshipped by practitioners,
then those wicked guardians cause the destruction of their place.
Having thoroughly understood this ritual for the Kṣetrapālas from the *Aghorīpañcaśataka*,
the foremost of practitioners will attain their desired siddhi.
Afterwards, an offering (bali) should be presented to the host of Mothers and Bhūtas.

O Queen of the Gods, [one should offer] to the lords of beings (bhūteśvara) and to the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla) on the outside. Om! To the various beings of manifold forms who dwell within the earth and the intermediate space, and to those who reside in all the worlds from Dhruva up to the end, and who occupy the directions beginning with Indra.
May all, with delighted minds, accept this bali offering.

Through the conjunction with the utterance of *svāhā*, they shall be satisfied; one should cast it forth while reciting [the mantra]. Having worshipped them in due order with prostrations, perfumes, and flowers.
From the east to the northeast, and downwards and upwards on all sides—
in the corner positions are the Kṣetrapālas and even the outcaste Śvapacas.
Having offered the bali-oblation to their sons and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), O fair-faced one, [proceed].
Then, having bathed and performed the *uddhūlana* (sacred ash application), one should adopt whatever posture is desired.
The ritual offering to the spirits (*bhūtabali*) accompanied by mantras has been proclaimed in the *Śrī-svacchanda*;
their essential nature is described in the *Śrī-devyāyāmala-śāsana*.
Vultures, jackals, and hawks, as well as swans and cranes;
likewise ruddy geese, curlews, ravens, and owls; furthermore, antelopes, herons, cats, wolves, and monkeys.
All the goddesses, messengers, and yogins, as well as the guardians of the fields, always assume such forms within this [mandala] while wearing illusory bodies. (82a)
Men see them, and the goddesses see them there;
nevertheless, one should offer an oblation to those who have been created in such a manner.
[This concludes] the Knowledge of Spirits.
Having emerged from the sacrificial hall, he then offered oblations outside to the Mothers of the Directions,
the Mothers of Skanda, those who move on earth and those who move in the sky,
as well as the Kākinīs, Śākinīs, Ḍākinīs, and Lāsikās.
One should offer libations in due order to the cremation grounds, the lords of spirits, those dwelling in celestial palaces,
and the guardians of the fields;
then, having discarded the garments, one should perform all the rites for the virtuous.
One should properly perform the *ācamana* (sipping water) with water and ashes;
for one established in lifelong celibacy (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacarya*), residence in a householder’s home is not permitted.
Then, clothed again in garments and so forth, he performs other rites such as the *nyāsa* (ritual placement).
Having worshipped Śiva, who was honored upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), for the purpose of performing the fire-ritual (agnikārya),
and having fully worshipped him as the refuge of the Viśvānara fire of action,
the illustrious one named Dharmaśiva then offered an external oblation (bali) there.

Thus has the procedure for worship been described by Śambhu as it was taught in the Āgama; may it lead to the attainment of auspiciousness for those of pure heart. Now, the fire-sacrifice (agniyajana) will likewise be explained. Thus ends the chapter on worship in the *Nityādisaṅgraha*, extracted from the Āgamas.
(82b) Oṃ, salutations to Śiva.
Hereafter, I shall explain the fire-ritual as proclaimed by Śiva.
On a level, pure plot of ground, free from all thorns and debris,
the mantra-knower of the gods should construct an altar (vedi) adorned with lotuses;
according to the measurement of the eastern girdle (mekhalā), that is proclaimed as Rudrāṇī.
Behind that, one should have a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) constructed, endowed with all auspicious characteristics;
it should be circular for all mantras and bestows the fruits of all undertakings.
From the middle of the enclosure wall, the tiers (mekhalās) should be arranged like a waistband.
It should be extended all around, following the dimensions of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
This is called the altar-mound (*vedī*) of the pit in the *Vāmadevīyasaṅgraha*.
One should begin the fire from the southeast of the seat of yoga (*yogapīṭha*), which is in the east.
To the south for the sake of pacification; to the west for one who desires prosperity;
to the north for the sake of pacification and for the sake of attaining wealth;
and to the southeast for the attainment of knowledge and for the sake of accomplishing yoga.
In the southeast for the destruction of enemies, for victory, and for wealth;
in the southwest for the increase of one's own lineage and against all factions of the enemy;
in the northwest for expulsion, and for rites of subjugation and attraction.
Or else, one should propitiate [her] for the fulfillment of all desires before the God.
This was spoken by Maheśa regarding the Yakṣiṇī in the Pārameśvara:
"The eastern [section] should be square, while that in the southeast is in the shape of a vulva."
In the south, it is a half-moon; in the southwest, it is considered triangular.
In the west, it is known to be circular; in the northwest, it is hexagonal.
The shadow of the feet in the northern direction, within the domain of the Lord of the Eightfold Path (Īśa),
should be known as facing north; O fair-faced one, that which is toward the east and southeast is proclaimed as facing east,
and likewise that which is toward the south and southwest is proclaimed as facing east.
The wise know the western wind-pit (vāyukuṇḍa) to have a northern face;
likewise, the northeastern pit is proclaimed to have a northern face and to be oriented toward the east.
It should possess three ridges, a beautiful womb (suyoni), and be provided with a well-fashioned altar (vedi).
On a pure and beautiful sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should draw the most excellent fire-pit (kuṇḍa).
Thus it is seen in the directions and intermediate directions according to the venerable Bṛhatpiṅgalāmata.
Now, the fire-pit as described in the treatises on characteristics (lakṣaṇa-śāstra) is measured by fists and so forth.

The tip of the Veda (the triangle), the womb-section (the hexagon), the crescent moon, the circle, the six-cornered figure, the lotus, and the eight-cornered figure— their positions are established in order starting from the eastern direction.
[These correspond to] victory, slowness, peace, decay, the southern solstice, and movement.
The attainment of the fruit of nourishing knowledge is like the presence of the quarters of the directions within the body.
Having understood the strength of the sacrificial materials and the task at hand, one should perform the rite with two, four, five, or eight hands, as well as the ritual of *naladraha*.

Fifty, a hundred thousand, a million, a hundred thousand, ten million, and a crore— these are the numbers for the arrangement of the fire-oblation (homa). Thus, Dharmaśiva stated that there are fifty-six [such arrangements].
