The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) may have three girdles (mekhalā) or even just one.
For a pit measuring one fist (muṣṭhi) in size, the two girdles [of the single-girdle type] should be two finger-breadths (aṅgula) each.
Alternatively, there may be another pair of girdles, decreasing by one finger-breadth each.
In the case of a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring one cubit (*hasta*), the first rim is six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) [wide],
the second is four finger-breadths, and the third is three finger-breadths.
For a fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring four cubits, the first girdle (*mekhalā*) facing east shall be eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) wide;
the second shall be six, and the other [third] four finger-breadths.
For a pit measuring six cubits, the first girdle should be made ten finger-breadths wide.
Another [girdle] is eight finger-breadths wide, and the third is six finger-breadths.
For an altar of eight cubits, the first girdle (mekhalā) shall be twelve finger-breadths;
the second shall be ten finger-breadths, and the third eight finger-breadths.
Whatever the form of the pit (kuṇḍa) and the girdles (mekhalā),
the measurement of twenty-four parts should be used for the construction of the central lip (oṣṭha).
A navel (nābhi) should be made in the center of the pit, following the line of the girdles.
Here, however, the width resembling the form of a horse has eight fingers;
with a length of twelve fingers, its width is then eight fingers.
For the remaining [parts], the increase in width is considered to be two fingers each.
Three [types] are not prescribed for those born from the *kuṇḍa*; listen now to their characteristics.
Having first drawn a line in the east, there should be two fish-diagrams (*matsya*) therein.
For all [of them], the field is square, extending equally on all sides of the field.
One should take half a corner of the field and then rotate that half-field;
one should likewise rotate another [half] as far as the limit of that field.
When the field has been divided into five parts, one should place one part outside.
Therefore, having performed that conjunction, one should become like the petals of a lotus.
One should divide the field into five parts and discard half of another;
likewise, having discarded half of the other part, it becomes equal to that again.
Having performed the rotation of the thread, one should place a half-moon there;
the field, divided into five parts, should have two parts placed on the outside.
Leaving those two sides and grasping the middle from that [line], one should mark it with the measurement on both corners as well. Having laid three threads there, the triangle is clearly removed.

When the field has been divided into nine parts, one should lead [the cord] out by half a part from there; taking that very center, it shall become a circle. When the field has been divided into eight parts, one should lead [the cord] out by one part.
Therefore, having grasped the center and having thus defined the boundaries,
one should mark all the corners; there, by laying down six lines,
that pit (kuṇḍa) becomes hexagonal and endowed with auspicious characteristics.
The lotus should be made equal to a [standard] lotus, complete with a pericarp and petals;
one should give it depth and cause the tips of the petals to be visible on the outside.
O Bird, having first divided the field into twenty-four parts...
And he who should subsequently destroy one part everywhere;
having taken a corner from the center, he should thereafter mark it in those directions.
O Bird, from the intersection of the lines there, an eight-cornered [figure] shall arise.
Thus, the arrangement of the eight types of fire-pits (kuṇḍas) should be understood as described by the rays.
For a pit with one girdle or five girdles,
there are six arrows [units] for each, or alternatively, the five girdles are formed by the wings of the arrows in successive order.
These types of fire-pits (kuṇḍas) are considered to be six finger-breadths [in height] each;
such a distinction regarding the girdles (mekhalās) is observed in some scriptures.
One should adjust the dimensions of the pit so that no defect arises.
Likewise, for the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, [the length] may range from one cubit up to the desired number of cubits;
however, for the teacher and the disciple, a cubit increased by one finger-breadth grants all desires.

O Goddess, one should carefully fashion [the image] at twenty-four finger-breadths; because otherwise there would be a defect in the *vāstu*, it should be increased by one finger-breadth. An increase of one finger-breadth is taught for the sake of prosperity in the *Bhairavaśekhara*.
Thus, having understood the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one shall attain the desired goal.
This concludes the description of the characteristics of the sacrificial pit.
As for the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, they should be made of solid wood from a milk-exuding tree.

The ladle (*sruk*) and the spoon (*sruva*), made from excellent trees, are praised for the rites of pacification (*śānti*) and nourishment (*puṣṭi*). In other cases, they should be fashioned according to the specific intention and the nature of the rite. Their length is thirty-six finger-breadths, measured by the span of the arms.
No staff should be used for a vessel that deserves a six-part division; rather, the staff should emerge from the *kumbha*.

The top of its pedestal (*pīṭha*) should be four finger-breadths [in height], and that pedestal should be like the interior of a lotus. In the middle of the staff, it should be made two finger-breadths long and circular.
The altar (vedikā) should be made four finger-breadths in height, beautifully adorned with various designs,
and very elegant. It should be square,
resting upon a lotus at its base, and five finger-breadths in length above that.

The excavation should be made three finger-breadths deep; above that, it should be rounded by means of a circular turn and adorned with *tilaka* marks measuring half a finger-breadth. The neck should be made one finger-breadth wide, turned out by one-third of its width.
Likewise, on the two sides, an auspicious face measuring six *aṅgulas* should be made.
From those [proportions], one should gradually reduce the two lips by two parts on both sides.
The tip of the face is one-third of that, and its two sides are two parts.
One should fashion and pierce it with a measurement of the little finger;
one should make the root-base very deep and provided with three branches.
The central top-surface should be marked with a lotus, well-rounded at the neck with a measurement of one finger-breadth;
it should be four finger-breadths long, well-turned with two compartments at the tip,
fashioned according to the prescribed design, and filled with lac.
The *sruk* ladle should be full of four *palas*; the *śakti* is the *sruk*, and Śiva is the *sruva*.
The *kunda* is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), and likewise, the fire is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).
Thus has the characteristic of the *mṛtyujit* *kunda* been proclaimed as the sacred site (*tīrtha*).
Henceforth, I shall explain the characteristics of the components of the sacrifice.
The sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*) should be from trees suitable for sacrifice, free from defects, auspicious,
one *prādeśa* in length, and in thickness slightly greater than the little finger.
Thus have the sacrificial fuel-sticks been described in general according to my compendium. The fuel-sticks should be produced from sacrificial trees or fashioned from milky trees;
they may also be made from *pālāśa*, *akṣoṭaka*, *api-bhrū*, *bilva*, or those born from the *arjuna* tree.
These [leaves] are pleasing to the mind according to their specific region and species;
they should not be too thick, should be fragrant, and free from worm-holes or cracks. Even if the bark is deficient in fibers, it is acceptable provided it is free from defects such as insects.
For the sake of accomplishing the task, one should pile up the wood so that the ends are not overly dry.
They should be covered with fresh sprouts and purified with unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
One should arrange the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) at twice the measurement of those [logs].
The distinctions regarding the regions and the fuel have been stated in the Siddhānta Ānanam:
"The fuel sticks should not be too thick nor too thin; they should be struck with the fingers. They should be straight, free from defects, auspicious, and of even length for a virtuous rite."
In the case of the most undesirable [rites], the sacrificial sticks are said to be split at the ends and without bark;
likewise, the wooden fuel-sticks should be provided in double or triple quantity.
In the Vidyāpurāṇa, the characteristic of the Lord’s [liṅga] is said to be twofold:
"That which is broad, split at the base, short, crooked, or excessively thin,
as well as that which has two faces, is thick, or long— such a one must be avoided with great effort."
A wide [line] bestows long life; a split [line] is known to cause disease. A short [line] destroys progeny, and a crooked one likewise destroys good fortune.
A broken [line] leads to total ruin, while a double-faced [line] destroys success.
The gross [form] indeed creates obstacles and certainly causes one to sleep for a long time.
Now, the sevenfold observances (niyamas) are specifically described for those who,
out of desire, are engaged in the service of the Blessed One in every way.

Therefore, listen to the distinction of fruits resulting from the oblation among the materials for the *homa*. O Six-faced One, that which resides in the seven kinds of fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and clarified butter (*ājya*) belongs eternally to those whose souls are devoted to the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*).
The fruit is indeed sevenfold and generally eternal: peace, which is like the supreme state of one whose fuel is fully kindled, and for the perpetual worshiper,
good fortune, which is considered equal to the divine worlds by virtue of its celestial flowers.
With perfumes, sandalwood,
and excellent incenses prepared together with ghee and mixed with *guggulu*, one attains health and the fulfillment of all desires;
by performing additional oblations (*adhihoma*) therein, there is indeed great prosperity even in times of great distress.
Through this oblation, the practitioner obtains the desires cherished by the mind,
as well as long life, health, sovereignty, and a multitude of virtuous daughters, along with sons and grandsons, all attained through the clarified butter used in those burnt offerings.
Furthermore, for this [deity] who is slightly differentiated by division, there is again a six-faced [form].
By means of the fuel of the sevenfold [group], the fruit arising from the differentiation of desire is attained. (86a)
Now, understand this with an attentive mind:
oblations made from wood of excellent trees, mixed with honey, milk, and clarified butter,
should be twelve finger-breadths in measure, or otherwise one span (prādeśa) in length.
The fruit arises from the *aśvattha* tree, and the fuel-sticks lead to the state of fearlessness.
Those who cut down the *tāmasa* [ignorance] will indeed not have to cut it themselves;
for that which is obtained through the principle of *āśraya* (reliance) and others, and that which is acquired through diligent effort from another source—[all these are attained].
Whether it falls by itself at the proper time and through its own destiny, or is struck down by elephants and the like,
O Lord, it is not perceived as a transgression of the dikṣā;
otherwise, there would be a great fault due to the intentional cutting of it oneself.
There would be no need for expiation for devotees by cutting down that tree.
O lotus-eyed one, great prosperity is attained through the offering of fuel-sticks of *nyagrodha* wood; indeed, even greater is attained through the offering of those made of *udumbara* wood.
For those who are deceased, debts arise for their descendants very quickly.

(3) For practitioners of mantra, however, the fruits of using fuel-sticks from the *pālāśa* tree and performing oblations are the attainment of wealth arising from enjoyments, the acquisition of land, and the destruction of enemies.
Reverence for Brahman, discernment, and serenity are the supreme mantras.

(4) O Six-faced One, hear now the fruit of the sacrificial fuels (*samidh*) of those who have reached the state of the waters, horses, and buffaloes: the destruction of pride and freedom from rebirth. (5)
One desiring a wild elephant should offer oblations made from sandalwood.
Likewise, for the sake of bringing men and women under one's control, or for the sake of desiring a maiden,
one should offer sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*) produced from the red sandalwood tree, O son.
For the accomplishment of all the elements, for the cessation of *rājayakṣman*,
and for the attainment of the maṇḍalas and villages, O son, in due order.
Those made of *phalgu* wood, as well as those produced from *drākṣā*, sugarcane, and *kramuka*,

and those born of *amṛtavallī*, should be used for the *homa* for the sake of conquering untimely death. Those produced from *apāmārga* are prescribed for the sake of conquering diseases known as *lāna*.
Sāla and tāla trees, as well as other materials, are beneficial for the successful accomplishment of rites;
those made from madhūka and abhaya trees are for the purpose of destroying wounds and injuries;
and those consisting of bamboo wood are for the attainment of the fruit of the Śabdabrahman.
Garlands made from the *plakṣa* tree cause one to abandon laziness (9).
O Son of Pārvatī, flowers, trees, wealth,
and sacrificial fuel destroy defects such as pride and arrogance, and they bring about the attainment of delight.
Likewise, there is the child-seizing spirit known as Kumāra, who is broad;
and those born from the Madana tree, as well as those made of terrifying wood—
the results for those offerings to the hosts of Piśācas follow in due order.

The accomplishment of the *avaivartika* [state] is difficult to attain, as is the accomplishment of a *yakṣiṇī*. Likewise for the raising of a *vetāla*. For the sake of attaining the power of *rocanā* and *añjana*, one should use fuel derived from black *aguru* and the great wood known as *śiṃśipā*.
Those produced from the *nārikera* (coconut) tree and likewise those born from the *akṣoṭa* (walnut) tree should indeed be offered constantly for the pacification of drought;
[they are used] when drought has subsided and for the warding off of all thunderbolts.

Homas made from the wood of the citron tree (*mātulaṅga*) are for the attainment of *trāpti* as well as in the rite of nourishment (*āpyāyana*). Homas made from the wood of the *sāraṅga* tree are indeed for overcoming defects of the senses and for the provocation of the bodily humor *vāta*.
The Āprās and the Āpratakīyas originate from Karamandaka;
[they are found] in the rites concerning Prasannā, Kanyakā, Veśa, Svapna, and Mānavaka.
O son, the *kapittha* together with the group of *sida*, as well as that which arises from the *bhavya* tree,
the *ṭaṅka*, *pālevata*, and the moon-like juice of the *kakṣikāraka* tree—
this is prescribed for the destruction of all fevers and for enmity.
The *kādamba* [is used] for eloquence of speech, and the *cāṇpaka* for the reduction of graying hair. The collection of sacrificial fuel-sticks produced from the *śrīparṇī* tree destroys wrinkles;
know it to be a destroyer of all diseases, a vessel for speech, and a warder-off [of obstacles].
A bundle of *haridrā* fuel-sticks produced from the *dhanañjaya* tree,
as well as a collection of fuel-sticks originating from the *putrajīvaka*,
brings stability to the mind through hymns to the Sun arising from those trees.
They bestow supreme intelligence and an irresistible splendor.
All [sticks] produced from milk-exuding trees grant everything at all times.
Those produced from the Palāśa, Khadira, Aśvattha, Nyagrodha, and Udumbara trees likewise grant all things.

These [mantras] grant all desires to practitioners who seek their fruits. A hundred oblations of ghee mixed with lac, offered six times by one desiring welfare, is a fire-sacrifice that fulfills all wishes.

O son, the king of mantras bestows sovereignty upon those who have offered a measured number of lotuses with the first fuel-stick as their oblation; however, through the offering of red lotuses, it grants great fortune. Furthermore, by performing this [rite] once, one attains the state of being a commander over regional kings.
The destruction of mantras is brought about by the offering of white lotuses (*utpala*) at the conclusion of the *homa*.
When propitiated with flowers in this manner, he bestows great prosperity.
O Fire-vehicled One, the fruit of red lotuses is obtained through the act of oblation (*havana*).
Together with a multitude of male and female servants, he bestows either a city or a great capital after a long time upon a village or a hamlet; such is the mantra-form. (87b)
O son of Umā, from the offering of white, fragrant flowers like white lotuses,
one obtains fruit like that of red lotuses; likewise,
from the offering of those that are perfected, fragrant, and pleasing to the mind.

Indeed, from the offering of flowers that are blue and black, and well-known, the fruit should be understood as that which is proclaimed for the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*). [This applies also to] those that are green,
yellow, suitable for ritual action, and fragrant.
From the offering of flowers, there shall be the fruit arising from flowers. [This is] the second [offering], the flower-fuel.
From the offering of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and flowers—
Longevity, health, sovereignty, and immense prosperity shall arise.
O Son, for those who seek knowledge, those afflicted by fear, those desiring offspring, and those seeking wealth,
the mantra-soul eternally bestows whatever is desired by their minds.
The third is *gandhamasit*. O son, know that from *śrīvāsa* sprinkled with clarified butter, from *vajra*, and from *guggulu*— each in succession— one obtains cattle, sons, and abundant wealth.
The fourth is the Dhūpasamit rite. By offering curd, milk, and rasālā, the Supreme Lord bestows a great creation and satisfaction arising from the fruit of one's birth.
Worldly happiness, health, and the attainment of genuine prosperity are obtained through the fifth [offering], the *kṣīrasamit*. Furthermore,
by means of an oblation of sesame seeds (*tilahoma*), one attains liberation from debt arising from one's lineage.
O you whose vehicle is the lion and the peacock, [this leads] to the supreme increase of the seeds of other disciplined ones,
as well as the supreme growth of lifespan and the absence of decline; indeed,
it brings about the supreme growth of one's own side and the total destruction of enemies.
By means of oblations of rice preceded by barley and wheat,
and by means of the best of mantras, the practitioner shall indeed obtain everything without delay.
O Six-faced One, by offering oblations of jaggery-rice, milk-porridge,
and likewise of mung-bean and black-gram rice accompanied by ghee along with the mantra,
one obtains imperishable fame and worship that fulfills all desires.
One who is devoted to the rites of the Śarava-mantras and tantras shall attain [success].
By offering oblations of fruits such as the bilva and āmalaka, the Supreme Lord bestows his entire personal splendor and power.
The sixth fuel is also mentioned here:
from the offering of cow-derived clarified butter, the accomplishment of knowledge arises;
from that of buffalo-derived [butter], O Mahāsena, there comes supreme stability of the body.
By offering oblations of goat-flesh and clarified butter in this manner, one who knows the mantras shall obtain great vigor, splendor, and strength, endowed with a twofold nature.
From the offering of barley-meal mixed with ghee, the pacification of disease arises.
O Six-faced One, O Son, having combined seven fuel-sticks mixed with sugar and honey,
along with nutmeg and the other previously mentioned substances,
one should perform the daily libation (*mantratarpaṇa*) with them as a single offering.
Together with the green sprouts of dūrvā grass and white sesamum seeds,
his supreme sovereignty, strength, vigor, sustenance, fame,
incomparable prosperity like that of the kāśa flower, and the highest accumulation of merit [shall increase].

The Blessed One, being perpetually satisfied, swiftly bestows the eternal pacification of intoxication, delusion, and lack of discernment. [The seventh [offering] consists of clarified butter and fuel.]
Thus everything has been shown by Śiva, the remover of inauspiciousness:
through the oblation of fuel-sticks and other materials into the fire of the Six-faced One, the fruit is great.
In this authoritative scripture of the *Saṃhitā*, I shall speak in brief according to one's desires and so forth, just as it was revealed by Viṣṇu.
Garuḍa said:
O Blessed One, O Beloved of Kamalā, O Abode of Śrī, O Lord of the World!
The quantity of the materials for the oblation has not been truly known by me. O Sovereign of the Thirty-three Gods, please declare the determination regarding the sequence of substances.
The Blessed One said:
"Excellent, excellent, O one of great intelligence! I shall explain to you the sequence and the rules for the Mānava sacrifice; listen with focused attention and truth."
First, the fuelwood is enumerated as being of eight kinds:
from *pālāśa*, *khadira*, *carū*, *śamī*, and red *candana*;
it is also said to be from *bilva* and *akṣoṭa*, or, in their absence, from trees that produce milky sap.
With water containing *puṣpākhyā*, *mallikā*, *jāti*, *priyaṅgu*, and *bakula*;
and with *mālatī*, *caṃpaka*, *udāra*, and *kunda* flowers for the second [offering]. In the absence of these, it is prescribed that one should offer parched rice grains (*lāja*) mixed with sugar.
That third [incense] for Dhūsara consists of guggulu and aguru;
it is combined with mṛgajendra, turuṣka, śuktikā, and saffron, as well as sandalwood. Now hear of another, the eighth variety.
The fifth [type] is said to be prepared with sugar, ghee, honey, curd, and *kardūra*, combined with white cardamom; listen now to the eightfold [description].
Likewise, sesame seeds, unhusked rice, *rājika* (black mustard), and *māṣa* beans—these seven are to be taken.
Then, lotus seeds, apāmārga, and mustard seeds [should be used] eight times;
they are then infused with sixty-day rice mixed with ghee and sugar, consecrated by the mantra of the Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī.
The seventh [stage] is called "Accomplishment" (*abhyasaṃpannā*), which follows immediately after that [the sixth].
It consists of the preparations made with *karaja*, *bilva*, *yākhya*, and previously prepared *āmalaka*,
along with the powder of *madana* and *akṣa*, and subsequently with *kundura*.
Guduchi combined with milk, fresh butter mixed with sugar;
then māṃsī smeared with ghee, followed by eight parts of ghee and sesame seeds;
likewise, vacā and the two types of haridrā, combined with ghee and sesame seeds.
Dates, licorice, and grapes, as well as resin (sarjarasa), should be impregnated with ghee;
thereafter, the leaves of the mango, jasmine, bilva, betel nut,
and banyan trees should be added.
One should cause [the patient] to be given *kāryā* and *śatāvarī* mixed with ghee;
immediately after that, *bhūtakeśī* with milk,
and then *muktā*, *sahadevā*, *pṛṣṭhaparṇī*, *bṛhatī*, and *kaṇṭakārikā*.

Likewise, Garuḍavega and Ghṛtākṣa are proclaimed. And the "five nectars" (pañcāmṛta) consists of sesame, linseed, and rice, as well as clarified butter, milk, and honey; this is declared to be the five nectars.
One should cause cow's milk to be given together with padmaka, uśīra, badara, nāgakeśara, kunda, ruda, dūrvā grass, and mustard seeds;
and then, O Bird, one should offer mustard seeds after all the others.
Others, for the sake of attaining enjoyments, should offer oblations with consecrated substances that purify;
however, for the sake of liberation, one should perform the fire-sacrifice using only unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
I shall now state the prescribed measure for this collection of sacrificial materials.
Sesame seeds are known to be equal to ghee, while unbroken grains are recorded as being twice that amount.
Village grains are equal to ghee, whereas forest grains are recorded as being twice that amount.

Parched grains (lājā) should be equal to half the amount of ghee, and fruits should be equal to the ghee. Flowers should be offered according to the measure of the oblation (āhuti), and incense should be of that same measure. One should likewise offer the honey-mixture (madhuparka), fruits, and so forth, according to this same measure during the fire sacrifice (homa).

O Lord of Birds, one should offer guggulu, kunduru, vacā, kuṣṭha, and mṛdvīkā in a measure equal to a fourth part of the clarified butter; other substances may be half that amount, or even less according to one's ability and availability, and thus one should perform the oblation.
At the conclusion of the fire offering (homa), one should perform a libation (tarpaṇa) outside for the assembly of spirits,
as well as for the guardians of the directions and others who dwell in the netherworld and the sky;
[this should consist of] clean, cool water mixed with parched grain, curd, and boiled rice.
And for the libation (tarpaṇa), one should offer white mustard seeds along with unbroken grains (akṣata).
Thus has the eightfold classification of the seven types of sacrificial fuel (samidh) been succinctly described by Viṣṇu in the Pārameśvara-vihagendra.
An oblation of sesame seeds mixed with ghee bestows all desires;
for the sake of attaining wealth and grain, an oblation of guggulu resin with ghee brings about vast success— whether inferior, middling, or superior.
One shall obtain Śrī by means of white lotuses for the purpose of clarified butter and by offerings of bilva fruits.
O fair-faced one, through the oblation of sesame seeds smeared with milk, the rite of pacification (śāntika) is accomplished;
likewise, attraction (ākarṣaṇa) is achieved with white and black [seeds], and nourishment (pauṣṭika) with yellow and black [seeds].
O lady of excellent hips, one should employ these in sequence to remove disease:

with *kunda* flowers for the sake of obtaining a son, with *aśoka* for union with a beloved, with *jātī* buds for the accomplishment of all tasks, and with *vakula* flowers for union with a *gandharva*.
The Nāgas [were born] from the Nāga maidens, and the Siddhas from the Siddha maidens; the Apsarases from Caṇpaka, and the lords of men from Phalguṣa. (90a)
O lady of excellent hips, anointed with ghee, accompanied by the mantra, the purohita,
and joined by the queen and her son, he comes under control, O fair-faced one;
and by means of *kadamba* flowers, even a *yakṣiṇī* comes under his control.
"One should accomplish the Vidyādharī through *kuvyakas*; there is no doubt in this.
Thus, even in the *Svacchanda Śāstra*, the fruit of the substances for the fire-oblation (*homa*) is recorded:
"From an oblation of curd, nourishment (*puṣṭi*) arises; from milk, peace (*śānti*) is produced."
Through the oblation of cow-derived products with clarified butter, there shall be supreme nourishment;
through the oblation of red flowers and clarified butter, supreme nourishment shall occur;
and through the oblation of red flowers and clarified butter, one shall attain supreme good fortune.
One should remove a spider-bite with blood and clarified butter; a swelling is removed by barley and blood.
By offering oblations of equal parts of sesame and clarified butter, one may destroy fistula-in-ano.
By offering oblations of clarified butter, honey, and sesame, one removes the pain of fever caused by a wound.
By means of goat meat, consumption (rājayakṣmā) is quickly destroyed.

By means of *nāra* and pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*), one may release [the patient] from spirits (*bhūta*) in an instant. O Bhairavī, by means of oblations of fat, marrow, and muscle-tissue, as well as blood and clarified butter, [one achieves the same].
Indeed, by one thousand and eight recitations, epilepsy is destroyed;
and by an oblation of pure, fragrant *kāpila* ghee performed one thousand and eight times, all diseases are destroyed.
Thus has been told to you the attainment of fruits through the various substances used in the worship of Aghora, as enjoined by Bhakṣyabhairava; hereafter,
I shall speak specifically regarding the accomplishments (siddhis) of the sky, the earth, and the netherworld.
One should offer the best, the middling, the inferior, and even the very lowest; indeed,
one should offer the best by means of gain and the middling as well.

The mantra-practitioner should offer oblations according to the rule, in accordance with what is available: the *madhyamā* [oblation] by means of [cow’s] milk, and the *kanyasā* by means of even inferior substances.
The best is said to be that called *nāra* (human fat), and the middling is known to be that produced from the earth (ghee).
But the younger brother of Phalguka [obtained] a portion known as *phalavrīhi*.
That which is struck by a banner, struck by a fish, suspended, or prepared by force—
this is to be known as the "Monthly" (*māsa*), the best, which bestows heroic accomplishment (*vīrasiddhi*).
That which is broken by untimely death, likewise struck by a thunderbolt of vajra,
or afflicted by cold, wind, and heat, should be known as superior or middling.
Furthermore, that which is worn out, seized by disease, or dead from being tormented by hunger and thirst [is inferior].
The flesh of the Śavarī fish is the best, while that of others is inferior.
Furthermore, a bull that is not emaciated, nor afflicted by disease, nor worn out by cold or heat, and which is either tawny or very beautiful, is excellent for sacrifice.
That which arises from a steady-sensed elephant is middling; that arising from a bull is superior.
That produced from a lion or a tiger, as well as buffalo, horse, and donkey meat, is middling. Deer, goat, and wild ox meat are superior.
Moist, dry, or well-formed, yet destroyed by old age and disease—this flesh is devoid of bliss; it is middling or inferior. It is variously white, speckled, plump, horned, or fresh.
That which is complete in its constituent elements (*dhātu*) should be known as the best of the inferior; meat produced from sheep and goats is the middling of the inferior;
[meat] originating from dogs, jackals, oxen, cats, rabbits, and mice [is likewise inferior].
One should know that according to the quality of what is obtained,
it is classified as "inferior-inferior" based on the number of flowers used for the oblation, such as the lotus (*padma*), the blue lotus (*utpala*), or the *savaduha*.
Among all those growing on land, the latter should be known as superior.
The offering (*homa*) of fruits such as the *bilva* and others is considered inferior.
For daily offerings in the cemetery (*pitṛvana*), the best [plants] are those that grant the accomplishments of heroes (*vīrasiddhi*).
One [oblation] is offered at a *liṅga* on a mountain peak; those of medium and superior quality are also offered there.
Or, at a crossroads or beneath a solitary tree, or in the house, the inferior ones are to be offered.
All others are to be offered everywhere, according to the specific sacrificial rite (*medha*).
Through the highest [practices], the highest perfection is attained—the eightfold qualities beginning with *aṇimā*.
Through the middling ones, one indeed attains the power of moving through the air (*khecaratva*) and union with the Yoginīs.
One attains the perfection of moving on earth (*bhūcarī-siddhi*), the dissolution [of obstacles], and the destruction of mechanical devices.
By means of the *kanyasa* [mantra], one may bring about subjugation (*vaśya*), possession (*āveśa*), inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*), eradication (*uccāṭana*), and so forth.
Whatever the practitioner desires—the fulfillment of all wishes—shall come to pass. With ten thousand recitations of the *sumana* [mantra], one becomes dear to the *gandharvas*.
When an oblation is performed with blue lotuses, one becomes beloved by all.
By means of *jātu* flowers, an excellent maiden comes under one's control at that very moment.
Through oblations of sesame seeds and barley, success is achieved and the destruction of disease occurs.

The increase of rice is always achieved by means of rice soaked in ghee and milk; whatever the practitioner offers as an oblation, that very thing shall become inexhaustible. Whatever fruit a man may obtain through a thousand bhāras of ghee, [he obtains by this].
A man would not be equal to the tenth oblation, nor would he be equal to the *tantrava* [sacrificial vessel].
This is the supreme secret; it should never be disclosed. Scholars [who do so] incur censure and are held in contempt.
By that [means], improper conduct is to be purified;
without the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), no spiritual awakening (*vṛddhi*) arises here.
In the Sārasvata doctrine, the results for the highest accomplishment (*uttamasiddhi*) and so forth are proclaimed as follows:
there are oblations of superior substances, and the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is performed with a tenth part of that.
Those who know the tradition say that the recitations of the great earth-mantra (*mahākṣmā-japa*) are classified as "superior" (*uttama*) and so on.
One should perform the rite twice for the medium [offering] and thrice even for the inferior one.
Using clarified butter, guggulu, human fat, and mahāmāṃsa,
or with sesame seeds and so forth, one should perform it nine, six, and three times respectively.
The Mahākṣmājasamoha-homa is prescribed in the Mālinīvijaya. [This concludes] the procedure for the seven-fold oblation with sacrificial fuel and so forth.
But when one is seized by death and overcome by Time, O Dear One...

Having seen [the danger], one should then worship Amṛteśa for the sake of warding it off. By invoking the name of whichever [deity] one worships the Lord Mṛtyujit, one quickly crosses over death; this is my truth, not a false word.
One should perform the oblation with sesame seeds mixed with white sugar and saturated with ghee and milk,
using sacred fuel-wood, in a circular fire-pit with three enclosures,
while reciting the name of the person for whom the rite is intended, accompanied by the great ritual of protection.
Great peace shall swiftly come even to one who has gone to the abode of Yama.
Alternatively, by means of milk mixed with sugar, or by itself, or through an oblation of fragrant ghee poured into a vessel made from the wood of a milky tree; |||
When satisfied, it destroys death; there is no doubt that it brings an end to death.
[This is] the Mṛtyuñjaya Homa.
A fire kindled with fuel from a milk-tree destroys fever in an instant.
Combined with sesame, rice, honey, clarified butter, and milk—
this offering of fifty oblations wards off all malevolent beings.

Thus ends the procedure for the pacification of fever and other ailments. O observer of noble vows, by performing oblations with pills of guggulu, whether cast into the fire or otherwise, nourishment quickly arises even for one whose body is emaciated.
Thus ends the section on the Fist-offering (muṣṭi).
By performing seven oblations of rice, one who desires wealth shall become a possessor of wealth.
[The materials are] sesame, rice, honey, clarified butter, milk, together with sugar.
One should perform the oblation as before in a fire-pit kindled with excellent fuel.
By this truth, falsehood shall be born as great [evil]; [therefore] peace!
Peace! Peace!
By offering oblations with excellent fuel-sticks into a fire of excellent luster, one attains all desires; this is the truth and not otherwise.
One should perform the desired oblation with the specific aim of attaining the red [fire].
Thus has been declared the fruit [of the rite] for Mṛtyuñjaya according to the distinctions of the ritual acts.
Now, by means of those sesame seeds, disease is destroyed and peace is produced;
thereafter, there shall be the return of prosperity through all kinds of wealth.

Subjugation and other rites are accomplished with corals; and the success of the *astra-mantra* arises from offerings of seven types of grain mixed with unbroken rice and clarified butter. O Goddess, even a barren woman gives birth when [the rite is performed] with lotus seeds mixed with flowers.

In all these oblations, O Goddess, ghee mixed with the appropriate substances should be used. However, that oblation which is devoid of clarified butter (ājya) should be performed intentionally for the purposes of eradication (uccāṭana) and killing (māraṇa), O Goddess; it should not be otherwise devoid of ghee.
In the absence of all [other] substances, an oblation with clarified butter (ājya) is recommended for the destruction of fever,
epilepsy, possession by spirits, and the like, as well as for the removal of spider-bites and pustules.
An oblation of *putrajīvika* seeds serves to ward off all malevolent influences.
(92b) For the sake of attaining gnosis, one should offer sesame seeds with honey;
for the purpose of driving away enemies, however, one should offer the fruits of the *kaṇṭakārī* plant.
For the sake of achieving subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), one should offer oblations combined with curd and ghee.
The homa performed with *dolāja* seeds brings success; that produced from sesame seeds leads to liberation. And for the purpose of causing the death of enemies, *ananta* is offered as an oblation.
One should place the name of the target (sādhya) in the center, accompanied by the syllable *phaṭ* and surrounded by fire above and below; then one should perform the night-oblation (*niśihoma*).
Thereafter, one should offer white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*) equal in number to the Meru mountain.
O Great Goddess, this [is] the enemy in the mandala of the enemy, and not otherwise.
Thus it was spoken by Śarva regarding the Śrīkaṇṭhī; now the authoritative proof is stated:
"One should speak of the barley, the mṛgī, the sesame seeds, and so forth, joined with five branches."
The sacrificial ladle (*sruva*), honey, milk, ghee, alms-food, liquids, and so forth;
curd in the hands, within groves, and not that which grows from roots or is divided into three pieces;
and whatever edible things are prepared as appropriate, characterized by their joints and protective coverings.
The creepers of the fingers of the eyes possess unimpaired fruits and flowers;
the mantra and all the sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) are marked with sesame for the sake of the location.
One should speak of those that are very small or large, possessing bark, free from wounds, and auspicious.
One should offer five oblations each, in sequence, of jujube, *iṅguda*, grape, and so forth; likewise,
rice mixed with curd, milk, and other substances, characterized by mouthfuls,
or even that which rises in flames from the ladle or clings to it like sesame seeds.
The *kāsāraṅga* is like a ball of dough or oil-cakes,
while the *guggulu* of *umāhiṣākṣa* is like pills or jujube fruits. (93a)
The portions of the paste (kalka), of the *madana* and other fruits, and of the *māṣa* beans should be like chickpeas (*caṇaka*).
Thus ends the measurement of the substances for the fire-oblation (*homa*).
A seat (*viṣṭara*) made of thirty strands of *barhis* grass is prescribed.
Green and heart-pleasing *kuśa* grasses are not equal [to these] by their very nature.
Made from *darbha* grass thirty-six *tāla*-lengths long and consisting of thirty-six blades,
[one should fashion] the supreme sword of awakening (*bodhāsi*) with its hilt (*veṇī*), consecrated seven times with the *Śivāstra* mantra.
For the sake of the ritual measurement (*prādeśa*), one should prepare two sacred blades (*pavitra*) made from the tips of *darbha* grass, tied together with a double knot;
these destroy obstacles and defects, and are radiant with the splendor of their qualities.
As prescribed for fifteen or twenty-one sections (*kāṇḍa*), one should fashion them in this manner for both hands.

The vessel for Śiva’s *arghya* should be made of gold, silver, copper, or earth, filling the hollow of the palms; it may be adorned with lotuses or sunflowers, circular, free from cracks, and provided with a conch,
a mother-of-pearl shell, a horn, or leaves of the *palāśa* or lotus.
These vessels made of cow-products, even without horns and the like,
are established for prosperity when they measure six finger-breadths in diameter and three finger-breadths in height.
Vessels made of clay should be prepared from the fourth part of a *praṇīta* [measure], or from a *tolaka*, or from mustard seeds.
This characteristic of rice and other grains has been illustrated in the *Mṛgendra*.
Here, the Lord explains it as he has taught, according to his will:
that vessel for the arghya-offering should be one span in width and circular in circumference.
The surface is declared to be level with half [the height] above and below;
and just as it is placed by the pervasive one (vibhu), it remains well-established.
If the half [of the vessel] intended for Śiva should fall elsewhere, [it is not a fault].
In that kingdom, the elevation of the lowly occurs constantly;
and at that time, there is always an abundance of clarified butter in the royal court.
For indeed, the stability of the king and of the kingdom depends upon the *praṇītā*.
Therefore, one should always ensure that these three have firm foundations.
The water-channel, however, should be shaped like a golden nose and straight at its tip.
The *ājyasthālī* (clarified butter vessel) is likewise auspicious when provided with a single nose;
the *praṇītā* (water vessel) should be provided with a handle shaped like a neck, or it may be without that. One should fashion it surrounded by a jar (*kumbha*) and joined with an ear and a rim.
The elevation of the neck is one-fourth [of the height], and its mouth is twice as wide.
The water-pot (karaka) and the neck itself have the shape of a *unmatta* flower.
Below the neck, the girdle (*kāñcī*) rises up and is equal in width to the mouth.
Then, from the footprint of the Vardhakī of the Kalaśa,
who is long-limbed, firm-standing, and of a single color, there arises the food offering (naivedya),
as well as the water for honor (argha), perfumes, flowers, white mustard seeds, rice grains, and barley.
One should provide kuśa grass and dūrvā grass along with dhanyā, as far as they are available; likewise,
flowers that are very fragrant, with unbroken petals, fresh, and pure— even if they lack scent— should be used, while one should avoid those that are otherwise unsuitable.

One should avoid even fragrant flowers that turn foul-smelling, as well as those with a pungent scent, those that are withered, and buds. Blue lotuses (*nīlotpala*) and the like should be accepted, provided they are otherwise pleasing to the senses.
Likewise, bound and unbound garlands, as well as leaves and fruits;
fragrances that are heart-pleasing and sweet-smelling, yet devoid of animal products;
and similarly, various types of incense as well as diverse garments.
The height of the [mandala] for the teachers should be four times its own width;
for the practitioners and others, it should be two feet less by two finger-breadths.
The seat of the teacher should be equal to the seat of Śiva;
above it, there should be a canopy made of auspicious cloth of the same size.
It should be four finger-breadths wide, according to the ritual manual, and conducive to comfort.

It is without knots, free from tangles, and the supreme bringer of all accomplishments. A rosary made of *raudrākṣa* seeds, or of *pautrajīvaka*, which is even, uncracked, auspicious, or beautifully fashioned from lotus seeds (*pauṣkara*), is likewise excellent.
Or else, a crystal [vessel] that is stainless and free from the heat of the sun and so forth,
containing one hundred, half of that, or a quarter [of the beads], joined with a *sāvitrī* knot;
as well as food fit for eating, chewing, sucking, licking, and drinking, as traditionally prescribed.

The sacred thread, the mantra according to the rules, and the food offering (naivedya) are proclaimed as such. The sacrificial porridge (caru), prepared with milk, clarified butter, and mantras, becomes "consecrated by the residue" (saṃpātita).
Likewise, the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) should be neither burnt nor overcooked.
One should offer *śama* cooked with a hoof-scraper, placed in a potsherd and drenched in clarified butter;
likewise, cow’s ghee and other offerings, barley-gruel mixed with sesame,
and auspicious vessels filled with ghee, made of various grains and metals.
Lamps suspended from a staff or arranged in streams are also considered auspicious.
Sesame seeds, parched grain, barley, ghee, honey, curd, boiled rice, and milk—
this oblation is remembered as the supreme means of satisfying the deities of the maṇḍala.

Oil, black-gram rice, meat, kṛsara, fish, and honey— this, in brief, is the offering dear to all beings, consisting of oblations. Furthermore, according to the Vidyāpurāṇa, this is the defining characteristic of the excellent sacrifice.
(94b) According to the ritual procedure, first of all, the mere performance of the fire offering is prescribed;
if one hundred and eight *pala* of clarified butter are offered.
Then, double that amount of rice and barley should be prepared;
sesame seeds are known to be equal to the ghee, while sugar should be half of that.
One should know that milk is equal to that [sugar], and ghee again should be half of that [milk].
O auspicious lady, this five-fold nectar (pañcāmṛta) brings peace and nourishment to men. O beautiful one, there should be [seven] palas of parched grain (lāja),
and here, O Pārvatī, there should be seven palas each of the seven types of grain.
Māṃsī, the two types of Haridrā, Kuṣṭha, Śaṅkhapuṣpī, the pith of Bilva, Devamuni, Nāgakeśara,
Śaileya, Caṃpaka, Surāhvā, Vacā, Kharjūra, and Mustaka.
The various medicinal herbs known as dūrvā are proclaimed to be effective when moving [through the body]. One should offer seven palas of each individually into the sacrificial fire (jātavedas).
In that same manner, there should likewise be twenty-seven gurus [of the mantra].
O Maheśvarī, there should be seven *palas* each of mustard seeds, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*),
and *śigru*; likewise,
the *śrīphala* fruits should be like sesame seeds, while the other fruit is equal to *śāli* rice.
The betel nuts should be equal in size to the *śrīphala* fruit, and the nutmegs half that size.
Likewise, one should add the substance called *madana*, as well as other ingredients such as *kākolaka*.
O lady of dark belly, three and seven *palas* of sandalwood should be given.
One *pala* and one *karṣa* should be offered into the fire, followed by three *palas* of fresh butter mixed with white sugar and saffron filaments. (95a)
O Dear One, one should offer two karṣas of guggulu resin and twice that amount, a pala, of mahiṣākṣa;
thereafter, one should perform the oblation with curd-rice.
Then, one should offer the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) accompanied by many ritual materials.
Richly adorned with silk cloth, endowed with the sacred thread and other ornaments,
provided with betel, and accompanied by flowers, water-offerings (*argha*), and so forth—
one should offer there whatever one desires or has obtained.
Thus, he who gratifies the Supreme Lord, the God residing in the fire,
attains Śiva before long and enjoys divine pleasures.
This [method] regarding the substances for the *homa* has been declared and demonstrated in the Vāthula [Tantra].
Thus ends the section on the auxiliary elements of sacrifice.
Now, the propitiation of the lordly elephants is accomplished on the day of the Sun;
it is employed among medicinal herbs for the sake of increasing nourishment and health.
On the day of the Sun, one should perform rites for peace and prosperity; on that day, one may plant various medicinal herbs and bury treasures consisting of accumulated wealth.
On the day of Mars, success is especially established here.
Through Mercury, there is the acquisition of knowledge and success in subterranean caves on the day of Jupiter.
Alchemy, elixirs, and the eightfold debate—all these are accomplished on the day of Venus; of this there is no doubt.

Having performed the rites of killing, driving away, and so forth, by means of *vetālas*, swords, and other such means, on the day of the Son of the Sun (Sunday), success is attained; there is no doubt in this matter.
Once one has understood the ritual taught by Śikhākāmeśvara, the rite becomes accomplished.

Thus, where the common collection of substances and so forth is to be consumed by fire, one should then carry [the materials] to the sacrificial ground, which is always in use and situated within that [area]. (95b)

Having gazed upon Śiva on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and other such sites with extensive offerings according to one's means, and having received permission, he should proceed to the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) accompanied by the *argha* offering for the sake of satisfying its mantras.
Having driven away obstacles in the eight directions, he should install the eight names of the sections (*kāṇḍa*).
Having wrapped that head with armor and with a triple-strand thread,
one should worship the weapons and the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) all around them for the purpose of dispelling hosts of obstacles and for the protection of the sacrifice.

Meditating upon [the deity] seated upon a lion-throne, resembling blazing, radiant light in the form of his own weapon, he should then worship the guardians of the gates. He should perform the purification of the elements (bhūta-śuddhi), the tilaka, and the consecration of his seat and himself.
Having placed Śiva within oneself, one should contemplate the desired horse as having been created;
then, having placed the partless (niṣkala) Śiva, one should meditate, "I am Śiva.
One should place upon the head a white turban consecrated with the root mantra.
One should wear a turban after the ritual placement (nyāsa), like a cloth band of reality;
it should be twelve finger-breadths in height and well-fashioned with the fifth [digit].
One should adorn one's own body with perfumes and well-decorated flowers.

One should prepare a mandala with perfumes on one's own right hand; by rotating it according to the prescribed rite, one thus performs the "Hand of Śiva" (śivahastaka). Having placed that radiant [hand] upon one's own head with the Śiva-mantra, [one should proceed].
One should contemplate oneself as the agent, non-different from Śiva:
as the witness of actions in the mandala, the protector of the sacrifice in the water-pot (kalaśa),
the locus of the fire-oblation in the fire, and the liberator of the disciple.
(96a) "Well-grasped in its own nature"— the Guru should cultivate a very firm conviction that "this Lord, who has five supports, is indeed I myself."
Having placed eight jars made of the five grains, adorned with cloths and garlands, and established upon seats of the *praṇava* (oṃ),
the mantra-practitioner, holding the sword of knowledge in hand, should worship the peaceful Vidyā.
Placing the navel of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍanābhi) at the forefront, one should perform the consecration of the pit;
this was stated by Somaśambhu in the Karmakāṇḍakramāvalī.
Thus ends the rite of making [the disciple] Śiva-like (śivīkaraṇa).
At the time of commencing the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) are first performed;
once it is completed, all [other rites] are to be carried out in their proper sequence.
Thus indeed has the rule been shown for the sake of victory, according to the Mata [Tantra].
One should sprinkle the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), endowed with its proper characteristics, with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra (astra).
One should veil it with the armor-mantra (kavaca) and scratch [the lines] with a blade of darbha grass empowered by the weapon-mantra.
Having lifted [the earth], one should then sprinkle it again with the weapon-mantra, O beautiful lady.
He should perform filling and leveling here;
he should carry out sprinkling and pounding with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*).
He should also perform sprinkling and drying with that same weapon-mantra.

The worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, the consecration with the sword-mantra, and the "vajrification" (vajrīkaraṇa) with the weapon-mantra (astra); the lines are threefold, east-west and north-south;
that which has one line facing north is proclaimed as the "vajra."
With that very sword, one should fashion the fire-pit, strewing it inside and out with darbha grass blades pointing eastward; this is for the purpose of constructing a house, and not otherwise.
Thus end the consecrations of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
On the southern side of the pit, one should prepare a seat made of dry cow dung,
a grass mat (viṣṭara), and flowers, having first offered a prostration.
With his own name joined with the word *mada* and ending in *namaḥ*, he should establish Brahmā by means of that very vocative form and worship him with flowers and so forth,
along with incense and other offerings, according to the sequence prescribed in the *Vṛha*.
At the crossroads within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should first place a seat (viṣṭara) made of two darbha grass blades with their tips pointing east using the Praṇava mantra; upon that seat,
one should place a flower and worship [the deity] in the heart.
Having thoroughly worshipped Yāgeśī with the mantra beginning with *praṇava* (Om) and ending with *namaḥ*,
she who is dark as the petal of a blue lotus, possessing most beautiful eyes,
and adorned in all her limbs according to the characteristics prescribed for mantras.
Having meditated upon the Goddess in this manner, one should establish her in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
standing with her head bowed as if rising at the time of menstruation;
one should worship her with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings while reciting the Bhava-mantra.

O Goddess, the knower of mantras should display the mudrā for the sake of [the deity's] presence, from the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) until the conclusion of the worship of Vāgeśa. This has been declared in the Śrī Svacchanda and other texts; now, [I shall explain] the birth of the fire.
Thus ends the generation of Vāgīśī. The lower fire-drill (adharāraṇi) made from Śamī wood, horse-wood, or Arka wood— characterized by a height and width of eight, twelve, or ten [aṅgulas]—
is the source for the upper drill.

The male organ is six finger-breadths long; when the circle [of the body] is exceeded by the arms, that [line] is for the sake of joining them together, being situated in the middle between those two limbs. (97a)
Reciting the Gāyatrī mantra while uttering the name of Śambhu,
one should firmly place [the image] in a vessel amidst bees and consecrate it with fire according to the prescribed rite.
Thus has this been declared by Raṇita regarding the two manifestations of birth.
Thus ends the procedure for the fire-drill (araṇi).
Having taken either a fire-drill set or one produced from a sun-crystal (sūryakānta),
[one should place it] in a vessel made of metal, copper, or clay, or even in a new one.
One should place the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) in the northeastern direction, facing it directly.
In this manner, one should procure the fire according to the procedure taught in the Jayā-saṃhitā.
Fire is declared to be of two kinds: the new (nava) and the domestic (māhānasa).
Likewise, fire is said to be of two kinds: consisting of mantra and [ordinary] mantra.
The domestic fire is to be consecrated, but the new [fire] requires no consecration.
That which consists of mantra is described as being produced from a *pippala* tree containing a *śamī* tree within it.
Whether it be from a sacrificial post or from another source,
or if the fire for the Agnihotra has been brought from the kitchen; or if it has been taken according to the prescribed rite from a Vaiśya who is wealthy in cattle, or even from one's own household.
The fire that is without mantras, which is new, and that which is known as the domestic (māhānasa) fire—
these five consecrations, beginning with *garbha*, must be performed for it in sequence.
This specific fire is also pointed out in the *Pauṣkara*.
Furthermore, for the fire that has been brought forth, the fivefold consecration (*saṃskāra*) must be performed:
inspection and so forth according to the scripture, veiling with the *kavaca* mantra,
and offering five oblations with the *praṇava* for the purification of the flesh-eating portion.
Thereafter, one should perform the universal transference of fire into the three [elements] in three ways.
A wise person should perform this consecration as taught by the venerable Mṛtyujit.
Alternatively, when the fire is blazing,
one should again cast [the oblation] with the right hand into the center of the heart-dwelling [deity], as if by the wind that carries the funeral pyre;
and one should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) as before— this is another rite for the fire of Śiva.

Having beheld Him in the form of Śiva, the practitioner of mantra should gradually perform the internal dissolution of that [deity] within himself; thereafter, he should perform the fire-oblation (homa). The procedure for the fire, which is devoid of the purificatory rites (saṃskāra), has been shown in the *Śrīpūrva* (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra).
Then, one should kindle the fire with blue-colored blades of grass emerging from the mouth [of the vessel].
It should not be done with a winnowing fan, nor with a bowl, nor with the hand, nor with a cloth.
Then, taking the fire-vessel, one should sprinkle it with auspicious water while reciting the Astra-mantra.

Then, having veiled [the fire] with the *kavaca* mantra, one who knows the ritual procedure should worship it with the *praṇava*. Having meditated upon the fire— arisen from the forest and so forth, extending from the beginning to the end of the worlds—
as being like semen (*śukra*), one should [infuse] consciousness into it with the *praṇava*.
Having fully worshipped with the six limbs by means of the *amṛta* mantra,
one should meditate on oneself as Bhairava and meditate on the fire as being like a seed-syllable.
With the *śiva* mantra, one should cause [the fire] to descend by circling it three times outside the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Having cast [the seed] like a seed in a womb with the Bhairava-mantra and the auspicious water (śivāmbhas), the wise one,
having recited the Astra-mantra, should cover the womb. Then,
with Darbha grass and the Dhruva-mantra, he should establish the enclosure (akṣavāṭa).
One should fashion [the protection] in the four directions using *darbha* grass alone with the *astra-mantra*.
Having recited the mantra seven times over a *darbha* blade that has been fashioned like a heron’s claw,
one should bind it upon the right hand while mentally recollecting the *astra-mantra*.
(98a) Therefore, for the sake of protecting the one whose womb contains fire, the rite of impregnation (*garbhādhāna*) should take place.
One should indeed cause a drop of water to fall here with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) using the tip of a *darbha* blade.
One should again perform worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using the *śikhā* [mantra].
One should offer three oblations with the *uttara* [mantra] and one oblation with the *śikhā* [mantra]. For the conception of a male occurs in this manner; he is not produced from a female womb.
One should fashion the parting of the hair with the tip of a darbha blade held in the right hand;
one should likewise fashion the neck, the shoulders, the waist, the arms, and the shanks.
Having thus designated each limb, the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) shall be performed.

One should perform worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and offer three oblations with the head [of the ladle]. One should conceive of the fire as having three parts—the eastern, middle, and western—corresponding to the regions of the mouth, heart, and feet; and at the conclusion of the *homa*, one should perform the *tritatvaka* rite.
Having conceived the five faces— the central, eastern, southern, northern, and western— with three oblations each using the upward-facing [mantra],
one should worship the remaining [faces] with three oblations using the downward-facing [mantra].
Having mentally assigned the *netra* [mantra] with the *netra* [mantra],
one should perform all [the rites] with sesame seeds at each of the three faces and at each of the three *tuti*s (sections),
following the sequence of eight, three, ten, and eight *aṅga*s.
Having fashioned the remaining faces, one should then form the body of sesame (tila).
Afterwards, one should assign the limbs and the heart-mantras in their proper sequence.
One should offer three oblations with the right [face] and three oblations with the head.
The parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*) is thus [concluded]. Now, the birth-rite (*jātakarma*) is described:
one should fan the fire with the *astra* mantra and worship it with the very same mantra.
One should offer three oblations with the eastern [mantra] and likewise three oblations with the cloth itself;
thus, by means of these two mantras, the birth-rite (jātakarma) is accomplished.
One should sprinkle the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the Astra-mantra for the immediate purification of the birth-impurity (sūtaka).
Thereafter, one should cause the faces to vanish with three oblations using the very [mantra of] the faces.
The faces are to be purified by means of the sword [mantra] through three oblations.
In the sprinkling of the faces, there are three [oblations] for each face.

One should sprinkle the sides of the sacrificial pit with auspicious water while reciting the Astra-mantra. Then, having spread the sacrificial grass (darbha) with its tips pointing eastward, arranged from south to north,
one should likewise place the enclosing sticks (paridhi) and the spreading grass (viṣṭara), starting from the north, with their tips pointing eastward and westward.
All of them [should be worshipped] with weapon against weapon on the eastern seat;
Rudra should be established on the southern [seat], Viṣṇu on the western seat,
and Sadāśiva on the northern [seat], each marked with the word of their own name.

O Goddess, one should first remember the fixed [seed-syllable] and then assign the name in the peaceful state. One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, while not forgetting their respective forms.
Above the girdle, one should worship the World-Protectors with the syllable *praṇava*.

For the sake of protecting the newborn infant, Brahmā and the other deities should be worshipped by you. Then, having removed the bracelet situated on the right hand and taking hold of a flower, the Lord should assign a name in the presence of Śivā.

Having performed the recitation with the *kavaca* mantra, one should offer oblations of perfume, flowers, incense, and so forth. With the face turned upward, one should offer three oblations; then again, three with the *kavaca*. Having thus generated the divine fire marked with the names of Śiva, [one should then address] the gods.
One should dismiss Sāvitrī to her own place with the *praṇava*,
having worshipped her with flowers and other offerings, and indeed with three oblations each.
The fuel-sticks (samidh) are to be offered according to their respective domains, measuring one cubit in length;
twenty-four in number, they are for the purpose of satiation at the tip of Śiva’s fire. These five purificatory rites (saṃskāra) have been proclaimed in the Svacchandabhairava.

In the absence of ghee, the performance of the *jātakarman* rite is accomplished by means of sesame seeds, leaves, excellent *vātakuśa* grass, and fruits. The naming ceremony is performed with the mantra: "Oṃ, salutation to Śiva, to Agni."

Having uttered this, one should cast the flower; the worship and so forth are performed with the *kavaca* mantra. One should perform the ritual procedure for naming with the *īśa* mantra. The fire-oblation (*homa*) is performed with the *īśāna* and *varma* mantras; thus is the fivefold consecration (*saṃskāra*).

Or, due to the absence of the fire-oblation (homa), one should perform the five purificatory rites (saṃskāras) through recitation (japa). These rites are especially intended for when the sacrificial materials are unavailable; they are thus honored. This concludes the consecration of the fire (agnisaṃskāra).
Having heated the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles in the fire, one should sprinkle them with auspicious water while reciting the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
Enveloping them with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), one should rotate them three times in the Śiva-fire.
Then, one should wipe them with water using the tip of a *darbha* blade while reciting the weapon-mantra, and subsequently touch them.

Again, having whirled them over the fire, one should sprinkle them with the water of Śiva. Having touched the *darbha* grass with another [implement], one should whirl them over the fire again and heat them. Having cleansed them with the water of Śiva, one should touch them with the root-end of the *darbha* grass.
Then, one should place the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles face down upon the blades of *darbha* grass;
they should always be worshipped by the wise to the south of the fire.
Once they have been placed, they should be heated over the fire, sprinkled with water, and wiped clean with *kuśa* grass.
"One should cleanse the tip with the tip, the middle with the middle, and the base with the base"—
thus it is stated in the *Svacchanda*, *Hāṭakeśvara*, and *Vyāsa-samāna*.
The state of being composed of the powers of will (*icchā*) and the rest arises precisely from that triad. Furthermore, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles are threefold;
by placing them [therein], one should heat them thrice with fire.
By that [realization], they were born contented and turned away from the state of wood.
Those three conceptualized states are fashioned from the three powers (*śakti*).
By means of those [powers], touching the three locations, there is the contemplation of peace (*śāntabhāvanā*) in everything.
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles are established by direct instruction; Sadāśiva is the mass of power (*śaktipiṇḍa*).
The Power that pervades all levels of existence (*adhvan*) is conceived as the vessel (*āsrug*).
A specific refinement has been made for these two according to the ancient scripture.
Thus ends the consecration of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.
One should perform the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*) as one does for the *śravaṇa* and other rites.
Having sprinkled the clarified butter with the *astra-mantra*, one should veil it with the *kavaca-mantra*.
One should heat it in the Śiva-fire with the Astra-mantra and expel [impurities] with the Kavaca-mantra.

O Goddess, having circled it three times around the fire-pit (kuṇḍa), one should establish it. Then, the vessel of clarified butter (ājyapātra) should be placed within the womb [of the pit], together with its float and its ladle.
Taking two tips of *darbha* grass, one should fashion a *pavitra* measuring a span (*prādeśa*) with a knot in the middle;
this is the prescribed *pavitra*, and one should perform the ritual with it well-soaked.
Then, holding that *pavitra* with the thumb and the ring finger—
Turning away from three doors and likewise facing toward three,
he should sprinkle [the site] with the *astra* mantra alone by means of the fire of Śiva.
Having taken up a bundle of *darbha* grass and a torch, he should gaze upon the vessel of clarified butter (*ājya*).
Then one should perform the *nīrājana* rite, and then the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*).
Having uttered the *dhāman* weapon-mantra, one should cast a firebrand into that fire.
The practitioner of mantra should recognize [the deity] by its very abode and sprinkle it with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra (astra).
Having empowered it with the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), he should effect its emission with the Dhruva-mantra. Then, by reciting the Bhairava-mantra once, he should perform the worship.
The consecration of the clarified butter (ājya) is declared in the venerable Svacchanda-śāsana:
that which is purified by all four—by fire, by mantra, by the purifier (pavitra), and by the eye—is *ājya*; anything else is merely ghee (*ghṛta*).
This specific procedure for the illumination of ritual action has been declared by the venerable Dharmaśiva.
Thus ends the consecration of the clarified butter (ājya-saṃskāra).
One should perform the joining of the mouths [of the ladles] with three oblations using the [respective] faces.
One should perform the joining of that face with the [mantra] beginning with *apara*.
In this way, the joining of the gentle (Saumya) face is accomplished.
The junction of the faces is proclaimed to be performed by the application of three oblations (*āhuti*).
Thus ends the section on the Orientation of the Faces.
The face situated upon the primary head is the principal one, while the others possess the status of qualities.
For one desiring liberation during initiation, the upward-facing face holds primacy.
Indeed, the Pāñcāla, the Pāñjana, and other various Siddhis—
all of which culminate in Sadāśiva— one should offer as oblations into the eastern face.
This applies likewise to rites such as killing, driving away, creating enmity, and paralyzing.
Through oblation in the southern face, supreme accomplishment will be attained;
likewise, rites for pacification, nourishment, good fortune, and attraction,
as well as the accomplishment of ascending to good fortune, one should always perform the oblation in the northern face.
In the west, the application of the daily rites is proclaimed;
for the consumption of the clarified butter is indeed to be offered into the upward-facing [flame] in the west.
O lady of excellent hips, one should then place a *darbha* blade in the center of the clarified butter vessel with the *Bhairava-mantra*; thereafter follows the ritual procedure.
One should simultaneously deposit three portions across the three channels (*nāḍī*) in a single moment.
One should conceive of Suṣumnā as situated in the middle part and Piṅgalā on the right;
one should conceive of Saumyā on the left for that light which comes through the path of Iḍā.
Having thus conceived the three parts and having filled [the vessel] with clarified butter, one should perform the oblation.

With the Bhairava mantra itself, ending with "agnaye svāhā," one should take the portion belonging to Agni and cast it as an oblation of clarified butter with the *drū* mantra. Regarding the portion belonging to Soma, while reciting [the mantra] ending with "somāya svāhā," [one should proceed].
One should offer an oblation of clarified butter (ājyāhuti) with the *dhruva* mantra, preceded by the *praṇava* and beginning with the word "dhāma.

Having filled the *sruva* ladle with clarified butter— beginning with the *praṇava*, containing the word "dhāma," and ending with the word "svāhā"— one should perform the *homa* sacrifice using the two verses beginning with "agnīṣomā" and ending with "svāhā."
In the bright fortnight, the procedure is thus; in the dark fortnight, it should be otherwise. When the moon is in its waning phase, the sun indeed becomes known as "Fire" (Agni), as before.
One should offer the oblation from the center of that solar fire.
"For on the new moon day, the moon indeed enters into the center of the sun.
Thus end the Cākṣuṣī oblations. Following this, however, there is an oblation for Bhairava for the purpose of consuming [the sacrificial food] by means of his mouths.
In the Cūḍādhyāya, however, the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) for the fire are established as ending with the washing (kṣālana).

For the purpose of the consumption [of the oblation], one should offer a single portion of the previous [substances] to all. Having uttered "Bhairava," Śivāgni is the bestower of all accomplishments (siddhi).
One should subsequently lift up the fire, establish it in the vessel, and preserve it;
the arrangement of the three junctions of the faces is according to the Svacchanda-śāstra.

Thus it has been said: for the sake of accomplishing the *caru* and other offerings, the wise man, having consecrated the fire in a separate pit, should establish it according to the prescribed rite (*varma-kṣita*).
Or, for the purpose of daily ritual, he may remain established in the abbreviated procedure (*sāmāsika-vidhi*).
In the *Śrīmṛgendra* as well, the procedure for the sake of the fire has been prescribed:

"One who knows the scriptures should not offer oblations into a fire whose flames are directed upward, nor into one whose flames are agitated by smoke, nor into one that is only faintly glowing, nor into one that is too small."
One should perform the *paryeṣṭi* (searching) for the rites of pacification (*śānti*), nourishment (*āpyāyana*), and so forth, as well as for the *mṛtyuñjaya* and other mantras.
[The fire] is auspicious when its flames curve to the right, outshining the moonlight, and it is used for the attainment of good fortune, attraction, progeny, fruits, roots, and other such siddhis.
He shines like a pomegranate flower or coral;
he is beneficial for [rites of] inciting enmity, eradication, causing disease, withering, deluding, destroying, and so forth.
He possesses dark blue or black flames and is accompanied by smoke. He is beneficial for his own [destruction].

For the attainment of elixirs, the essence of flavors, health, stability, sovereignty, and other perfections; for the great yogi of the knowledge of reality, who is like turmeric, saffron, *karṇikāra* flowers, and the moon, to proceed toward divine accomplishment.
With a flame resembling crystal, accomplishing mixed and unmixed purposes;
in the *Candrarāja*, the fragrance of jasmine or the scent of *mallikā* flowers;
for rites such as pacification (*śānti*), the substances are camphor, agallochum (*aguru*), and saffron.
In rites for averting misfortune (*ariṣṭa*), one should use marrow, fat, and muscle; in rites for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), the Kadamba, Ketakī, Bimba, Caṇpaka, and so forth;
and [in rites for subjugation], the substances consisting of Kapi, Guggulu, Dantī, Śaṭī, Vacā, and Yavāsa.
In the Mahodaya, the arrangement of objects suitable for ritual action is established by words.
These two—form and fragrance—are revealed in the Mṛgendra as belonging to fire. (101b)

I shall fully explain the characteristics of fire, which grant success in all undertakings. One must diligently understand the sixfold characteristics of fire, which are endowed with color, sound, crest, smoke, resonance, and fragrance.
White, red, yellow, green, or even black— any single,
stable, glossy, and captivating color is praised.
[This applies to] white varieties of flowers, as well as conch and crystal.
The color of lotus fibers and the moon is white and pure; the auspicious color of red flowers and gold is known as yellow, like the belly of a palm tree and the navel.
The color of fire is desired to be green, like that of green flowers,
jasmine, and emerald; however,
for black varieties of lotus, as well as for swords and collyrium, it is black.
Having a color like sapphire or great sapphire, white and auspicious;
having a shape resembling a linga, a temple, a lotus, a mountain, or a banner;
and being auspicious when resembling a lion, a garuḍa, an elephant, or a bull—such is the auspicious [mark].

Glossy, turning clockwise, well-formed at their tips, compact, and unbroken— such tufts of hair are praised like the plumes of a chowrie. Those hairs described as black are auspicious, provided they have the fragrance of smoke.
The sound of flutes and lutes was like the cry of the cuckoo and the bee, and like the throat of the peacock; the roar of fire was equal to the sound of conchs and kettledrums,
while the trumpeting of elephants and the lion’s roar were hushed.
The fragrance of excellent aromatic substances, the scent of fire and ghee,
and a fragrance equal to that of various species of fragrant flowers bring about success.
The fire,
impelled by obstacles, becomes agitated, unbearable, and produces crackling sounds like that of smoke;
therefore, the practitioner should perform the *homa* with the *bahurūpa* mantra.
Indeed, when the fire is offered oblations with the Aghora mantra accompanied by the syllable *e* and the *kāra* ending in *m*, then the fire, along with its modifications,
[consumes] that which is sinful and originates from the sacrificer.
Vāmadeva shall destroy the sin committed by killing a Brahmin;
Bahurūpa shall utterly annihilate the sin born from stealing the property of one’s own caste;
and having committed adultery with the wife of a guru, Tatpuruṣa shall burn away that sin.

May Īśāna wipe away that great sin, arising from contact with [the sacrificial materials] either collectively, individually, or in combination, which has been committed by him through the clarified butter (*ājya*).
He is white in color, yet pale; he possesses a foul odor, yet he is indeed the one to be consumed.

The one who has entered the fire announces the murder of a Brahmin; the red one, the drinking of liquor; the yellowish one, theft; and the green one, the sin committed with a woman. The black one announces the sin born of association.
When the fire, being offered with the aforementioned oblations,
ceases to remain in its natural state, then one should offer the oblations by means of the *aham* [syllable] alone.
When the fire is well-kindled with abundant fuel for the oblation and possesses brilliant luster—
One should offer oblations into a fire that is smokeless and bright for the successful accomplishment of one's rites.
If one should offer oblations into a fire that is smoke-filled and not yet fully kindled,
there will be a loss of the ritual efficacy, and the sacrificer himself shall perish.
Fragrant with the scent of kuṅkuma, resounding with the music of flutes and lutes,
its flames whirled to the right, and it was exceedingly radiant with a smooth, glossy color.
Always blazing and unwavering, indeed intensely radiant,
with the color of a lotus or a blue water-lily— such is the fire that accomplishes all purposes.
These characteristics, such as the color and other signs of fire, have been declared in the Pauṣkara scripture.
One should know that in a white form there is auspiciousness; in one with the luster of crystal, progeny and fortune;
in one resembling a ruby, sovereignty; in one like the moon, happiness and prosperity;
and in one resembling yellow orpiment, wealth, increase, and the enhancement of splendor.
When the *gāyatrī* is recited over clarified butter (*ājya*), happiness and the accomplishment of mantras arise.
Whatever substance the sacrificial fire conceives within its womb,
it is said to grant that fruit swiftly, increasing wealth and grain.

Having seen the fire blazing but lacking its proper color, making noise, and devoid of the three auspicious signs (the *śreyas-traya*), one should avoid it for up to three days; likewise, one should avoid performing oblations (*havana*),
the satisfaction through mantras (*mantratṛpti*), and food [offered there].
When the fourth day has arrived, one should begin the fire-oblation (homa) therein. However,
he who offers oblations without first discerning the form of the mouth [of the fire] shall perish prematurely,
