falling away from both seen and unseen fruits.
If a fall of fire occurs at the crown of the head, there is loss of wealth; if it falls on the heart, there is loss of riches;
if it falls on the two sides, there will be the destruction of kinsmen; and if it falls on the back, there is the destruction of the family.
Therefore, with every effort, one should remember this with a happy mind.
In that very place, one who is diligent in performing expiation should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
This has been declared according to the *Sārasvata-mata* through its various distinctions of fruit.
Having thus understood these characteristics, one should satisfy Śiva within the fire.
If that which has fallen from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is offered again out of grace,
yet one does not cast it back into the fire out of greed, then that which has been vomited by him is censured.
Furthermore, on the northern side of the pit, to the left of the grass mat (viṣṭara), [it should be placed].
(103a) One should prepare a refined vessel there, filled with water;
one should place therein a pure strainer joined with flowers, unbroken rice, and sesame seeds.

Having invoked [the deity] with the *praṇava* and other mantras, one should always worship Viṣṇu by means of the very vocative address "O Viṣṇu," having thus established Him. Then, with a welcome, a seat, water for the feet (*pādya*), and the guest-offering (*argha*), one should address Him as follows:
Whether the sacrifice has been commenced for the sake of the sacrificial animal or for the sake of the practitioner himself,
O Blessed One, by Your grace may there be flawlessness in my portion. The *praṇītā* and the *sthiti-vijñapti* have been proclaimed in the *Śrī-svacchanda*.
Then, while uttering the *praṇava*, one should worship the eightfold Śaiva [deities] in the world within the eight full jars,
according to their pervasion of the earth and the directions. Likewise, one should offer eight lamps to Śiva located in the direction of fire (the southeast).
The eight jars have been specified by the illustrious Dharmaśiva. Thereafter, O Goddess, one should perform the sacrifice in the fire and worship Bhairava;
on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), however, one should worship Ananta and the others according to the prescribed rite.
Having meditated upon the five faces in the fire, one should visualize whichever face is desired for whatever rite is intended; then,
having conceived that central face according to the dimensions of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
one should contemplate nine tongues established within each face.
Eight [lines] starting from the east are for the central [deity], while one is praised as being directed toward the directions for the sake of specific desires.
[These lines] bestow sovereignty, act as a mother, grant death, cause enmity with enemies, bring about subjugation, perform the rite of attraction (uccāṭana), grant wealth, and bestow liberation.
Bestowing all accomplishments, one should therefore perform the oblation in the center;
indeed, with the *pūrṇāhuti* alone, by means of Bhairava, for the purpose of conceiving the tongues [of fire].
Then, one should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* itself with Bhairava.
Having grasped the tip of the flame with the heart-mantra, conceived as the consciousness of fire,
and having visualized it as residing within oneself, one should then imagine the yoga-throne.
Following the tongue [of the flame], one should place the skull-cup at the navel;
having recognized the stalk as extending up to the heart, one should visualize a lotus there,
endowed with eight petals, white in color, and of great brilliance.
One should conceive of the infinite there, beginning with the feet of Dharma and so forth;
one should likewise fashion the form of Agni, beginning with Oṃ and ending with Śiva.
Then, with the *dhruva* mantra, one should again perform the ritual of unfastening (*utkīlana*) for that which resides in the crest and the heart.
One should cast [the offering] into the fire with the *recaka* breath; that [fire] is of the nature of Bhairava as the embodied form (*mūrti*).
Having thus conceived it as the embodied form endowed with the thirty-eight *kalās*, one should then project the path to be purified (*śodhyādhvan*) at the time of initiation, O fair-faced one.
Having worshipped Bhairava according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures,
the union of the faces occurs through the two faces, and from that, the union of the channels arises.
Having uttered the root mantra, he [the deity] emerges through the mouth of fire.
One should recite the mantra, which has but a single meaning, while standing upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with the tuft of hair (śikhā) resting there.
O fair-faced one, one hundred and eight oblations should be offered into pure clarified butter;
here, for Bhairava, the ten-part portion (daśāṃśaka) should be offered for the faces and limbs.

One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) for the eight Bhairavas and the ten Lords of the World (Lokeśas) according to the [prescribed] number. Having recited the root mantra, one should offer a single full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Furthermore, this is for the sake of removing any deficiency or excess and to ensure there are no flaws.
Afterwards, O fair-faced one, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed according to one’s desire.
Having thus regularly performed what is taught in one’s own Tantra for rites such as pacification (śānti),
one should offer oblations in this sequence, soaked with clarified butter (ājya), for the sake of a good rebirth.
In the past, she was made of sacrificial wood from the beginning and end of the Brahma-tree;
she was known as Kausumīgandhā, with Madhuparka as her womb.
Having offered the oblation known as *ājya*, one should then present another auspicious *pūrṇāhuti*.
This may be performed a thousand times, a hundred times, or according to one's faith and capacity.
One should then separately gratify [the deities] with the previously mentioned desirable materials.

Then, having mixed all those substances together, saturated them again with the three sweets (trimadhu), one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) for the satisfaction of each individual substance; or, O Six-faced One, when all the materials for the fire-oblation (*homa*) are assembled, one may offer a single oblation using all of them together.
Thus, the fire sacrifice (homa) has been observed in the Īśvara-saṃhitā as following one's desire;
such a sacrifice should be performed according to the specific rite.
For the purpose of pacification (śānti), there should be an offering of dūrvā grass, but for nourishment (pauṣṭika), it should be ghee alone.
For the purpose of subjugation (*vaśya*), one should offer fragrant substances mixed with sesame seeds.
For expulsion (*uccāṭana*), one should offer crow feathers; for killing (*māraṇa*), poisonous substances;
and for the rite of causing enmity (*vidveṣa*), the feathers of an owl and a crow.
For attraction, one should use white mustard seeds combined with pungent oil;
likewise for the propitiation of a Yakṣiṇī and for women who worship the Buddha.
By offering oblations of Nāgapuṣpa flowers, even Nāga maidens will become submissive.
Then, one desiring to accomplish the attainment of Apsarases should offer lotuses and water-lilies.
For the propitiation of the four castes, one should offer grains along with sesamum.
O best of Brahmins, by the oblation of bilva fruits, the practitioner beholds prosperity.

By means of a hundred thousand oblations of *guggulu* resin together with pills, the most excellent practitioner shall accomplish the *Padmamālinī* rite; by performing it with a target of ten thousand,
he obtains all his desires, especially when he has renounced them.
One should perform the oblation in its entirety with substances smeared with honey, milk, and ghee.
That which has been relinquished is fully described; one should avoid it in cruel rites.
The gross [form] is said to consist of the mantra, while the subtle possesses the body of the *bindu*.
The Supreme is said to consist of Śakti; meditation on Śiva is both supreme and non-supreme.
One who knows the distinction between Bindu and Nāda is a contemplator of Śiva and Śakti.
"The Lord Śiva has declared that one attains the desired accomplishment.
Having performed the fire-oblation (homa) as prescribed at Hāṭakeśvara-rakta,
the preceptor should subsequently perform the expiation (prāyaścitta) ordained by Śiva."
In the performance of ritual action, there is no distraction of mind for one who exceeds the prescribed number;
having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one becomes purified through atonement.
Now I shall describe to you the procedure for the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
With the upper body erect, the neck straight, and the feet placed evenly,

one should position the base of the *sruk* ladle at the level of the navel with its tip facing upward and held comfortably. O Goddess, having placed the *sruva* spoon upon the *sruk*, it should likewise be turned face down.
Having placed a flower at the tip of the *sruc* ladle, held together with a blade of *darbha* grass,
and grasped it with both hands in the manner of a hollowed cup (*tattāvuka*),
one should then drench it with clarified butter and perform the act of consecration (*abhimāna*).
I alone am the supreme reality through the division of the higher and the lower. Reality is indeed one everywhere; one should not cause anything else to exist.

O fair-faced one, he who has cast darkness into the jar of sixfold variety— [Note: The text provided appears to be a fragment from a tantric or Śaiva philosophical work. The final line refers to the "sixfold variety" (*ṣaṭprakāra*), which typically denotes the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) or the six categories of existence in certain systems.]

Having projected the path [of the offering] into the ladle— from the common conceptualization within the child [disciple] in the fire of the maṇḍala— [placing it] in the center of the station of the vital breath (prāṇa) situated between the two nostrils;
and having made the prāṇa and apāna equal, one should cast it into the receptacle of the ladle.
By means of the *vasudhārā* practice, one should cast [the breath] into the fire.
One should lead the root of the sacrificial ladle from the region of the navel to the range of the tip of the nose.
In whatever manner one offers the stream, in that same manner one should exhale the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
One should offer that into the fire with these two [mantras], using a stream of water accompanied by a smile.
One should also offer ceremonial rinsing water, sandalwood paste, and preparations such as betel leaf.
Having worshipped Him with devotion, one should offer supreme prostration;
then, having dismissed Śiva with the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) added to each of the three worlds beginning with Bhūḥ,
one should offer four oblations either sequentially or simultaneously.
Then, having worshipped the fire and drawn out the *śumbha* [offerings] with the weapon-mantra ending in *phaṭ*,
and having performed the rite of "forgive me" (*kṣamasva*) using the *saṃhāra-mudrā*,
he should [withdraw] those situated within the radiant perimeter by means of inhalation (*pūraka*) and the heart-mantra.
One should establish [the fire] within one's own heart-lotus with supreme devotion.
Regarding the dismissal of the fire, the procedure is that which has been declared in the sequence of the Karmakāṇḍa.
One should wipe away the residue of clarified butter from the *sruc*, the *sruva*, and the vessel for the clarified butter.
Having thrown that [substance] into the midst of the fire, one may perform whatever rite one desires.
With it, one should apply the *tripuṇḍra* on the forehead, on the ears, on the two arms,
and on the region of the navel for the sake of great longevity and the grace of Śiva.
One should pour that water from the *praṇītā* vessel in all directions;
by that, the spirits and the officiating priests residing in the quarters are satisfied.
This which was proclaimed by Saṅkarṣaṇa is for when the previous [rite] has been lost at its conclusion.

At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, having applied the *tilaka*, the sins accumulated over seven lifetimes are destroyed; therefore, one should carry that sacred ash. A human being does not obtain such a fruit even through a thousand sacrifices.
This was taught by Nandin to the sages in the *Nandīśvara-āgama*. Having brought the foremost of all cooked offerings and having prepared two mandalas,
one should present the inner and outer oblations in the southeast, near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Rudras in the east; to the Rakṣasas in the southeast; to the Nāgas in the southwest; to the Nakṣatras in the northwest; to the Viśvedevas and the Rāśis [in the north]; and to the Kṣetrapāla in the center of the four corners. (105b) The seed-syllable Oṃ and the word svāhā are used everywhere. In the second maṇḍala: Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Indra. In this manner, there are the eight world-protectors from the east to Īśāna. To Brahmā above and to Viṣṇu below.

In the center of that [maṇḍala], an offering (bali) and libation (tarpaṇa) should be made for the Guardian of the Field (kṣetrapāla). Then, outside the maṇḍala, offerings should be made for the crows and other such beings.
Likewise, the concluding fire-rite (agnikārya) performed upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or the [liṅga] has been described;
now the procedure for the caru-oblation at the midday junction (madhyasandhyā) shall be told.
In this teaching, there are two kinds of *caru* and two kinds of *puroḍāśa*:
one is called the *śivacaru*, and likewise the *vidyeśacarū*;
one is the *śivapuroḍāśa*, while the other consists of the *vidyeśvara*s.
The consecration of the vessel for the *caru* has been proclaimed by Maheśa;
likewise, the procedure for other substances and vessels therein is as follows:
first, there is the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) of the *caru* vessel seven times.
The ritual application should be performed according to the rules with the Sadyojāta mantra; milk, or indeed water, should be consecrated with the Vāmadeva mantra;
and rice grains sprinkled with ghee should be consecrated with the Aghora mantra.
The neck of the vessel for the sacrificial porridge (caru) should be wrapped with kuśa grass that has been wound around it.
Ghee and milk [should be offered] through the mouth, and curd likewise, according to the prescribed rule. Thus is the ritual procedure for the Śiva-caru, beginning with the offering to Īśāna.
For all the Śiva-mantras whose essence resides upon the Yoga-pīṭha, one should offer oblations with the Aghora-mantra and the Śiva-gāyatrī, and then dismiss them. Thereafter, the caru-oblation,
having been offered with the Āghāra and Sampāta rites and consecrated by recitation, should be performed by Śiva.
It should be performed by the God of all selves, the god of gods, who possesses many forms,
or likewise by Īśāna as the Lord, according to the available oblation.
Having filled the *sruva* ladle with pure clarified butter from a cow,
one should there recite the mantra of Uparicara as prescribed;
then, having offered it into the fire with the utterance of *svāhā*, one should shake the *sruva* over the *caru*.
This *sampāta-homa* is enjoined by rule everywhere;
the *sampāta* should be performed one hundred times, or even as many times as possible.
Then, the *kuśāgra-mantra* should be recited eight hundred times in detail.
That cleansing should be performed by Maheśa at the region of the throat;
indeed, the smearing with cow-dung should be done only once.
Then, pressed with the thumb, it should be offered to Śiva with the *hṛdaya* mantra.

It should then be divided into three parts and placed in three vessels. The first portion, honored with flowers, is to be offered to Śiva; the second is to be offered as an oblation into the fire; and the third belongs to the practitioner.
In vessels made of gold and jewels, or of silver and copper; in the absence of such vessels, in auspicious earthen ones,
or in those made of plantain, blue lotus, royal jasmine, sunflower, or water-born lotuses.
The practitioner should offer oblations to Śiva and likewise to the fire with the middle leaves of the *palāśa* tree, combined with ghee and honey. Alternatively,
his own portion may be prepared with honey alone or with ghee alone.
The Śivacaru has been described, which liberates one from all sins,
pacifies calamities, and destroys all obstacles;
it is equal to the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and Tulāpuruṣa penances when performed according to the prescribed rules.
Having eaten the *śiva-caru* but once, one obtains the merit of having performed it a hundred times;
likewise at the equinoxes (*viṣuvat*), the solstices (*ayana*) of the sun, at the *viśvapada* [festivals],
at the commencement of the *ṣaḍaśīti*, and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
During the *vyatīpāta* yogas, the *caru* offering should always be presented to the deity.
On the day of one's birth star (*janmanakṣatra*), the *caru* should especially be consumed.

A householder who has previously observed celibacy should always eat the *śivacaru* offering; by consuming that *caru*, he indeed obtains the supreme fruit of that *caru*. Having consumed the *caru*, the wise man should not eat anything else at all.
Even one who drinks liquor should abandon it, or else always [abandon both] with true devotion.
The practitioner, however, should always consume the *caru* oblation and the *āvartana*.
Thus, he shall attain the accomplishment (*siddhi*) desired by his mind, free from all obstacles.
The sacrificial oblation (caru) for the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśvara) is to be prepared with one's own heart-mantra.
The oblation may be prepared from rice-flour, wild millet (nīvāra), śyāmāka, or even rice grains;
or likewise from wheat, barley, and kaṅku.
One should cook the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) with the powder of these very [grains],

according to the rule, using full quantities of clarified butter on two earthen plates that are equal and two finger-breadths thick. The Śiva-puroḍāśa is to be prepared in this manner, and it should consist of five potsherds.
The hoof should finally be made with its tip no larger than the palm of one's own hand;
it must be made level with great effort according to the prescribed rule.
If it is crooked, it causes the fear of disease; if burnt, it brings about death itself.
A sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) that is perfectly cooked accomplishes all desired aims.
Both the qualities and the defects of the sacrificial cake have been proclaimed;
indeed, one such quality of the sacrificial cake is also possessed by the practitioner who performs the rite.
The sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) representing Śiva should be prepared with nine portions (avadāna).
The sacrificial cake for the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvara) should be made with five portions.
Portions are prescribed as nine in all the directions and in the center.
In the four directions as well as in the center, there are indeed five portions (*avadāna*).
Having offered the portions of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) in sequence,
the knower of mantras should himself eat the remnants of the offering and give them to someone else.
(107a) The sacrificial cake along with the oblation must never be given by the officiating priest to anyone other than the Guru, according to the established rule for one who knows the ritual.
In this manner, O friends, the sacrificial pap (caru) and the cake (puroḍāśa) must be prepared by the practitioner.
However, when the fire has not been offered to Śiva and has not been consecrated by the proper rites,
the practitioner himself, being intoxicated [by the power of the mantra], must cook another sacrificial pap.

Immersed in this [mantra], [one offers] salutations with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) everywhere to the Self of Supreme Śiva; to the Self of Sadāśiva; to the Self of Īśvara; to the Self of Vidyā; to the Self of Māyā; to the Self of Kalā; to the Self of Niyati; to the Self of Puruṣa; and to the Self of Pradhāna. [The sequence is: Īśvara, Vidyā, Māyā, Puruṣa, Pradhāna—exactly thus.
In the *Śrī Pauṣkara*, the accomplishment of the *caru* and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is twofold.
I shall now speak of that water with honey, and the determination regarding the wandering for alms (*bhikṣāṭana*).
Brahmā said:

O Lord, for those practitioners who possess only *kuśa* grass as their wealth, who are poor and ascetic, you have provided this means of subsistence through the *caru* offering; what other way of livelihood could there be?
The Supreme Lord said:
Vegetables, the roots of ritual action, and various fruits constitute the sustenance for the best of practitioners— those who are poor and devoted to austerity.
One who eats food should first practice [the consumption] very gradually;
the practitioner should increase the morsels of vegetables and so forth until they reach the desired amount.
The wise one should [regulate] the morsels of food according to his internal disposition.

The first morsel of the vegetable [consists of] the heart, the channels, and so forth, as they naturally exist; the second morsel, consisting of the intellect, the self, and the inner being, is to be taken as it naturally exists, beginning with the *sauhitya* (satisfaction).
Once that has become one's own, the wise man should increase the second [morsel] during that consumption.

In this manner, the practice should be performed until only vegetables and the like remain as food for the lord of practitioners; then, having entered the forest which abounds in tubers and roots and is augmented by fruits and vegetables, [he should continue].
(107b) Otherwise, if one were to suddenly abandon the [proper] food and eat only vegetables and the like,
pain would surely arise in the stomach and in the limbs.
Burning of the limbs, breaking pain in the head, burning of the throat, as well as vertigo,
loss of appetite, trembling, and dysentery arise; or else,
the wise man should avoid bulbs, roots, fruits, and the like.
The practitioner of mantra should subsist on grains, oil-cakes, and parched grain flour;
even for these, one should first perform the ritual of conquest (*jaya*) as one does for roots and tubers.
One should consume roots, tubers, fruits, vegetables, and alms-food obtained from twice-born men.
The practitioner of mantra should consume vegetables and other such foods that are easily obtained, non-burning to the stomach, sweet, soft, light, and phlegm-increasing;
however, the mantra-practitioner should avoid grains such as *kaṇa* and similar items.
One should maintain one's livelihood by means of alms and take refuge in prosperous places.
Alms are said to be of four kinds for high-souled practitioners:
*mādhūkara*, *svayaṃ-datta*, *sāntānika*, and *ucita*.
Alms gathered by wandering from house to house is known as "the honey-gathering" (mādhukara) alms.

When a practitioner himself receives enough alms to fill his bowl, it is considered "self-given. That by which the filling of the bowl is accomplished while one is seeking alms is likewise [accepted].
It has been said that this alms-food of mine should always be accepted;
for it is designated as "alms for the sake of progeny" (sāntānika).
Furthermore, it is intended that alms be given to one who has entered [the house] for the purpose of begging.
One should practice this fourfold mode of mendicancy as the livelihood of a monk.
Whether there is gain or loss, one should maintain an even mind, free from a turbid nature.
One should avoid those households where women are constantly intent on jesting.
One seeking alms should carefully avoid from afar that house where there is immediate slaughter of meat and revelry takes place.
One seeking alms should avoid that house from afar in every way.
One should practice begging for alms among the four castes who abide in their own duties,
as well as among fallen twice-born men and those who have cursed themselves.
A seeker of alms who is practicing for success should not wander for alms among houses.
A wise man should never step upon the shadow of another,
nor should he ever walk downwind from another person.

One must never, under any circumstances, perform a funeral rite for gurus, Vedic scholars, those who have renounced the world, pregnant women, or those overcome by fear, if it has not been properly completed by another.
Indeed, through physical contact and even conversation, calamities arise in various ways;
moreover, afflictions and most unbearable diseases torment him.
Therefore, applying diligent effort, the practitioner of mantra should wander for alms.
The learned man, having equipped himself according to rule with the five ancillaries of knowledge,
should wander for alms without negligence, while recollecting Lord Śiva.
When the second pressing of the Soma has been prepared, he should purify his alms-bowl.
The wise one [should act] indeed with the Vāmadeva mantra and the Sāṅgu weapon.
A vessel— whether made of metal, clay, split bamboo, or strong bamboo, or even one placed within a date-palm leaf-cup, or made of leaves in the absence [of others].
The bamboo staff should have the girth of a thumb, be even, round, straight, and firm; it should be thus bound and held, free from blemishes.
Having placed the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyādhipa) upon the heart with the mudrā of the Multiformed One (Bahurūpa), [one should proceed].
Likewise, one should place the Brahmaśiras at the crown with the mudrā of Īśāna;
and Rudrāṇī at the crest-lock with the mudrā of Īśāna.
One should place *Puruṣṭhuta* on the two breasts with the *Bahurūpa* mudrā;
and the *Astra* on the hand and the staff with the *Sadyojāta* mudrā.
One should perform this placement (*nyāsa*) in sequence using those respective mudrās.
Then, having offered [the food] to the deity and the guru according to the prescribed rule,
the wise man, seeking alms, should enter the village while recollecting Lord Śiva;
he should likewise strike the path three times with his staff.
Having cleared the directions with the Astra-mantra, the wise man should place Īśa within the solar disc—
either as the All-Self, Aghora, Gāyatrī, or Śiva himself—
and while mentally reciting the Pratyaṅgirā, he should wander for alms.
The knower of mantras should not accept alms with an empty body;
rather, while reciting the *Pratyaṅgirā*, he should diligently receive alms.
The *Svastipratyaṅgirā* is said to consist of three syllables, beginning with the *praṇava*.

For indeed, whatever is unfit to be eaten by the twice-born should not be accepted by the wise from one who is intent on begging for alms. Even if meat should ever be given in such alms through ignorance, it must not be taken.
In that case, however, there would be no fault; the fault lies in giving [meat] knowingly.
One should never accept alms containing meat unknowingly.
A practitioner of mantras should collect alms that are neither too small nor too large.
It should not be used excessively, nor should it be praised too much.
One should perform the worship of deities and guests, offer oblations to the gods,
and likewise present the *vāstu-bali* as well as offerings to the crows and the sun.
One should accept only as much as is necessary and not from excessive abundance;
furthermore, one should never eat leftover alms-food oneself.
Having wandered for alms, he should return to his own home alone;
a knower of the Self should not seek alms at another's house.
Having reached his own home and having performed the cleansing of his legs...
Having bathed or touched ashes, one should perform the purification of alms-food.
Having silently sprinkled it with water and likewise illuminated it with a firebrand,
one should touch it before the Deity and oneself with the five mantras.

One should praise the remainder [of the food] and set aside a portion for the gods and the crows; this is the purpose for the gods and others, serving as food for guests. Having offered that alms-food into the fire, one should then consume what has been prepared for oneself.
One should eat the remainder from the aforementioned vessels, preceded by water.
One should not eat to excessive satiety, nor should one excessively emaciate the body. The practitioner of mantra should drink very pure water that has passed through the three substances.

One should never eat fresh food immediately after a meal, nor at an improper time, nor during the night; yet one may eat even stale grains and likewise fresh vaṭakas, provided they have been eaten from a vessel.
Modakas filled with food fit for eating as pieces, sesame modakas, well-prepared aśokavartis, neck-encirclers (grīveṣṭhas), honey-heads (madhuśīrṣakas),
and salt-filled embryo-mounds (garbhotkaras), even those many days old.
The practitioner of mantras should consume faultless and unrepulsive *maṇḍakas*,
as well as incenses, *varvara* incenses, wick-incenses, and flour-cakes;
likewise, *svastikas*, *lopikās*, and those resembling puffed beans.

The practitioner of mantra should eat stale foods after consecrating them in the fire. He may consume *śaṣkulī* cakes that have been prepared long ago while wandering about, as well as side dishes that are fresh, provided they have been purified by the ritual preparations prescribed in the scriptures.
(109b) That alms-food may be accepted without hesitation by one observing a vow, or even by a householder;
for even one who has been consecrated does not eat food until he has performed his midday ablution.
For him who has performed the midday rites after five muhūrtas have passed, the auspicious mantras established in the sacred seats (pīṭha) turn their faces toward him;
while he is eating, those mantras become destroyers of inauspiciousness.

The gods, ever-renewed Siddhas, and Rishis established in austerity, possessing the Three Jewels, diligently attend upon the midday libation. When the Guru has eaten before his eyes, only then should the practitioner eat.
Having bowed his head to Śiva, the God of gods, in his absence,
this rule for the alms-round as spoken in the venerable Pauṣkara has been declared. O Brahmin, O Sage, listen with a one-pointed mind to the procedure for eating.
Just as food is eaten by the castes who have been purified according to the auspicious teaching (Śivaśāsana),
so too should the place of eating be pleasing to the mind, freshly smeared with cow dung,
strewn with heaps of flowers, covered, and perfumed with incense.
There, the wise one should prepare a mandala with cow dung,
using fresh water, or with ashes, or even with clay;
it should be made square and level, neither too long nor too wide, by the learned.
One should construct it with uneven finger-breadths in width, making it larger than a cubit;
or even half a cubit longer, or exceeding that by uneven finger-breadths.
One should likewise fashion [the seat] for the Guru according to a measure three times [that].
Then, one should cover it without gaps using the leaves as prescribed;
one should also place many of those prescribed leaves there.
One should arrange water-vessels along with conch shells, mother-of-pearl, and bowls.
A seat made of *śrīparṇī* wood or fashioned from cow dung—
either circular or square, level, and thirty-two finger-breadths in measure. (110a)
It should not exceed one-third or one-fourth [of the width] even in length.
It should be provided with a clean cloth cushion, worshipped, and likewise fumigated with incense.
Therein, a protective barrier should be made either with ashes or with clay.
One should have it fashioned from rice flour or even from wheat powder,
with one line, two lines, or even three lines.
[The practitioner] should be clothed in white garments and anointed with white perfumes.
Anointed with yellow pigment (rocanā) and wearing white garlands,
his entire body consecrated with the *sakalīkaraṇa* rite and having performed the placement of the *pratyaṅgirā* mantras, the wise man,
seated upon that seat facing east, should partake of the meal.
Pure, wearing white garments, bathed, and with their forms consecrated by worship— such are those attendants of yours, Pratyangirā, whom you have obtained, all of equal complexion.
Some among them should be assigned as providers of food, and likewise some as providers of water.
Some have hands marked with signs, and likewise some have hands that are deformed;
among those of low caste, there are even lower ones, and among those of high caste, there are likewise superior ones.
Those who give them food and drink are considered to be persons whose food should not be eaten.
One should not fan [the fire] with the hand, nor with a cloth, nor with a peacock feather;
one should fan it with a palm-leaf fan and with a *mādhura* fan.
Therein, one should meditate upon Pratyamgirā in the *praṇītā* vessel according to the true principle.
One should likewise receive water from the water-vessel for rinsing the mouth and so forth;
first, one should accept the water prepared in vessels—
water that is scented with incense, fragrant, cool, light, sweet, and perfectly pure.
The most excellent of those who eat should accept food according to the custom of fishermen:
whether it be parched grains, or snacks, or sweet cakes, or savory delicacies. The *sakthu* (barley meal) should be eaten moistened with ghee and seasoned with *saindhava* salt.
(110b) They may be prepared with sauvarcala salt, or even with sea salt; or they may be mixed with sugar, jaggery, or candied sugar, or with inspissated juice.
One with a phlegmatic constitution (śleṣmala) should avoid split and tender meat. One with a bilious constitution (pittala) should avoid sugar and candied sugar, as well as well-cooked marrow-bones.
One whose nature is dominated by wind (vāta) should avoid the aforementioned marrow-bones that possess the specified characteristics.
One should first drink water with curd, or even with meat broth, or with sour gruel, or with parched grain flour; but never with milk. One should not eat to excessive satiety, nor ever at night.

One should not eat again after having taken [the meal], nor should one grind the teeth. One should not eat with hot water, nor with water containing salt; one should not eat them with *kāñjika*, nor with *śukra* unless there is phlegm.
One should certainly not offer food mixed with oil-cakes, nor those accompanied by oil-cakes;
nor with black gram, nor with horse-gram, nor indeed with kidney beans;
nor with *kalāja*, nor with chickpeas, nor with lentils under any circumstances.

One should not eat with *murmā*, *mayoṣṭha*, or *niṣpāra* leaves, nor with *vara* leaves; nor with vegetables, tubers, or roots, nor with *piṇḍis*. One should not eat with sesame oil, nor with oils from the *iṅguda* tree grown in the sky (*nābhaseṅguda*).
Neither with honey-ointment nor with white mustard does it become impure;
by discarding it, one should discard only that specific portion.
Thus, for one who eats the thigh bone, there is equality with those who eat meat.

Having washed both hands, one should then eat the food in the order of its sweetness. For one whose constitution is always balanced by the food itself, one should first receive what is offered; such a person remains stable like a *maṇḍaka* (a small cake).
Then, having well-steamed mung beans, or even *madgupūpa* cakes,
one should offer various side dishes (*avadaṃśa*) seasoned with ginger.
A wise person should take a morsel with *cidbhiṭa*, *parpaṭa*, and various kinds of *paṭola*,
as well as with steamed vegetables, *atikā* greens, and very tender herbs,
provided there is no distortion of the mouth.
One should first receive the milk-rice (pāyasa) and never [receive] what has been left over.
Likewise, one should eat foods cooked in ghee that have been broken with the teeth;
a wise person should not consume any morsel that has been broken by a stick.
Likewise, one should offer even frogs accompanied by various condiments;
thereafter, drinks and gruels that are out of season should be presented.
At the end, the practitioner of mantras should request liquid offerings, saying, "Do not [refuse] this."
Either boiled or strained curd with its whey,
or even curd mixed with black pepper, cumin, and salt; or the entire quantity of curd combined at the end with milk, sugar, and candied sugar.

Whatever cooked food has been brought by another during the effort of eating must indeed be given while it is still half-eaten and after it has been encircled by fire. One should purify the vessels with water while reciting the Vāmadevya hymn.
The food received in the vessel should be consecrated with Vedic mantras.
Having taken the *apośāna* water, the knower of mantras, having partaken [of it] with the *Īśāna* mantra,
should then eat his meal in silence while reciting the *Puruṣa* mantra.

Holding the vessel with the left hand and pressing it with the thumb, the wise one should offer five oblations into the fire of the body for the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth. First, while seated, he should mentally project himself [into the vessel] with the mantra: "I am seated."
Making the self the lower fire-drill (araṇi), one should awaken the other self as the fire.
By the offering of oblations of breath, the three groups of five are pleased—
those bound to the great elements, preceded by the internal self and so forth.
(111b) The internal, the elemental, and likewise the divine— [these correspond] respectively to earth, water, fire, air, and space.
By the offering of the subsequent oblation, the three groups of ten are gratified—
those who are considered to be the speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals,
as well as the ears, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose.
The three groups of five— the internal (adhyātma), the elemental (adhibhūta), and the divine (adhidaivata)—
are gratified by the offering of equal oblations.
These [groups], preceded by the internal and so forth, are indeed bound to the subtle elements (tanmātra).
By the offering of oblations to the vyāna breath, these deities are pleased:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and likewise the Supreme Lord;
Śiva and Sadāśiva, as well as all that is stationary and moving.
For indeed, the entire world— including gods, asuras, and humans— is [contained] within the vessel that rests upon the earth. Having thus offered these five oblations,
one may then eat as one desires, using either what remains on the ground or what has been lifted up from it.
One should eat sweetmeats (*modaka*) from jeweled bowls made of gold or silver;
milk-rice (*pāyasa*) from an earthen vessel; honey and clarified butter from vessels of metal;
and milk from vessels of copper, or those made of gold or silver.
In the absence of those, he may eat from things produced on water or land;
however, he should never take his meal from vessels made of both [materials].
Furthermore, he should eat at a place where he eats alone and no one else eats.
One should never drink water that remains as an offering (hutaśeṣa).

At the time of the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), one should not eat; nor should one eat while lying down or while standing up. One should not eat too early in the morning or too late in the evening, even if one has been defiled by wandering about after voiding excrement or urine.
Or if one has been defiled by feces or urine, one should perform whatever purification is required before taking up [the vessel].
One should not use a vessel where there is a mixture of discarded flower offerings (*nirmālya*).
Upon seeing flies, insects, hair, or the like in his food, he should discard it;
he should wash his hand and likewise that very vessel. Having taken other food, he should eat while remaining established in the prescribed rule.
When an internal affliction has arisen, one should perform an ablution according to the prescribed rule;
the self-possessed person should consume ghee with the ring finger.
Then the wise man should perform the recitation of the Vāmadeva hymn one hundred and eight times.

Once the maṇḍala has been prepared, the wise practitioner should not eat even a single fruit from it today; for the food would be consumed by the Rākṣasas who abide as attendants of the deity. Furthermore, food should not be eaten by the practitioners if they rise immediately after [the ritual], nor should it be consumed by them at that time.
For one who observes silence for a hundred years, it may prolong life;
yet a practitioner who is impure should not take even a single step anywhere.
For obstacles caused by children indeed corrupt the practitioner.
Having eaten the food as prescribed,
the self-possessed person should cleanse his hands and feet with water for the sake of removing all traces of oiliness and residue;
he should use either fine powdered cow-dung or simply urine.
For the purpose of removing oiliness, odor, and stains, mustard paste should be applied.
One should sprinkle water on one's own right foot while reciting this mantra.
With the right thumb, one should likewise moisten the big toe of the right foot with water.
Then, having consumed betel-leaf and likewise used a tooth-stick,
and having again performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) correctly, he should consume an aromatic mouth-freshener.
Having sipped water once more, he should offer the sacrificial gift (nivedya) to Śiva and likewise to his guru.
One who knows the mantras should perform the expiation with the Vāmadeva mantra;
having formed the aparigha-mudrā, one should recite it nine times,
placing [the fingers] beginning from the little finger of the left hand.
With the Vāmadeva mantra, one should perform the four consecrations in sequence;
likewise, the thumb as the fifth is joined together with the other, the little finger.

One should cause the remaining [food] to enter [the mouth] with the right hand, ending with a salutation. One should place the left little finger at the navel while reciting the mantra, and the right thumb at the mouth; this is known as the "excellent enclosure" (*parigha*).
Food is indeed the most excellent of all things, and the enjoyer is known as the Puruṣa;
therefore, the Lord who causes one to eat is to be understood as the Supreme God.
Even while eating among outcaste dog-cookers, one is not tainted by this sin.
One should recite the Śivadā Gāyatrī in front of the giver of food.
For whomever one thus eats food, that person’s lineage up to the seventh generation shall be rescued from this most difficult-to-cross [ocean] of worldly existence.
The Brahmins and others should eat in a single row according to their seniority.
The space between the rows should be thirty-two finger-breadths, like a circle of the sky.
When the meal is finished, there should be a distribution of food among the kings and those who have eaten.
The Ācārya should eat alone, and the Sādhaka likewise alone.
The Putraka and the Samayajña may eat according to their own wish in a communal row;
those seated in the row should eat while being mutually affectionate toward one another.
This is the rule for the meal of householders belonging to the four castes.
For ascetics, it has been previously stated that [the meal consists] of *caru*, portions of grain, alms, and so forth.
The mantra-words for the *arghya* offering are as follows:
Oṃ, I am the heat of Viṣṇu within the lunar orb; I am completely enclosed by Agni and the others—svāhā! Thus is the visualization of the self.
Oṃ, having made the self the lower fire-drill (araṇi) and the vital breath the upper fire-drill, I churn with the churning-stick that which is to be churned, just as it was churned by Rudra.

(113a) Having awakened the fire within oneself with "Svāhā," and having taken water for rinsing the mouth (*āpośāna*), one consecrates the food with: "To the subsidiary vital airs—the Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya—Svāhā. Then, having sipped the remaining water with "Oṃ, you are the spreading of the nectar (*amṛtopastaraṇamasi*"), one offers the five oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhutis*) without touching them with the teeth, saying: "To Prāṇa; to Apāna; to Samāna; to Udāna; to Vyāna. After eating, one should sip water again with "You are the covering of the nectar (*amṛtāpidhānamasi*)."

The Self indeed resides in the right foot as the all-pervading one, higher than the highest; I sprinkle him with water who is established at the tip of the big toe. Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer, and Śiva is this entire world.
"Śiva worships everywhere; he who is Śiva, I am indeed that very one. Thus ends the Bhojana-gāyatrī.
This is the rule for eating as seen in the Pauṣkara-śāsana.
Now, I shall briefly describe the supreme procedure for eating:
having sipped water and purified oneself, one should sprinkle the alms-food once;
having cleansed it, one should offer it to the deities, the fire, and within oneself.
Having constructed the maṇḍala as previously described, one should place three vessels therein.
Having performed the consecration of the vessel intended for the *argha* offering, one should fumigate it.
Then, having projected the *saṅga* mantra upon that auspicious vessel within the cavity of the moon-maṇḍala, [one should proceed].
Having intentionally prepared the vessel of nectar within the *mṛtyuñjaya* (death-conquering) fold,
and having offered it to the God in the heart while consecrated seven times with the *śiva-mantra*,
one should extract the fivefold oblation (*pañca-havis*) for the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, using the [mantras] beginning with *Īśāna*.
Having visualized the *droṇakalaśa* vessel upon the head, one should contemplate *prāṇa* in the heart;
*apāna*, known as *samāna*, in the anus; and *udāna* in the navel and throat.
Having placed the subtle elements (*tanmātrās*) in the navel and the joints, one should thereafter drink the *apośāna*.

The mantras, the gods, the Gāyatrī, the tantras, the medicinal herbs, and the mountains— along with those situated in the realms of Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar— are satisfied by the consumption of the food of vital breath. (113b)
The Aśvins, Vāyu, Vāruṇa, Agni, the eight classes of divine progenitors (devayoni), Yama, the Apāna breath, and the Vyāhṛtis become pleased along with the Kinnaras;
as do the rivers, mountains, oceans, the netherworlds (pātāla), the elephants, the hosts of ancestors, and the sages.
Satisfied and filled by means of the *samāna* breath along with the vital airs (*marut*), they support the world below through *māyā*. O Earth-protector, their paths are thus augmented;
for by means of the *udāna* breath, they all become filled by half [of that capacity].

From Brahmā down to Śiva, all are pure, abiding in the reality of the pure Self; and through the supreme delight of the pervasive Lord (Īśā-vyāna), all the powers (śaktis) are satisfied. Thus it is declared in the great tantra known as Lalitā within the Śiva-āgama.
Having eaten in this manner according to the prescribed rule, one should worship the Guru with devotion.
One should carry out his command through the actions of mind, speech, and body.
[This includes] listening, studying, reciting, explaining, and reflecting upon the scriptures.
The lord of practitioners should perform the *vyāna* breath-control, free from the channels (*nāḍī*),
until the time of twilight arrives; so indeed it has been stated in the *Śrīvāmadevapaddhati* in the present context.
If, at the time of eating, one should touch one's own leavings,
a penance is declared according to the specific caste of the person involved. Regarding the touching of another's leavings, [the purification] occurs through the grace of these [deities].
Purity is attained simply by touching [water] and by reciting [the name of] one's own caste.
For the Brāhmaṇa caste, the Lord is the mantra known as Tatpuruṣa;
Aghora is for the Kṣatriya caste, and Vāma is proclaimed for the Vaiśyas.
Sadyojāta, however, is for the Śūdras; Maheśa is the origin of all things. The Brāhmaṇa emerged from his mouth; his limb is of the nature of Puruṣa.
The Kṣatriya was born from the two arms, and that is known as the limb of Ghorā. The Vaiśya arose from the thighs, and they know that to be the limb of Vāmā.
The Śūdra was produced from the feet, and that is remembered as the limb of Sadyā.
The Vedic mantras are established as the lords of their own kin;
however, from contact with one of a lower caste, one must fast for a day and night.
In that situation, the knower should recite the two Jātīśa mantras while remaining in a single place.
One should recite [the mantra] for one day after contact with a Kṣatriya, and for two days after contact with a Vaiśya.
After contact with those of the lower castes,
Śiva residing within the maṇḍala must be worshipped by all members of the castes through the rite of caste-elevation.
The extraction (*uddhāra*) of one's own *jāti* is proclaimed by means of its own lord;

the insertion (*nikṣepa*) is performed with the suffix *svāhā*, while its projection (*kṣepa*) is done with the syllable *phaṭ*. Having thus performed the extraction of the *jāti*, the Guru should cause them to be recited.
In this way, purification arises from the mere touch of one of an external caste;
likewise, through the rite of initiation by a guru, there is the elevation of one's birth.
However, when the guru is absent, the knowledgeable disciple should perform the rite himself.
Even if he has desisted from the three [lower] castes, a Brāhmaṇa who is initiated into Śiva may,
without hesitation, eat the food of those who have been initiated,
even if they belong to the Kṣatriya or other castes, provided they are endowed with purity and right conduct.

A twice-born man who avoids the food of those [sinners] shall undergo expiation. If a twice-born man of a certain caste does not eat the food of another caste when invited, his vital energy (*ojas*) belonging to the lord of that caste and his own vital energy belonging to the lord of his own caste become purified together in one place.
One, two, or even three days are prescribed for his purification;
this is the sequence of recitation (japa) ordained for those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes.
Alternatively, upon seeing the mandala of the Lord of the Jātis, one becomes completely purified.
(114b) Furthermore, whether by means of undivided or divided [sections], or from a teacher or by oneself alone,
the mandala of the Lord of the Jātis is four-cornered, with four gates, four arms, and four spokes,
consisting of a four-petalled lotus.
Īśāna is in the center of the pericarp; Tatpuruṣa is on the eastern petal; Bahurūpa is on the south; Vāmadeva is likewise on the north;
and Sadyojāta is on the west—all of these are remembered as the Lords of Birth (Jātīśvaras).
This mandala of Īśāna is indeed fit for worship in its entirety.
Puruṣa is in the center of the pericarp, and Īśāna is on the northern petal.
The remaining deities are situated exactly as they are in the Vaiśya-type mandala.
One should not eat food from a minister, nor from other ascetics (liṅgins) here;
however, having eaten out of necessity, one must recite the mantra of Liṅgeśvara one hundred times.
For the Lord is multiformed among wandering mendicants and those bearing sectarian marks.

Likewise, Vāmadeva is remembered as the lord of the Pāśupatas who bear the marks of impurity on their faces, as well as those clad in white and red garments; and similarly, he is the lord of other wearers of sectarian marks and even those who bear the marks of householders.
Those who bear the skull-emblem (kapāla-liṅgin) are proclaimed to be persons whose food should not be eaten. If one should eat their food through negligence, one must undergo initiation again.
Having first performed the removal of the emblem (liṅgoddhāra), the wise man himself should then perform the initiation.
Whichever Lord is proclaimed as the presiding deity of a particular *liṅga*,
by that [deity] the extraction of the *liṅga* is performed through the act of depositing and raising it up.
Whichever mandala is proclaimed for whichever Lord of a [particular] caste, [that is to be used].
The mantrin should construct that very same mandala for the Lord of the Linga;
indeed, the Jātīśa-maṇḍala is known as consisting merely of the ritual placement of the seats.

The external placement (nyāsa) of the seat has been declared; now its internal placement is being taught. The internal placement is established through its divisions, and those divisions are now being described. The internal placement is arranged with the Brahmans as well as the limbs (of the mantra).
The ritual placement (nyāsa) for all [deities] should be performed by those assuming external forms as previously described;
likewise, it should be done by those assuming their respective forms in the center.
All [deities] have their heads in the Īśāna direction, and all have the faces of Tatpuruṣa.
All [mantras] whose heart-mantra is Aghora are proclaimed to have the Vāma as their secret;
all those whose form is unknown are proclaimed to be Brahma-mantras.
One should assign the Brahmāṇīs as the secondary Brahmās (upabrahmāṇi) for all of them.
The ritual services, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and so forth, should be performed for Śiva;
indeed, everything up to the conclusion of the worship should be done in sequence with the [mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta.
One must not consume the food of a Śaiva without first ascertaining his spiritual status (gocara).
Those whose name is Śivāṅka are remembered by you as the Śuddhaśaivas (Pure Śaivas).
The Kaumāras are indeed the Śuddhaśaivas, arisen from the pure substratum (śuddhādhikaraṇa).
It is not merely by their name that they are called Śuddhaśaivas.

Their stability consists in the tradition of the discourse on Dharma and abiding by right conduct. Those who are pure Śaivas and bear names marked by Śiva are to be known as *punarbhavas*; others are likewise [known] as *svāyambhavas*.

Those who abide in a state of purity do not proclaim their identity as Śaivas in the world; however, those virtuous ones who, while belonging to other sects, remain established by resorting to the Śaiva path,
are declared to be "reborn" within the teaching of Śiva.

Even those who have taken up the ascetic marks (*liṅga*) on their own are remembered as being of self-originated descent (*svāyambhuva*). They possess no traditional scripture from a guru, nor do they undergo the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) that consist of Śiva;
these lowest of men will become a source of corruption for the Kali age.
Having themselves inferred the Śaiva scripture that had been stolen by bandits,

those who were previously divided from the state of independence and followed other sectarian marks take recourse in the knowledge of Śiva at the end of their own nature, becoming self-existent ones. (115b)

But those Śaiva teachers who, having performed the rite of formal initiation (*upasadana*), become proficient in the scriptures, are to be known as "reborn" (*punarbhū*). Those who are called "self-born" (*svayambhū*) are said to be of two kinds, established in their respective observances (*samaya*).

O Brahmin, their food is not to be eaten by a Śūdra, just as iron is not fit for consumption; yet, when pierced by the mantras of Śiva— Sadyojāta and the others— in due order according to that very same rite, they no longer return to the state of iron.
Just as a vessel previously seen to be flawed attains purity through fire,
so too a vessel corrupted by birth becomes pure through the fire of mantra.
Brahmā said:
The transformation of iron into gold has been seen through the means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
here, however, the twice-born status of one who is pure is established through inference (*anumāna*).
For that [inference] which functions as an established fact concerns an object not perceived by the senses.
But that which is established by direct perception does not require the demonstration of the unseen;
indeed, the means of valid cognition have been proclaimed solely for the sake of establishing what is well-observed.
That which is an object of direct perception is established by direct perception alone.
Nothing is perceived here that establishes the existence of a [real] recipient;
for while the substantiality of iron and the like is seen, its state as gold is likewise perceived directly. Only the bare object is to be grasped, not the demonstration of a relationship.
Just as iron may become gold, so too does the status of the twice-born exist even among Śūdras.
Since the human species is one and the same, how can the state of being twice-born be established? For when the physical body is identical, it is devoid of any distinguishing characteristic.
The conceptualization of a universal [such as "cow"] regarding the right side of an inauspicious body is merely a conventional designation; it is not established by direct perception.
Furthermore, if every twice-born man were established by direct perception as being produced from all seeds, that would not be the case;
for there is no reason here whatsoever [to prove it] through propositions, logical reasons, or examples.
Setting aside the authoritative scripture (āptāgama) thus spoken by Śiva, you think as follows:

"The means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) have indeed been declared for the sake of establishing objects of knowledge (prameyas). But what can be established by means of valid cognitions regarding the Lord, who is himself not an object of knowledge?"
For he whose infinite powers and likewise his activities are unimpaired— indestructible, universal in form, and accomplishers of all purposes—
it is thus that the twice-born status of the castes is established by the powers of Śiva.
O Lotus-Seated One, when that is established, everything else is indeed established from the outset:
namely, sharing the same bed and seat with her, likewise eating together,
acting as a benefactor to all, and a livelihood that is beyond reproach.

But one should act according to one's own will, and certainly not by the injunction of the scriptures; for the scripture establishes a fixed rule, and one must abide by that established rule. Thus, at that time, [one follows] such and such a rule of the teacher.
O Lotus-born One, by that [teacher] and by that [method] at that time, according to the established rule of the teacher;
and also by the established rule of the practitioner’s own place,
and by his own established rule, even with a son.
The Blessed Lord spoke thus in the *Pauṣkara-pārameśvara*: Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain in brief the determination of the phonemes (*varṇa*).
For the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and others, [the distinction] exists according to their respective castes;
however, there is no caste-prescribed [status] therein, nor even color such as white and so forth. All have arisen from the womb and the male organ; the single Jīva remains equal.
Therein, the omnipresent deity is perceived by the eye of wisdom;
[he is not seen] by those whose minds are defiled by ignorance and sin, and whose selves are governed by false teachings.
If their purpose is merely idle chatter regarding birth,
there is no cause for this direct perception of the living soul (*jīva*).
Furthermore, those with corrupt minds sometimes engage in critical debate against the proponent of examination.
Neither the Vedas nor the Upaniṣads, nor even the vision [of them], bestow strength or liberation through mere caste.
In this regard, those who do not know the distinction from Brahman remain beyond duality, established in the Supreme.
Alternatively, for living beings, there is the dwelling in the womb, which is filled with impurity.

For one who is seen to have arisen from semen, what purification of caste is there in that state? Indeed, when the body— composed of bones and sinews and sustained by an equal life-force— is destroyed, what purpose is there in caste at all?
Wherein pleasure and pain are equal, and creation is uniform as being of the nature of the womb— therein,
how can there be purity in the body as long as knowledge is not stainless?
One who does not rely on the white sacred thread, the topknot, nor the words of the Vedas [is pure].
In some places, Brahmins emerged from the mouths of those reciting;
there, where the Vedas were indeed studied, the sacred thread and the topknot were prescribed. Where Brahmins are merely artificial, what would be the use of birth?

What woman is proclaimed as a virtuous wife (*satī*) who, upon seeing a man, goes under the sway of passion like a female deer, her senses overwhelmed by intoxication? For in this world, even the gods beginning with Brahmā are proclaimed to be born from a womb.
What need is there to speak of humans or animals in this regard?
If a Brahmin, though established in a wrong occupation by the force of his birth, were to ascend upwards;
yet even a Mātaṅga, though established in righteousness, would not attain the vision of liberation.
O twice-born ones, let other scriptures be set aside for now; people know those Brāhmaṇas as established in dharma through the sacred revelation (śruti), whose souls are bound by austerity,
who understand the rules for the bonds of the individual soul (paśu-pāśa), and who follow the knowledge of Śiva.
For they are celebrated as the subjects of the God of gods;
thus it is stated in the *Candrahāsa* and in the *Muktaja* and other Āgamas.
Due to distinctions such as the initiatory rites (*samayī*) and so forth, caste (*jāti*) is proclaimed to be but one.
Among humans, where is the purity of either family (*kula*) or caste?
One should adopt that pure conduct through which, by means of its purity, all forms of purity are attained.
In this context, the description of the castes of the devotees has been mentioned incidentally.
Now, at the third libation, one should perform the twilight ritual (*sandhyā*) as before;
the rites beginning with *mārjana* (sprinkling water) are to be performed as previously described, ending with the satisfaction of the mantras.
Having performed these, one should enter the sacrificial hall and carry out the recitation according to the prescribed rule.
Then, having prostrated before the Lord of Gods, one should enter the auspicious temple,
which is filled with lamps such as the *nirmalā* and others, and is delightful with the fragrance of incense.
Having ascertained that the place is prepared with auspicious scented waters, radiant with scattered flowers,
provided with canopies, fine cloths, and an umbrella, secured by protective measures,
well-guarded, free from dualities, and devoid of fear, one should cause the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) to be performed there.
Or else, one may descend onto auspicious ground that has been cleared of obstacles;
or upon a couch provided with a cotton mattress and draped with beautiful cloth,
which has been sprinkled with water from the *astra* mantra— upon that, one should place a lotus.
An eight-petalled lotus, white and radiant,

with filaments and a beautiful pericarp; having ascended that auspicious seat with his own name preceded by *praṇava* and ending in *namaḥ*, the practitioner, whose body is adorned by the mantra, should sleep there.
Having purified the directions with the scripture, one should then cover them with the armor-mantra.

One should meditate on Smara at the region of the head, using his own name preceded by the *praṇava* and joined at the end with a salutation (*namaskāra*). Likewise, one should meditate on Rati on the right side.
Likewise, one should visualize Prīti on the left side, along with a multitude of celestial couches;
and there, at the foot of the bed, one should likewise place Kāmadeva.
According to this procedure, the householder who is a spiritual guide (deśika) should sleep.
Mindfulness is his attendant; his bed is made right there with pure grass,
or upon a piece of bark pierced by thorns, or on ashes, or on a deer-skin.
Having first fashioned a lotus there as before,
the lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) should then sleep upon a bed of ashes while meditating on the god Maheśvara,
either upon his head, or on a cloth, or on a consecrated full water-pot.

Or else, having worshipped mentally, one should contemplate one's own head as being at His two feet. Then the supreme practitioner should meditate upon Rudra together with the Goddess, and immediately thereafter, upon the auspicious Gaṇeśāna.
Having recollected [the deity], the wise practitioner should sleep facing either the east or the south. When midnight has passed,
he should rise from his bed and then perform the cleansing of the waist, followed by a bath of ashes as prescribed.
Then one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with water drawn out during the day;
for water is not recommended once the sun has set.
Alternatively, having bathed with previously collected water, one should perform the rite while reciting the two mantras.
One should worship the deity with the mind, or else remain established in one's own true nature;

or else, the recitation (japa) should be performed through the practice of yoga and meditative absorption (samādhi). Having done this, the practitioner of mantra should sleep again until the exhaustion of the night.
One should perform the ritual actions as previously described, accompanied by song and instrumental music.
This divine and meritorious rite dedicated to Maheśvara bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Now, I shall declare the regulations for those who sacrifice to Śiva, as spoken by Śiva himself.
Just as all castes and those of lower castes go to Śiva,
and just as the waters of city-tanks and mountain torrents attain oneness upon reaching the Gaṅgā,
so too, through contact with the mantra of the Lord, the fourfold caste system becomes Śiva.
Śrī Devī said:
"O Maheśvara, tell me how the maintenance of the teachers and others is to be carried out;
by what cause can that be accomplished for those who are destitute of wealth such as [traveling] provisions?"

The Lord: Their withdrawal occurs through their own function; that function arises from the field of experience. Sacrifice is to be performed by means of functions arising from a good field of experience, and stability is maintained by them.
Śiva, Jyotis, Śikhā, and Sāvitra—these are the domains;

they further undergo a fourfold division according to the distinctions of the stages of life (āśramas). The observance of these stages of life has been ordained for those who know the traditional rules (samaya).
For the sake of the stability of the sons [of the lineage], for the accomplishment of the practitioners of mantra,
and for the authority to bestow grace upon the teachers (daiśikas), this is desired.
I shall state their names and the conduct of those in the stages of life (āśramins) in due order.
The Prājāpatyas, Mahīpālas, Kāpotas,
and likewise the Granthikas are to be known as the successive stages of life (āśramins) among those initiated into the sphere of Śiva:
the student (brahmacārī), the householder (gṛhastha), the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), and the mendicant (bhikṣuka).
The Vṛtarāṣṭras, Śakas, Kaṅkas, Gopālas, Kuṭikas, Vetālas, Padmas, and likewise Haṃsas;
the Tuṭikas, Māṭharas, Guḍikas, and those known as Daṇḍas reside within the sphere of light (jyotigocara).
The *śikhā* known as *sāvitra*—these eight are thus proclaimed.
I shall now describe their observances (*vratas*) in brief:
Vedic study, service to the teacher, and the restraint of all the sense organs.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, and observance of one's commitments—
this indeed is the Prājāpatya vow which a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) twice-born man should practice;
or it is called Prājāpatya for a householder (bhautika) who seeks spiritual perfection.
Its function is traditionally held to be the protection of the earth, as well as sacrifice and nourishment.

Since kings protect the earth from those who seek wealth unasked and from those who have been bestowed upon the twice-born, they are known as Śāntis (pacifiers) through their subduing of poison and other dangers.
Since they indeed protect [the people], they are celebrated as "protectors of the earth" (*mahīpā*).
Furthermore, there is the previously mentioned medical treatment, restoration, and likewise the petitioning.
Likewise, wives endowed with auspicious marks should be taken from the six castes,

according to the ritual of initiation and consecration, or by means of mantras enjoined in the Vedas. Furthermore, other purificatory rites, beginning with those pertaining to the womb, must be performed in their proper sequence.
One who gathers grain fallen on unplowed ground like a pigeon,
or sows seed there like a pigeon— he is like a pigeon.
The worship of the gods and guests is certainly ordained for these three.
Approaching one's wife during her fertile period, refraining from sexual union with others,
as well as other prescribed mental acts such as self-praise and the like;
first worshipping Śiva and others, and indeed the renunciation of ritual action (karma-saṃnyāsa).
And meditation on Śiva for all [practitioners] at night is prescribed according to one's desire.
All this has been explained as it was indicated, in due order, regarding the spheres of perception (*gocara*).
O Goddess, the general rule has been laid down; now I shall tell you the specific details.
It was constantly practiced by great beings with restrained senses, lifelong celibates, and those committed to the ultimate goal;
and likewise by practitioners of mantras who were compassionate, even when they had not yet attained their goals.
O Goddess, such are remembered as the practitioners (sādhakas) of Vṛtarāṣṭra.
Those who always move about in concealment, whether practicing vows or religious duties, pursue only their own self-interest; they alone are the secret ones on earth.
Those who reside depending on a single river or lake,
having achieved perfection through that alone, are indeed proclaimed as *kaṭvas*.
Subsisting on alms, with senses subdued, he should remain standing together with the cows as they move toward the cow-pen.

The sage who always dwells in a cow-pen together with the cowherds is known as a *gopa*. Those pure ones who practice celibacy together with their wives and abide by the *asidhārā-vrata* (the blade-edge vow) are declared to be *kuṭikas*.
Those who,
together with their wives, undertake pilgrimages to sacred fords while subsisting on whatever they happen to obtain,
are proclaimed to be Vetālas in that very state.

Those who do not eat and do not speak even during the day without having seen the sun are known as those desiring sovereignty (*rājyakāma*). Those who are devoted to the lotus-oblation (*padmahoma*) are said to be *haṃsas*. And those who possess the yoga of arisen knowledge are called *advaitins*.
Furthermore, in this section, I shall explain their knowledge in its entirety.
They constantly exhaust themselves through arduous penances such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa;
even those who eat only a single *tuṭi* [of food] are the *tuṭikas*, the best among practitioners (*sādhakas*).
Those householders who, being deceitful, made their wives the source of their livelihood through agriculture and remained devoted to domestic chores were known by the name Māṭhara.
But those [who subsisted] on eight pills the size of a mouthful...
Those who subsist on bulbs, roots, fruits, and water are indeed Guḍikas.
Those who carry a staff like a scepter and are devoted to the vīrāsana posture at night are Daṇḍins;
those practitioners who are constantly devoted to the all-pervading void (vyomavyāpin) are also Daṇḍins.

Thus, the sixteen divisions of the Śaivas have been proclaimed; they should conduct themselves according to their own respective modes of life as prescribed for their particular sphere. Those who have been initiated by whichever [division] are designated by the name of that specific sphere.
The duties of the stages of life (āśramadharma) have been declared; however, [the practice] may occur according to one's own will and resolve.
These [mantras] are designated as belonging to the foremost of the twice-born (brahmins), while those marked by the group [of letters] beginning with 'ra' belong to kings and others.
Likewise, those known as *śakti* are proclaimed for all women.
Thus, the conduct for the duration of one's life has been briefly explained. Now hear the general daily routine for the teachers and others, which pertains to a single day and night:
[it consists of] rising from home, bathing, yoga, staying [in meditation], exposition, and likewise the daily duties.
The nights are known as the activities; for the Guru, they consist of meditation and praise.
For the disciple, they likewise consist of recitation, worship, fire-rituals, abiding [in discipline], and study of the scriptures. (119b)

The reception of ministers, worship, remaining [in the lineage], and likewise the examination of the scriptures; for the spiritual son (putraka) and others as well, private study and service to the Guru;
hearing [the teachings on] sacrifice and so forth at night—all these are acts of meditation and praise performed by everyone.
"The mode of subsistence according to one's own capacity has thus been briefly explained;
the occasional mode should likewise be applied as appropriate.
Thus is the Vidyā declared in the Purāṇas, which should be adopted by those who have taken refuge in Śiva."
Especially because of the breath and even the *āmala* fruit of the Goddess,
the Śiva-lineage described by Śaṅkara, Bhairava, and others is not Vedic.
That womb consisting of mother and father is common to all beings.
From the union of semen and blood, a body is formed consisting of six sheaths;
it should be known as impure, though it appears endowed with qualities through [karmic] impressions.
At that time, the womb, which is essentially composed of mantras, is established at the moment of conception and thereafter.
From that, the Brahmins are said to be born; otherwise, one is pure through the six sheaths (*ṣāṭkośī*).
Even there, the qualities of the self (*ātmaguṇa*) are supreme; without them, [true status] is not seen.
Due to the lack of refinement by these qualities, one is neither a "Brahmin by word" (*śabdabrāhmaṇa*) nor a true Brahmin.
One who is unrighteous exists as the essence of Śiva or the essence of Brahman;
yet, from the world of Brahman, he falls away from that state.
He is a *brātya*, a performer of rites for the powerful, one devoid of merit, one who has fallen from his station, and a mere kinsman of Brahman.
The soul whose primary essence is the principle of Brahman does not likewise attain the principle of Śiva.

Because he possesses the five limbs of the *praṇava*, the twice-born one is Śaiva and endowed with five qualities. Having joined him with the status of a Brahmin of Brahman, and having performed the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) from the beginning by means of oblations;
Having offered oblations for all rites from conception until the cremation ground along with all the constituent elements,
and having offered forty-eight oblations for each of the stages of life (āśramas) individually,
one should purify the seven worlds and unite them within the principle of Brahman.

Having offered the eightfold Brahman and purified it, it should be joined to the fivefold group and so forth. Through successive union, he who is united with Śiva is indeed the Unsurpassed (Anuttara).
What distance can there be for him, as he perceives the characteristics of the path therein?
Therefore, after due deliberation, one should speak of Śiva and the Brahmin, O twice-born;
for although [the universe] is infinite and immeasurable, it is perceived through the form of logical reasoning.
There is a vast difference between a Śiva-dvija and a [mere] brāhmaṇa.
By means of the Vedic dharmas, even the gods and sages are gradually liberated.
For what purpose were all those beginning with Brahmā, the best of ṛṣis, initiated?

Lord Śiva has the Vedas as his seat; the Vedas are the servants of Śiva. Therefore, one who knows the Vedas is a devotee of Śiva, for he knows the eternal Śiva, who is to be known through the Vedas. Having worshipped Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra, they are auspicious ones who worship the Cause of all causes.
There, being disciplined and having become Śiva, the initiated ones know the principle of Śiva.
Therefore, one who has long observed the vow should always abandon this worldly caste;
having abandoned pride in caste, silent and maintaining the vow of Śiva, he is Śiva himself.
Having understood all this from the *Mukuṭa*, the practitioner shall become a possessor of siddhi. O true devotees, place this flood of jewels of words, extracted from the oceans of scriptures,
upon your necks during the union with the beloved Devotion.
O All-pervading Lord, you indeed whet the afflictions on all sides, yet your wisdom remains unimpeded;
even while revealing [the truth] within their hearts,
O Ocean of Compassion, please hear my words.

"May these two [hands] quickly wash away the afflictions that shatter this continuum through a flood of devotion, and swiftly lead [the soul] to that unborn state where Your servants go forever. Having heard this petition offered with devotion by Takṣaka, O Śambhu, quickly cast upon him Your glance filled with the nectar of grace;
then, uttering auspicious and noble words from Your pure mouth, ensure that the people remain diligent in meditation, recitation, worship, and other such practices for You."
Thus ends the section on worship composed by Rājānaka Takṣakavarta; may there be auspiciousness.
Now follows the supreme propitiation of the mantra for the sake of the practitioner’s accomplishment.

Having extracted from other treatises the essential core concerning the illumination of the subject matter of mantras for rites such as pacification (*śānti*) and so forth, that which is appropriate for the practitioner will now be explained.
For it is observed in the world that some who possess supernatural powers (*siddhi*) are actually harmful.
The pinning down of mantras, as well as their piercing,
deluding, terrifying, drawing away, paralyzing, and immobilizing; furthermore, the causing of enmity and the state of being a counter-protection.
Evil ministers bring about the total destruction [of the state].
Thus, indeed, do the injurers strive in ten ways;
therefore, with every effort, one must remain well-guarded above [them].
One should diligently perform sacrifice, fire-oblation, and recitation in one's own home;
for by means of these, such as the "kindling" (dīpana) rites, practitioners achieve success,
while malevolent spells (kṛtyā) employed by others— such as the Khārkhadaka and similar incantations— are destroyed.
Through the application of *Pratyaṅgirā*, one destroys many wicked ones.
O lady of excellent vows, having understood that this alone is the supreme mantra-discourse for all, the practitioner of mantras should employ it according to the characteristics of the mantra.
Illumination, awakening, striking, consecration, purification, as well as the placement of fuel; satiation, the state of protection, and nourishment as the ninth.
Thus, he who understands the ninefold mantra-discourse in its entirety truly understands the means for accomplishing the mantra-attainment. Furthermore,
O Dear One, the elevenfold mantra must also be known.
I shall explain the correct application by which masters of accomplishment attain success, as well as the distinctions approved in all the scriptures. (121a)
The *sampuṭa*, the *grathita*, the *grasta*, the *samasta*, and the *vidarbhitā*;
then the *ākrānta*, the *ādyantagarbhastha*, and the *sarvatoddhṛta*; likewise the *yuktividarbha* and the *vidarbhagrathita*.
