Thus, the mantras are assigned in eleven ways, bestowing all accomplishments (siddhis). Having understood everything without exception— namely, the accomplished (siddha), the to-be-accomplished (sādhya), the self-accomplished (svasiddha), and likewise the state of being an enemy (aritva)— one should practice the discourse on mantras.

He who knows in this way the pervasion of rising and setting, meditation, and the mudrā according to their true nature— he is omniscient, the doer of all, and the best of practitioners. O Goddess, [he is so] by means of these and other such distinctions and variations of states.
O Dear One, when cultivated, the great mantras become givers of fruit.
Therefore, with every effort, one should apply oneself to knowledge;
O Goddess, for this king of mantras, there is no doubt.
The Supreme Lord is the nourisher of all mantras;
by him the mantras are strung together like clusters of gems upon a thread.
Abiding within his womb, the mantras become bestowers of both supernatural powers and liberation.
The supreme, all-pervading deity, the source of the arising of the fruits of all accomplishments;
the all-encompassing, auspicious in every way, facing in all directions, and imperishable;
the fulfillment of all mantras and the protection that is strength on every side.
It is the source of all mantras, bestowing liberation and success, and is auspicious;
O Goddess, for that mantra there is no doubt.
Even if practitioners are pierced by these thousands of defects, [the mantra remains effective].
Those seized by Vināyakas and those tormented by chronic diseases;
kings fallen from their kingdoms and oppressed by foreign realms;
those whose sons have died and whose wives have been lost, deprived of both and stripped of their fortune. (121b)
Teachers or practitioners who have turned their backs on the attainment of mantra-siddhi;
women who are childless, unfortunate, barren, or whose husbands are hostile—
endowed with thousands of such miseries and defects.
Having seen those Dānavas in the world indeed corrupted by the aforementioned defects,
[this] has been declared thus in brief in the *Mṛtyujitsārasaṅgraha*.
Furthermore, I shall explain in detail the nature of the *dīpana* and other [rituals].
O highly fortunate one, for illumination, there is the conjunction of the *praṇava* at both ends;
for awakening, there is the salutation (*namaskāra*); for impurity (*mala*), there should be the utterance *svāhā*.
For consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one should employ the mantra ending with *vauṣaṭ*.

One should employ the syllable *phaṭ*, joined with both [the preceding and following elements], for the purpose of striking. By means of the seed-syllable *lā*, likewise unaccented (*asvarita*), the mantra becomes powerful; it provides protection and the state of being guarded.
One should then recite that [mantra] ten thousand times encapsulated by Mṛtyujit.
When the mantra has been recited according to this procedure, protection will be established.
Furthermore, it should always be performed with the syllable *vāṃ* in an interspersed manner.
The mantra for nourishment (*āpyāyana*) is as follows:
it is described in the venerable *Ucchuṣmatantra* and other texts as being preceded by the *dīpana* [invigoration] and so forth;
it is enclosed at the beginning and end by the syllable *Oṃ*, and is illuminated by the secret power (*guhyaśakti*).
The illumination of all mantras is supreme for accomplishing all siddhis;
it is enclosed by the syllable Oṃ at the beginning and end, and interlaced with the syllable Hūṃ.
This awakening and illumination grants success even to those mantras that have not yet been mastered.
Enclosed at the beginning and end by the syllable Oṃ and interlaced with the syllable Oṃ,
this is the "striking" of all mantras, which destroys those who are arrogant.
Enclosed by the syllables *ṛ* at the beginning and end, and interlaced with the syllable *vīṃ*,
this is the consecration that renders [the substance] nectar-like (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), the sprinkling (*seka*) which causes the nourishment of the mantra.
Enclosed by the syllable *ha* at the beginning and end, and interlaced with the syllable *huṃ*, [is the mantra for] the empowerment of the mantra.
Furthermore, there is another method for purifying all mantras that brings success:
it is enclosed between the syllables *ṛ* at the beginning and end, and interlaced (*vidarbhitam*) with the syllable *vīṃ*.
This is the supreme burning and purification of all mantras.
If a mantra does not succeed for a practitioner despite his recitation,
he should perform the purificatory rite according to the procedure seen in the scriptures.
He should then recite that mantra while mixing it with *śiva* (ashes) and offer oblations (*homa*) mixed with meat.
Arise! This mental mantra succeeds even for a slayer of a Brahmin.
It is enclosed by the syllables *ṛ* at the beginning and end, and interlaced with the syllable *vīṃ*.
Those who have been pinned down, burnt, severed, or terrified [by other means]—[this mantra overcomes them].
They know the supreme *amṛtīkaraṇa* (the rite of immortalization) for these [mantras].
Next, I shall describe the *āpyāyana* (the rite of nourishment), which bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*) upon mantras that have been burnt,
severed, deprived of potency, drawn away, or likewise paralyzed.
And those fierce reciters of spells, agitated, greedy, and provoked—
angered by the insults of others possessed of blazing splendor,
and mutually opposed, they shall steal away the potency of the mantras.
The fourth among the secret and non-secret mantras is the one of great power;
the seed-syllable *kliṃ* is joined with all mantras as a means of nourishment,
especially by teachers, practitioners, disciples, and those who know the samaya.
The mantra, which is honored by the Omniscient One, is recited according to the ritual procedure.
Having first determined its recitation according to the rules, one should cause it to blaze forth.
The mantra becomes ignited, possessing the form of the sixty-sixth letter, *rakāra*. Having restrained its beginning and end, one should indeed recite it five thousand times.
O Goddess, this is certainly an illumination; of this there is no doubt.
By this procedure, [the mantra] joined with the letter *ra* at the beginning and end should be recited.
Having meditated upon the fiery concentration (*āgneyī dhāraṇā*), he abandons the practice of sleep.
Upon seeing that supreme practitioner, [the deity] becomes the bestower of the fruit of accomplishment.
For those practitioners who have reached awakening and are free from doubt, having made a firm resolve,

[the deity] is struck with the staff of power (śaktidaṇḍa) and joined with the letters beginning with *ra* and ending with *na*. Then, invoked by the word "existence" (*sattā*), they are discerned and proceed to bestow the fruit.
When all the hosts of mantras have their cravings for enjoyment dispelled,
and having understood the form described in the meditation, fashion them in the likeness of uśīra roots;
having seated them upon the lion-throne, one should consecrate them with a water-pot.
One should consecrate a thousand [times] with the deity Paramākṣara;
having performed the sacrifice in the east, the preceptor should perform the consecration.
Thus, this Vidyā-consecration shall bestow the fruit of great bliss.

O fair-faced one, even after the practitioner has abandoned that impurity without remainder, the mantra may still become defiled; listen now to the method for its purification. By reciting [the mantra] with the final letter placed in the middle, the purification is accomplished.
By means of merely a thousand recitations, those practitioners who have made a firm resolve [attain their goal].
However, those mantras that are devoid of sacrifice (yāga) and likewise devoid of fire-oblation (homa),
their syllables blazing with garlands of flames, should be known as "fire-like" (niritvat).
The [mantras] ending in *svāhā* and *vauṣaṭ* are to be recited during the rites of the festival days.
By merely reciting them a thousand times, there is satisfaction through the syllable *oṃ*.
Through the application of *māyā* at the beginning and end, it becomes an object of the mind.
By merely reciting it fifty times, the city of concealment arises;
indeed, the fifth [syllable], which has the color of strength, is the immortal syllable situated within the *bindu*.
This is accomplished by a thousand recitations; of this there is no doubt.
Thus has the application of the assembly of mantra-knowledge been explained for the practitioner according to this rule; by this, the practitioner shall become a partaker of success.
And in the Devyāyāmala-śāstra, the Moon-crested Lord (Śiva) has declared:
Intoxicated by the pride of power and arrogance, like those in a swoon,
they do not see even though they see, and they are utterly deluded even though they know. Therefore, for this reason, the God of gods has issued a restrictive command of his own authority.
In this way, the mantras are illuminated and proceed toward an increase in awakening.
O Dear One, having performed the natural recitation (*japa*) according to the *tantra*,
one should likewise perform the illumination of the mantra and the ritual action.
The one of great austerity should recite the mantra conjoined with the *praṇava* at both its beginning and end;
thereafter, through the practitioner’s application, he performs the ritual acts.
O Lord of Gods, [the scripture] declares this "illumination" (*dīpana*) in the *Umāyamala-śāsana*.
A mantra, ignited by means of illuminations, is bestowed once its birth has been attained;
setting aside other births, it shall manifest accomplishment.
Once awakened, it becomes aware of whatever has been performed by the practitioner.
A mantra will undoubtedly bear fruit from its seed; there is no doubt.
Illumination occurs through a tenth part [of the recitation], awakening through a hundredth part, and the planting of the seed of the mantra occurs through a thousandth part of the recitation.
In the Vidyāpurāṇa, the illumination [of the practice] according to the divisions of caste is described:
for all mantras indeed, that which has emerged from the seven streams is the supreme secret regarding the differentiation of rites, the unsurpassed root of accomplishment.
I shall explain in brief, according to their true meaning, the *saṃpuṭa* and other [methods],
without which, O lady of excellent hips, the accomplishment of ritual actions does not arise.
One should first write the entire mantra, followed immediately by the name of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
Furthermore, one should write the mantra in this manner; it is declared to be "encased" (saṃpuṭa).
It should be known as bringing about peace and nourishment, and as accomplishing sovereignty over the three worlds.
Each syllable of the name of the person to be acted upon (sādhya) is to be encased individually by the syllables of the mantra.
The "grathita" (strung) is declared to be the supreme performer of subjugation and attraction.
A wise practitioner should place the mantra at the beginning, the end, and likewise above and below [the name].
When it is situated in the middle of this, it is known as "grasta" (swallowed).
In all rites of sorcery, such as those for killing and the like, one should employ [the following]:
one should first write down the entire object to be addressed, and afterwards the mantra, O Great Lord.
In this way, it is taught that the whole is twofold.
For the purpose of inciting enmity or eradication, one should employ [the mantra] without hesitation.
First, the name to be addressed should be placed, and then the mantra should follow once;
this is known as the "interlaced" (vidarbhitam) form, which destroys all wicked beings.
For the protection of all worlds, he likewise brings the universe under his control.
When the target (*sādhya*) is overcome by the mantra wherever he may stand, he becomes subdued;
therefore, he immediately bestows the accomplishment of all aims.
One should first write the mantra once, and likewise three times again at the end;

one should write the name in the middle of it—this is known as the "measured" (mita) [mantra], beginning and ending with it. One should also write the mantra at the beginning, at the end, below, and above.
This mantra is said to reside within the womb of all those to be accomplished (*sādhya*). It effects killing, eradication, and subjugation of gods, asuras, and humans;
likewise, it performs the immobilization of weapons, ships, armies, intellect, the womb, and so forth.
O Goddess, when joined [with the appropriate seed-syllable], it quickly brings about the truth; it is not otherwise.

One should first write the mantra three times, and likewise write it again at the end. When the name is written once in the middle, one should know that [mantra] to be "facing in all directions" (sarvatobhadra).
It pacifies all calamities and destroys great death;
it generates all prosperity and bestows immortality upon the deceased.
O auspicious lady, when employed according to the prescribed rite, it successfully accomplishes every purpose.
One should first write the mantra, then the name, and then write the mantra again.
Having thus performed this threefold arrangement, it becomes one that is considered through proper reasoning;
it is declared to be the remover of all fevers and the crusher of spirits and epilepsy.
It is remembered as the supreme bestower of enjoyment and the pacifier of all diseases.
Having performed the *vidarbha* (interlacing) of each individual syllable of the name to be accomplished (*sādhya*) within the mantra,
one should arrange another [mantra] as previously knotted at its beginning and end.
This supreme characteristic of the mantra, when composed with the *vidarbha* technique,
is said to effect the attraction of all things and bestow the fruit of all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).
It destroys old age, poverty, the flood of suffering, death, and misfortune.
Through pacification, enrichment, subjugation, as well as inciting enmity, expulsion, and killing;
through paralyzing, immobilizing, causing possession, deluding, nourishing, and so forth—one shall accomplish whatever mantra is desired by the mind when it is properly applied. (124b)
Everything that has been said and unsaid, employed across various scriptures, has indeed been declared here;
this most secret [teaching] is common [to all], bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The characteristics of all mantras have been explained in the Kubjikāmata.

That which is situated within the womb (*garbhastha*), as well as that which is described as "swallowed" (*grasta*) and "surrounded on all sides" (*sarvato vṛta*), and that which is said to be "trampled" (*ākrānta*)—these two types are to be known as "surrounded on all sides.
This procedure for writing has been declared; it is thus written and likewise recited.
One should surround that which is "overpowered" (ākrānta) on all sides with the mantra;
likewise, when it is situated within the womb and swallowed, one should place the mantra in the cardinal directions.
That which is "overpowered" should be understood as being enclosed on all sides, just as it has been described.
This procedure for writing has been declared; now the procedure for recitation (japa) is being stated.
Since the mantra is at the beginning and end, with the name [of the practitioner] in the middle, it is "encased" (saṃpuṭa).
First there should be a syllable of the mantra, and then a syllable of the name of the one to be accomplished (sādhya).
One should recite the mantra in this manner; this is declared to be the "strung" (grathita) form.
All that is to be known regarding *prakṛti* begins with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ends with the word of salutation (*namaḥ*).
First the mantra, then the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*)—this is to be known as the "interwoven" (vidarbhitam), performed once.
First, the object to be accomplished (sādhya) should be joined with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and other syllables;

then the ritual action (*karma*), and then the mantra. This becomes the supreme form, either as an encapsulation (*sampuṭa*) at the beginning and end, or likewise with the object situated in the middle.
From that, the wise should take the middle portion and apply it three times;
for this is known as the "interlaced" (vidarbha) arrangement, which bestows success in ritual action.
One should arrange the mantra three times and the object of the rite three times, beginning with the *praṇava* (OM) and ending with the words "namas" and "anta."
This method of application is declared to be known as *vidarbha*.
One should employ [mantras] of the common and middling classes in the *śāmbhava* and other [mudrās];
for they possess extreme potency and power, being self-luminous and of great strength.
Thus, the mantra is elevenfold; he by whom it is known partakes in accomplishment.
Everything else is merely verbal, yet no statement is contradicted.
O twice-born one,
one should observe that mantras consist of either one, three, or many syllables;
those with more than these are known as impure (*malina*), provided they are not endowed with [the proper] characteristics.
The deities of the mantras are to be known as superior, inferior, and middling.

Those with vertical strokes (ūrdhvamātrā) are to be known as the Svaras; those with downward strokes (adhaḥmātrā) are always the Asuras; those with horizontal strokes (tiryaṅmātrā) are remembered as the Yakṣas, and those with [curved] strokes are declared to be the Gandharvas.
By those possessing only the upward [breaths], there is the power of moving through the sky; by those possessing the downward [breaths], the supreme state of the Asuras;
by those possessing only the horizontal [breaths], the human state. Thus is the collection of various accomplishments:
with the superior [breaths] the accomplishment is superior, and with the middling [breaths] it becomes middling.
The accomplishment of a human woman is achieved through common means; therefore, one should resort to the supreme [means].
Just as a head that has been severed does not truly grow back here again, so too for those who rely solely on the elevated *piśāca* measures, no foremost accomplishment is found.
One should recite a mantra obtained in a dream, or even one spoken by Prasena;
for actions performed in dreams are accomplished by means of mantras proclaimed by Śiva.
Therefore, one should perform the rite of the "dream-child" (svapna-śiśu) and cause Prasena to descend [into the dream].

Whether it be what is written on the ground, obtained from tradition, or inherited through family lineage; or wherever one’s innate disposition (bhāvāṃśaka) may lie, there should be devotion toward that deity. One should accomplish a single [deity] until success is attained; one should not practice a variegated mixture [of many].
"Or one may accomplish another [aim] separately for the sake of compassion toward living beings;
having counted the desired [syllable] with the Guru, one should then recite it.
Thus it was proclaimed by Maheśa in the Hāṭakeśvara Śāsana.
Now, the classification of castes, established according to their respective duties,
is proclaimed in due order for the purpose of distinguishing the mantras.
Through their connection with the [specific] vowels, they attain presence within the state of mantra:
the short vowel burns away sins; the long one certainly effects eradication;
the protracted (pluta) vowel is to be employed for nourishment and indeed for the rite of liberation.

If one who has eyes as wide as a lotus, possessed by wrath, performs the recitation with a short vowel joined at the beginning and end and ending in the syllable *phaṃ*, he shall kill. If joined at the beginning and end with the syllable *hūṃ* and using a long vowel, he will certainly cause expulsion.
This [mantra] for inciting enmity (vidveṣa) should be employed, provided with the syllables *phaṃ* and so forth.
Furthermore, rites for pacification (śāntika) and nourishment (pauṣṭika) should be performed with a protracted vowel (*pluta*).
At the time of initiation, one should perform the rite of the unification of the principles (*tattvasandhāna*).
One should lengthen the one to be accomplished by joining it with the syllable *phaṃ* and so forth;
having become a great sinner oneself, one should properly place [the mantra] upon the head.
Then, indeed, one should enter that [being] by way of the path of the arising of the inner essence (*nigarbha*).
Having entered into oneness with that [object], one should draw it back again by means of that very same [power].
Having joined the limbs to the limbs, one should unite the mind with the mind. One should extract the self of the person to be acted upon, like a thread situated within the interior of a lotus bud.
Whatever action is performed, its name is traditionally known as the *upapada*.
One should mutter that [name] conjoined with its locus, joined with the name, and interlaced [with the mantra].
A mantra for worship is not traditionally held to be one that lacks the nasal dot (*bindu*) and the *praṇava*.

In the rite of pacification (*śānti*), one should end with "home svāhā"; in the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*), one should draw [the mantra] toward oneself. In the rite of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), the mantra is preceded and followed by the syllable *namaḥ*, encapsulated by the syllable *hrīṃ*. Furthermore, in the rite of attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*) and in the rite of inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*), it is bound by the syllable *hūṃ* at the beginning and the end.
One should employ the application ending in *phaṭ* for the purpose of killing; likewise for paralyzing, immobilizing, deluding, punishing, restraining, binding, causing enmity,
insanity, suffering, and the like, as well as for bringing about displeasure and the destruction of one's undertakings.
In cases of binding through hostile views, in acts of deafness and blindness,
in mental derangement, in the affliction by great diseases, and in the splitting of the mind,
the mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra enclosed between the syllables *phaṭ* at the beginning and end.
For immobilization, [the mantra] ends with the visarga; for cutting, it ends with *cchindidanta*;
for drying, it is *bahudhāśūnya*; likewise, for the generation of passion, [it is the same];
for pinning, the word *tiṣṭhati* is used, conjoined with the seed-syllable of concentration (*dhāraṇā*).
A mantra ending in *e* or *ā* thoroughly effects the binding of the mouth.
A *ya* or *va* situated at the end brings about eradication (*uccāṭana*).
For the attainment of what is desired, it ends in *ma*; for cessation (*nivṛtti*), it is joined with *svā*.
In the rite of burning (dāha), the root mantra is employed as it is pervaded by two *repha*s (the letter *ra*);
in the rite of summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*), it ends with the letter *gha* and is applied to the eight petals.
In the rite of encapsulation (*saṃpuṭa*), the vowel *i* is used here, while in the rite of causing enmity (*vidveṣa*), the vowel *ī* is proclaimed.

The syllable *kṣo* is for the subduing of wicked beings and the like, as well as for rites of pacification (*śānti*) and nourishment (*pauṣṭika*). The syllable *ma* is for the destruction of poisons, whether stationary (*sthāvara*) or mobile (*jaṅgama*). Here, the syllable *ja* is for the act of refreshing or increasing, while the syllable *ra* is for the rite of burning.

The syllable *huṃ* is to be employed for killing, while the syllable *ṭha* is used for neutralizing poison. Written upon the eight spokes starting from the eastern one, it accomplishes its own specific purpose when visualized as intensely blazing from the big toe up to the crown of the head.

Having entered [the body] and turned it face downwards, one should by means of oneself [imagine] the locus of the apāna breath as resembling burnt wood; having thus contemplated the target whose body has been abandoned, the severance of the mantra is accomplished.
There shall be pinning down, as well as delusion, and likewise the loss of splendor;
there is also the severing of protection—this is true, there is no doubt in this matter.

And he becomes hated by all; the mantra of one for whom the name is written between two enclosures of the letter *ka* does not succeed. Outside of that, one should draw the world of fire (*vahnibhuvana*), adorned with eight *ra* letters.
Having written [the name] and placed it where a skull is joined with another in a vessel,
there is no doubt that for whomever it is done, a severance of the mantra occurs; indeed,
his success is lost, and he becomes hated by all.
The mantras situated in the northern direction should always be written as they arrive in their primary order,
all facing toward the central deity; whichever deity is in the center,
then [the mantras] become fruit-bearing, provided they always abide according to their respective positions.
When written in reverse order, they perform acts such as inciting enmity and eradication;
indeed, when moving in the rightward direction, they bring misfortune if they go in the reverse order.
Thus, according to the distinctions of their classes, one should employ them as desired.
The minister named Śrīmad Varmaśiva declared:
"O Goddess, that single mantra is manifold; likewise, meditation bestows its own specific accomplishments, whether it be in the dual, the non-dual, the mixed, the Ekavīra, or the Yāmala."

In every manner prescribed by all the scriptures, it shall become a bestower of accomplishment. Just as the wish-fulfilling gem in this world grants the fruits of whatever is desired, even so does the King of Mantras accomplish whatever is intended.
The supreme and most powerful abode of the seventy million mantras;
yet those mantras which are devoid of meditative realization (bhāva), lacking power, and obstructed;
as well as those deficient in phonemes, mantras, and so forth, and bereft of the guru’s oral tradition.
Those oral traditions of the *trasva* that have perished because they were obstructed by being abandoned by the scriptures do not succeed,
O Goddess, even when recited thousands of times as desired;
for those who are unaccomplished and hostile are devoid of all constituent parts.
O Goddess of the Gods, by this mantra Amṛteśa, which is enclosed between the first and last syllables and thus bound by the initial letter, [the dead] are restored to life. (127a)

Indeed, when recited without effort, they grant one's desired objects without a doubt; O Goddess, these nine are renowned as bestowers of everything, and this is not false. Thus is that supreme deity, Amṛteśa, free from all ailment.
It is taught as abiding in its own nature, all-pervading, [eternal], and constant.
In the ultimate sense, neither form nor color exists for it;
for the auspicious Lord consists of everything and consists of all scriptures.
Pervading all mantras and bestowing all accomplishments,
it is stainless like a crystal threaded upon a white or other colored string; indeed,
wherever it is colored by this or that, it reflects itself everywhere.
Just so, the Lord of Gods, being established in all the scriptures,
bestows upon all practitioners the fruit they desire.
Therefore, among all the currents [of tradition], He shines like a wish-fulfilling gem.
Indeed, when meditated upon according to the distinction of states (bhāva), He bestows the fruit of all the Āgamas:
Śiva, Sadāśiva, Bhairava, and likewise Tumburu;
the All-pervading Lord who assumes the forms of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire.

Since the Lord consists of knowledge, and knowledge exists in many forms, he is called "Tattva" because he protects those who are constrained and bound. Because he delivers one from death, he is called "Mṛtyujit" (the Conqueror of Death); therefore, he is not to be grieved for.

Thus, he bestows immortality and is remembered as Amṛteśa; for by whatever state of being [the practitioner] approaches him, he becomes the giver of that very fruit. The practitioner who always meditates upon him in the form of Sadāśiva—
He whose body becomes that of Sadāśiva—of this there is no doubt.
For he is common to all and the bestower of grace upon all;
he is indeed Sadyojāta, Aghora, and the forms of Puruṣa and Īśāna.
By this [mantra], O fair-faced one, the heart and other [limbs] are to be installed;
by this very mantra, one should likewise arrange one’s own seat.
Thus indeed did the Supreme Lord declare in the Mṛtyujit Tantra.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, destroyer of Tripura, please explain in that same manner for the benefit of your disciples the mantra consisting of pure syllables which was previously mentioned by you.
Thus, the fourteenfold cycle of saṃsāra has been described.
Among those, the eightfold creation of the gods has been proclaimed.
From Brahmā down to the Piśācas, O beloved, human beings are portions of that [creation].
Then, O Daughter of the Mountain, that which is established and declared in the scriptures is told by me in brief, as it was spoken regarding the Piśācas and others:
"The portion of a Piśāca is one who is addicted to strong liquor, hypocritical, and joined with sin."
One who betrays gods, the twice-born, and teachers; one who causes fear to friends; one who is always deceitful until the end of danger; one who eats everything and sells everything;
and one who is devoted to impure paths at all times—such a person is utterly despised.
"Nothing succeeds for him," said the Blessed Lord Śiva.
"Born from a portion of Nairṛti, he will always be a seeker of deceit;
he is constantly a kidnapper of maidens, as well as wrathful and fickle."
A worldly person should always be intent upon fire-worship;
being excessively proud, he should always strike [his enemies] through sharp deception. O Dear One, his success will be constant in the practice of cruel mantras.
Constantly intent on acquiring wealth, a portion of a Yakṣa, he is fond of his own wife;
desiring fish, meat, and delicacies, he is greedy and acts with arrogance.
Likewise, he immediately consumes strong liquor and wine.

One who desires to master the collection of weapons should always devote themselves to the study of the treatises; for even in that case, O fortunate one, success is attained by relying on unwavering practice.
O fair-faced one, he is skilled in song like a Gandharva, devoted to the guiles of a hunter,
constantly proud of his heroism, and fearful of the scriptures;
he frequents women in secret and is desirous of all things.
A man who is constantly devoid of attachment, lacking friendship,
ever deceitful, fraudulent, devoted to temples,
and unstable in all undertakings, is one whose portion is that of a Gandharva.
A meat-eater, arrogant, cruel, wrathful, and fond of excessive food; always intent on great battle and devoted to the conquest of enemies;
he should constantly carry weapons and hold all things in high esteem.
Intolerant yet always powerful, devoted to hating the gods,
and born from the portion of a Daitya, he is eternally a vessel for the netherworlds and other realms.
The portion of Indra, possessing fiery brilliance, shall always accomplish all his undertakings.
He shall always be devoted to the gods and the twice-born, a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
a promoter of all scriptures, and a constant composer of poetry. He shall be a believer endowed with sincere devotion, and ever intent upon the practice of celibacy.
That man shall be of virtuous character, devoted to righteousness, and an incarnation of Indra;
he will possess a fine residence, have many sons, be devoted to Brahmanas, and be thoroughly versed in the scriptures.
He will be a knower of dharma, grateful, a donor, and dear to his own kin.
Attached to the abode of the deities, devoted to his guru, and learned in the scriptures—
such is the Prājāpatya [birth], O Great Goddess, which bestows the perfection of creation.
He is a portion of Soma, handsome to behold, and affectionate toward all people.
A man who is devoted to the worship of gods and brahmins becomes a portion of Soma;
he is an ascetic, ever self-restrained, with a bright countenance and conquered senses. He is intent on recitation and worship, self-controlled, learned, and a follower of the scriptures.
An excellent man who is a portion of Brahmā and a devotee of Brahmā attains perfection;
he is devoted to the worship of the gods, eloquent, and his speech is dedicated to Brahman and truth.
Devoted to sacrifice, ever-diligent, tawny-hued through his illusory power (*māyā*),
a slayer of enemies, eternally free from desire, and intent upon hating the Daityas—
such a man becomes an incarnation (*aṃśa*) of Viṣṇu, engaged in both restraint and favor.
An incarnation of Rudra, you have squinting eyes and are tawny-hued, yet free from deceit.
You are a master of illusion who transcends illusion, devoted to the worship of the deity.
Arrogant and ever prone to anger, you do not laugh at anyone.
O Goddess of the Gods, the yogi who knows the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, who is radiant, devoted to the mantras,
endowed with the perfection of mantra, intent on recitation, engaged in ritual action,
and purified by all mantras, attains success.
O lady of excellent complexion, even mixed activities arise;
knowing this portion [of the disciple], O Goddess, the wise Guru, who is proficient in the Tantras,
bestows grace according to the disciple's own nature.
In this way, O Goddess of gods, the practitioner intent on the mantra attains success;
or wherever devotion is firm, that is a portion of the Great Intellect. But regarding meditative realization, O Goddess of gods, it clearly becomes a distinct portion of that.

One should also examine the mantra according to the division into *siddha* and *sādhya*. That which is established (*siddha*) and situated at both the beginning and the end bestows middling accomplishment. O Goddess, that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) resides in three places; it does not bestow accomplishment here.
It is self-established for the foremost of practitioners and is indeed accomplished without deliberation.
O Mother of the Gaṇas, it should be known as eternally indestructible;
there, too, I shall declare the procedure by which one should investigate it.
The wise one, having first written the name, should place it within the syllables of the mantra;
O Pārvatī, he should not, however, separate the mantra itself.
The preceptor should fill the syllables of the mantra with the letters of the name;
he should then count the *siddha*, *sādhya*, *svasiddha*, and *ari* [syllables] by means of calculation.
Furthermore, the wise one should count the *mātṛkā* (alphabet) excluding the *kūṭa* and *śaṇṭha* [consonants].
Having deliberated upon the result therein, one should then commence the bestowal of the mantra.
O Pārvatī, that which is taught by an enemy does not succeed at all;
likewise, O beautiful one, having examined the enemy and the sādhya, [one must consider] if it is situated at the side.

Then, it is declared that [a name] is "bestower of success" (siddhiprada) if it is situated between two "accomplished" (siddha) syllables. That which is situated between both "to-be-accomplished" (sādhya) syllables is established as "accomplished" (siddha) when it occupies the middle position.
Wherever there is an enemy (ari) situated in the middle between two positions of accomplishment, [it is likewise determined].
O Mother of the Gaṇas, one should consider that [mantra] which bestows middling success as indeed harmful to the enemy;
a mantra established in the "sādhya" state, even if it possesses abundant self-success, bestows success;
however, one should examine a mantra that is "svasiddha" (self-accomplished) as being fearful to the enemy and devoid of success for oneself.
One's own *siddha* [mantra] situated at the side of the enemy bestows success; of this there is no doubt.

Having thus analyzed the mantra according to the categories of enemy (*śatru*), neutral (*madhya*), and one's own *siddha*, that which is situated within one's own *siddha* and occupies the middle position is remembered as the most excellent.
Then, O Goddess of Gods, the practitioner attains success; there is no doubt in this matter.
Having first considered this section as stated in the Vīṇāśikhottara, I shall now fully explain the procedure exactly as it is taught in another scripture.
First, one should spread out the Mātṛkā, excluding the *kūṭas* and the *śaṇṭhas*.
Having worshipped it according to the prescribed rule, one should write the mantra beneath it.
Likewise, the measures (*mātrā*) of the conjuncts are distinct according to the various divisions of the *ajāla*.
Having written the name below, according to the sequence of the syllables of the mantra—
whether it be a name well-known in the world or a birth-name,
or that which may have been bestowed by the Guru through the falling of flowers for ascetics.

The characteristics and the constituent parts (*aṃśaka*) of both the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the means of accomplishment (*sādhaka*) should be known; they are taught as fourfold: *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and [the fourth]. The syllables of the names of the mantras are distributed according to the sequence ending with the Mother-letters (*mātṛkā*).
The practitioner desiring success should count the syllables of the mantra until it is fully realized.
It is considered "all-accomplishing" (sarvasiddha) when its results—both seen and unseen—are well-established;
"all-effective" (sarvasādhya) when it is indifferent [to external conditions]; and "self-accomplished" (svasiddha) when it bestows success.
Likewise, an enemy [mantra] is said to be artificial for the practitioner; of this there is no doubt.
One that is perfected at the beginning and perfected at the end bestows the fruit of all accomplishments.
However, that which has the *sādhya* syllable at the beginning and the end is considered difficult to accomplish.
But he who is "accompanied by the Siddha" (sasiddha) at both the beginning and the end attains success very quickly.

Where there is an enemy at both the beginning and the end, that [mantra] destroys everything in an instant. However, one that is to be accomplished (sādhya) at the beginning and at the end bestows its own success with double the effort.
That which is established at the beginning and that which is to be accomplished at the end require fourfold merit.
When that which is to be accomplished is at the beginning and the end while that which is established is in the middle,
it requires an excess of recitation for both the established and the to-be-accomplished ends.

A *siddha* [letter] enclosed by an *ari* (enemy), or likewise one that is itself *asiddha* (unaccomplished), should be known as causing the total destruction of the practitioner; of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, a *sādhya* [letter] separated by a *siddha*, or even one separated by its own *siddha*, [is likewise ineffective].

The mantra of the practitioner will be accomplished without obstacle; of this there is no doubt. Whether the enemy is separated by one who has attained success or even by one who is himself successful, he does not become an adversary in that case, but rather merely endures hardship.

But that which is established through the intervention of another goal to be accomplished, or even through the intervention of one's own [prior] accomplishment, may be established only with great difficulty; it should always be avoided. When an accomplishment is intervened by an enemy, or when it becomes one's own accomplishment [only after such interference], [it is likewise problematic].
Having observed such characteristics from afar, one should avoid [the mantra] entirely.
A mantra corrupted by an enemy should never be brought near.
Having unified, according to the prescribed rite, both the perfected Śaiva mantra and one's own perfected mantra, [one should proceed].
Furthermore, one should multiply both the *sādhya* and the *ripu* by ten; then,
having multiplied them, one should subsequently divide the two resulting heaps by eight from the *siddha* heap and by twelve from the *ari* heap.
One should indicate those months which correspond to the remainder in the "enemy" heap (*arirāśi*).
As for the remainder in the "accomplished" heap (*siddharāśi*), those become the watches (*prahara*);
during that watch in that month, one should perform the reception of the mantra (*mantragrahaṇa*).
Having consumed the desired *caru* offering at that time during the day, the practitioner, being composed in mind, attains success within that very month; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, having understood the constituent parts of the mantra and having correctly realized certainty within oneself.

One who desires supreme accomplishment should offer the *arghya* oblation to the mantra. Those beginning with *a*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, and *ta* are known as the waters; those beginning with *ā*, *ai*, *kha*, *cha*, *ṭha*, and *tha* are known as the winds.
The letters *ī*, *ū*, *gha*, *jha*, *ḍha*, *dh*, and so forth, as well as *bha*, *ba*, *ha*, *na*, and *bha*, are remembered as the *nābhasa* (ethereal) class.
*O*, *au*, *aṃ*, and *aḥ* are proclaimed as the final members of their respective groups; these are the *taijasa* (fiery) letters. Thus, the total number of letters in one group is forty-five.
The *gaṇa* is to be known from the nine [syllables] in the *mātṛkā*; of this there is no doubt.
If the first syllable of a mantra is seen anywhere to belong to the *māhendra* [class], they know that to be the practitioner's own *kula* in this world.
In this very way, one should know that the auspicious mantra is fivefold: pertaining to wind, water, space, and likewise fire.
The Vāruṇa [element] is the enemy of the Pārthiva, and the Māruta of the Āgneya.
The Māruta is situated as the enemy of both the Māhendra and the Vāruṇa.
Likewise, the Vāruṇa is the enemy of the Āgneya, and the Taijasa (Āgneya) is the enemy of the Vāruṇa.
Because all the principles (tattvas) are equal,
one who possesses the intent for their own welfare should avoid the union of the mutually contradictory syllables of the mantras born of the five faces, even if it pertains to the etheric realm.
Indeed, one must not only gather mantras, but especially embodied beings—
enemies, kinsmen, sons, and those who are essential, as well as friends, those to be accomplished, and those beneficial or harmful—
having understood them through substances, medicinal herbs, and elixirs.
This examination of the seed-syllables is not to be performed for mantras consisting of one, three, five, or thirty-two syllables, nor for a mantra of seventeen syllables.
This applies to those [mantras] that consist of a single hero (ekavīra), great peaks (mahākūṭa), or the nature of Śiva and Śakti.
The Sauras, Baudhas, Hatās, Vaiṣṇavas, and Nārasiṃhikas— among them,
this investigation of the Siddhas and Sādhyas does not exist.
From the forty syllables, there is an increase of one syllable at a time.
The mantra at the end, numbering sixty-three, grants all desires.
Those mantras which are perfected through the command (*ājñāsiddha*) by the grace of the Yoginīs,
and those mantras which have been obtained [otherwise], bestow the fruit of all desires.
All this characteristic of mantra has been fully explained in the Western [Tantra].
Having known this, his mantra will be swiftly accomplished; of this there is no doubt. (131a)
The practitioner— sincere, steadfast, and conversant with the injunctions of all the scriptures— having reached a site of accomplishment (siddhakṣetra) as desired, should,
accompanied by his own assistants and free from fear, perform the formal adoption of the liṅga as described below.

A wise person should worship a linga facing west; in its absence, one facing east. However, a linga with a face toward the Kaurava direction (the northeast) is not recommended for the sake of attaining success.
One should also avoid a linga that is stacked on top of another or a linga with a face.
One should worship a deity established by the ṛṣis that is to be accepted, or one previously worshipped by the gods,
or a self-manifested (svayambhu) deity, or one made of crystal;
or likewise one made of gold or jewels, shaped like a parasol, which bestows success.
Or even one resembling a hen’s egg, which bestows the accomplishment of mantras;
once it has been installed according to the rules by a high-souled preceptor,
one should worship that liṅga situated there, together with its ancillaries and accompanied by the collection of mantras.
Always, according to the previously mentioned procedure for the ritual of union with the *liṅga*,
one should construct a firm temple for the sacred field facing either east or north, which is auspicious;
if a western door is unavailable, one should avoid facing south.
The best of practitioners should diligently avoid facing the intermediate directions.
Alternatively, there may be a central door according to the indications of the architectural layout (*vāstu*).
These are, in sequence: *svabhadra*, *maṅgala*, *bhadra*, and *vardhamāna*.
One should mark these doors in the directions starting from the east,
in all temples and in the houses of kings;
these locations should be established, for they especially bestow success.
The thirty-two door-designations have been declared by means of the names of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*).
They are to be employed in all household affairs and beloved undertakings. In another tantra, it is prescribed that there shall also be eight arrows in the cardinal directions.

One should bind [the site] with a trident pointing upward and a wheel at the bottom, consecrated with the great weapon-mantra; furthermore, one may bind it with the five jewels or with a rope made of goat-hair.
One should also perform the binding of the directions with *khadira* wood or mustard seeds.
The seat was filled with cotton and covered with a deer skin;
there he sat, wearing a black antelope skin and holding a meditation strap and a rosary.
That dwelling was provided with incense, flowers, and fruits, and was radiant with its own splendor.
One should thus fashion a rosary made of ruby,
or one made of *putrajīvaka* and lotus seeds, which is recommended for all rites.
Alternatively, one may make it of gems or crystal, which bestows one's own specific accomplishments (*siddhi*).
One should fashion one hundred and eight [pieces], or half of that, or even a quarter.
In the center, Meru must be made, either of the same material or of another.
One should empower it with the Astra-mantra and meditate upon it as blazing like fire.
One should constantly revolve [the breath] along the lower part of Meru;
one should not revolve above Meru, nor should it become composed of sound.
One should always perceive these three—the self, the deity, and the radiant [breath]—as one.
The practitioner, having sprinkled it with water while reciting the Astra-mantra, should take up that which has been worshipped.
For rites such as pacification (śāntika), one should draw [the substance] starting from the little finger;
for subjugation (vaśya) and so forth, the ring finger is used; and for attraction (ākarṣaṇa), the middle finger is prescribed.

One should perform all rites involving harsh actions with the index finger, but all others with the thumb. A wise person should perform the recitation (*japa*) neither too slowly nor too clearly, neither with water in the mouth nor while making a sound, neither without counting nor with a distracted mind.
Japa is threefold: whispered (*upāṃśu*), vocal (*vācika*), and mental (*mānasa*).
The fruit of these is proclaimed to increase a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and infinitely, respectively.
A wise practitioner of mantra should perform the japa facing either the east or the north.
Having uttered the root mantra,

one should contemplate the syllables of the mantra as being strung upon the power (*śakti*) inherent in that root mantra. And one should contemplate that power in the supreme void, nourished by the supreme nectar.
The mantra situated within that [Nāda] bestows the fruits of all desires.
Residing within the pericarp of the heart-lotus is the stainless power of Nāda;
there, the mantras are strung together like clusters of gems upon a thread.
For those who have bathed in the supreme nectar-essence indeed become [liberated].
But when the supreme reality— omniscient, omnipresent, and imperishable— is known, the mantras,
together with the lords of mantras, enter into a state of servitude.
When the wise practitioner recites the mantra through the yoga of total tranquility,
that yogi, situated in the midst of the assembly of deities, conquers death with ease.
There is no other mantra without *nāda*, and *nāda* is established as the vital breath (*vāyu*).
That power which carries the wind, whose nature is the touch of pure consciousness—that is declared to be the power of mantra; there is no other mantra, nor is there any recitation.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Rudra, Īśvara, and Śiva himself [are it].

The eightfold division of Śiva, as well as Vidveṣa and Bhairava—those mantras beginning with these are proclaimed as Śāmbhava. Umā and the others are declared to be the Śaktis: Lakṣmī, Gaurī, and Sarasvatī.
Jayā and the others, as well as Raktā and the others, and likewise Kālāntakaraṇī—
these and other such great goddesses are Śākta, O best of the twice-born. So too are the female messengers (dūtīs), the Mothers (mātṛs), the servants (kiṅkaras), and those who go before.

Likewise, the piśācas and yakṣas are proclaimed to be of the nature of the atom (āṇava). Whether walking, standing, sleeping, or waking, the practitioner who has made his resolve [should remain focused].
One whose self consists of the mantra established in its power certainly becomes a partaker of supernatural attainments (siddhi).
One should contemplate that very mantra which possesses whatever power it has;
that [power] is perceived there, within the earthly principle (pārthiva-tattva) of the individual soul (āṇava).
The practitioner should always know that which resides within the pericarp of the heart-lotus as the "casket" (samudga) of all embodied beings, the cause of the individual souls (āṇava).
Above that, they say, is the Śākta [state], characterized by the awakening of the mind.
From the heart-lotus upwards, however, is the principle of Śakti, which is intensely radiant.
Therein reside the red mantras as far as the end of Nāda (nādānta).
Furthermore, from the "end of the twelve" (dvādaśānta) to the middle of the eyebrows and the crown of the head, there are indeed lights.
Likewise, the subtle sound (*sūkṣmanāda*) resides eternally within the point (*bindu*);
thus is the arising of mantra proclaimed, which is the supreme method for recitation (*japa*).
One should perform the recitation in its proper sequence through the manifestation of the form of the *yuga*.
In the Tretā age, the mere completion of the study [of the Veda] as enjoined for the Kalpa is required;
in the Dvāpara age, O Goddess honored with the best of vowels, the recitation is said to be twofold;
but in the Kali age, O Goddess, the practitioner of mantra attains success through a tenfold recitation.

At the conclusion of the recitation (*japa*), the fire-oblation (*homa*) should be equal to it, or half, or even a tenth or a hundredth part, according to one's own means. It should be performed with sesame seeds or rice grains, accompanied by the five ancillaries (*pañcāṅgika*).
Whether with clarified butter, fuel-sticks, or incense such as guggulu and pills;
or even with wild flowers, bilva fruits, or lotuses and water-lilies—
the practitioner of mantra does not achieve success without recitation, nor does one become a possessor of accomplishment without offering oblations.
In this world, nothing that is not worthy of worship is worshipped; how could there be anything other than playful meditation?
Success is attained through austerities, mantras, vows, and the Cāndrāyaṇa fasts.
Through the performance of the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances, and by the practice of the *tulāpuruṣa*,
the fivefold accomplishment (*sādhana*) of the mantras is thus described;
for him in whom the signs of success arise, his perfection (*siddhi*) becomes manifest.
One has a vision of deities in a dream and great conversation with them;
one may even devour the moon and the sun in the sky,
or drink from the Gaṅgā, the ocean, or a great river in a dream.
Or one whose head is severed and drenched with blood,
or who drinks blood in a dream, or undertakes the Great Vow (mahāvrata);
or who consorts with an excellent woman, or climbs to the top of a tree.
(133b) Impelled by the Supreme Lord, those who are attached to the essence of innate bliss [attain it].
That day is declared to be a festival that yields both natural and artificial fruits.
Even one devoid of knowledge and yoga who worships on a Kula festival attains self-awareness; such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
The hero’s vow, the attainment of power, the union with the beloved, as well as the rites of killing, eradication, inciting enmity, subjugation, and attraction—
all of these are accomplished by him spontaneously on the day of the festival.
One should perform a special worship according to the prescribed rite on the family festival (kulaparvan),
with flowers, incense, offerings, and various kinds of foods— both solid and soft— as well as with drinks produced from water, the air, or the earth, and with consecrated liquors.
One should worship the Supreme Lord according to the Yamala ritual on the ninth day of the dark fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa at the onset of night,
during the first half of the second watch, under the conjunction of Āditya (the Sun) and Uttaraphalgunī.
O Pārvatī, the second festival occurs on the ninth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa at the arrival of midnight,
when there is a conjunction between the moon and the constellation Citrā;
and it occurs on the full moon of the fifteenth day of Māgha at the arrival of midnight.
The third festival, known as Kaulika, occurs during the conjunction of Maghā and Bṛhaspati.
The fourth festival is said to take place on the twelfth day of Phālguna during the conjunction of Tiṣya and the Moon,
when the sun has reached the middle of the sky.
O Pārvatī, when the moon is in Uttaraphalgunī and the sun has reached the middle of the day,
on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the fifth festival occurs; likewise,
on the eighth day of the month of Vaiśākha, there is the conjunction of Mercury and the Śravaṇa asterism.
O fair-faced one, the sixth festival occurs at midday during the dark fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha; O Pārvatī,
the seventh festival occurs on the ninth day of the dark fortnight in the same month, at midday,
when there is a conjunction with the Moon and the water-god (Varuṇa).
On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, when the sun has reached the meridian,
the conjunction of the moon with Mūla and the sun constitutes what is declared to be the eighth *parvan*.
Furthermore, on the eleventh day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, there is the conjunction of the moon with Rohiṇī and Venus.
O beautiful lady, the ninth festival occurs at dawn during the dark fortnight;
O Goddess, the tenth Kaulika festival occurs on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, when there is a conjunction with Viṣākhā and Jupiter, at the rising of the Sun.
O beloved, on that bright ninth day of the month of Āśvayuja,
neither the position of the planets, the lunar mansions, nor the specific time of day is taken into account;
for then the goddess Vidrāviṇī, who is fond of her heroic brothers, appears.
Like a mother, she eternally bestows accomplishment upon those who desire it.
This eleventh chapter is the great source of success for the Kula.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, at the onset of night—
The twelfth [day] is proclaimed to occur during the conjunction with the moon in Śravaṇā.
Having obtained this fivefold occasion— consisting of the lunar mansion, the planet, the time, the day, and the fortnight— one shall attain the Kaulika accomplishment.
Among these five, the day is the most important; one should reflect upon it.
The specific festivals have been declared; now hear from me the general ones.
The fourth, the fifth, and likewise the ninth are accomplished within a month.
The fourteenth and the twelfth days of both fortnights,
as well as the birth day and the consecration day of one's preceptor and oneself.
The ancestral rite (śrāddha), the warding off of calamities, the appearance of deities or portents,
worldly festivals, the transit of the sun (saṅkrānti), dreams, commands, and even gains;
as well as the commencement and conclusion of the exposition of secret scriptures— these are the occasions for [the recitation of] the *Rudra*.
Likewise, the arrival of the guru or the circle of gurus at one's own home;

the acquisition of knowledge and the acquisition of scriptures through devotion to the rules of conduct; meeting with yoginīs and association with those belonging to one’s own spiritual lineage and so forth.
Thus, the general characteristics of the *parvan* have been declared in twenty ways.
Here, the specific conduct of the *kula*-yogins is praised.
Having performed the ritual of the *parvan*, one should perform the *mūrti-yāga* according to the prescribed rule.

And when the sacrifice to the image is impossible, one should satisfy only young maidens who possess breasts and flowers, who are free from physical defects, and are beautiful. In all the Kula practices, the Kula personage is rich in the arts.
O Goddess, he by whom the Self is known is an authorized one and possesses accomplishment.
Thus, the procedure for the festival has been declared in two ways according to the opinion of the Lord of the Cakra,
following the distinction between the Kula and Siddhānta traditions, as desired by practitioners.
One should fulfill the incompleteness of daily worship and the like by means of every possible form of worship;
here too, one should fulfill any deficiency through the Pavitraka rite.
In the absence of wealth, one may perform it even with *kāśa* or *kuśa* grass.
If one possesses wealth but does not perform [the rite], how could there be freedom from hell and disease?
However, in the event of the omission of the *pavitraka*, one should always recite the mantra as penance;
having become purified, one should perform it again—such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
(135a) Initiation is in vain, knowledge is in vain, and service to the guru is in vain,
if one does not perform the *pavitraka* rite; but if one performs it, that [initiation and so forth] becomes fruitful indeed.
Śrī Devī said:
"O God, bearer of the trident, I wish to hear in truth about the Pavitrārohaṇa; tell me briefly its origin and the procedure for its performance."
Bhairava said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly wise one who brings grace to the worlds!
That which has been called the 'Purifier' (pavitra) is the means for accomplishing dharma, artha, and karmas."

O lady of beautiful countenance, all has been rendered pure for the sake of the *pavitra* rite by the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, piśācas, uragas, kinnaras, bhūtas, hosts of sages, and others such as the kṣetrapālas and rākṣasas.
Whether by teachers, practitioners, those established in the observance, or by spiritual sons—
whoever has been initiated and is constantly devoted— if he does not perform the *pavitraka* rite,
the obstacle will certainly destroy the worship performed throughout the year.
The *pavitraka* was ordained by me for the purpose of protecting the worship;
one should prepare the *pavitraka* either upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) or within a mandala.
The younger brother of Vāsuki, whose name is Pavitraka, [is the deity presiding over it].

"O Goddess, I was gratified by him through his fierce austerity and devotion. Then I said to him, 'O serpent, choose a boon. [He replied: 'The worship, recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites performed for a year [have been completed]'"—so it was said.
O Goddess, I have granted this to him who would not perform the *pavitraka* rite,
whether in the month of Āṣāḍha, or Śrāvaṇa, or even at any other time.
It is declared that the performance in Āṣāḍha is the best, while in Śrāvaṇa it is considered middling.
In the month of Nabhasya, during the month of Kanyā, it is proclaimed that this is the purifying rite (*pavitra*).
Otherwise, one who desires his own welfare must not perform it at any other time.
In the Kṛta age, it was made of gold; in the Tretā age, it was produced from silver.

In the Dvāpara age one should make it from copper, and in the Kali age from cotton thread. It should be very strong, well-twisted, and spun by the daughter of a twice-born man. Having tripled the thread and twisted it three times, one should prepare the *pavitraka*.
With this [mantra] one should wash the thread; with the Vāmadeva [mantra], one should tie the knots.
Having purified it with the Aghora [mantra], one should dye it with the Puruṣa [mantra].
One should then install it in the northeast; such indeed is the sequence.
O Goddess, listen as I declare to you those deities who reside within the nine threads:
the first is Oṃkāra, the second is known as Soma,
the third has Vahni as its presiding deity, and the fourth is named Brahmā.
The fifth has Nāga as its deity, and the sixth is Śikhidhvaja;
the seventh has Sūrya as its deity, while Sadāśiva is ever-joyful.
In the ninth, all the gods reside—these are the nine threads.
One should perform one hundred and eight, fifty, or twenty-five;
these are declared to be the superior, the middling, and the inferior [counts] respectively.
That which consists of one hundred and eight is said to bestow both spiritual accomplishment (siddhi) and liberation (mukti).
O lady of excellent vows, it is said that [this rite] bestows fifty perfections for the sake of attaining longevity.
For the purpose of purification, however, it should be performed with twenty-five [strings];
ten knots should be tied at intervals of four finger-breadths.
The first is named Kriyā, the second is remembered as Pauruṣī;
the third shall be Vīrā, and the fourth Aparājitā.
The fifth is named Jayā, and the sixth is likewise Vijayā;
Ajitā is to be known as the seventh, while Sadāśiva is the eighth.
Manonmanī is the ninth, and Sarvatomukhī is the tenth.
These names of the knots have been told in brief.
Now, the sacred thread (pavitraka) should be made according to the measurement of the *liṅga*.
In the *ajāteṣṭi* [rite], it should be known as sixteen digits (*kalā*); in the *vāmadeva*, thirteen.
In Aghora there are eight kalās, four kalās in Puruṣa, and five kalās in Īśāna; thus all have been declared. O Goddess, he who knows these thirty-eight kalās in the Pavitraka [rite]—
Alternatively, O fair-faced one, there are nine knots [made] at a measurement of two finger-breadths or even one finger-breadth;
they should be smeared with saffron, red ochre, or turmeric.
The wise man should find delight according to his own capacity.
On either of the two sides, on the seventh or even the thirteenth lunar day,
the *adhivāsa* and the *pavitra* should be offered there according to the prescribed ritual.
Then, having bathed with water and other substances, with his body armored by mantras,
he should bathe the *liṅga* with milk,
curd, and ghee, and then dry it with powders made from barley and wheat, combined with astringents and fragrances.
Having bathed [the image], one should anoint it with camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood;

one should worship it according to the prescribed rule through rites seen in the scriptures, accompanied by auspicious sounds of "May merit increase! and "Victory!", as well as conchs and musical instruments.

O Goddess, the mantra-practitioner, with hands purified by mantras, should offer the *pavitraka* [sacred thread]. Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Puruṣa, and Īśāna—these five are the Brahmās; to them one should offer the *pavitraka*. (136b)
One should place the tooth-stick in the east, the earth in the west;
having placed the ashes in the south, one should pour water in the north.
Likewise, one should place the flower in the northeast and the yellow pigment (rocanā) in the southeast.
Having placed sandalwood in the northeast, the preceptor should cast the *īśāna* [mantra] there;
he should also scatter the fourfold [ingredients] in the northwest and distribute them over all the limbs.
He should perform the encircling of the pedestal for the temple and the monastery.
In the absence [of these],
one should worship Caṇḍīśa, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgīśa,
Gaṇādhipa, Vṛṣabha, Ṣaṇmukha, and likewise Nandirudra, together with their rays, within water vessels.
One should likewise thoroughly purify Viṣṇu and the Goddess on all sides;
one should satisfy the other deities with [the appropriate] offerings.
Having worshipped the guardians of the quarters and others, the practitioner of mantra should give [the gifts].
Together with singers and dancers, one should perform an auspicious sacrifice.
O Goddess, one should perform worship especially;
having done so according to one's means, O Goddess, one should offer the sacred thread (*pavitraka*).
Having recited the Aghora mantra one hundred and eight times, O deer-eyed one, one should first encircle the liṅga, then oneself, and then the temple;
together with the initiated and consecrated followers of Maheśvara.
In this manner, the *pavitraka* rite must indeed be performed for all the deities;
one should employ whichever mantras reside in each particular place right there.
The preceptor must always perform the *pavitraka* rite.
Thus, he who performs the *pavitraka* rite without understanding the pervasion (*vyāpti*) obtains no fruit whatsoever; his exertion is in vain.
Alternatively, he who, out of greed for wealth, does not perform the *pavitraka* [is likewise lost].
He goes to a terrible hell until the dissolution of the earth;
and at its end, O Goddess, he shall again enter a hundred animal births.
That fool might as well try to crack parched rice with his fingernail or strike the sky with his fist.
O fair-faced one, everything performed by one who does not act out of greed becomes fruitful when done according to the rite joined with mantra and purified;
such a person attains all siddhis and goes to the world of Śiva.
One who bestows upon the twice-born the earth bounded by the seven oceans and adorned with elephants when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu,
obtains a fruit equal to that from the performance of the *pavitraka* rite according to the prescribed rules.
Together with twenty-one generations of his lineage, he shall attain the world of Śiva.
He should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Guru, as well as to the *putraka* and the *sādhaka*.
Furthermore, it should be given to one who performs austerities, to a devotee, to a devotee of Śiva, and even to a twice-born (*dvija*).

One should not give a gift to him who reviles Śiva, the scripture, the guru, or an ascetic; both of them shall go to hell. One should give one's entire possession to the guru, prostrating and asking for forgiveness.
O Goddess of the gods, when he is pleased, the supreme state is attained.
There is no mother like the Guru, nor father, nor kinsmen;
for he effortlessly delivers mortals from the terrible bondage of saṃsāra.
For one who perceives a multiplicity in the teacher’s knowledge of Śiva, in the mantra, and in Śiva himself, or who harbors hatred toward them,
everything given to him and everything consumed by him becomes entirely fruitless.
Having understood this, those of great wisdom should indeed take refuge in a true guru for one night,
three nights, or even five nights.
Alternatively, for seven nights, or even at the Guru’s discretion,
one should perform worship and ask the Lord for forgiveness after withdrawing the *pavitraka*.
The knower of mantras should offer oblations with the *astra-mantra* and the *śiva-mantra*.
O Goddess, when the purifiers have been withdrawn, one should ask forgiveness from the Guru.
O lady of beautiful countenance, one should give him a sacrificial fee according to one's ability;
or else, the worship of the Guru should be performed with bulbs, roots, and fruits.
On all auspicious signs, during planetary transits and eclipses, and on the eighth and fourteenth days— on both the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights—
the preceptor should be honored by the practitioner and diligently provided with food.
O Goddess of the Gods, by his eating, it is as if I myself have eaten;
his ancestors dance for joy and go to heaven satisfied.
However, if he is not in the presence of his guru, then first [the offering] should be made to the five classes of beings (*pañcayoni*).
"He should be brought [there] with effort; one should not inflict punishment upon him.
Or rather, O Goddess of Gods, being pleased with him, he attains the eternal state.
Knowing this, if any man should treat him with contempt..."
He goes to a terrible hell from which there is no rebirth.
This *pavitrārohaṇa* was proclaimed by Śiva in the *Vāmadevya*;
it is also taught in the twenty-four thousand-verse *Saṃhitā*.
The specific detail here is as taught by the illustrious Somaśambhu:
the *pavitraka* (sacred thread) rite must be performed to fill any deficiencies in the entire procedure of worship;
otherwise, the practitioner of mantra will suffer a fall from his accomplishments (*siddhi*).
Furthermore, on the fourteenth day of the months beginning with Āṣāḍha, as well as in the months of Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada,
[the rite] should be performed on the white and black [fortnights], specifically on the fourteenth and eighth days.

During these three months, the sacred thread (pavitra) of Śambhu is prescribed as superior, middling, and inferior respectively; otherwise, it causes harm. During the three months beginning with Āṣāḍha, Janārdana is indeed asleep.
The rule concerning the *pavitra* prescribed in the Sūtra is threefold:
it is not considered a mandatory (*nitya*) injunction because it is not to be performed every day;
rather, this is recorded as an occasional (*naimittika*) rite due to its fixed timing.
The fruit of this [rite] is proclaimed to be the removal of obstacles and so forth;
and since this has been polished by the supreme gods through the Śiva-āgamas,
it is clearly known as the occasional *pavitraka*.
One should daily prepare the *pavitra* for the perpetual worship with mantras, flowers, fruits, and so forth; even at other times, one should fashion it every day.
[It is dedicated] to Agni, Brahmā, Varuṇa, Gaṇeśa, Nāga, Skanda, Sūrya, and Śiva.
O Sugovinda, one should worship Durgā, Smara, Śambhu, and the gods who consume nectar. For all these deities, the *pavitraka* (sacred thread) must be prepared,
beginning from the first lunar day (*pratipad*) and continuing in sequence until the fifteenth day.

In the Kṛta and subsequent ages, the *pavitraka* is made respectively of gold, silver, or copper; in the Kali age, it may even be made of cotton according to one's means. It should be spun by daughters of twice-born men, doubled and then tripled [in strands].
A thread that has been washed, dried, and is pure— another such [thread] may also be employed.
The *praṇava*, the Moon, Fire, Brahmā, the Nāga, the Peacock (Śikhin),
the Sun, Sādākhya, and all the gods [are assigned] respectively to the nine knots.
One purifying thread (*pavitraka*) should consist of one hundred and eight strands;
likewise three [such threads], or half of that, or twenty-seven,
or eighty-one, or thirty-eight strands.
The space between [the lines] should be made equal to fifty [units].
They should measure twelve finger-breadths in width and eight finger-breadths in breadth,
or they may be four finger-breadths in the measurement of the width of the liṅga.
In the same way, the *piṇḍikāsparśidatta* [thread] dedicated to all deities,
the *gaṅgāvatāraka*, which is purifying and exceedingly beautiful, should be prepared;
it is a washed thread knotted by Guhyaka with an unborn goat’s hair.
Having purified it with the *bahurūpa* face-mantra, one should color it. With red sandalwood, saffron, musk, camphor, *rocanā*, turmeric, and red ochre— one should color it with any one of these.
Ten knots should be made, or according to the number of the principles (tattvas);
or the interval may be one, two, four, or as many finger-breadths as is aesthetically pleasing.
[The knots are] Prakṛti, Pauruṣī, Bījā, and the fourth is Aparājitā.
Jayantī, Vijayā, Ṣaṣṭhī, Ajitā, and then Sadāśivā;
thereafter Manmanī is proclaimed, and the tenth is Sarvatomukhī.
As for the additional [days], they should be made as beautiful and the knots (granthi) should be equal.
On a jeweled surface, a sacrificial mound, a bamboo mat, a wooden plank, or a self-arisen stone,
one of the purificatory rites should be performed as appropriate and according to one's preference. For Caṇḍīśa, Ravi, and Vahni, the excellence of the thread is like that of Śiva.
Otherwise, one should provide a purifying thread (*pavitraka*) for each of these individually:
upon one's own image, on Gaṇādhīśa, at the feet of the Guru, on the book,
and on the guardians of the directions, the pitcher, and so forth.
The sacred thread (*pavitraka*) for the *liṅgas* may measure from one cubit up to nine cubits.
From twenty-eight [units] down to twelve, it is reduced by ten units at each step.
The intervals between them, according to the sequence of the measuring line, start at two finger-breadths and end at one finger-breadth.
The knots and the mental [constructions] are likewise [determined by] the extent of the *liṅga*.
On the seventh or the thirteenth lunar day, having performed his daily rites and being pure,
he should adorn the sacrificial hall with silk cloths and other ornaments during the afternoon.
Having performed the occasional twilight worship (saṃdhyā) and especially the libation (tarpaṇa),

the Guru, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and the ritual assignment of mantras to the limbs (sakalīkaraṇa), should worship the Sun on the consecrated ground that has been marked out with lines, while holding the offering (argha) with the syllable Om (praṇava).
Having sprinkled water over the doorways with the Astra-mantra, one should worship them in order, beginning from the east.
Thus, at each door-jamb, one should worship two Gaṇas.
Having worshipped the door-keepers and others according to the prescribed rite with the [Aksara] mantra, as in the daily ritual.
Having entered through the western door, one should worship Vāstunātha.
Having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), the special arghya offering, the sprinkling of one's own head, and so forth,
one should consecrate the sacrificial materials as before.

Water, milk, tips of *kuśa* grass, rice grains, jasmine flowers, sesame seeds, along with white mustard seeds, *darbha* grass, *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice, flowers, and sandalwood— this is declared to be the eightfold *arghya* offering, performed with the heart-mantra and the other [limbs].
Having thus performed the Śivahasta [rite],
[the teacher]— Śiva, the omniscient one, beginning with the letter *a*— is preeminent among those who know the *samaya*.
The Guru, bearing the sword of knowledge, should meditate in this manner upon that which transcends all.
Having reached the region of Nirṛti,
one should cast the water for the *argha* offering and the *pañcagavya* while facing north, all around the sacrificial mandala,
which has been well-consecrated by purificatory rites such as those performed at crossroads, as well as by the rites of inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*) and so forth.
Having scattered those [grains] there, one should gather them together with a tuft of *kuśa* grass;
one should prepare those [tufts], which resemble the moon or the half-moon, for the purpose of a seat.
One should worship Nirṛti, the elements (dhātus), and the gods (gīrvāṇas) at the door, as well as Lakṣmī.
Then, one should place the pitcher facing west, situated upon all kinds of grain;
with the Praṇava mantra, one should then worship Śiva mounted on his bull and Pārvatī seated upon a lion.
One should worship Lord Śiva together with his limbs (aṅgas) in the pitcher (kumbha), and the Weapon (astra) in the Vardhanī vessel.
One should worship the guardians of the directions, beginning with Śakra and ending with Viṣṇu and Brahmā, in their respective quarters.
Then, having properly taken up the Vardhanī, which follows behind the pitcher, [one proceeds].

The mantra-practitioner, reciting the root mantra, should cause the command of Śiva to be heard from the east up to the northeast; he should then circulate this unbroken stream of water all around, in the form of a weapon, for the sake of protection.
Having first placed the *kalaśa* [vessel] and the *śastālu* to its left— [in the case of] a vessel containing a complete throne— one should worship the Deity, O fair-faced one;
[one should worship] the weapon in the *vardhanī* situated at the *praṇava*, and [the weapons] for the two bodies.
One should perform the union of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga* by means of the *liṅgamudrā*.
Having placed the sword of awakening (*bodhāsi*) within the *kumbha*, one should then perform the recitation of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
Then, with a tenth part of that [recitation], one should offer the *vardhanī* vessel and request protection.
Having worshipped the four-armed Gaṇeśa,
who resembles the petal of a lotus, who wields weapons, and who is the warder-off of obstacles,
in the northwestern direction, one should bathe the deity with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and other substances according to the prescribed rite.
Then, having performed the consecrations of the sacrificial pit and other rites, one should worship the face of Śiva with the previously mentioned procedure using the fivefold offerings. (140a)
Having prepared the sacrificial pap (caru) according to the rules and purified it with the oblation of the *saṃpāta*,

one should divide the food into three parts by means of the distinction between the deity, the fire, and the self. Having offered a portion to Śiva and the fire, one should protect the portion within oneself.

And a tooth-stick made from a milky tree, twelve finger-breadths in length, should be placed in the east; either by means of the *nara* mantra or the *varman* mantra. Ashes should be offered in the south, either with the *rūpin* mantra or the *śikhā* mantra.
Earth should be offered in the west with the *sadyojāta* mantra or the *hṛdaya*;
in the north, one should offer an *āmalaka* fruit to the God of gods;
and pure water should be offered with the *vāmadeva* mantra or the *śiras*.
In the northeast, one should offer water with the Īśa-mantra or the root mantra; likewise,
fragrant *pañcagavya* placed in a leaf-cup should be offered in the northeast, and *rocanā* (yellow pigment) in the southeastern direction.
One should place agallochum in the southwest quarter and the four equal measures in the northwest; all materials for the fire-oblation along with uncut *kuśa* grass,
as well as a staff, a rosary, a loincloth, and an alms-bowl, should be made of silver.
One should offer collyrium, saffron, oil, an applicator stick,
a hair-comb, betel, a mirror, and also yellow pigment (rocanā) in the north. One should also offer a seat, sandals, a vessel, a meditation-band, and a parasol.
One should offer [oblations] to Īśa in the northeast with the mantra of Īśa for his satisfaction.
