In the east, O Nara, one should offer *caru* mixed with clarified butter, along with mantras, perfumes, and so forth.
Whatever among these is incomplete, one should mentally conceive that as being present.
Having taken up the purificatory blades (*pavitra*) that have been sprinkled with water from the *astra-mantra* and purified by the *saṃhitā-mantras*, he brought them into the presence of Pāvaka.
Having covered himself with a black antelope skin and other garments, while recollecting Śiva—
the imperishable protector and witness of all rites who consists of the year—
he should perform [the rite] again with the mantra collection using the formulas "svā" and "heti."
One should purify the sacred objects and the twenty-one enclosure lines; then,
resorting to the sacrificial hall, the site of the bull, and the temple,
one should envelop the two agents with the five-threaded armor-mantra.
Having offered a fragrant purifier (*gandhapavitraka*) to the worshiped Sūrya,
having prostrated, sipped water for purification (*samācamya*), and performed the ritual placement of mantras (*nyāsa*) and vows (*vrata*),
one should offer a *kuśa*-grass purifier to the gatekeepers beginning with Nandin.
Having entered, he should offer that [vessel] to Brahmā as the lord of the site;
he should offer the purifiers (*pavitra*) to the weapons and to the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) by their respective names;
and he should offer them to the jar of Śiva, to the jar of the waters, and to the jar of the *lambodara* (Gaṇeśa).
Having worshipped Vighnanāyaka, one should then honor the lotus-feet of the Guru.
One should adorn oneself with a purifying substance preceded by perfumes.
Then, having smeared oneself with all medicinal herbs, one should remain free from the sense of "I" (māna).

Having prepared a sacred thread (*pavitraka*) that has been fumigated, enriched with flowers and incense, possesses a single knot and few strands, and serves as an invocation for the means to attain the fruits of the four aims of life (*caturvarga*),
one should join the palms in *añjali* and recite the invocatory words situated therein.
It is as follows:
Oṃ! To the Lord who fulfills all deficiencies in the ritual procedure regarding this sacrifice, O Master, I address you, the one who brings about the attainment of your will.
Grant success to those who have been born into the state of both consciousness and the unconscious;
O Śambhu, who are entirely and at all times the Three-eyed One, salutations to you—be gracious to me!
Or else:
"You are invited, O Lord of Gods, together with the Goddess, the lords of the Gaṇas,
the Mantras, the world-protectors, and your retinues. At dawn, I shall offer the sacred thread (pavitraka) unto you."
"And I shall observe the rule by your command, O Supreme Lord.
Having thus addressed the God, and having consecrated [the offering] with the *recaka* breath while reciting the root mantra up to the end of "Śiva," he should present it to Śiva.

Having performed the recitation, the hymn of praise, and the prostration, one should ask Śambhu for forgiveness. Having offered the oblation of cooked rice (caru) according to the prescribed portion, one should give that to the Śiva-fire. Then, according to the specific names of the directions, one should offer the external bali-oblation in all directions.
Others, however, say that one should offer the *kṣetrapāla* bali in the north-western direction.
Having sipped water (*ācamana*), one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) which fulfills any deficiencies in the ritual procedure.
Having performed the *pūrṇāhuti* and the *vyāhṛti-homa*, one should conclude with the purificatory rite (*pāvana*).

Then, one should offer four oblations according to the prescribed rite. O Śivā, one should then unite, by means of the ritual consisting of the connection of the channels (nāḍī), the deity worshipped in the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) with the deity worshipped in the mandala.
Having placed the armor-mantra (*kaṅkaṭa*) and the weapon-mantra (*astra*) upon a vessel made of bamboo or similar material,
one should then place the purificatory threads (*pavitrāṇi*) there in the heart [of the deity],
either with the *kalās*, the *vāruṇa* [mantras], or with mantras expressive of Brahman.
Alternatively, one should consecrate the purificatory items with the root mantra;
one should then apply the heart, armor, and weapon mantras over them.
Having thus encapsulated them, one should perform the rite with another substance.
Having wrapped it with armor-like threads and honored it with the collection of ritual ingredients (*aṅgasambhāra*),
one who is bowed in devotion should offer it to the Lord of the World for the sake of protection.
Once it has been worshipped with flowers, incense, and other offerings, [one should offer it] to the manuscript of the *Siddhānta*.
Having bowed at the feet of the guru, one should offer the *pavitraka* with devotion.

Having gone outside and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), one should partake of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and the tooth-cleansing twig (*dantadhāvana*) in sequence upon three mandalas made of cow dung.
Self-restrained, girded with mantras, and having performed the vigil of chanting,
one who desires worldly enjoyment should lie down upon a bed of darbha grass while remembering the Lord with his own mantra.
One who desires liberation should likewise lie down in this same manner.
Having fasted and being composed in mind within a structure made entirely of ashes, the practitioner of mantras,
having risen early in the morning and performed his ablutions with a concentrated mind,
should perform the twilight worship and enter the sacrificial pavilion.
Having taken up the purificatory materials and without having dismissed the presiding deities,
one should place them in a pure vessel upon a prepared maṇḍala in the northeast.
Then, having dismissed the Lord of Gods and removed the floral offerings (nirmālya), [one should proceed].
As before, having performed two daily oblations on the purified ground,

one should especially perform an extensive occasional worship (naimittikī pūjā) in the sun, at the door, among the guardians of the directions, in the water-jars (kumbha), in the cauldron (sthālī), and in the fire of Śiva.
One should perform the satiation of the mantras and the expiatory oblation (prāyaścitta-homa) with the Śara-mantra;
having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one should slowly present the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having offered the purifying thread (pavitra) to the Sun and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should then present that [thread].

Then, having seated himself upon his own seat in the presence of Śambhu, [he should worship] the guardians of the directions, beginning with the door-keepers, as well as the water-jars and the vardhanikā vessels. (142a)
One should offer the *pavitra* to oneself, to the *gaṇas*, and to the lineage of gurus. Then,
taking the *pavitraka* and facing the ritual jar (*kalaśa*),
while recollecting the Lord who is Time itself, one should address Śaṅkara as follows:
Oṃ! O God, O Soul of Time, whatever has been seen by you in this rite of mine—
whatever was performed with difficulty, abandoned, maintained, concealed, or otherwise done—
all that has been rendered pure by your will, O Śambhu, through my very life-breath which is entirely yours.

Oṃ, fulfill, fulfill the vow of sacrifice for the Lord of Restraints, svāhā! Having recited the root mantra ending with *māyā* within the *ātmatattva* (the principle of self) which is protected by the Lotus-born [Brahmā] up to the end of *prakṛti*, one should worship Śiva with the purifying thread (*pavitra*).
In the *vidyā-tattva*, at the end of the *vidyā* [mantra], protected by Viṣṇu as the cause,
one should recite up to the end of *Īśvara* and then place the sacred thread.
Likewise, in the *śiva-tattva*, at the end of *Śiva*, protected by Rudra as the cause, one should do the same.
Having recited the mantra ending with Śiva, the purifying thread (pavitraka) should be given to him.

O observer of good vows, having recited the root mantra ending with dissolution (laya), one should give the Gaṅgāvatāraka [thread] for all the principles (tattvas) that are to be protected by all the causes.
Having joined his hands in a gesture of offering flowers, he should petition Śiva with devotion:
"You are the refuge of all beings; you abide within the moving and the unmoving.
O Supreme Lord, you are the witness of all creatures through your inner movement."
In deed, thought, or word, I have no other refuge but you.
Whatever I have performed for you daily— whether deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, deficient in materials, or lacking in recitation, fire-offerings, and worship— [may it be accepted].
O Maheśvara, fulfill that which is incomplete and deficient in words. O Maheśāna, you are yourself pure, the purifier, the destroyer of sins;
by you, the entire world—both the stationary and the moving—is sanctified.
"O Lord, whatever vow has been broken by me through the occurrence of deficiencies—
may all of that become unified, strung together by the thread of Your command.
Having offered the recitation to the God and performed a hymn of praise with devotion, [he spoke thus].
With a steady mind, one should meditate upon Śiva, who is contented with whatever has been offered.
This should be done for four, three, or two months, or even for half a month;
or for seven days, five nights, three days, or even a single day.
Having received the vow as instructed by the Guru, the practitioner,
having prostrated and asked the Lord for forgiveness, goes to the vicinity of the fire-pit;
likewise, even when Śiva resides in the fire, he offers the fourfold set of purifiers.
Then, having offered his own *pavitra* as an external oblation (*bali*) to the guardians of the directions,
he should offer a *pavitraka* of his own prescribed measure to the book of the Siddhānta. Having thus offered the *vyāhṛti* oblations, he should then present four oblations according to the rule.
Then the Guru, who is Śiva himself, should be worshipped with garments, wealth, and ornaments. When the Lord Guru is satisfied, Śaṅkara becomes satisfied;
for him, the entire annual ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) becomes complete and fruitful.
The Supreme Lord has declared that he with whom the Guru is fully satisfied is truly successful.
Having thus placed the sacred thread upon the Guru,
one should devotedly feed those who bear the sectarian marks (liṅgins), as well as brahmins, the blind, and the destitute.
Having worshipped with garments and a sacrificial fee according to one's ability, one should say:
"By this gift, may Sadāśiva, the Lord of Gods, be pleased with me.
Having performed the morning bath and other rites, the wise man should recite the purificatory verses (*pavitrāṇi*).
Having worshipped the Lord with the eightfold offering of flowers, one should ask for forgiveness. Having performed the daily and occasional rites in detail as before,
and having offered the sacred threads (*pavitra*), one should bow down and worship Śiva in the fire.
Then, having performed the expiation with the Astra-mantra, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Desiring liberation, one should then perform the dedication of the rite to the God, saying:
"By Your grace, may the fruit of my action be effective for me."
One who desires enjoyment [of worldly fruits] should say: "O Lord, let this rite not be a cause of bondage for me.
One should unite Śiva, who resides in the fire, with Śivā by means of the application of the navel. Having placed the collection of mantras in the heart, one should dismiss the fire.
Having sipped water and entered within, he should place the *śambhara* offerings contained in the jars and bowls upon Śiva, and then dismiss them with the forceful utterance, "Forgive me.
Having dismissed the guardians of the quarters (*lokapāla*) and others, he should take the purifying thread (*pavitraka*) from Īśa.
When Caṇḍeśvara is present, having performed worship and offered the *pavitraka*,
one should offer his *nirmālya* and other remains to him along with the *pavitraka*.
Alternatively, one should worship Caṇḍa on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) or on a seat (*pīṭha*) as previously described.
"Whatever annual rite has been performed by me, whether deficient or excessive,
may it become complete through your command, O Caṇḍanātha. Having thus informed Caṇḍeśa, and having given [the offerings], praised, and dismissed him.
One should cast whatever remains of offerings and the like into a blind well or into the wind.
Having thus worshipped Caṇḍeśa and purified the ground with cow-dung and water,
one whose body is now cleansed should bathe [the deity] and then bid him farewell.

Even one who occupies five *yojanas* [of space] should perform the rite of purification (*pavitraka*) in the presence of the Guru according to this procedure; he shall obtain his desired fruit. This is the ritual for the *pavitraka*. Now follows the ritual for the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-caturdaśī*).
Having prostrated before the Blessed Maheśvara, who was seated upon the central throne of Kailāsa, Kārttikeya, filled with humility, first questioned him. Kārttikeya said:
O Blessed One, Supreme Lord, O All-pervading One, you previously spoke of the meritorious procedure for the vow known as the worship of Śiva. Accordingly,
on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, Śiva, the benefactor, is to be worshipped there.
For indeed, O Lord, [this] is the proclamation [made] out of a desire for the welfare of the devotees.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"Excellent, my child! You who act for the benefit of the devotees; [I shall explain] in brief."
Listen to the procedure for the vow, accompanied by the name-mantras:
the mantra of supreme grace (*prasāda*), the all-pervading space (*vyomavyāpin*),
the deliverer (*avatāraka*), the multiformed one (*bahurūpī*), the conqueror of death (*mṛtyujit*), or else the six-syllabled mantra (*ṣaḍakṣara*), [to be recited] with devotion.
Or, at the time of initiation, whichever king of mantras has been pointed out by the Guru—
whether it be the section on daily rites (*āhnika-prakaraṇa*), the procedure for recitation (*japa*), or the rules for meditation (*dhyāna*)—
Śiva brings about His presence through the mere utterance of these.

Although these have been declared by me to be great sinners, they are also removers of sin. Those desiring the fruit of their heart's desire should worship the omnipresent Lord Śiva with these [mantras], having adopted pure devotion on the fourteenth days of the dark fortnights.

Listen now to those names by which [the Lord] is addressed during the months beginning with Phālguna when the Soma sacrifice is performed: Śiva is said to be in the month of Phālguna; in Caitra, Rudra and Vṛṣākapi;
in Vaiśākha, Hara; in Jyeṣṭha, [Īśvara]; and in Āṣāḍha, Tryambaka is remembered.
O child, Śrīkaṇṭha is in the month of Śrāvaṇa; the omnipresent Bhava is in Bhādrapada;
Īśāna is in Āśvayuja; Śarva is in the month named Kārttika;
Mahādeva is in Mārgaśīrṣa; and the Lord Paśupati is in Pauṣa.
In the month of Māgha, the Lord Maheśvara is to be worshipped by those seeking liberation under these names; from Mārgaśīrṣa onwards, Mahādeva Hara is to be propitiated.
Listen with devotion, my son, to the names by which He is to be honored.
Haṃsa, Śuci, Jyotirūpa, Kapardī, Brahmā, Unmana,
Mahāhaṃsa, Visarga, Mahāpuruṣa,
Prāṇa, Īśvara, and Śiva— these are recorded as the twelve [forms] at the end.
There, in the month of Phālguna, the pure-souled one with restrained senses,
having gathered together on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, should worship the Supreme Lord;
he should offer sacrifice to the Liṅga with various kinds of bathing waters filled with sacred sites (tīrthas).
With fragrant curds and milk, as well as ghee and honey;
with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), flowers, fragrant incense and lamps;
and with various kinds of food—both solid and soft—as well as fruits, roots, and drinks, according to one's ability.
Having worshipped the All-pervading Lord with recitations, hymns of praise, prostrations, songs, dances, and so forth, and having bowed down with devotion, she should thus petition Śiva:
"O Lord, I worship you this morning; please grant me your presence there."
"O Lord, out of affection for your devotee and likewise out of compassion for the distressed," [the devotee says].
"So be it," is said by Him; then, with a mind imbued with faith, one should contemplate Him.
Having eaten, and then remembering the Lord, one should use the tooth-stick.
One should sleep while recollecting that [mantra], and should utter it when one stumbles or falls while walking;
having risen in the morning, one should worship Śiva according to that very same procedure.
One should address this sign:
"O Maheśāna, since you are present here, having fasted today, I shall worship you;
therefore, remove all obstacles there and grant me faith and devotion."
"O Blessed One, O Śambhu, remain thus present within this *liṅga*.
Accept this worship, O God, out of compassion, for you are fond of devotion.
Having said, "So be it," one should contemplate that it has been spoken by the All-pervading Lord with a focused mind.
Then, having risen at dawn, one should perform worship with special care.
One should worship that which resides in the *liṅga*, that which resides in the fire, and likewise that which resides in the Guru and the Vidyā.
One should give gifts according to one's ability to cows, Brahmins, and ascetics.
Having satisfied them, he says to them, "O Blessed One, may you be pleased.
When they have said, "May Lord Śiva be pleased with you," those endowed with faith should request the Lord with devotion: "This fourteenth day is mine to be honored."
Having been worshipped by your grace, grant me my desired fruit;

for you, O Supreme Lord, are the recitation, the one who recites, the object of worship, the act of worship, and the worshipper; likewise, you are meditation, the object of meditation, and the meditator.
Having bid farewell to the Lord of Gods with devotion, one should eat food prepared with milk.
Remaining celibate and composed, one should subsist on the food of sages for three days.
In the absence of a linga, one should worship on a stone slab or in a vessel filled with water.
One should offer ritual baths with devotion and perform everything as prescribed.
In this manner, one should complete the vow after twelve months, at the end of the month of Māgha.
Upon the completion of the fast, one should again address the Supreme Lord in this way:
"O Lord, by Your grace, the propitiation of Śiva has been completed.
Destroy my omissions regarding the rules of conduct and fulfill all my desires."
Having made this request, he should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins according to his ability.
When this is done, whatever desire may be in his mind shall be attained unfailingly, and he shall go to the eternal Brahman.
O son, the fruit of this vow has been described by me as being attained through a single recitation;
however, I am unable to describe the fruit for those who have performed it throughout their entire lives.
Or, for those who worship the mandala, there is no doubt that they shall attain my own state.

Whatever fruit is obtained through all the ascetic penances and sacrifices of every sacred ford, as well as through vows and meditations— that fruit should be known to be multiplied countless times by the completion of this vow.
A woman endowed with faith, having performed this completion of the vow, [attains that merit].
Having abandoned womanhood, one shall attain the status of a Gaṇapati of the Lord;
whatever is desired by the mind, that one shall obtain without effort.
One desiring liberation [should perform] the breaking of the vow (pāraṇa) in the month of Kārttika, beginning from Mārgaśīrṣa.
But by performing [the rite] without aiming for a fruit, one attains the eternal Brahman.
This entire rule applies also to the bright twelfth days (dvādaśīs);
therein too this fruit is proclaimed, as are these names of the Lord.
On full-moon days, as well as on the fourth and ninth lunar days,
one should observe the rule of fasting or otherwise take a single meal at night. O child, on the day of the fast, a man should do so regardless of his circumstances.
One who worships Mahādeva with devotion at the *liṅga* attains the imperishable state.
He who, day by day, worships the Lord of Gods according to the prescribed rite—
He surely eats, he surely drinks, and he stands upon the earth in a state of intoxication.
By the sight, conversation, remembrance, or even the touch of him,
the sin of men who are great evildoers is reduced even to ashes.

Therefore, O son, those who desire the fruit of all perfections should always worship the god Śiva with devotion, faith, and according to the prescribed rites. This is the conclusion of the scriptures, uttered by Śiva on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight.
The procedure for the vow has been fully described; now the Śivarātri rite is being told.
Now begins the Śivarātri rite.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, stainless Maheśvara!
By your grace, I have heard the Śiva-dharmas many times.
Yet even now I have a doubt; please sever it, O Supreme Lord.
O Lord, since you are eternally present,
how is it that this most excellent lunar day (tithi) named Śivarātri is considered sacred? At what time did it originate, and what fruit is obtained by observing it?
What is her ritual practice, and what is the nature of her observance of vows?
What are her sacrifices, fire-offerings, vows, recitations, image-worship, and ritual adoration?
And what kind of gift is given for her, and at what time is it bestowed?

O Lord, what should be done in the drinking assembly, both externally and internally, as well as the *cakrayāga*— with whom should one perform these there? O Supreme Lord, tell me this excellent and secret question.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret which bestows liberation upon mantras—
the wheel of the higher and the lower, established in the venerable seat of Ujjayinī.
"In the past, I was requested by the Yoginīs while seated upon a throne;
why then have you requested the Lord, whom you have seen just as I saw him?
At that time, I told you that he had been invited for the sake of a sacrifice."
You have said once more, "I shall come together with you.
Having beheld your form, I have indeed reached a state of supreme wonder;
for if it were not so, the expansion [of its nature] would be difficult to traverse even here.
For this reason, having placed her within the body and concealing her,
one should perform the *ḍāmara* wheel-sacrifice (*cakrayāga*) in the illustrious seat of Ujjayinī.
O blessed lady, that wheel is most terrifying, wherein the three worlds are dissolved;
it is completely filled with various kinds of dust, with the most excellent of drinks,
and with manifold offerings.
Having performed the primary sacrifice and its subsequent rites right there, they attained completion.
Then all the deities were delighted and engaged in dancing;
O Goddess, I remained in their midst, dancing with joy.
Thinking, "The goddess is dancing with me," they created an opening there;
the Mothers then carried you away and presented you to the goddess. You were then devoured by the Yoginīs, and the deities were filled with joy.
And they danced together with me for as long as two days. Then, all having rested, you were meditated upon by me in my heart;
yet, O Goddess, I did not see you, and I was overcome with great wonder.
As soon as they were thought of by me through meditation, they devoured them; then, enraged, I seized the Lord of the Discus (Cakreśa) from the surface of the earth,
whirled him about, hurled him into the sky, and then cast him back down to the ground.
The entire wheel was shattered and reduced to fragments by me;
the yoginīs were struck down and destroyed, fleeing in the ten directions. Whose head was not broken? Whose arms, thighs, and shanks were not shattered?
When the discus had been thus shattered by my wrath as I was intent on destroying the sacred seats (pīṭhas),
all those deities became transformed into discs before me. Bowing low with palms joined in reverence, they offered a most wonderful hymn of praise.
O lady of beautiful countenance, I have been gratified by songs, instrumental music, dances, various kinds of drinks, and diverse offerings of garlands.
When I was pleased, the Yoginīs addressed me with these words:
"For what reason, O Lord, are you angry? Command us, O Great Master!
There, I indeed said to them: "Where has my Goddess gone?"
The gods spoke again: "O Lord, where has that Supreme Goddess gone? Why was she, the Mother of the World and Queen of the Gods, hidden away within your body?"
"She is delicate and fortunate; for that reason, she has been protected by me.
When they had spoken thus, the yoginīs prepared to speak again:
"Why was this done by you, while we have acted in such a manner?"
O Śambhu, that has been done for their sake; therefore, O Maheśvara, abandon your anger.
Be gracious, O God, Lord of Gods, for you are indeed the bestower of grace upon all.
I have indeed related these words of all of them to you.
"Hand over the Goddess to me, so that I may be satisfied once again.
Then the Supreme Goddess was reconciled by all the goddesses;
having performed the reconciliation with the word "Umā," they presented her before him.
When she was indeed entrusted to them, I was then truly pleased.
By means of the discus, I accomplished everything exactly as commanded.
Thereafter, O Goddess, that lunar day became celebrated in the mortal world.
This Śivayāminī was bestowed upon me by the Yoginīs according to the prescribed ritual and with due ceremony; however,
due to the incapacity of my body or perhaps due to the collapse of the kingdom at some time, [it has been lost].
O Pārvatī, since there is a loss of worship, recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth for those rites that have been performed [but not completed] as specifically instructed by the Guru; (147a)

From hatred toward ascetics or from the transgression of the established rule, a very great fault arises; therefore, one should observe this vow. It is on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna.
O Goddess, that night was formerly designated by me as "Śiva-niśā.
Having bathed, wearing white garments, with a single-pointed and concentrated mind,
liberated from all dualities, and solely intent upon the meditation on Śiva—
Having observed a fast or kept a night-vow (nakta), one should perform the rites beginning with the aspiration (yāśā) in due order.
First, having prepared a consecrated mandala there,
the work consisting of the drawing of lines must be performed, followed by the worship according to one's own tradition.
And [he should prepare] very beautiful jars, filled with all kinds of medicinal herbs and fruits,
joined with gold, wrapped in cloths,
smeared with sandalwood paste, and adorned with garlands of flowers.
One should prepare [the pillars] richly adorned with the splendor of canopy-cloths, decorated with bells and chowries,
equipped with *kāṇḍa-pratisara* cords, provided with full vessels (*pūrṇapātra*),
and made auspicious with various kinds of flowers of diverse beauty.
Having performed such a sacrifice, one should commence worship therein.
Worship should be performed during the twilight with extensive offerings according to one's means.
One should fumigate with jewels such as water-offerings and incense, and with refined incenses.

Having prepared many rows of lamps, one should present them there; likewise, various kinds of food offerings—many sorts of things to be chewed and eaten—and numerous oblations, one should offer with devotion. (147b)
And one should offer as sacrificial food (naivedya), according to one's wealth, large cattle, buffaloes, goats, and beautiful rams, as well as fish, tortoises,
and donkeys; or else, one may offer animals made of flour in the sacrifice.
One should thus offer up the great sacrificial animals—anger, greed, and desire.
Having thus satisfied the sacrifice, one should thereafter commence the recitation (*japa*).
One should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) at the conclusion of the recitation, and then worship the All-pervading Lord within the image.
Having satisfied [the deities] and offered the *digbali*, one should then gratify the lords of the field (*kṣetreśas*), the Viranāyakas,
and all the deities beginning with the Guru and the yogins.
Together with the preceptors (*daiśikas*) and practitioners (*sādhakas*), one should pass the night.
After the ritual worship of the image has been performed, one should then carry out the vigil (jāgara).
With songs, instrumental music, prostrations, recitations (japa), fire offerings (homa),
and the sounding of the *huḍukka* drum, one should repeatedly ring the bell while contemplating the wondrous form of the deity’s body.
There were indeed various musical instruments and likewise dances;
there were also delightful songs accompanied by hosts of gods,
and many transformations of form were to be performed.
Having thoroughly contemplated all the principles (tattvas) through the movements of the wheels (cakras),
and having established oneness with them, one attains thereafter the state of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya)—
that which transcends the divisions of time and its parts, all-pervading and imperishable.
One should meditate upon the supreme Śiva, who is composed of eternal bliss and is peaceful.
The seventeenth digit (kalā), which has arisen from the supreme nectar (parāmṛta),
has flowed forth as the form of Mahābhairava.
With that wine, one should hold a circle-gathering (*cakragoṣṭhī*) together with them.
Having fed all of them while in the form of supreme bliss, one whose own self is delighted by bliss should thus perform the great festival.
Just as one should perform [the rites] on the thirteenth day, so should one perform them for three days—
namely, worship, recitation, fire-oblation, giving, and indeed the feeding [of the community].
Alternatively, one may hold a great festival for five or seven weeks according to one's capacity.
Or else, one who is solely devoted to Śiva should observe a single night;
he should perform this meritorious Trayodaśī, which bestows union with Śiva,
with a spirit of devotion and free from stinginess regarding his wealth.
Whosoever are devotees of Śiva who observe this lunar day in due order,
they go to the supreme abode where I dwell with Umā.
There is no man equal to me, nor is there any woman equal to you.
A sacrifice equal to Śivarātri has never occurred before, nor will it ever occur again.
He who performs this sacrifice day and night every year,
endowed with a spirit of devotion, shall attain union with Śiva.
Endowed with devotion to Śiva and dedicated to the dharma of Śiva,
he uplifts twenty-one generations of his lineage and goes to the world of Rudra.
Whatever merit is found in all sacrifices and whatever fruit is found in all gifts—
A mortal who observes the Śivayāminī vow obtains that fruit;
even he who performs it only once during his lifetime, or even for the sake of sport,
shall dwell in Rudraloka as long as the moon and stars endure.
This procedure for Śivarātri has been told by me out of affection for you.
Whoever hears this with devotion shall go to the abode of Śiva.
As long as that mortal remains, so long do the prosperity and other blessings endure.
For that wise one, indeed, obstacles are eliminated;
he shall obtain that fruit which is gained by bathing in all sacred fords. (148b)
He attains the fourfold aims of human life and becomes a partaker of merit.
This determination of Śivarātri has been fully declared for the Goddess;
its greatness was likewise proclaimed by Śiva in the Ḍāmaraśāstra of the Dūtis.
Elsewhere, the fruit has been proclaimed in many ways according to one's desires.
[End of] the Ritual for Śivarātri. This manual, titled *Nityādisaṅgraha*, is completed; it is the work of the venerable Mahāmāheśvara Ācārya Śrīmat Takṣakavarta. May there be auspiciousness!
Oṃ, salutations to the gurus beginning with Śiva; may there be auspiciousness for all.
